title: What to do if your credit card debt is starting to feel overwhelming
full_content:
Struggling to pay off your credit card? These simple tips could help
Whitney Restall got her first credit card just a few months after finishing high school.
"I never prioritised paying it off … I'd max it out and then the bank would be like, 'Oh, would you like to increase your limit by another thousand dollars?' And then I'd max it out again," she says.
Whitney, who lives in Wagga Wagga, NSW, on Wiradjuri land, and only paid the minimum repayments for years, is far from alone.
Credit card debt was the third most common reason for calls to the National Debt Helpline (NDH) last financial year, and the second most common reason for seeking help via chat.
With the cost of living continuing to rise, what steps can you take if your credit card is starting to feel like a problem?
First, get clear on your spending
NDH coordinator Vicki Staff, from Brisbane/Meanjin, says you need to get on top of your financial situation by creating a basic budget.
This means looking back over your bank statements, noting your income and what you are spending your money on.
"It's only once you've got that real clarity around what it costs to live that you can come up with an amount that you might be able to offer to a credit card provider," she says.
If you're not quite sure where to start, Moneysmart.gov.au has a free budget planner.
Associate professor Kirsten MacDonald, from Griffith University's Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics, on the Gold Coast/Kombumerri land, recommends examining your spending habits with a critical lens.
"What are you actually buying on the credit card? Is that a want or a need?" she says.
"Find out what you have got that's extra and perhaps cut back on some discretionary spending."
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
Financial hardship and revolving credit card debt
The next step is to assess what level of help you need with paying off your debt.
If you're experiencing financial hardship, you have a legal right to ask credit providers to change their loan terms.
The definition of "financial hardship" is quite broad, and includes situations like poor health, a recent job loss, or being hit with unexpected expenses.
But Dr MacDonald says people who struggle with credit card debt aren't always enduring financial hardship.
They may instead experience what she calls "revolving credit card debt", where money does get paid off a card, but the debt mounts again and the cycle continues.
"People who have more money might not be in hardship … but they could certainly still have cashflow difficulties or just be spending a whole lot more on credit cards than they need to," Dr MacDonald says.
This was Whitney's reality for almost 10 years.
"I've had my debt since the first two weeks of my full-time job out of high school in 2015," she says.
"That was just life to me … and, I'm sure, a lot of other younger people out there."
Here's how to get back on track
If you're not experiencing financial hardship but you need some extra strategies to help pay off your debt, Moneysmart recommends checking your card's interest rate and looking for a lower option.
If you're paying a high interest rate, Moneysmart suggests doing a balance transfer to a card with a lower interest rate or a zero-interest period, or transferring your debt to a personal loan with a lower interest rate.
However, Dr MacDonald says it's important to pay careful attention to fees and conditions.
Sometimes you can end up paying a higher rate for balance transfers with a promotional period if you don't pay off your card in time or miss a minimum monthly payment, according to Moneysmart.
If you need to pay off multiple credit cards, or have other forms of debt such as a loan, debt consolidation is worth considering, Dr MacDonald says.
"Can we combine the credit cards, or have we got a credit card and another type of loan that has the potential to actually combine it?" she says.
"For some people, they would be best to go and talk to their bank and see whether or not they can combine some of their personal loans or credit cards with their mortgage."
If you are considering this option, Ms Staff says it's important to crunch the numbers first or get some advice.
"When you consolidate all of your debts into one loan, it might have a lower interest rate, but it may still cost you more over time because it's going to take you longer to pay off," she says.
To avoid adding more debt to your card, Ms Staff suggests cutting up your card or lowering your credit limit as you pay it off.
"If you want to keep your credit card but you don't want to get too far into trouble if something happens again … there are low-cost credit cards out there with lower limits, lower interest amounts, lower annual fees," she says.
And if you still need help, Ms Staff recommends calling your bank and asking to speak with their hardship department.
"You might even be able to ask for what we call a repayment holiday," she says.
If your bank isn't willing to make an agreement you think is fair, you can lodge a complaint with them, Ms Staff says, and failing that, appeal to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.
You can also get advice and talk to a financial counsellor by contacting the National Debt Helpline.
Proving it is possible to pay off an overwhelming credit card debt, Whitney decided to knuckle down to pay off her card about two years ago.
She made a basic budget, cut back on unnecessary expenses, and put 10 per cent of her pay into an emergency fund.
It took her about six months to bring the balance down to zero, and she has now cut the card in half and cancelled the account.

title: Creators of Untitled Goose Game turn Australia into a playground
full_content:
Big Walk video game transforms Victorian coastal wilderness into giant playground
There's nowhere quite like Wilson's Promontory, the Victorian national park that lies at the southernmost tip of mainland Australia.
The coastal destination boasts a beach with sand so fine each footstep makes a squeak like treading on a dog toy, a dramatic range of granite mountains, and a scenic landscape studded with boulders tinged rust red.
And Wilson's Prom can now lay claim to the co-operative video game Big Walk, a game that, unusually, prioritises (mis)communication and relaxed house party vibes as players escape puzzle rooms scattered across its vast expanse.
For its developer, House House, the Melbourne studio behind 2019 breakout Untitled Goose Game, there was more behind the chosen location than its awe-inspiring geography.
"It's such a magical place," says co-founder Jake Strasser, who has spent the last six years hand-placing every rock in the game's loose 1:20 scale recreation of Wilson's Prom.
"It has a kind of magnetism to it."
When Strasser's partner proposed to him at Wilson's Prom on a mid-production research trip, the already magical place became even more special.
Meanwhile, fellow co-founder Stuart Gillespie-Cook is a regular visitor to his relative's farm in nearby Fish Creek in South Gippsland.
Using lidar scans that provided a 3D map of the national park, the team produced an unusually naturalistic space, scattering puzzle rooms across the landscape to become what Gillespie-Cook compares to "a big outdoor sculpture garden".
Big Walk's convincing rendition of the Australian bush came about thanks to the team's deep familiarity with the area, bolstered by a week-long research camping trip and on-location recording to gather sights and sounds specific to the region.
That included a sound designer pounding Squeaky Beach with their fists to record its unmistakable sounds.
Such detailed recreations of Australian nature are rare in this medium, with other examples, such as Death Stranding 2: On The Beach often taking dramatic ecological and geographic liberties.
"I guess why a lot of games don't do it is because it's incredibly laborious to make a whole bunch of plants," Strasser says.
The team's 3D artist, Kalonica Quigley, rectified that gap by developing 3D models for 80-100 native plants, which Strasser faithfully placed in the virtual landscape according to Victoria's Ecological Vegetation Class, used to categorise localised flora ecosystems.
"We'd break it up into a bunch of different biomes, like you have in video games," says Strasser. "But instead of snow biomes and lava biomes, we had salt marsh and wet eucalyptus forests and dry eucalyptus forests."
While video game logic determined the variety of environments in Big Walk, the geographic foundation of Wilson's Prom gave the game its own quirks and an unruly, unorthodox character to match the real wilderness.
"A lot of the paths are designed so that you feel like you're the first person who's ever walked along there. You're being guided by an invisible hand that you never fully see," Gillespie-Cook says.
"[There aren't] explicit bushwalking paths — you feel a bit intrepid choosing where to go."
Playing make-believe
Like the best camping trips, Big Walk is about the people you're with as much as the view.
Players communicate by voice chat whenever they're close-by. When forced to split up, they're required to engage in long-distance charades, using outstretched arms, hand signals, flashlights, laser pointers — anything they can put their hands on — to try to bridge the communication gap.
As an example, a puzzle may set a task like asking one player to climb a mountain to identify a symbol. They then try to communicate what they see, often using frantic gestures, to another player watching their movements through a telescope.
The result is an entertaining cycle of planning and execution —either a memorably muddled success or a botched attempt that ends in reconvening to laugh, debrief and try again.
Creating and exploiting communication gaps in this way is more akin to social games like charades or Pictionary than conventional escape room or devious adventure-game puzzles.
Gillespie-Cook sees this as an underexplored space compared to pure mechanical puzzles.
Games of moving blocks, deciphering codes and finding hidden items lack the communication, comprehension and delegated teamwork tested by Big Walk.
"Drawing a squiggle is a fun thing to try and communicate to someone else," says Gillespie-Cook.
"It's the game of seeing a horse in the clouds and pointing at it to your friend but we codify and gamify it.
"A really early lesson we learned is that those kinds of logic puzzles preference a certain type of thinking," Gillespie-Cook continues, comparing their intended approach to the make-believe games and assigned roles played by kids.
"If puzzles are completely solvable by one person, that person is generally going to step up and solve the whole thing. Then everyone else is going to be a bit bored."
Stumbling onto the latest trend
Big Walk's six-year development cycle was a long lead time for an indie studio, even with the financial buffer provided by the success of the 2020 BAFTA Games winner Untitled Goose Game.
"When we started Big Walk, we really thought this is a non-commercial project," Gillespie-Cook says.
"We've got some leeway. We could make a flop if we wanted to."
With development starting during lockdown, the meetings the team had in-game were their only way to stay connected. Other, faster teams were working on similar ideas, too.
In the last three years low-budget, often quickly designed online multiplayer games with an emphasis on social hangouts built around the same 'proximity voice chat'' tools used by Big Walk have become a post-COVID industry phenomenon.
These online co-operative games, such as shooter Lethal Company, mountain climber Peak and hide-and-seek game Meccha Chameleon, have sold between 10-20 million copies, with waves of imitators looking to emulate their success.
House House started ahead of the trend. Nearer release, they feared their prolonged work on the game (by their own admission, they enjoyed working on it too much) had taken so long they'd missed it entirely.
Big Walk came out in early August. In less than a week it has already sold in excess of 1million copies, more than double the 400,000 visitors who come to Wilson's Promontory every year.
"It feels fun to be swept up in it," says Gillespie-Cook, who still regards himself as a newcomer to online multiplayer games after a lifelong aversion to the format — despite having spent the last six years making one.
"It wasn't until lockdown where I found I needed them. It turned out to be really good to connect with friends and I realised I've been missing a huge trick here."
Big Walk is out now.

title: Record Jetstar profits fuel pay fight over 'rock bottom' wages
full_content:
Jetstar's profits soar as passengers face more fees and workers push for a bigger share
In short:
Jetstar has posted a record $492 million in earnings in the six months to December.
The Australian Services Union (ASU) says about 900 airport operations workers are demanding more pay as negotiations stall.
What's next?
Jetstar said in a statement negotiations were ongoing, and it was committed to reaching a new deal.
Jetstar is making record profits while passengers are being slugged more fees and now workers say they want a bigger slice of the airline's success.
The Qantas Group's low-cost carrier posted a record $492 million in underlying earnings in the six months to December, up 12 per cent on the previous year.
Yet the Australian Services Union (ASU) said about 900 Jetstar airport operations workers were now effectively being paid at award rates, after the Fair Work Commission's annual wage increase overtook their expired enterprise agreement.
Jetstar said in a statement negotiations were ongoing, and it was committed to reaching a new deal.
"We're continuing to meet regularly with the ASU to progress negotiations … that includes pay increases, while continuing to deliver low fares to our customers," a spokesperson said.
Earlier this month, Jetstar announced passengers will need to pay extra to access the overhead lockers from next year, in a bid to streamline boarding, with the new fees adding up to $52 per flight depending on the route.
The move was described as a "money grab" by travel agent Lynton Jones from the Savvy Traveller.
Industrial relations academic at the University of Sydney and a former Qantas employee, Troy Sarina, said lower pay rates at budget airlines were not unusual.
"There is lower rates of pay at the low-cost carrier compared to a legacy airline, because that's how the airlines differentiate themselves in the marketplace," Dr Sarina said.
He said labour was one of the biggest costs facing airlines, after aircraft and fuel.
But Dr Sarina said Jetstar's profits raised questions about how much of its success should flow to employees.
"There is a deliberate choice that needs to be taken … to what degree are those profits shared?" he said.
'We've hit rock bottom'
The bargaining dispute, which has been underway for several months, covers 929 Jetstar airport operation workers, including customer service staff who check-in flights, handle bags inside the terminal and marshal the aircraft out on the tarmac.
These workers typically earn $29.45 an hour.
An ASU survey conducted to help with their negotiations, which covered most of these workers, found 96 per cent said their wages were failing to keep pace with the cost of living, more than 70 per cent had cut back on essentials or taken on extra shifts, and almost a third had gone into debt.
Jetstar customer services officer Emma*, who has worked for the airline for more than a decade, said workers had seen their wages steadily lose ground.
"This is the first time in 15 years we've hit rock bottom with our wages,"
"It's really disappointing to see that over time that has just slowly been eroded, particularly in the last four years."
She said she had been forced to cut back on her children's activities and has put off extra household spending to keep pace with rising costs.
"We are the lowest paid in the industry and it's completely disheartening to be honest," she said.
Workers are seeking pay parity with Qantas, arguing staff performing comparable roles can earn significantly more despite working with the same corporate group.
Dr Sarina said the pay gap reflected the different industrial arrangements between the two airlines, with Qantas traditionally offering higher wages and conditions.
The union says a worker with equivalent skills and seniority at Qantas can earn about 18 per cent more than a Jetstar employee performing similar duties.
ASU assistant national secretary Scott Cowen said Jetstar's current bargaining position remained tied to the Qantas Group wage policy of 3 per cent annual wage increases.
"Now our members working at Jetstar are being paid just the bare minimum legal wage by the company until a new agreement is reached," he said.
"Our members work hard every day to make sure that Australians can get to their destinations working for Jetstar and they deserve their fair share of the profits."
No protected industrial action has yet been commenced, although union survey results indicate strong support for escalation if negotiations fail to progress.
Extreme weather on the tarmac
The ASU survey found more than half of Jetstar workers reported symptoms of heat exposure, while almost six in 10 said they had "felt pressured" to keep working in extreme temperatures.
Workers said the tarmac can be far hotter than official readings as heat radiates off concrete and bitumen.
Some described temperatures so intense their shoes softened and warped beneath their feet.
"We've had members report to us before where they've had nail polish on their toes get caught to their stockings. That's how hot the tarmac can be," Mr Cowen said.
Emma said she had experienced the impact firsthand while pregnant.
During a shift she spent about 30 minutes marshalling aircraft in extreme heat before returning inside the terminal.
"I didn't even realise at the time how badly the heat had affected me until I walked back inside and became physically ill," she said.
The union said concerns about heat were significant enough to warrant specific protections in the next enterprise agreement, including mandatory paid breaks linked to temperature thresholds and stronger controls around rostering and tasks during extreme weather.
Employment lawyer Lisa Qiu from Citation Group, who specialises in workplace safety, said employers had an obligation to minimise heat-related risks.
"The law requires employers to do everything that is reasonably practicable to eliminate those risks associated with working in the heat," she said.
However, Ms Qiu said the Airline Operations Ground Staff Award already contained heat-related allowances and break provisions for some workers, although these generally only applied once temperatures exceeded 46 degrees Celsius.
Under the award, workers are paid an extra 85 cents per hour when the temperature is between 46 and 54 degrees.
Jetstar said it operated in destinations ranging from snowfields to tropical regions and had "a range of policies and procedures" in place to support employees working in "challenging conditions".
"We regularly review these in consultation with our people and their unions," a spokesperson said.
The ABC understands the airline had introduced some additional uniform options last year, including shorts for workers at Queensland airports, along with scarves, gloves and reimbursement for thermals for workers in colder climates.
The union argued those measures did not go far enough and was seeking enforceable heat protections written into the next enterprise agreement, including mandatory paid breaks tied to when temperatures went above 35 degrees.
Dr Sarina said concerns about conditions on the tarmac were not just a workforce issue.
"If there's something not right with the baggage handlers or something going on in the tarmac, then obviously that will impact people being able to get on their planes, to get their luggage on the plane and for the plane to arrive on time," he said.
New baggage policy raises fresh concerns
The dispute comes against the backdrop of Jetstar's recently announced cabin baggage changes.
From February 2, 2027, passengers who want to store a cabin bag in the overhead locker will have to pay extra.
But it will mean removing the 7-kilogram limit, and travellers will be able to take on bags up to 10 kilograms.
The union has raised concerns the new system could increase manual handling risks if workers are required to assist passengers with heavier carry-on bags.
It is also seeking clarification about how the changes could affect the role of cabin baggage officers who currently monitor luggage compliance at airport gates.
Mr Cowen said frontline staff often found themselves dealing with passenger frustration over company policies.
"We are concerned that a new, probably unpopular cabin baggage policy will just add to those pressures if they're not managed appropriately by the company," he said.
Dr Sarina said debates over wages and conditions were ultimately about more than pay packets.
"If there is a perceived inequity in the way that work pay and conditions is set up, it can lead to decrease in motivation and also people feeling a degree of lower morale," he said.
*Emma's name was changed for privacy reasons.

title: Pauline Hanson is backing WA on the GST, but she hasn't always
full_content:
Pauline Hanson changes position to back WA in GST carve-up debate
In short:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson previously argued the WA GST deal was not fair, but three years later she has endorsed the carve-up.
Senator Hanson's change of heart appears to coincide with her closer relationship to billionaire mining magnate Gina Rineheart, who resides in WA.
What's next?
The prime minister has endorsed a deal extension until 2029, with a final Productivity Commission report on the GST expected by the end of the year.
Call it the Gina effect.
Pauline Hanson has undergone a remarkable transformation when it comes to the politics of the GST.
Three years ago, the One Nation leader stood up in parliament and called out the "huge benefit" Western Australia had received from a 2018 GST deal, opposed by every other state and territory.
At the time, she was arguing that the North-West Shelf gas development off WA should be included in a future gas reservation scheme, when she strayed into dicey territory with the GST carve-up.
"Is it fair that 93 per cent of Commonwealth-owned natural gas should benefit just 10 per cent of Australia's population?" Senator Hanson asked the chamber in September 2023.
"My view is no.
"Western Australia receives a huge benefit without compensating the other states because of the passage of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Making Sure Every State and Territory Gets Their Fair Share of GST) Act 2018."
In another speech delivered in March, Senator Hanson said the WA government was "addicted to Commonwealth-owned petroleum resources".
She noted the billions of dollars in royalties WA received from offshore gas projects were not included in calculations that underpinned the GST distribution.
Now, it appears, her view has evolved.
GST stoush continues
Amid a brawl between the states over the Morrison-era deal, which the Productivity Commission last week labelled a "costly mistake" that only benefits WA, the Queensland senator has emerged as a defender of the west.
The deal guarantees states a minimum return of 75 cents in the dollar, or no lower than NSW and Victoria, after WA's share fell to below 30 cents.
"No, I'm not pulling anything from WA," Senator Hanson told News24 last week.
"Yes they do have the mining and they're a progressive state, but they've actually done business and encouraged business there, so the GST was increased.
"What's Victoria doing? They've destroyed the whole gas industry down there, the mining sector.
"These states cannot rely on other states to prop them up."
Senator Hanson now endorses the deal, despite her own state complaining the carve-up was broken and that Queenslanders were being dudded.
"For years, Queensland has been denied its fair share. This report proves it," Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki said on Friday.
Close relationship with Rinehart
The change of heart appears to coincide with Senator Hanson's increasingly close relationship with billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart, who is born and bred in WA, where the GST is a very big deal.
Mrs Rinehart has become One Nation's biggest backer, gifting Senator Hanson a plane and helping finance the minor party's extraordinary rise in Australian politics.
One Nation is locked in a fierce battle with Labor in the upcoming Secret Harbour by-election, which could deliver the minor party its first lower house seat in the WA parliament.
With growing pessimism about the prospect of a Labor victory, party sources have told the ABC the contest would be a useful learning curve for future battles with One Nation.
Hands off WA's GST deal, Cook says
Keenly aware of the sensitivities, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese played down the prospect of any changes, noting the Productivity Commission inquiry had been commissioned by the former Morrison government and had only delivered an interim report.
On a visit to Perth in 2024, Mr Albanese also signed a guarantee that there would be no changes to the deal.
After talking to Mr Albanese on Friday, WA Premier Roger Cook declared the agreement would remain, dismissing the Productivity Commission as a bunch of "east coast clowns" and its report as "dodgy, deceitful and dumb".
"My message to the Eastern States is this: Hands off WA's GST deal," Mr Cook later posted on Facebook.
Leaving no one in doubt about their position, the federal WA Liberals proclaimed: "Over our dead bodies will they take a cent from Western Australia!"
Even Teal independent Kate Chaney, whose electorate covers Perth's leafy western suburbs, pushed back on the widespread criticism, calling the current GST arrangements fair.
The Productivity Commission will hand down its final report by the end of the year.

title: What happens if property prices drop 20pc? Ask New Zealand or Canada
full_content:
analysis
Why the Kiwi and Canadian property bubbles burst and what we can learn
If it's a glimpse towards a possible future you're after, it's always worthwhile taking a peek across the Tasman.
For when it comes to the economy, the Kiwis don't do things by halves.
They were the first to raise interest rates in the aftermath of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and they lifted them at a cracking rate, among the quickest on the planet, in what appeared to be a deliberate bid to drive the economy into recession.
As for real estate, whether up or down, the Kiwis go hell for leather.
New Zealand's property boom left Australia in its dust. And the resulting bust has been far greater than anyone expected to happen here.
But it is worthwhile examining what has driven the slump and what we could learn.
Canada too has never recovered from its pre-COVID property market records. And just like New Zealand, its real estate has been on a steady decline for the past four years.
Australia, meanwhile, has only just begun its descent. Sydney and Melbourne have been in decline for several months, while, at a national level, the trend has turned negative as growth in even the tearaway cities like Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide has evaporated.
Research group Cotality argues that the sustained growth we've experienced over the past five years has left Australian households with enough reserves to weather a storm.
But what made Australia different to its Pacific neighbours?
The obvious contrast was in interest rate policy.
Both New Zealand and Canada hiked interest rates far more dramatically than Australia, curbing demand for housing finance from 2022 onwards. Unemployment was also far higher than here.
Immigration also played a major role. Australia has maintained levels of arrivals that far outweighed dwelling construction ever since the pandemic — ensuring shortages — while Canada imposed heavy restrictions to limit arrivals, including students.
In New Zealand, net migration came to a standstill as the country's high unemployment rate prompted an exodus of Kiwi workers across the Tasman to take advantage of a more buoyant economy.
Meanwhile in Canberra, the immigration debate is only just beginning.
It is playing out as buyers have already begun a retreat from Australian real estate, sparked by interest rate hikes and a fundamental shift in tax policy as incentives for investors have been wound back.
Diverging paths
Australian housing may be among the world's most expensive, but New Zealand and Canada did their best trying to catch up after the global financial crisis.
From 2010 onwards, New Zealand real estate surged an incredible 164 per cent until it peaked in early 2022.
That's after accounting for inflation. In nominal terms, the price movements were even more extreme but, when comparing different countries, stripping out inflation provides a more accurate reflection.
Canada experienced a similar surge, up about 150 per cent.
On this side of the ditch, our property prices, while coming off a higher base, rose just 40 per cent after inflation over the same period.
But after the invasion of Ukraine, our paths diverged quite radically. Canada and New Zealand began a long slide into property losses.
Canadian housing prices have shed about 20 per cent since then, while the Kiwis have dropped close to 30 per cent once inflation is included; in one of the longest property market downturns in its history.
Australian real estate, on the other hand, began a gentle U-turn in 2023, even as interest rates were being pushed higher, accelerating back towards record levels as rates were cut last year.
But that is about to change.
Loading
Why the difference?
Interest rates played a major role.
The New Zealand Reserve Bank set a blistering pace in its quest to kill inflation, sending the official cash rate to 5.5 per cent, way above its Australian counterpart, which restrained interest rate hikes with a 4.35 per cent peak.
The Bank of Canada pushed interest rates far higher than Australia's too, pushing its official rate to 5 per cent.
And that played through into the broader economy.
New Zealand retreated into recession several times as the rate hikes stifled growth. Unemployment, meanwhile, only avoided surging to embarrassing levels because of the number of Kiwis who fled the country.
While the country's population has grown since 2022, a large number of residents, many of whom are younger and highly educated, left for higher-paid positions in Australia.
That has helped take pressure off the housing market.
Meanwhile in Canada, the unemployment rate climbed to 7 per cent in 2023 and since then the economy has been hit hard by the imposition of US tariffs under the Trump administration.
In some cities, including Toronto, unemployment has surged to 9 per cent, dampening demand for housing and accelerating declines.
Negative wealth and population
In New Zealand and Canada, the housing downturn is beginning to ricochet through the broader economy, highlighting the challenges the RBA and the federal government may face in the near future.
Household spending is restrained, and retailers are struggling in both countries, hindering efforts to revive economic growth.
Australia's economy is already sluggish, with growth expected to come in at less than 2 per cent this year, giving the RBA little wriggle room to use interest rates to keep inflation in check.
A string of retailers has shut in the past 12 months, and even market darlings like JB Hi-Fi have been under fire from investors as difficult trading conditions are expected to weigh on performance.
Given the extent to which property is ingrained into the Australian psyche, the political blowback from an extended downturn is likely to gather pace.
Australian households are among the world's richest, coming in third behind Luxembourg and Belgium, according to a UBS study.
That's down to our booming property market. And while that incredible rise in wealth has driven consumption on the way up, a prolonged or steep drop in housing values is likely to undermine demand across the broader economy.
Canada, which embraced immigration curbs two years ago when it slashed net overseas migration, is now examining ways to put a floor under the housing market, including bailing out property developers.
Many cannot sell without realising enormous losses, but can't afford to sit on finished properties indefinitely.
That has prompted Prime Minister Mark Carney and his British Columbia counterpart to initiate a plan to buy up unsold apartments and convert them into affordable housing.
The great Kiwi real estate slump, meanwhile, has begun to steady but shows little sign of a turnaround.
Housing here is still in short supply. But demand has dropped sharply.

title: Albanese government reduces home care waitlist by changing counting method
full_content:
Albanese government reduces in-home aged care waitlist by changing method of counting
In short:
The federal government has changed the way it counts the number of people waiting for in-home aged care funding.
As a result, more than 53,000 people who would have previously been counted have been taken off the official waitlist.
Using the previous method, the number of people waiting for full funding would be higher than it was before the aged care royal commission was announced in 2018.
A Four Corners investigation can reveal the true number of people waiting for full aged care funding at home stands at almost 154,000 — not 100,000 as officially reported.
More than 53,000 people, who in the past would have been counted on the waitlist published by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, have been excluded since government reforms started in November last year.
This has happened because the department has a new method of counting, which means people receiving interim funding have been excluded from the waitlist.
Prior to the reforms, people received interim funding in the form of a lower-level package.
They remained on the official waitlist until they received their approved package.
If the waitlist were counted using the same method applied for the nine years prior, the waitlist would be at its longest since before the aged care royal commission was announced in 2018.
Under the new system which started on November 1, once someone begins receiving an interim payment of 60 per cent of their approved funding, they are taken off the official waitlist — even though they have not yet received full funding.
More than 90 per cent of people being granted funding under the Support at Home program are provided with an interim package of 60 per cent, which they remain on for an average of 10 weeks before getting their full funding.
This change is one of the key reasons why the waitlist numbers appeared to drop immediately after the government's "once in a generation" reforms came into effect on November 1 last year.
Official figures of the waitlist before Support at Home was introduced showed that on October 31, 2025, there were 107,281 people waiting for their full aged care funding.
That waitlist dropped to 94,963 on December 31, 2025, after those receiving interim funding were excluded from the waitlist.
When Four Corners put these findings to Aged Care Minister Sam Rae, he denied there had been any change, saying "the waiting list has always been manufactured or calculated the way that it currently is".
Asked directly whether the current waitlist included people receiving interim funding, Mr Rae said they did not. "No, once people receive the care package at the level that they have been assessed for, they no longer count [on the official waitlist]."
A spokesman for the minister sent a statement later, saying that "to have people remain in a queue when they are already receiving their allocated level of care would skew the distribution of places".
More than 4,800 people died in 2024–25 while waiting for their approved home care funding.
'Unacceptable'
Former acting Inspector-General of Aged Care Ian Yates said it was "unacceptable" that the government had changed its reporting method.
"The government needs to come clean and at least report these [people on interim funding] as an additional figure in their reports so they can be monitored," he said.
The department's latest figures put the waitlist at 100,191 at March 31, but using the method applied consistently since reporting began in 2017, the true figure is 153,909.
Four Corners uncovered the discrepancy after comparing evidence given at Senate estimates on June 2 this year, where officials disclosed that people on interim funding had been taken off the waitlist, meaning 53,718 people had been excluded as of March 31.
Combined, it means the number of people waiting for full funding is 153,909.
In May, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged problems in the system, saying "the state of aged care is not good enough," and pointing to "billions of dollars of additional funding in the budget".
Demand for aged care has increased dramatically since the royal commission was announced, with the number of people receiving home care jumping four-fold to more than 364,700.
Also potentially adding to the bottleneck is that more assessments are being completed.
Since the reforms, the average number of completed assessments has risen from 46,500 per quarter in 2017-18 to more than 79,700 per quarter in March 2026.
Labor's record
In its first three years in power, Labor released fewer home care packages than the Coalition did during its last three years in power — averaging less than 37,700 per quarter compared to more than 45,700 under the Coalition.
This was also below the average during the royal commission, of 41,445 per quarter.
Natalie Siegel-Brown, who recently resigned as Inspector-General of Aged Care, told Four Corners that restricting funding to help people stay at home amounted to a false economy.
"It might look like a saving in the short term, but in that wait time, decline accelerates … and we end up paying a much higher cost for them to go into residential aged care," she said.
On average, it costs the commonwealth more than $117,000 a year to subsidise a person in residential aged care, compared with less than $30,000 for care at home.
Since the Support at Home program was introduced, Labor has boosted its output, roughly doubling the number of packages released per quarter, compared to its three-year average.
Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said, "While we know there's much more to do … our methodical work to secure more care for more older Australians than ever is making a material impact".
Watch Four Corners' full investigation, The Waiting Game on ABC iview.

title: Russian bank fires economist who said Moscow losing 'war of attrition' with West
full_content:
In short:
Andrei Klepach, the chief economist of the Russian state development bank VEB, has been fired.
It follows an address at a financial forum in which he predicted a social crisis and warned Russia was losing its "war of attrition" with the West.
The comments mark a rare critique by a senior figure at a state institution of the costs of the war in Ukraine.
Russian state development bank VEB has fired its chief economist over remarks in which he said the country was falling behind the West and China and suffering mounting economic damage from the war in Ukraine, two sources familiar with the matter said.
Andrei Klepach, one of Russia's most prominent macroeconomists, made the remarks to a financial forum in May, but they were reported in Russian media only last week.
"We are falling behind. We are losing both the technological and economic competition in the world. And we are losing it not only to China and the United States, in some ways we are losing it to Ukraine too," he said, adding that this was due to Kyiv receiving financial support from the West.
"We will not win the competition in this war of attrition. We have the illusion that everything there [in Ukraine] will collapse. It has not collapsed and will not collapse. Our costs are mounting,"
The speech, published on the website of the Nikitsky Club — a forum of economists, academics and government officials — and in which he predicted a social crisis, marked a rare public critique by a senior figure at a state institution of the costs of continuing the war that Moscow launched in 2022.
Mr Klepach has held several roles at economic institutions and worked at the economy ministry for 10 years before joining VEB.
VEB, which finances state projects, confirmed in a written response that Mr Klepach was no longer its chief economist, but did not say why. Mr Klepach, who was appointed to the role in 2014, also confirmed his dismissal to Reuters.
Mounting pressures from Ukraine
In the speech in May, Mr Klepach highlighted Russia's resilience to Western sanctions but said pressures were mounting due to Ukrainian strikes on energy and logistics infrastructure.
He pointed to rising income inequality and a slower GDP growth rate than in the US and Ukraine.
In July, the Russian central bank suggested the economy might not grow at all this year. Over the summer, repeated Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and warehouses of top online retailer Wildberries have created supply shocks, raising inflation risks and public unease.
President Vladimir Putin has said the economy was stable despite what he called external attempts to undermine it.
"Economically we will not collapse, but our lag will continue to grow, with all the resulting consequences," Mr Klepach said in his speech, predicting a social crisis could arise "precisely when nobody is particularly expecting it".
There is currently no sign of serious social unrest in Russia, amid tight wartime censorship, protest bans, long jail sentences for dissidents and the growth in influence of the Federal Security Service, the main successor agency to the Soviet-era KGB.
Mr Klepach also criticised what he called Russia's over-dependence on China and said uncoordinated monetary, budgetary, and industrial policy had contributed to this year's economic slowdown.
"The quality of governance is almost constantly deteriorating," he said.
"Decisions are being made all the time that have an extremely low level of justification but long-term strategic consequences."
War critic jailed
Mr Klepach's dismissal came on the same day a prominent opposition politician was sentenced by a Russian judge to 11 years and one month behind bars.
Lev Shlosberg, a senior member of the Yabloko party, had previously criticised Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Yabloko, the only official political party in Russia overtly opposing the war, also saw itself barred from upcoming parliamentary elections.
The moves against Mr Shlosberg and Yabloko highlight the Kremlin's intolerance toward any criticism of the war, now in its fifth year.
It was the second trial for Mr Shlosberg in the past two years.
He has also been designated a "foreign agent", a label that carries strong pejorative connotations in Russia and brings additional government scrutiny. He was convicted of violating the foreign agent regulations.

title: Options are slim for new Australia Test cricket batters
full_content:
In short:
Australia's nine wicket loss to Bangladesh in the first cricket Test has raised more questions about the positions of some batters in the side.
Pundits have raised a series of names of other batters who could replace the two players under the most pressure, Marnus Labuschagne and Jake Weatherald.
What's next?
Australia plays the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay on Saturday, with live updates and radio commentary on ABC Sport.
Australia's nine wicket defeat at the hands of Bangladesh have thrown up yet more questions about the state of Australian batting.
Twin failures by opener Jake Weatherald and number three Marnus Labuschagne have only increased the pressure on both batters.
Moreover, the repeated failures of the battling line-up, with the exception of Steve Smith and Cam Green in Darwin, have continued a pattern which was partially masked by last season's Ashes success.
Labuschagne hasn't scored a century since July 2023 — 22 Tests ago — during which time he's averaged just 25.23.
Jake Weatherald is averaging 20.36 in his six Tests since the beginning of the Ashes last summer, with just one score above 50.
The question is, does Australia make changes now ahead of the second Test starting in Mackay on Saturday?
Skipper, Pat Cummins, openly mused on the subject in his post-Test press conference on Sunday.
"I think that's the question over the next couple days," Cummins said.
"We'll sit down and have a think; the selectors will have a think.
"Is there something there that's going to take us forward, or is it something starting to become a trend that we think needs to be changed?
"So, it's trying to work out, do you need to intervene now, or do you let it play out and think [the current group] is the way forward?"
Australia's head coach, Andrew McDonald, said the disastrous display in Darwin was clearly not good enough.
"Call it a trend, call it what you will, we believe our players are better than what they're putting out there at the moment," he said.
"And that falls on us as coaches as well; our job is to get the best out of playing group.
"I think if you go back to the original squad [of 13] that was picked, it was quite skinny.
"I think Bailes, George [head selector, George Bailey] left it very open as to you know, we could add depending on what we saw going through."
The obvious problem is that we are in the middle of winter season and most batsmen last played first-class cricket around five months ago.
It means the selectors don't have recent form to go off and so any decision about bringing in a player from outside the squad of 13 is going to rely on hunch as much as hard facts.
If it's the current group, the only other batter available in the squad is Josh Inglis, who scored 100 on debut against Sri Lanka in January 2025, but was dropped after his fifth Test during last summer's Ashes series.
Inglis last represented Australia in the white ball format playing One-Day Internationals and T20 matches on the tour to Bangladesh in June.
The 31-year-old wicketkeeper-batter played five matches in this year's IPL for the Lucknow Super Giants, scoring 266 runs at an average of 53.2 and a strike rate of 186.
Inglis opens for Australia in the short forms of the game but hasn't batted higher than four in Test cricket and bats in the middle order for Western Australia in the Sheffield Shield.
Is he the long sought-after answer to open for Australia? His record and usual batting position suggests not.
If not Inglis, then the selectors will have to look outside the current squad where pundits are putting forth names including Matthew Renshaw, Sam Harper, Nathan McSweeney, Cooper Connolly, Campbell Kellaway, Sam Konstas and Kurtis Patterson.
Queenslander Renshaw was part of the wider squad that trained in Brisbane before the Sri Lanka series and is a possibility to replace Weatherald as opener.
He scored 499 runs in six matches at 49.9 in last year's Sheffield Shield, with three centuries and a 50.
While those numbers don't scream "pick me", they are actually a stand out in what was a disappointing summer for Australia's first-class batters: his average was second only to Jack Edwards's 51.75 for batters who scored more than 300 runs.
Former Test opener and Queenslander, Matthew Hayden is a fan of the 31-year-old.
"I want to see Matt Renshaw and I've been saying this for at least 12 months. I think he is match fit," he told Channel 7.
"I think the selectors knew what he was, now I want to see what he actually is."
Renshaw was also a member of the Australian side that played limited overs matches against Bangladesh in June.
He played the last of his 14 Tests against India in Delhi more than three years ago when he came in as a concussion sub for David Warmer and scored just 2.
Victoria's keeper/batter Sam Harper scored the second most Shield runs last year behind his teammate and former Test player, Peter Handscomb.
Harper scored 677 runs at an average 35.63 in his 11 matches which included Victoria's loss to South Australia in the Sheffield Shield final played at the end of March.
Of late, 29-year-old Harper has been part of the Galle Gallants title winning side in Sri Lanka's T20 competition, the Lanka Premier League.
He was the second highest scoring batter in the competition with 425 runs at an average of 38.63 and a strike rate of 163.46.
The question around Harper, who has proven himself a successful T20 batter over the years, is whether he could translate last year's Shield runs to the Test arena, and possibly even step up a level?
One player who has been playing regular first-class cricket is the former Test opener, Nathan McSweeney.
McSweeney was drafted into the Test side two years ago to replace the retired David Warner partnering Usman Khawaja at the top of the order.
He lasted just three Tests, where he made 72 runs at an average of 14.4.
More recently he's been playing for Northamptonshire in England's One-Day Cup and County Championship Division Two.
His record in eight first-class matches for Northants has been solid, scoring 589 runs — placing him fifth on the run-scoring charts — at an average of 49.08.
Batting at number three, he captained South Australia to last season's Sheffield Shield title and, at 27, he has added leadership qualities, more experience and maturity since he last played for Australia.
Cooper Connolly is the other former Test player who's been mentioned in dispatches.
Connolly played his one and only Test in Sri Lanka, where he batted at eight scoring four runs.
He hasn't played a first-class match since last March — one of four he played for Western Australia — scoring 216 runs in total with a top score of 70 and an average of 30.85.
He was part of the Australian team on the limited overs tour of Bangladesh highlighted by his man of the match performance in the third ODI where he scored 149 as an opener alongside Inglis.
Earlier in the year he scored 107 off just 59 balls for Punjab Kings in the Indian Premier League to become the youngest ever overseas centurion in that competition.
The Western Australian will turn 23 this year and so has youth on his side and is sure to play a part in Australia's Test side in the future.
The question is: Is he ready now?
Another youngster whose name keeps coming up is Victoria's Campbell Kellaway, who scored 509 runs in the last Shield season with one century and two 50s at an average of 26.78.
Kellaway was a member of the Cricket Australia XI which beat Bangladesh by an innings in a warm-up match in Darwin before the first Test.
Unfortunately, he was bowled for a duck off five balls.
Another young gun, Sam Konstas, has failed to grab his chances at the highest level.
The New South Welshman is unbelievably still only 20 but seems to have packed more into his brief career than many more senior players.
The five Tests he played following his dynamic Boxing Day debut against India two years ago have netted Konstas 163 runs at an average of 16.3.
Like Kellaway, he failed in the recent tour match against Bangladesh scoring 1.
Konstas is a constant in the selectors sights with a credible 660 runs in last season's Sheffield Shield at an average of 33.
The issue seems to be taming the impetuosity and proving he has the temperament to grind out a Test innings.
The forgotten man in Australian cricket is 33-year-old Kurtis Patterson.
Patterson scored 619 runs for NSW in the last Shield season at an average of 36.41.
His two Tests against Sri Lanka in 2019 included a not-out century but he was a victim of timing, squeezed out of the side as David Warner and Steve Smith returned from bans following the sandpaper scandal.
Patterson was a member of the CA XI, scoring 53 batting at number three which shows he's still in the thinking of selectors.

Australia's nine wicket loss to Bangladesh in the first cricket Test has raised more questions about the positions of some batters in the side.
Pundits have raised a series of names of other batters who could replace the two players under the most pressure, Marnus Labuschagne and Jake Weatherald.

title: Why this future star has 'goosebumps' over triathlon's future
full_content:
How AusTriathlon's new high performance hub is set to prepare the future for gold in Brisbane 2032
The future of triathlon in Australia is looking very bright — particularly on the Gold Coast.
And 19-year-old rising star Aspen Anderson is hoping to play a big part in that future.
Last week, AusTriathlon formally opened its new high performance hub at the Miami Aquatic Centre, a home for the sport's best athletes and coaches, as well as the future, developing talent through the Ascent Academy.
It's a move that positions the Gold Coast right at the heart of the multi-sport universe leading into the 2032 Olympics.
The proposed location of the triathlon events at those Brisbane Games is the Gold Coast, and that is something that has Australia's top athletes very excited.
"I think having a home, for a home Olympics is really special," Anderson told ABC Sport on the Gold Coast.
"Sometimes it [training] is a bit of a slog when you have to put the headphones in and you're just trying to get it done.
"But knowing that there's always someone that can go for a ride with you, yeah, it definitely helps.
"It's like a strength in numbers kind of thing. Some days when you're not feeling great, they're always there to lift you up and someone's always got a smile on their face, and on your hard days, they might be having a great day, and vice versa, when you're having a good day, you can help a friend out too.
"This hub is definitely a great step forward, it's been hard in previous years where you're kind of just floating between venues. Now, having this locked in is really exciting."
Reigning World Champion Matt Hauser agreed, saying the hub was a huge step forward for the athletes.
"For sure I wouldn't be able to do this sport if I was just training solo, seven days a week across the three sports," Hauser told ABC Sport.
"I think it's a really important dynamic that you also get that racing exposure in training and you're able to push each other and go to another level than you would have previously without someone there pushing you.
"Having that culture piece, having everyone on the same path and knowing that when you're putting the hard yards in, when your heart rate's maxing out, when you've got a sore body at the end of the week, everyone's in the same position and they're motivated to get to the same place as you are is, I think, really important, especially when we move towards Brisbane 2032.
"Everyone wants success for the country … so to be on that journey together and have that centralised program here in Miami now is, I think, really powerful."
Anderson noted that Hauser has "led the way" in bringing Australia back to the top step of world triathlon.
The 28-year-old claimed the world title on home soil in Wollongong last year, becoming the first Australian since Emma Moffatt in 2010.
It put Australia back on top of the triathlon world after a lengthy absence, and with the global hiring of new high performance coaches like British former European champion Non Stanford-Royle and Germany's former world champion Daniel Unger, hopes are that Hauser's success will be just the latest in a long line of triumphs.
Anderson herself is clearly on the right pathway to emulating some of the greats of the past.
A double gold medallist from the Youth Commonwealth Games in Trinidad and Tobago in 2023, the Victoria-born teenager made her World Triathlon Championship Series debut earlier this season.
At the event in Quiberon, France, in June, Anderson led off Australia's mixed team relay to a sensational fourth place finish.
"I was really fortunate to get to experience the mixed team relay," Anderson said.
"I loved it. It was so fun, it's short enough that you're still with all the best of the best, like I'm lining up next to [Luxemburg's European champion] Jeanne Lehair and [French mixed team relay world championship gold medallist] Emma Lombardi, and I'm like 'wow, these are people that are performing on the biggest stages and here I am, just hey guys'.
"I had a bit of a fangirl moment but it was a great experience."
Fresh from that fourth place, a couple of weeks later Anderson made her full individual World Championship Series debut in Hamburg, finishing 38th as the second-youngest of all the competitors in the race.
"I wasn't even planning to do World Series races this year, that was not even really on the cards, and then I think I just had a little bit too much momentum and they were like, 'oh, let's just go for it,'" Anderson said.
"Hamburg was another extreme … the crowds and everything, it was insane.
"It was definitely a big step up but it wasn't as big as everyone made it seem, I think maybe I over-hyped it a little bit in my head.
"But now I know what it's like and I know what to expect for next time. Every race is different though, so you never know what to expect."
Anderson will race in Weihai, China, at the end of the month, and has also been named to the Australian under 23 squad for the 2026 World Triathlon Championship Finals in Pontevedra, Spain, later this year.
This too came somewhat as a surprise for a teenager well and truly on the fast-track to the top.
It's made the prospect of a home Olympics all the more tantalising.
"It's always something in the back of your mind," Anderson said.
"I'm someone that's really realistic, so I don't want to get ahead of myself, I'm kind of taking it race by race or day by day and really enjoying the process of doing that.
"But yeah, there's some days where you just get goosebumps thinking about it, just, wow there's an Olympics literally out the front door; there's talks of it being in Tallebudgera or Currumbin, and if it's in Currumbin that's literally where I live, so that would be something you could write in a fairytale ending.
"Cassie [Beaugrand, Paris 2024 Olympic champion] and what she did at her home Olympics, I think it's … yeah it literally is giving me goosebumps now thinking about it.
"Having the support of a home base going for something like 2032 is insane — and LA would be a lovely stepping stone for that, it would be lovely just to dip the toes in the water and still be competitive and then I think, yeah, it would be lovely to have a fairytale ending in Brisbane."

title: Josh Burns on the personal cost of being Jewish in parliament
full_content:
Josh Burns didn't set out to be the 'Jewish guy in parliament'
He's from the Labor party and is Jewish. She's from the Animal Justice Party and happens to be pro-Palestinian.
The partnership sounds incongruous on paper, yet Victorian MP Josh Burns has just welcomed a baby girl with fellow MP Georgie Purcell, an animal rights activist and vegan.
Together with Mr Burns' seven-year-old daughter from a previous marriage, the couple divide their time between Ms Purcell's farm in Kyneton and their Melbourne home in Josh’s electorate of Macnamara, where they juggle their respective parliamentary duties.
The pair finds it "funny" when they are called political rivals, and stress they have "shared values".
"But we do talk about things. We have robust political discussion," the MP told Annabel Crabb on ABC iview's Kitchen Cabinet.
A 'normal Australian'
Elected to the lower house in 2019, Mr Burns never set out to be the "Jewish guy in parliament" but he felt "thrust" into the national spotlight, nonetheless.
"I'm just a normal Australian," he said.
When his grandparents arrived in Australia from different parts of the world they ended up in "this little community … I'm now privileged to represent".
That community includes the Melbourne suburb of Caulfield, Australia's most populous Jewish neighbourhood and where the federal MP grew up.
But in a post-October 7 world, there have been "really difficult issues" he's had to contend with as not only a parliamentarian, but also as someone who is Jewish.
His electorate is also where you'll find Ripponlea, home to the Addas Israel Synagogue that was fire-bombed in late 2024 in an incident police have said was a politically motivated attack.
It's a scene all too familiar to Mr Burns. Six months earlier his own office was targeted when, according to police, at least five people smashed windows and painted the phase "Zionism is Fascism" on the wall.
"I remember after the Adass Synagogue was burnt down and I stood there looking at a synagogue literally in ruins and in flames [with] this crisp, burnt smell in the air.
"And you think, 'I've seen this in history before' and 'How can this be happening in Australia?'"
'We are a very complex people'
It's a question that would be echoed in the aftermath of the Bondi Beach terror attack that claimed the lives of 15 people when two gunmen opened fire on a Jewish community event marking the start of Hanukkah.
Mr Burns remembers the moment a member of his staff rang to tell him shots had been fired at the popular beach.
"I knew my mum was taking my daughter to the Melbourne Hanukkah event and you're like, 'Well, what is this? What's going on? Is this something that's a national attack?'"
He called his mum urging her to stay home and then rang the Prime Minister's office.
"I've got to try and make sure our country is responding to this in a way that actually remembers who we are, what our country is [and] what our country represents," he said.
"That we are a migrant country, that people come here for refuge, for safety."
But it's come at a personal price.
"It's probably been the most difficult time of public life for me because it's so personal — it's so intrinsic to who I am," he said.
"And even when there were times when there was a conflict between being Jewish and what the Labor Government were doing, that's a conflict that's happening inside me."
As a Jewish member of parliament, Mr Burns says he is asked to distance himself from the Israeli government's actions "all the time", but he stressed that not everyone in the Jewish community is the same.
"We are a very complex people. We have a lot of different opinions. There's lots of different components of the community that make up the Australian Jewish community, even though it's such a small population."
And when it comes to having differing viewpoints to his partner, Mr Burns questioned why disagreeing with someone meant you could no longer associate with them.
"When George and I got together, there was a lot written about us as if somehow there was this conflict," he said.
"We spoke about the issue a lot and we spoke about how we would navigate it and how we would work together."
But he would never ask her to "diminish what she feels or what she wants to advocate for", he says.
"Nor would I be able to diminish my representation for the community I love and grew up in."
'How I'm wired'
Mr Burns also revealed something he's never spoken about before publicly: he was recently diagnosed with ADHD.
He said the diagnosis has given him "great strength" and it helps him focus on the things he really cares about.
"I definitely focus under the pressure and it's something I'm learning about myself, that it's actually how I'm wired.
"But also, in the day to day … if I don't consciously set out what I want to do and what I need to do throughout the day, I can get drawn in different directions really quickly."
It's helped him understand himself and has changed how he feels about his work as a parliamentarian.
"I wear glasses a lot of the time and with my glasses I can see clearly. It's the same as with ADHD," he says.
"It's a bit blurry but then when you are on top of it and you take your medication, you can just see clearly, and you can move through things and it's not daunting to start a task.
"You just think about what you need to do, and then you go and do it."

Caen drones bomba y un explosivista de las disidencias de las Farc en Briceño: golpe frontal al aparato explosivo del Frente 36
Operación militar en El Hoyo y El Roblal dejó la captura de alias la Mona, la incautación de material bélico y el hallazgo de un taller de explosivos.
En las veredas El Hoyo y El Roblal, en el municipio de Briceño, en el norte de Antioquia, tropas de la Fuerza de Despliegue Rápido N.° 7 del Ejército Nacional, en coordinación con el CTI de la Fiscalía General de la Nación, desarrollaron una operación militar sostenida que afectó directamente la capacidad logística y operacional de la Estructura 36 del grupo armado organizado residual de las Farc.
Durante la acción de las autoridades, se logró la rendición ante la justicia de una mujer conocida con el alias de la Mona, señalada de desempeñarse dentro de la organización como operadora de drones y encargada de la manipulación de cargas explosivas.
La infraestructura de esta integrante debilita las operaciones de tecnología armada que la estructura venía desplegando en la zona rural del municipio.
Entre el material bélico decomisado figuran tres vehículos aéreos no tripulados, de los cuales uno estaba destinado a labores de reconocimiento y dos estaban adaptados para el ataque mediante el lanzamiento de granadas artesanales.
En el mismo sitio, las unidades militares hallaron 30 granadas de 60 milímetros diseñadas para ser ensambladas en estos equipos, un fusil AK-47, proveedores, más de 950 cartuchos de diversos calibres y 80 eslabones para munición de 7,62 milímetros.
El reporte oficial da cuenta también del hallazgo de 25 artefactos explosivos improvisados, siete minas antipersonal, una rampa artesanal de lanzamiento, dos balones bomba y más de 100 kilogramos de material explosivo dividido entre R1 y pólvora negra.
A esto se suma la incautación de indumentaria de uso privativo de las Fuerzas Militares, entre la que se destacan uniformes camuflados, chalecos multipropósito, equipos de campaña y calzado táctico.
Finalmente, la ofensiva permitió la localización y desmantelamiento de un taller artesanal empleado para la fabricación de explosivos.
En el lugar se encontraron herramientas de taller como taladros, pulidoras, soldadores, baterías de 12 voltios, tres bolsas de balines y 30 metros de cable de energía.
Con este resultado, la Fuerza Pública neutraliza la cadena de producción de artefactos letales con los que este grupo pretendía atentar contra la población civil y la Fuerza Pública en la subregión.
Otros resultados en esa zona
Según reportes del Ejército Nacional y la Séptima División, el material bélico y las minas antipersonal estaban distribuidos en tres depósitos ilegales ubicados en áreas estratégicas de la zona rural.
La ubicación de estos artefactos representaba una amenaza crítica para las comunidades campesinas, dado que varios de los explosivos y trampas mortales se encontraban sembrados en las inmediaciones de caminos veredales por donde transitan a diario los pobladores de Briceño.
Especialistas en explosivos y demoliciones del Ejército realizaron la neutralización y la destrucción controlada de este arsenal bajo estrictos protocolos de seguridad, para prevenir accidentes directos sobre la población civil y mitigar el riesgo de confinamiento o desplazamiento forzado.
De acuerdo con las autoridades, la neutralización de este laboratorio y el decomiso de la tecnología adaptada para ataques aéreos frenan una escalada violenta en la subregión del norte de Antioquia, lo que devuelve garantías de movilidad y tranquilidad a los habitantes de la zona.

Adulto mayor murió tras sufrir fatal golpe en la cabeza al caer de una chiva rumbera en el sector turístico de Santa Marta: esta era su identidad
Las versiones conocidas hasta el momento indican que el hombre habría perdido el equilibrio cuando estaba sobre el vehículo turístico.
Las autoridades de Santa Marta adelantan una investigación para establecer las circunstancias en las que perdió la vida un hombre luego de sufrir una caída relacionada con una chiva rumbera en una de las zonas más concurridas del sector turístico de la ciudad.
La víctima fue identificada como Alexander Móvil Maldonado, de 52 años de edad, natural de Dibulla, La Guajira, y residente en el barrio Brisas del Nevado, en Santa Marta. Su fallecimiento ha generado consternación entre familiares, allegados y personas que lo conocían tanto en la capital del Magdalena como en su tierra natal.
El hecho ocurrió durante la madrugada del domingo en inmediaciones de la bahía de Santa Marta, específicamente en el área cercana a la calle 11 con carrera 1 y al parqueadero de la Sociedad Portuaria, un sector frecuentado por turistas y residentes durante los fines de semana.
Cayó al pavimento y sufrió un trauma fatal
De acuerdo con la información preliminar recopilada por las autoridades y testigos, Alexander Móvil Maldonado se encontraba en el sector turístico cuando se dirigió hacia una chiva rumbera. Por circunstancias que aún no han sido esclarecidas, terminó cayendo al pavimento y sufrió un fuerte golpe en la cabeza.
Las versiones conocidas hasta el momento indican que el hombre habría perdido el equilibrio cuando estaba sobre el vehículo turístico. El impacto le ocasionó un severo trauma craneoencefálico que le causó la muerte.
Según la reconstrucción preliminar de los hechos, la víctima había sostenido minutos antes una conversación telefónica con un familiar. Posteriormente cruzó la vía y se dirigió hacia la zona donde se encontraba la chiva, instante después del cual ocurrió el accidente.
Algunas versiones recopiladas por los investigadores señalan que la caída se produjo desde una altura considerable, circunstancia que habría incrementado la gravedad de las lesiones sufridas por el hombre.
Era oriundo de Dibulla
Alexander Móvil Maldonado era oriundo del municipio guajiro de Dibulla, aunque desde hacía algún tiempo residía en Santa Marta. Diversos reportes señalan que trabajaba como albañil y era conocido por familiares y amigos en los sectores donde desarrollaba sus actividades cotidianas.
Tras conocerse la noticia de su fallecimiento, comenzaron a surgir mensajes de solidaridad dirigidos a sus seres queridos, quienes ahora esperan el avance de las diligencias judiciales para conocer con exactitud qué ocurrió durante las horas previas a su muerte.
Luego del hecho, funcionarios del Cuerpo Técnico de Investigación (CTI) de la Fiscalía llegaron al lugar para realizar la inspección técnica del cadáver y adelantar los actos urgentes correspondientes. Una vez concluidas las diligencias, el cuerpo fue trasladado a las instalaciones de Medicina Legal en Santa Marta.
Paralelamente, los investigadores comenzaron la recolección de testimonios de personas que se encontraban en el sector al momento del accidente. También se adelanta la revisión de cámaras de seguridad ubicadas en la zona turística con el propósito de reconstruir la secuencia de los hechos.
Las autoridades buscan determinar si la caída obedeció exclusivamente a una pérdida de equilibrio o si pudieron existir otros factores relacionados con las condiciones de seguridad del vehículo o del lugar donde ocurrió el incidente.
Por ahora, el caso permanece bajo investigación y los organismos judiciales continúan recopilando elementos que permitan establecer con precisión cómo se produjo el accidente que terminó cobrando la vida de Alexander Móvil Maldonado en pleno sector turístico de Santa Marta.

¡Histórico! Centro de acopio de El Campín despachó 933 toneladas de ayuda humanitaria a zonas afectadas por el terremoto
Desde Bogotá se mantiene activa la operación para llevar ayuda a las regiones más golpeadas por el terremoto.
Mientras en las zonas más afectadas por el terremoto —Cali, Pereira, varios municipios de Chocó y Manizales— no paran las labores de atención humanitaria con miras a la fase de reconstrucción, desde Bogotá también se libra una carrera para hacer llegar alimentos, agua y otros elementos de primera necesidad.
Desde el centro de acopio instalado en el estadio El Campín ya fueron enviadas 933 toneladas de ayuda humanitaria, distribuidas en 79 envíos hacia las regiones afectadas por la emergencia. La titánica operación ha permitido llevar asistencia a seis destinos ubicados en cinco departamentos.
Risaralda es el departamento que más ayuda ha recibido, con 344 toneladas enviadas desde Bogotá. Le sigue el Valle del Cauca, con 236 toneladas, mientras que a Caldas han sido despachadas 157 toneladas y al Chocó, 138 toneladas. El Quindío, por su parte, ha recibido 58 toneladas.
Las cifras dan cuenta de la magnitud de la operación que se mantiene desde la capital para responder a una emergencia que, una semana después del movimiento telúrico, sigue dejando necesidades urgentes en distintos puntos del país.
Según el último reporte de la Unidad Nacional para la Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres (UNGRD), el terremoto deja hasta ahora 15 departamentos y 472 municipios afectados, con 185.996 personas damnificadas.
El balance también da cuenta de 287 personas fallecidas, 4.147 heridas y 194 desaparecidas, mientras que 355 personas han sido rescatadas durante las labores de búsqueda y atención de la emergencia.
En materia de vivienda, el reporte registra 127.608 viviendas averiadas y 26.392 destruidas, además de 197 edificios que colapsaron en los municipios golpeados.
Y frente a los servicios básicos, hay 304 centros de salud, 3.207 centros educativos y 4.059 centros comunitarios afectados.
La gran ‘ayudatón’ en Colombia ha sido una labor admirada internacionalmente. Desde todos los sectores sociales, el personal de salud, los rescatistas voluntarios y hasta músicos y artistas se han volcado a ofrecer centros de acopio, logística y, en algunos casos, a donar las ganancias de sus bienes y servicios para atender la emergencia humanitaria más grave del siglo.

China took a major step towards green modernization Saturday as its landmark Ecological and Environmental Code came into force, strengthening the legal foundation for harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature.
Adopted by China's top legislature in March, it is the country's second formal statutory code after the Civil Code.
The code comprises 1,242 articles in five chapters, covering pollution control, ecological protection and green, low-carbon development, among other areas.
It was formulated through systematic integration, compilation, revision and refinement of over 30 ecological and environmental laws, over 100 administrative regulations and more than 1,000 local laws and regulations.
China also celebrated its fourth National Ecology Day Saturday under the theme "Building a green foundation for Chinese modernization."

title: Once Upon a Time in the Middle East: A new frame on anti-war films
full_content:
By continuing to browse our site you agree to our use of cookies, revised Privacy Policy and Terms of Use. You can change your cookie settings through your browser.
A movie poster is seen in Wuhan, China, August 11, 2026. /VCG
A movie poster is seen in Wuhan, China, August 11, 2026. /VCG
From Schindler's List to All Quiet on the Western Front, anti-war films have always found an audience. This summer, a Chinese film is offering a fresh take, not from the battlefield but from the kitchen.
Once Upon a Time in the Middle East follows Xu Fu, a Chinese chef who finds himself caught up in a desperate struggle to save lives amid the flames of war in the Middle East.
His survival instinct isn't about fighting, it's about feeding people and holding onto normal life when everything around him is falling apart.
Moviegoers have called it one of the most emotionally powerful Chinese films in years. Some scholars have described it as China's first realist anti-war film.
There is already a buzz building overseas even before its international release. Viewers say it is challenging trite storytelling, bringing a perspective rarely seen in the genre.
One scene sums it up: a line about "peace and good food."
A movie poster is seen in Yangzhou, China, August 11, 2026. /VCG
A movie poster is seen in Yangzhou, China, August 11, 2026. /VCG
"Have a good meal" is a Chinese expression carrying an everyday wish. In the film it becomes a quiet act of defiance.
Traditional Chinese chopsticks, square at one end and rounded at the other, are sometimes said to embody the ancient Chinese idea of a square earth beneath a round heaven. Sharing food is more than a habit for Chinese people; it's an act of care and bonding. In the middle of war, this simple act takes on a new meaning.
"This film absolutely deserves the Oscar for Best Picture," one viewer wrote. Others said the film doesn't need to compete with anything else, it just tells its story.
In Once Upon a Time in the Middle East, the heroes aren't soldiers. They're ordinary people trying to hold onto their humanity. American soldiers appear too, not as saviours but as people caught up in the same mire.
A movie poster is seen in Kunming, China, August 11, 2026. /VCG
A movie poster is seen in Kunming, China, August 11, 2026. /VCG
As some overseas viewers have put it, the film is "undoubtedly one of the most direct and unvarnished critiques of Hollywood."
The film doesn't preach or tell you what to think. It just shows you a chef, a restaurant, a war and the small acts of kindness that survive.
The taste it leaves the viewer with is that "having a good meal" should be the norm for people everywhere.
