title: Jason Bateman Says ‘Uncut Gems’ Was “A Good Shorthand” for ‘Black Rabbit’
full_content:
Jason Bateman, one of the nicest men in Hollywood, has a real talent for playing assholes.
The wry everyman with a hidden vein of creep has become something of a Bateman archetype.
Think of his financial planner turned drug cartel enabler Marty Byrde in Netflix’s Ozark. Or Mark Loring in 2007’s Juno, the prospective adoptive dad revealed to be a boundary-crossing man-child. More recently, he’s been Clark Forrest, the local weatherman eager to scratch his dark sexual kinks in the HBO series DTF St. Louis. But with Vince Friedken in Netflix’s crime drama Black Rabbit, Bateman finally goes full scumbag.
When we first meet Vince, he’s hanging out in a low-rent Reno casino, waiting to do a shady deal with some shady folks to sell some (obviously pilfered) rare coins. The deal goes bad, violently so, and Vince hightails it back to New York, looking for a bailout from brother Jake (played by Jude Law), owner of Manhattan’s hippest restaurant. Vince brings his chaos with him. His outstanding gambling debts to a local mobster (Oscar winner Troy Kotsur, of CODA) threaten Jake’s business and the life he’s built away from his self-destructive sibling. Bateman even looks lousy: Vince’s greasy hair and untamed beard are a world away from his usual clean-cut presentation.
The performance earned Bateman an Emmy nomination for acting, while his work behind the camera on Black Rabbit also earned him a directing nomination — a fitting double recognition for an actor increasingly drawn to the other side of the camera.
“I remember thinking, ‘I bet the audience would expect to see me in the part that Jude ended up playing,’ ” says Bateman, reflecting on how he and Law were cast by Black Rabbit creators Zach Baylin and Kate Susman before it was decided who would play which brother. “It would have been more comfortable for me [to play Jake]. But I had a real good take on Vince. He’s a very broken guy. He has a sense of humor, but he’s very aware of what a failure he is. I’ve known a lot of people in my life like that, people who are just heartbreakingly ill-equipped to manage the things that they find themselves involved in.”
After his career as a child actor in ’80s family sitcoms — Little House on the Prairie, Silver Spoons, The Hogan Family — shows where “the big note is always: Make sure your character is likable,” Bateman says he finds it more “exciting” to play the noxious jerk. Even one as toxic as Vince.
“[Vince] starts pretty unlikable, and I play him pretty unlikable as well,” he says. “Then, by virtue of his bad decisions and getting backed into a bunch of corners, he becomes much more vulnerable and apologetic, and hopefully that earns it back in time for the ending to be satisfactory.”
Bateman was determined to test himself on Black Rabbit, and not just in front of the camera. He directed the first two episodes of the show. Baylin and Susman “basically asked me to do what I had done on Ozark and The Outsider,” he says, “direct the first couple of episodes and then oversee the whole project, hire the other directors and keep a consistency going from the first episode to the last.”
Bateman brought in his Ozark collaborators Laura Linney and Ben Semanoff to direct two episodes each of Black Rabbit and picked Justin Kurzel, who directed Law in the 2024 crime thriller The Order, to close out the show with its action-packed two-episode finale.
On Black Rabbit, Bateman the director takes the color palette and dark lighting of Ozark and roughs it up. Grainy, low-key cinematography from Igor Martinović and Peter Konczal and gritty production design from True Detective‘s Alex DiGerlando give the show a look and feel closer to that of ’70s noir.
The shaky handheld anxiety of the Safdie brothers is also a clear influence.
“Uncut Gems was something that was a good shorthand for all of us,” says Bateman. “It was something that was very current and took place in the same part [of Manhattan]. That visual style, the editorial pace, even the kind of soundscape really fits well to the writing and with what the two brothers are going through. But there’s a lot of anxiety [in Uncut Gems]. We knew if we had that level constantly through all eight episodes, it would be a bit much. So, we tried to throttle them on and off, onscreen and also with the writing.”
The one area of directing Bateman needed no help with was managing actors.
“It’s challenging for some directors that have never acted before or even taken an acting class. Being an actor myself makes that part of the job easier,” he says. “I understand what a really weird thing acting is, pretending to come up with all of these words right in the moment. I mean, really, it’s total bullshit. We’re all just professional liars.”
Bateman and Law come from very different acting backgrounds. Law came up in fringe and musical theater in Britain, while Bateman honed his craft on the sets of many a multicam sitcom. Their approach to performance is also distinct. Law imagined a backstory for Jake and Vince, a history from childhood to the moment we meet them onscreen. Bateman has no need for bios, preferring to work off the script alone.
But Bateman and Law’s chemistry onscreen in Black Rabbit is immediate. They are utterly believable as bickering brothers with a lifetime of shared trauma, resentment and lingering affection.
“We didn’t spend any time developing that; it just came naturally,” says Bateman. “Maybe I’m overanalyzing, but Jude is just such an incredible person and so professional, he’s such a good guy and we worked together so well — us having chemistry was just about the easiest thing in the world.”
The hard part was directing. “Acting is more comfortable, directing is more challenging,” says Bateman. “It’s something I have to work a bit harder on. But it is something that, at this stage of my life and career, I’m enjoying a lot because it calls on everything that I’ve learned over the last — what is it? — 45 years of experience.”
His first Emmy win, after decades in the business, came in 2019 for outstanding directing on Ozark. Bateman has finished shooting his second feature as a director, the crime comedy The Cackling of the Dodos, starring Sam Rockwell and Woody Harrelson, and has several directing gigs in the works, including The Partner, an adaptation of a John Grisham novel set to star Tom Holland.
“I still love acting immensely and pursue it, you know, 110 percent,” he says. “But I’m simultaneously looking at all of my options as a director, oftentimes on the same project. It’s incredibly rewarding for me, and incredibly challenging. Maybe I’m a masochist. But I’m looking at things that are right at the edge of what I think I can handle.”

title: Patrick Renna on ‘The Sandlot’ Fame and “Once in a Lifetime” Trip to Field of Dreams Game in Iowa
full_content:
Patrick Renna touched down in Iowa last week to attend the MLB’s Field of Dreams game in Dyersville, Iowa featuring the Philadelphia Phillies and the Minnesota Twins. The interleague matchup, which streamed live on Netflix, took place inside a newly built stadium just a ball’s throw from the original movie site used for the 1989 sports classic starring Kevin Costner, Ray Liotta and James Earl Jones.
“Theo Von, baseball players, great food and there’s a baseball game to see tonight at the Field of Dreams — it’s spectacular. It’s once in a lifetime,” Renna told The Hollywood Reporter of the scene during a brief interview against the backdrop of the house used for filming. As Renna recapped his experience, a line of fans formed over his shoulder as people waited for a chance to take a photo with the actor best known for starring in another beloved baseball classic — The Sandlot.
In a chat with THR, Renna opens up on the nostalgic moment, being starstruck by the MLB commissioner and his recent reunion with his Sandlot pals on the series Dugout Dads.
How did it happen that you were able to be here for the game?
The [Sandlot] guys came out a couple years ago but I couldn’t make it for some reason, and I had such major [fear of missing out]. The fact that this [site] is still standing here is so epic, and they built a whole stadium. It’s great.
You’re wearing John Deere merch. Did they bring you out?
Yeah, they brought me out. I have a partnership with them that I’m doing here, and we shot a little fun thing in the cornfields. They brought me out for the game and I head home tomorrow.
Anything baseball must always kick up a lot of interest around you and the film. What is it like to be so closely associated to this sport?
It’s a great sport to be attached to — it’s America’s pastime so it’s really special. The sport itself is almost nostalgic when you think about it; the experience of families watching the game together in the stands with all the food. It’s cool and it’s humbling. It doesn’t get lost on us how lucky we are to have been part of something like [The Sandlot]. We have now three generations of people coming up to us saying, “You’ve been in our living rooms for 30 years.” To be able to provide that is special.
What’s the other most common thing people say when they come up to you?
“You’re killing me, Smalls.”
It’s nice to see you embracing it, taking all the photos and engaging with the fans. Some actors lean into it, while others might say, “I’ve done 30 years of other work since then.” But you really enjoy it?
Yeah. As an actor, you kind of always worry about the things that you’ve done that are negative and you think to yourself, “Oh god, I hope nobody sees it.” But the great thing about doing something negative is that nobody sees it. So, yes, I’ve been working for 30 years but I haven’t topped Sandlot and that’s OK. It still gives me something to shoot for and hopefully I do. There are major movie stars that don’t have a movie like Sandlot. There’s something there for people, and all the credit goes to the director, [David Mickey Evans], who write, directed and narrated it. It was lightning in a bottle for a movie to mean something and become so important to families. It’s mind-boggling to even be in it it because it’s not really about me or the guys. It’s bigger than all of us.
How hard is it to be an actor today?
I do more producing and directing now. I have Dugout Dads coming out in August, which I brought all the Sandlot guys back for. That was fun. I’m an actor in that. But I don’t go out often [for acting jobs]. If something comes to me because I’ve been doing this so long, that’s exciting to me and I’ll do it. So acting isn’t that hard for me today because I just don’t do it often. I’m on the other side mostly now.
Can you describe the atmosphere here? You’re getting a lot of attention and I just saw you hanging out with Theo Von.
Super nice guy. Also, the commissioner of baseball is here. I was so starstruck and wanted to meet him. Theo Von, baseball players, great food and there’s a baseball game to see tonight at the Field of Dreams — it’s spectacular. It’s once in a lifetime.
Who are you rooting for between the Philadelphia Phillies and Minnesota Twins?
I got no skin in the game. I’m just looking for a good ball game that is hopefully high-scoring and down to the ninth inning. Maybe the Phillies? Maybe the Twins? I don’t know really. It’s going to be a good game either way.
Interview edited for length and clarity.

title: Paramount Demands That States Post $1.88 Billion Bond Amid Warner Bros. Antitrust Suit
full_content:
Paramount Skydance is demanding that the states suing to block its $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery post a nearly $1.9 billion bond ($1,884,726,092 to be precise about it), pending the outcome of the litigation.
In a statement Monday, the company, led by CEO David Ellison, says that the bond demand is based on settled federal law.
“Both the Clayton Act, the federal antitrust law upon which these suits are based, and other federal law expressly provide that plaintiffs are required to post a bond covering the potential harm from halting a transaction to litigate, so that if they lose, the injured party has a source of recovery for the damage caused,” the company said in a statement. “Here, every month of delay carries substantial and quantifiable financial consequences.”
Paramount counts Makan Delrahim, was previously the chief antitrust enforcer in the U.S. during the first Trump Administration, as its head of legal affairs.
“Paramount is seeking a bond based on the straightforward calculation of the maximum potential ticking consideration and financing costs from this litigation,” the company states. “But these are not the only costs of delay. By virtue of what will be at least an eight-month delay in closing, there will be no integration and no ramped-up investment in content, production, and creative talent by the combined company. Of course, in addition, employees of both Paramount and WBD are also harmed by the uncertainties caused by the delay.”
Paramount has been playing a hardball public pressure campaign since the lawsuit was filed, with threats to leave the state of California (realistic or not), as well as accusations that partisan politics are at play. Hollywood is divided on whether the states and company should try and settle or follow through with the trial, further complicating the effort.
But the bond is a tangible ask, one that would put taxpayers on the hook in a high-profile case.

title: Remembering Hayden Panettiere: From ‘Heroes’ to ‘Nashville’ to ‘Scream,’ 12 of Her Standout Roles
full_content:
News of Hayden Panettiere’s death shocked Hollywood — and the rest of the world — on Sunday.
While the cause of death is unknown, it’s understood that an investigation is under way. The actress was 36 at the time of her death.
As fans flock to social media to pay tribute to the actress, The Hollywood Reporter has rounded up a list of her most memorable roles, from her early beginnings as a child actor on soap operas to her critically acclaimed performances in Heroes and Nashville.
- 
			One Life to Live (1994-97), Guiding Light (1996-2000)
While Panettiere got her start in acting at just 11 months, appearing in a Playskool toy train commercial, she really kicked off her career in 1994, when she landed the role of Sarah Roberts in soap opera One Life to Live, leaving the show in 1997. From 1996-2000, she appeared in another soap, Guiding Light, playing Lizzie Spaulding.
- 
			A Bug’s Life (1998)Panettiere was part of an all-star voice cast that included Dave Foley, Kevin Spacey, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Phyllis Diller, Richard Kind, David Hyde Pierce, Joe Ranft and Denis Leary in this animated film, which followed an ant named Flik who is trying to protect his colony from a gang of grasshoppers. The actress voiced Dot, a friend of Flik. She was nominated for a Grammy in 2000 for best spoken word album for children for A Bug’s Life Read-Along.
- 
			Remember the Titans (2000)
Panettiere earned a Young Artist Award for playing Sheryl Yoast, the daughter of football coach Bill Yoast (Will Patton), who herself is obsessed with the sport. She has said that this film was her favorite acting experience. “This movie was my favorite movie to film,” she told Entertainment Tonight in 2023. “What an incredible time in my life. … I mean, you have no idea how many times in my life I have wished and prayed — if I had wished to go back to any time in my life, it would be going back to Remember the Titans.”
- 
			Ally McBeal (2002)In the fifth and final season of the legal dramedy, Panettiere played Madison “Maddie” Harrington, the long-lost daughter of Ally (Calista Flockhart). She appeared in 12 episodes of the series.
- 
			Ice Princess (2005)Panettiere starred opposite Joan Cusack, Kim Cattrall and the late Michelle Trachtenberg in this ice-skating film, adapted from a story by The Princess Diaries author Meg Cabot. While the movie underperformed at the box office, it’s garnered a cult following in the time since its release.
- 
			Bring It On: All or Nothing (2006)Kicking off a series of cheerleader roles, Panettiere starred in the third film in the Bring It On franchise (this one released direct to DVD). The actress played Britney Allen, a rich girl who is dating the star quarterback. But Britney is in for a shock when her father loses his job and moves the family to a more culturally diverse and less affluent area of Los Angeles. (The cast also included Solange Knowles-Smith, who starred as Panettiere’s cheerleading rival, and Rihanna, who makes an appearance as herself.)
- 
			Heroes (2006-10)
Panettiere was on Heroes for all four seasons of the show’s 2006-10 run. The show, featuring an ensemble cast that also included Milo Ventimiglia, Adrian Pasdar, Greg Grunberg and Ali Larter, followed a group of everyday folks who discovery they have superhuman abilities. Panettiere played high school cheerleader Claire Bennet, who discovers she has regenerating abilities. (Who can forget the infamous tagline promoting the show that focused on her character’s importance to the plot: “Save the cheerleader, save the world.”) The show became a cultural phenomenon, and the cast was even featured in Time’s “Person of the Year” issue as “People Who Mattered.” Panettiere won Teen Choice, Saturn and Young Artist Awards for her role. (The actress did not return for the 2015 miniseries revival, Heroes Reborn.)
- 
			I Love You, Beth Cooper (2009)Panettiere played yet another high school cheerleader in this Chris Columbus-directed teen rom-com, based on the novel by Larry Doyle. Her character, Beth Cooper, is wooed by school valedictorian Denis Cooverman (Paul Rust), who confesses he has a crush on her in his graduation speech.
- 
			Amanda Knox: Murder on Trial in Italy (2011)
In this Lifetime TV movie, Panettiere starred in the title role, with the story based on real-life events. The real Knox was tried and convicted for the 2007 murder of her roommate, Meredith Kercher, in Italy, before being acquitted two years later. In 2013, that acquittal was overturned, and Knox was retried and convicted of murder a second time. In 2012, an Italian court acquitted her yet again. The movie shows the events leading up to Kercher’s death and the 2009 conviction. (Knox and her family unsuccessfully tried to block the airing of the movie.)
- 
			Scream 4 (2011), Scream VI (2023)Panettiere played Kirby Reed in two films in the long-running franchise. Kirby is the best friend of OG character Sidney Prescott’s (Neve Campbell) cousin Jill (Emma Roberts). In Scream VI, it’s revealed that Kirby has become an FBI special agent who shows up to assist when the Ghostface murders start all over again, this time in New York.
- 
			Nashville (2012-18)Panettiere played ambitious, rising singer Juliette Barnes in the six-season series, set in the world of country music, which ran from 2012-18. Juliette began the series aiming to take over the crown of country music queen from Rayna (Connie Britton). The role earned her multiple awards and nominations, including two Golden Globe noms for best supporting actress and a Critics Choice Television Award nom for best supporting actress in a drama series.

title: Hayden Panettiere: Emma Roberts, Melissa Barrera, David Arquette, Viola Davis & More Pay Tribute To “Amazing Talent”
full_content:
UPDATED: Tributes are flooding in for Hayden Panettiere, the Scream and Heroes star who has died aged 36.
David Arquette and Melissa Barrera, who appeared on screen with Panettiere in the Scream franchise, all took to social media to post messages.
Arquette, who plays the loveable Dewey in Scream, posted simply: “I love you Hayden,” while Barrera, who acted with Panettiere in Scream VI, wrote: “Rest in peace sweet Hayden.”
Emma Roberts, who starred with Panettiere in Scream IV, penned a remembrance to the actress on Instagram: “rest in peace my sweet friend. you are so loved and you will be forever missed❤️”
Selma Blair, the Legally Blonde and Hellboy actress, wrote: “Blair wrote: “I love you. Don’t be gone. Please,” before following up with two similar messages. Blair had a small uncredited role in Scream 2.
Panettiere’s reps today confirmed the actress, who played Kirby Reed in Scream 4 and Scream VI, died aged 36 in South Carolina. Details are scant about her passing, but there is an ongoing investigation into the matter.
Others paying tribute include Rose O’Donnell, who wrote on social media, “Oh my god – heartbroken #hayden”, and One Tree Hill star Bethany Joy Lenz, who left a lengthy message, writing: “I’m crushed. I knew the wild little blonde. Was she nine? Ten? I was eighteen. She ran through the Screen Gem studio hallways at 222 E44th St. laughing and playing games in between blocking and camera rehearsals. Long, unruly curls trailing behind her.
“She knew her lines and everyone else’s. Her intelligence was astonishing. She understood scenes and nuance and human struggle like no child I’d ever seen on camera. And she’d sit with you for a great conversation, then giggle and go play. We’d connect on and off over the years, like the cousin in the family reunion who got famous and life moved her away — but I always felt such joy seeing her when we were lucky enough to cross paths.”
Viola Davis, who worked with Panettiere in 2006 on David Greig film Architect and in 2016 on courtroom drama Custody, wrote: “What an amazing talent you were….so gifted. Julius [Tennon, Davis’ actor husband] and I loved working with you….an old, wise soul with such a deep heart. I wish the world had more time with you because I had a burning curiosity about who you were becoming. I saw this beautiful Phoenix rising from the ashes.”
Another message came from podcaster Jay Shetty, who sat down with Panettiere a few months back for an emotional conversation about the actress’s career and difficult personal life. He wrote: “I can’t believe it. Our friendship had just begun and I was so moved by the conversation we shared earlier this year. My love and condolences to her family and fans.”
Panettiere was open about her well-documented struggles with depression and addiction. The birth of her daughter Kaya in 2014 brought postpartum depression, and she later split with the father, former boxing world heavyweight champion Wladimir Klitschko.
Panettiere was a child star who appeared in commercials and had a four-year run as Sarah Roberts on One Life to Live before acting in The Guiding Light. She made her big screen debut at the age of nine in A Bug’s Life and in 2000, she played the daughter of a coach in Denzel Washington starrer Remember the Titans. In 2004, Panettiere landed her first starring roles as the daughter of actor Bill Pullman’s character in Tiger Cruise on The Disney Channel.
In 2006, Panettiere landed her breakout role in NBC superhero series Heroes, playing indestructible high school cheerleader Claire Bennet, who had to juggle her normal life with saving the world from threats. Despite an initial plan to introduce new stars each season, the popularity of Panettiere and fellow star Milo Ventimiglia’s characters meant she lead all four seasons.
Panettiere appeared as Kirby Reed in three Scream films: Scream 4 in 2011, a cameo in its sequel Scream eleven years later and Scream VI in 2023. She played the best friend of Jill Roberts, franchise protagonist Sidney Prescott’s younger cousin.
The actress was also known for her leading role as rising country music star Juliette Barnes in Nashville, playing opposite Connie Britton. Much of the show’s drama — and a good portion of ABC’s marketingl campaign — centered on the rivalry between their two characters. Nashville ran for six seasons, first on ABC and then CMT.
News of Panettiere’s passing came to light today, with her family releasing a statement. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” her father, Skip Panettiere, said in a statement to ABC. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”
	More reactions as we have it.

title: Taylor Swift Praises Phoebe Bridgers’ ‘Lost Weekend’ as “An Absolute Triumph in Every Way”
full_content:
Taylor Swift is heaping some major praise on Phoebe Bridgers‘ Lost Weekend, as the pop star called Bridgers’ first album in six years “a gift” while wishing her one-time collaborator a happy birthday on Monday.
“It’s her birthday but she gave us a gift,” Swift wrote on her Instagram story Monday, accompanied by the album artwork for Bridgers’ third album. “Haven’t been able to stop listening. This album is an absolute triumph in every way. To write about grief with such vulnerability and detail, and to trust the listener with this much honesty. Happy bday @phoebebridgers I love you!!”
Bridgers made her much-anticipated return with Lost Weekend last Friday, marking the beloved indie star’s first new solo album since 2020’s Punisher. She’s taking the album on the road this fall with a phones-free arena tour set to begin in September in Indianapolis.
That Swift would be among the legions of fans listening in on Bridgers’ latest work isn’t surprising. The two are friends and Swift featured Bridgers on the Red (Taylor’s Version) track “Nothing New.” Bridgers also served as an opening act during Swift’s 2023 Eras Tour, playing nine dates on the tour at Nissan Stadium, Lincoln Financial Field, Gillette Stadium and MetLife Stadium.
While Lost Weekend marked Bridgers’ first solo album in six years, she’s hardly been off the scene, taking her career to new highs with supergroup Boygenius and their 2023 album The Record. The album won a Grammy for best alternative music album, while “Not Strong Enough” won for best rock performance and best rock song.
Beyond her music, Bridgers is also set to make her acting debut in Primetime next month as well.

title: Chris Pratt Seeks Violent Redemption in ‘The Terminal List’ Season 2 First-Look Images
full_content:
Chris Pratt returns as Navy SEAL commander James Reece in the first look images for The Terminal List season 2 unveiled on Monday ahead of an Oct. 21, 2026 premiere on Prime Video.
As Gabriel Luna joins the new season in the role of Freddy Strain, Reece is now on a journey of violent redemption that ties into his own family’s history. The second season, based on Jack Carr’s second novel, True Believer, sees Reece looking to uncover a vast conspiracy stretching from Moscow to Langley and allowing him a new purpose after finishing his list — a terminal list — of people he wanted to target for revenge in the first season.
“The psychological revenge story of season one expands into a globe-trotting espionage thriller, taking Reece across the Indian Ocean, Southern and Northern Africa, the Middle East, and Europe,” a synopsis from the producers reads.
The Terminal List was adapted from the first of Carr’s five novels built around the character of Reece, played by Pratt. The starry second season of eight new episodes — returning four years after the rookie season rolled out — includes returning cast members like Tom Hopper, Constance Wu, Dar Salim, Luke Hemsworth, Gabriel Luna, Costa Ronin, Olga Kurylenko, Yul Vazquez, Martin Sensmeier, Arnold Vosloo and Shiraz Tzarfati.
The Terminal List season 2 is executive produced by Pratt, Antoine Fuqua (who directed the original pilot for the series), showrunner David DiGilio, Carr, Kat Samick, Max Adams and Jared Shaw. The series is produced by Amazon MGM Studios, MRC and Civic Center Media.

title: Paramount+ Head Of Originals Jane Wiseman Outlines Programming Strategy One Year In: Female Dramas, Genre, Taylor Sheridan & Tyler Perry
full_content:
August 13 marked Jane Wiseman‘s one-year anniversary as EVP & Head of Originals for Paramount+. Coincidentally — and fittingly — it also marked the start of production for Discretion starring Nicole Kidman and Elle Fanning, which was the first big buy for the streamer’s new regime, led by Cindy Holland, Chair of Direct to Consumer, and her top programming executive, Wiseman, following Skydance’s acquisition of Paramount.
There have been 28 new series pickups since then across scripted, unscripted and kids and family and 16 renewals. There has been platform consolidation, with BET+ folded into Paramount+ and the Showtime name dropped from P+’s top tier.
The streamer’s sibling studio Paramount TV Studios has signed deals with top talent such as the Duffer Brothers and Issa Rae (shared with Paramount Pictures) and Liz Tigelaar (shared with CBS Studios). Meanwhile, Paramount+ is a little over two years away from seeing its most prolific creator, Taylor Sheridan, leave for NBCUniversal, with his close collaborator, David Glasser of 101 Studios, already there.
Watch on Deadline
And then, there is Paramount’s pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery which has been commanding attention for months, with its outcome and closing date in limbo amid a legal fight with state AGs.
RELATED: 2026 TV Cancellations Photo Gallery: Series Ending This Year & Beyond
In a wide-ranging interview with Deadline held on her one-year anniversary, Wiseman discussed Paramount+’s programming strategy and its different areas: female forward, genre and YA dramas — but not comedies — kids and family programming and unscripted. She spoke about Paramount+’s relationship with its top creators, Sheridan and Tyler Perry — who recently sold his stake in BET+ to Paramount — teasing more shows from both. Wiseman also talked about buying from sister studios Paramount TV Studios and CBS Studios and, for the first time in Paramount+’s history, from outside studios, too, about the future of the Star Trek franchise and the Showtime brand as well as building a slate with the WBD merger noise in the background and plans for Year 2.
“The fact that I can look back on these last 12 months and see what we’ve accomplished with the green lights and the renewals after looking at this incredible foundation that we started with, with all of our amazing Taylor Sheridan shows and with Star Trek and the Showtime shows and the CBS next-day shows, it really really hit home to us that we have so much, we have a lot to build off of,” Wiseman said. “So, although Paramount+ is only five years old, it feels like we’re really just getting started. So, the takeaway for me is that we have this incredible starting point but there’s so much room to grow.”
This is the second streamer Wiseman has worked at; she was also part of Holland’s core team at Netflix that built its slate from scratch and turned it into a formidable original programming player. (Wiseman has spent most of her career to date as a comedy executive at Netflix, NBC, Fox and Chernin Entertainment.) The assignment has been different with Paramount+, which had been around for several years with originals as well as access to the Paramount Pictures and CBS Studios libraries and next-day CBS programming.
Buying Volume
DEADLINE: There had been some expectation that when the post-merger Paramount+ regime came in, you would be going on a buying spree, which did not happen. Talk about your ramp-up approach.
WISEMAN: My dance card and phone sheet would say differently because I do feel like we are buying a lot. We are definitely developing a lot, we’ve announced seven scripted drama greenlights in the last 10 months, so it does feel like there’s volume. And then we have a lot on the runway that we haven’t announced yet. So, to me, what we don’t want to do is scale so big, so fast. We want to be very deliberate in our choices. We want to stay on strategy. We want to curate what we have, but we also want to take care of the the Sheridan audience, the Taylorverse.
Then we also want to look at our strategy in the female forward space as well as the genre. It does feel a lot, frankly, to me. We’re very busy behind the scenes. We’re working very closely with our friends at Paramount TV Studios and CBS Studios, and we’re also buying from outside studios for the first time in a long time, with A24 and MGM, just to name a few.
We have development with just about everybody in town, so the volume is increasing. But I also want to say we want to be the home where we buy something and we make it, we don’t want things to sit in development for years. We want to make sure that we’re deliberate in our buying. So that may seem like it’s less, I don’t feel that way because we want to greenlight everything we buy.
DEADLINE: Talk about your relationship with Paramount TV Studios and CBS Studios. And you mentioned Paramount+ opening up to third-party sellers for the first time, do you get a lot of incoming business from outside?
WISEMAN: We do, we get a lot. But what’s wonderful about our Paramount TV studio partners as well as our CBS studio partners that there’s so much trust. I’ve known [CBS Studios President] David Stapf for 20 years, I’ve known [PTVS President] Matt Thunell for 12 years, we worked so closely together in our last job, and we have a trust. And the fact that we have shows already on the service from both studios — we just greenlit Clueless and Ascent, we also have a lot of development. It speaks to our trust and our communication, and they’re filling the pipeline and allowing us to make these decisions easier as shows like Clueless and Ascent are really on strategy for us.
[Meanwhile], our show Trauma that we just greenlit is from Lionsgate, and we have a couple on the runway that are third-party studios. We’re working with everyone in town.
Programming Strategy
When Holland and Wiseman took over Paramount+, its original slate had a handful of cornerstones –Sheridan, who is behind the streamer’s biggest series, including Landman, Tulsa King, Lioness, and, most recently, The Madison; Glasser’s 101 Studios, which produces Sherdian’s series along with others, including MobLand; and the Star Trek franchise.
Word quickly spread to the creative community that the new regime was looking to supplement the existing lineup of largely male-skewing shows with female dramas. Signaling their arrival to the town, the first two bidding wars Paramount+ won with straight-to-series orders post-merger were for legal drama Discretion, starring Kidman and Fanning, and limited series Fear Not, headlined by Anne Hathaway. Both come from outside studios, A24 and MGM Television, respectively.
“We know that female forward ensemble shows, dramas, legal thrillers, soapy thrillers, are things that we were looking for,” Holland said at Paramount’s upfront presentation in May about the initial priorities.
Below, Wiseman goes over each aspect of Paramount+’s programming strategy.
Female Forward
DEADLINE: The expression I keep hearing about Paramount+’s programming strategy is filling white spaces in the lineup. Let’s talk about how you have been filling these gaps, starting with female dramas.
WISEMAN: As I said, when we started, we felt like we had a great foundation. You can look at the shows that come from Taylor and 101, they get big audiences. We just launched Lioness. We’re really, really excited about the viewing that’s coming from that show, and it’s both female and male, but it’s definitely a genre, I mean, Taylor’s his own genre, if you think about it.
So we wanted to widen the aperture, and, knowing that you already have men and women coming to the service — we have men coming, we have UFC, we have football, sports, and then we have an unscripted offering that we know can bring in women — we wanted to build on that, it’s all about building.
The female forward is in front of the camera, behind the camera, really getting women, intriguing them to come to the service and watch. And what was really exciting is that we just launched last spring The Madison and Dutton Ranch, which were from the Taylor Sheridan camp, but they over-indexed in women. So we felt like if you make shows for women, they will come.
Enter Discretion or enter Fear Not, that’s where we felt like if we could make shows for women but not alienate men; we want to make sure there’s something for everyone, and we feel like what was missing were those soapy character dramas. What I love about Discretion, just to pinpoint that one, when we first started, this was one of the first pitches that came in the door, and it was — I’m not kidding — it was a soapy female two-hander legal drama from Susannah Grant and Chandler Baker, starring Elle Fanning and Nicole Kidman, and we were like, bullseye, let’s go.
That was a pitch, but we felt some comfort with Susannah Grant because we’d worked with her before, and we also know how incredible she is. Chandler had just an incredible take on this female forward storyline, and then, we had two of the most incredible stars in the world in Elle Fanning and Nicole Kidman. So that one felt like a really no-brainer to us.
We’ve been developing female thrillers. We’ve been developing true crime. We’ve been developing soaps. We’ve been developing a lot. It’s not just one thing, it’s not one size fits all when we talk about female forward, which makes it exciting.
Prestige Fare & WBD Merger Impact
DEADLINE: A number of your buys look kind of prestige, something HBO would be doing. Did you adjust the strategy after the Warner Bros. Discovery merger was announced with a plan for Paramount+ and HBO Max to merge so your slate would be complementary to HBO’s?
WISEMAN: No. The strategy has not changed. From the day we walked in one year ago, it is still the same.
DEADLINE: How is the pending merger, especially the uncertainty surrounding it, impacting your strategy, if at all? Are you slowing down, are you pausing any efforts, programming or hiring-wise? Is there any wait-and-see approach?
WISEMAN: We came in a year ago with the goal of expanding our slate, and our commitment to that remains unchanged.
DEADLINE: And no other areas have been impacted, like staffing or buying, the volume of it?
WISEMAN: No. And, beyond the scripted dramas, we’re also playing in the unscripted space as well as kids and families. So we feel like we’re growing.
DEADLINE: And you have no issues with creatives with the merger and the limbo around it; you’re still not in shortage of great talent coming to you?
WISEMAN: Not in shortage.
Genre Build-up & ‘Star Trek’s Future
DEADLINE: Along with female dramas, genre has been a priority. You brought in top genre executive Chris Parnell to lead the efforts but haven’t announced any series. Where are you in the process and what areas are you focusing on? I’ve heard world-building, fantasy, romantasy. Everybody wants their Game of Thrones and Stranger Things.
WISEMAN: Speaking of spaces, the space is wide open. We’re the home of Star Trek, and we have series coming back. We’re going to have more. Yellowjackets, I guess, is also considered genre, and Dexter. But as far as new things coming to the service, true, we want our world-building, platform-defining genre series, and that can be grounded. In fact, we hope it is grounded because the best genre shows have relationships at the center.
What’s also exciting is that we have a Paramount library to choose from, titles that we’re investigating that you’ll hear from at a later date. And there’s nothing better than hearing an original idea for a grounded genre series that speaks to a lot of people. So the space is pretty wide open. And yes, you alluded to Chris Parnell, there’s no one better in that space, and there’s no one more in that space that I want on my team.
DEADLINE: Do you feel strongly about your development? Do you think that your signature genre show may be one that you already have in the works?
WISEMAN: I will say that when you’re developing these genre platform-defining shows, they do tend to take a little bit longer. But I would say for sure that there are a handful of titles, from our studio partners as well as a third party, that we are looking at right now, developing, and are on a very, very strong path to green light. I just can’t talk about anything right now.
DEADLINE: What is your plan for the Star Trek franchise? It is at crossroads with Strange New Worlds and Starfleet Academy ending and no new series greenlit. If I heard you correctly, you said that something is coming. Yes?
WISEMAN: Well, it’s one of the reasons why Chris is here as the resident number one fan of the Star Trek franchise. And there’s so many people in this building, by the way, that are. It is our goal and it is our job to figure out what the next bounce of Star Trek is. We’re talking to a lot of writers, we are leaning on CBS Studios, and it is imperative that we figure out what the next iteration is in this franchise because it’s just too important. We also are in touch with Paramount Pictures, they have a Star Trek movie that’s in development.
‘Clueless’, YA & Paramount IP
DEADLINE: You mentioned Clueless, the sequel series to the Paramount movie with Alicia Silverstone reprising her role as Cher. Talk about the decision to buy it after Peacock passed; I believe this came together very quickly.
WISEMAN: Clueless is a huge, huge property for Paramount, obviously. We’ve all been huge fans of the movie and everybody involved. When we heard that it was available and that it could be a way to bring it home, we did move very quickly. CBS Studios made it undeniable for us. Josh [Schwartz] and Stephanie [Savage] and Jordan [Weiss] are incredible creators. Sitting across the table from Alicia Silverstone and hearing her talk about the character, it just makes so much sense. We really wanted to get the band back together and celebrate it in an event series, and that really is what hit home for us.
DEADLINE: Why did you decide to eventize Clueless as a limited series and not do it as ongoing series? Could it still continue?
WISEMAN: We decided to make it an event series because it deserves to be an event. We feel like this is going to be something that people are going to come to in droves — already you can tell — if you want to get the cast back together, if you want to see where everyone is. It’s also a mother-daughter story, which I don’t want to overlook because we’re really excited about the next generation of Clueless. So, if I can leave it open-ended, I’d like to. But the idea is that this particular version of the show is supposed to be an event. It’s supposed to be open and closed where Cher is in her life and what she and her daughter are up to, and how we can bring the cast back to celebrate it.
DEADLINE: I’d heard, and you alluded to it multiple times, that the idea is to bring as many of the film’s cast back as possible, like Paul Rudd, Stacey Dash, Donald Faison, right?
WISEMAN: Oh, we would love it.
DEADLINE: But no one has a deal, correct?
WISEMAN: Beyond who we’ve announced, like Alicia, yes, correct.
DEADLINE: You mentioned the mother-daughter relationship, which is a YA element; obviously the original was a YA movie. You also have School Spirits. YA is such a hot area on streaming right now, are you ramping up that development too? There haven’t been announcements beyond Clueless.
WISEMAN: We are definitely developing in the space, and we want to take our time and be deliberate with our choices. Clueless, even though it is a mother-daughter show, it still feels there’s a big YA element, and we love School Spirits, we can’t wait for it to come back. We know that’s a space that’s important to our viewers, having this robust kids and family audience and then being able to have a bridge into adulthood, so we’re looking at it. It’s much more opportunistic. We’re definitely taking some swings in the space.
DEADLINE: In addition to Clueless, you have Cop Land, based on the Paramount movie, in development. Are there other Paramount titles that you are adapting for TV; is there a dream IP that you would like to tackle?
WISEMAN: Well, we are the home of Avatar in the animated space, and we could not be more thrilled with this movie that just launched, and then we have series that are coming. So we have a lot of Avatar Paramount IP coming, and then you’ve also reported on Garfield, which we’re really excited about in the kids space. Nothing else at this point to point to but knowing that we’re definitely working with our partners, and we’re really, really open to finding more IP from Paramount because it’s really important. It’s our home.
Comedic Pause
DEADLINE: On Day 1, Cindy Holland indicated that Paramount+ would not be doing original comedies, relying on next-day CBS sitcoms. It is ironic since comedy is literally your background, an area you’re you’re an expert in, so I’m sure it is a little strange for you not to be in the comedy space. Colin from Accounts is coming to an end, Crutch was canceled, you don’t even have a formal head of comedy. Is drama too big of a priority not to think about comedy?
WISEMAN: Well, first of all, thank you for calling me an expert in comedy, that is probably the best thing I’ve heard in a long time. I do love comedy, I grew up on comedy in my life. And it’s true, it is wonderful that we have the next-day CBS comedies. We are the home of South Park, which is one of the biggest comedies out there. I think the priority is one-hour drama. We talk about it in building blocks, and it’s not a never, It’s just not a right now. We’re just trying to find our space in the one-hour area.
DEADLINE: But there’s premium live-action comedy, something that CBS or South Park cannot offer.
WISEMAN: Yeah. The other thing I would say is, the dramas have humor; I always want to have humor in the content that I program and frankly watch. The actual comedy half-hour is just not something we’re programming right now. But again, we never say never. That is something that we want to make sure people know is that things come in opportunistically, and we jump on them when we know that it’s right.
Broadcast-Style Dramas
DEADLINE: Another area that you inherited on Paramount+ is broadcast-adjacent dramas like NCIS: Tony & Ziva, which was canceled. You have Criminal Minds: Evolution left. What is its future? I don’t know how those kinds of shows fit into your strategy, they don’t seem to.
WISEMAN: We just launched Criminal Minds Season 19, and we are big fans, we love how long-running that is. We’re going to 20, which is greenlit for 2027. Tony & Ziva, unfortunately, for the cost, it did not make sense with the viewing, although we were all fans of it.
DEADLINE: So if a show is performing, even if it’s a broadcast-type drama, it can still find a space on Paramount+?
WISEMAN: Yeah. Again, we have these incredible next-day procedurals from CBS. But if something works for us, and we feel like it’s going to work for us, we’ll take a shot.
Taylor Sheridan, 101 Studios, Duffers & Issa Rae
DEADLINE: You mentioned Taylor Sheridan a few times. How is your relationship with him going? He surprised everyone by writing every episode of Frisco King after his 2029 move to NBCUniversal had been announced. Can we expect more new shows for P+ before his deal is up?
WISEMAN: That is the hope, and that is the intention. We have Frisco King coming. We have a couple things that I can’t talk about, but we work very closely with Taylor and David Glasser. We have a really great relationship, and the idea that we have more Madison coming, we have more Landman coming, we have more Dutton coming, and there are a couple things that we’ve been discussing that we would love to get on the service before 29. But we know that his legacy will remain with us for many, many years to come because of all the shows I just mentioned.
DEADLINE: Mayor of Kingstown is the first one of Sheridan’s ongoing Paramount+ series that is coming to an end. Of his other longer-running shows, do you see Tulsa King continuing? There had been talk about it moving to New York.
WISEMAN: We’re about to announce the premiere date for Tulsa King Season 4, that one is coming out. It’s an incredible season. Sly [Stallone] is in great form in the show, and there’s going to be some surprises. But that show is continuing.
DEADLINE: Can it continue beyond Season 4?
WISEMAN: It could. Between Tulsa and Landman, which Taylor is writing right now. Frisco, Dutton, Madison, we have a lot of business, and we’re going to be in business for time to come.
DEADLINE: Moving onto 101 Studios. Is everything okay on MobLand after the behind-the-scenes commotion involving Tom Hardy. Are you locked and loaded for Season 3?
WISEMAN: Season 2 is unbelievable, it is so explosive. We just released the trailer. It’s firing all cylinders. I’m really excited about this season.
DEADLINE: And Season 3?
WISEMAN: We haven’t made a decision on Season 3 yet.
DEADLINE: Cop Land feels like a Taylor Sheridan or 101 Studios type of show, down to the title that is a cross between Landman and MobLand. Are you starting to think about a future after their departures, developing new series that would continue that legacy?
WISEMAN: It is early, and, again, the offering that we have is so robust. We have a lot in the pipeline, so it’s a little bit early. But Cop Land, besides being Paramount IP and from an incredible team and our sister studio FTVS, it felt like something that would go really well with the audiences that watch these other shows, so it felt like a good shot to take.
DEADLINE: Cop Land came out of James Mangold’s feature pact at Paramount. Have you started developing with other talent under big deals made right after the merger? The Duffer Brothers have a movie for 2028, but do you have anything with them or Issa Rae in the works?
WISEMAN: We’ve had incredible meetings with Issa and the Duffers, frankly. They’re very very busy, but it is truly the goal to have shows from both of them, and hopefully sooner than later with Issa. The Duffers are very busy with their movie but that doesn’t mean that they can’t shepherd series at the same time. We’re just trying to be respectful of their time.
Showtime Brand & ‘Original Sin’s Fate
DEADLINE: The future of the Showtime-branded series. Yellowjackets and The Chi are ending, leaving only Dexter: Resurrection. Are you developing shows to be in that brand, will it continue, or will any new series be Paramount+ originals?
WISEMAN: With shows like Yellowjackets and The Chi, which felt very female forward, we definitely want to develop shows in those spaces for women by women, so that’s not going to change. Really excited for the next season of Dexter to come out, it’s been on our platform for 20 years. As far as the Showtime brand, I don’t know that there’s anything really to say about it right now. In terms of brands, we just migrated BET over to a service, which was really successful for us, and we have some wonderful series coming from BET Studios, so I can speak more to that.
DEADLINE: To clarify, you’re not developing shows and say, these fit the Showtime brand, there will not be a tile or something on Paramount+ the way FX is on Hulu, correct? it’s not a separate lane that you’re developing in.
WISEMAN: No.
DEADLINE: Why did you decide not to proceed with Dexter: Original Sin Season 2, which had been announced pre-merger?
WISEMAN: I think that was right in the beginning. I know it was really deliberate, we wanted to focus on Michael C. Hall and his character with Dexter: Resurrection, and that was really important for us to continue that storyline.
DEADLINE: Any thoughts about 101’s The Agency, which started as a Showtime series before becoming a P+ original? How is the current second season doing? Could be more?
WISEMAN: It’s too early.
BET+ & Tyler Perry’s Arrival
DEADLINE: You just mentioned the BET+ migration being successful. Since then, you have renewed The Ms. Pat Show, you have The Varnell Hill Show coming up. Have you seen the BET+ slate bring new viewers to Paramount+? And how is your relationship with Tyler Perry, who is behind most BET/BET+ series?
WISEMAN: It’s a good question. And yes, we feel the migration was very successful. The audiences are showing up for sure.
Our relationship with Tyler Perry is very strong, and I’m excited for more content from him, as well as working closely with our friends at BET Studios, with some announcements to come.
DEADLINE: But we could expect similar volume of originals to what BET+ was offering, just on Paramount+, it’s not going to go down, correct?
WISEMAN: Correct.
Kids & Family Strategy
DEADLINE: In the kids and family space, you obviously have the Nickelodeon shows. But you also have ordered your own originals with the animated The Elephant & Piggie Show!, The Pigeon Show! and Garfield. Is there white space that Nickelodeon doesn’t cover? How do you decide what kids and family animated shows to do as P+ originals?
WISEMAN: Absolutely, the Nickelodeon brand is very strong and very important to Paramount, and we have a lot of offerings from the Nickelodeon studio. Elephant & Piggie and Pigeon and the Mo Willems universe in general was something that was really important to us. Preschool is we feel like a really important audience that we want to make sure we’re servicing, and the Mo Willems universe, it’s a crown jewel.
So we felt like that would be a perfect opportunity to program not just one series, but multiple series. We’re developing others, we’re working really closely with Mo Willems and Hidden Pigeon, and it’s been a joy, frankly.
DEADLINE: What about live-action family shows, like Percy Jackson. Is that something that you would do or will you rely on Nickelodeon’s output for it?
WISEMAN: We look to Nickelodeon. We have The Thundermans coming, the Avatar space is in that world as well. That is my group, small and mighty, and we are building out strategy for kids and family. We’re executing on that strategy with the announcements of the shows that we just talked about, and that is something that’s a big priority for us.
DEADLINE: In terms of your overall team, is it all built up? Are there more executives you would like to add, or are you keeping it lean and mean?
WISEMAN: I do like lean and mean. We feel nimble, we make really fast decisions, which I really like. And everyone has a direct line to me. Everyone has direct lines to Cindy. We built up last fall — I would say quickly — and then we took a pause and just we’re reevaluating what we need for the future. We’re about to go into production on four new shows, Discretion, The Best Of Us, Laird and Trauma, so ask me again in six months. But right now, it feels like the right amount of people.
Unscripted Priorities
DEADLINE: On the unscripted side, you have extensions of Paramount cable mainstays such as RuPaul, Teen Mom and Jersey Shore, you have ordered true crime shows, which have become a streaming staple, sports series to complement your live sports. Talk about mixing that with betting on new franchises that target young women like Making Love.
WISEMAN: Yes, and again, having this amazing foundation to start with football, with UFC, with next-day Survivor and Amazing Race. We thought we could opportunistically take some swings in the unscripted space that focuses on women, and that’s where the dating show Making Love comes in. That’s where Team Moms comes in and a few others that we’re going to announce shortly that will be female-focused, female-forward. We want to satisfy that audience because it’s a really big one.
DEADLINE: What other areas are you focusing on? True crime?
WISEMAN: We work really closely with See It Now Studios, Susan Zirinsky, she’s just a pro and has been programming here for a long time, and we’ve had an incredible experience. We have quite a few unscripted shows in the works that we haven’t announced. Handsome Devil came out in the first quarter and was so successful for us, that is true crime in its finest form. So that is something that we’re looking for as we continue, and we’re really looking to See It Now to help us with that. But also, we’re working with third parties as well.
DEADLINE: And Damla Dogan, who has been shepherding unscripted development for you, is she still a consultant?
WISEMAN: She is a pro, an expert in her field, and I’m so lucky to have her working on the unscripted content with us. She is currently consulting for us, but she is punching above her weight. She’s incredible and really helping us manage all of our shows.
Big Picture View
DEADLINE: Paramount executives have said that you won’t chase the volume of Netflix but you do seem to be following a similar strategy of trying to program for everyone, just in a different way, with some of the content coming from CBS, the cable networks, the movie studio and the film and TV library.
WISEMAN: As Cindy has said, we just want to have everyone’s favorite show. We really want to have a destination for people where they don’t even think twice about like, oh, I’m going to Paramount+ because I know my favorite show is on that service. And that’s why we talk about the scripted dramas, the unscripted, the kids and family, and we really are making a push. And it really comes down to the creators that we work with and wanting to be the best experience for people to tell their stories and to help them achieve their vision.
It all starts with the creator, with the filmmaker, and it’s not that simple, but it does feel like it for us because we get to work with the best in the business.
DEADLINE: If you have to grade the first year, what would you say? And what are the top priorities for Year 2?
WISEMAN: You know, and I say this with all sincerity: waking up every morning and being excited to come to work, and nothing is the same. Everything is different. It feels like a brand new day, and being able to work on these shows, these green lights, these returning shows – it’s a joy. So, if I can give myself a grade of joy, then I would give myself an A.
DEADLINE: And Year 2? More of the same?
WISEMAN: More of the same for Year 2, stay tuned. We have a lot. Although I would say in Year 2, we’re going into production on a lot of shows. So buckle up.

title: ‘All American’: Tensions High Within The Vortex Amid ICE Raid Aftermath & Fight For Beverly Coach In New Season 8 Clip
full_content:
EXCLUSIVE: Jordan (Michael Evans Behling), Layla (Greta Onieogou) and the rest of the Vortex are helping to pick up the pieces in Monday night’s episode of All American.
Deadline can share the above clip exclusively ahead of the episode, featuring the OG members of the Vortex presumably in the hours after both Amina (Alexis Chikaeze) and Preach (Kareem Grimes) were arrested by ICE agents while protecting students and faculty during a raid on South Crenshaw High School. In the clip, Jordan shows up to their home, where Layla waits with Coop (Bre-Z) and Breonna (Sasha Lance), with a box of doughnuts in tow.
“Doughnuts have a way of de-stressing even the worst situations,” he earnestly tells Layla when she questions the gesture.
It might’ve worked, if he hadn’t had to drop the news on Layla that KJ (Nathaniel McIntyre) is also missing after taking off in the middle of a fight between Cassius (Osy Ikhile) and Jordan.
Looks like they’ve got their hands full in this upcoming episode. Watch the full clip above.
Focusing on the three pillars that have always been at the heart of All American – football, family and friendship – Season 8 picks up six months after the football cliffhanger at the end of last season and will span just one week in our favorite Beverly and Crenshaw crew’s life. A week that will have them wondering if everything they’ve been through over the course of their lives has prepared them for this moment. A week that will ultimately reunite old with the new, friend with enemy, and alter the course of each of their futures forever.
The series stars Michael Evans Behling, Greta Onieogou, Bre-Z, Osy Ikhile, Alexis Chikaeze, Nathaniel Logan McIntyre, Antonio J. Bell, Kareem Grimes, and Lauryn Hardy.
All American is produced by Warner Bros. Television and CBS Studios in association with Berlanti Productions, with executive producers Nkechi Okoro Carroll (“Found,” “The Resident”), Greg Berlanti (“You,” “Brilliant Minds,” “The Flash”), Jameal Turner (“Rosewood”), Sarah Schechter (“The Flight Attendant,” “Riverdale,” “You”), and David Strauss (“One Tree Hill”).

title: Stephanie Koenig Joins Apple TV’s ‘Platonic’ For Season 3
full_content:
EXCLUSIVE: Stephanie Koenig (Lessons in Chemistry, English Teacher) has joined the cast of Apple TV‘s Platonic for Season 3 in a recurring role. She will play Alex, a lawyer who just began working at Charlie’s (played by Luke Macfarlane) firm.
From Nicholas Stoller and Francesca Delbanco, Platonic follows a platonic pair of former best friends approaching midlife (Seth Rogen and Rose Byrne) who reconnect after a long rift. The duo’s friendship becomes all-consuming — and destabilizes their lives in a hilarious way.
Season 2 picks up with everyone’s favorite pair of best friends as they contend with new midlife hurdles, including work, weddings and partners in crises. The duo tries their best to be each other’s rock, but sometimes rocks break things.
The cast also includes Luke Macfarlane and Carla Gallo.
Watch on Deadline
Platonic is produced by Sony Pictures Television, where Stoller’s Stoller Global Solutions has an overall deal. Byrne, Stoller, Delbanco and Conor Welch executive produce, along with Rogen, Evan Goldberg and James Weaver for Point Grey Pictures.
Most recently, Koenig was a series regular and writer on the FX comedy English Teacher. She played history teacher Gwen Sanders. Before that, she also had a main role as Fran Frask, starring opposite Brie Larson in Lee Eisenberg’s Apple TV miniseries Lessons in Chemistry. Koenig also recurred in the Paramount+ TV miniseries The Offer and HBO Max’s The Flight Attendant. She is repped by Green Management, Paradigm Talent Agency and Ziffren Brittenham.

title: Pierce Brosnan Joins Chris Hemsworth In Netflix’s ‘Extraction 3’
full_content:
EXCLUSIVE: Extraction 3, the latest entry in Netflix‘s action franchise starring Chris Hemsworth, has rounded out its cast with five additions: two-time Golden Globe nominee Pierce Brosnan (MobLand), plus Don Lee (Train to Busan), Joe Taslim (The Furious), Chi Lewis-Parry (28 Years Later: The Bone Temple) and Siena Agudong (Amazon’s upcoming Carrie series).
Lee joins after inking a deal to star in Tygo, a Korean-language entry in the franchise centered on his former child soldier turned mercenary, which is in post-production.
Extraction 3‘s logline is being kept under wraps, as are the roles of the other new hires. Pic is currently filming in Australia, with Idris Elba and Golshifteh Farahani co-starring alongside Hemsworth.
Watch on Deadline
Hailing from the Russo Brothers’ AGBO and Hemsworth’s Wild State, the Extraction films are based on the graphic novel Ciudad from Ande Parks and illustrator Fernando Leon Gonzalez. They follow Hemsworth’s Tyler Rake, an Australian mercenary taking on high stakes rescue missions the world over.
After directing the first two installments — both of which formerly held spots on Netflix’s Most Popular Films list — Sam Hargrave is back at the helm, working from a script by David Weil, based on a story by Ande Parks, Joe Russo & Anthony Russo.
Producers include Anthony Russo, Joe Russo, Angela Russo-Otstot, Michael Disco, and Ari Costa for AGBO; Hemsworth and Benjamin Grayson for Wild State; Hargrave; Patrick Newall; Eric Gitter; and Peter Schwerin. Shelby Malone and Steven V. Scavelli are exec producing.
Most recently seen starring in Netflix’s The Thursday Murder Club and Paramount+’s hit crime drama MobLand, heading into its third season, Brosnan is repped by CAA and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller.
Best known for roles in South Korean hits like Train to Busan and The Gangster, the Cop, and the Devil, Lee is repped by Chris S. Lee at B&C Group, Gersh, and attorney Stuart Rosenthal of GGSSC.
One of the stars of the lauded Hong Kong actioner The Furious, Taslim’s other recent credits include the Mortal Kombat films and the crime drama series Warrior. He is repped by CAA, Range Media Partners, and Brecheen Feldman Breimer.
A former professional mixed martial artist, Lewis-Parry plays colossal antagonist Samson in Danny Boyle’s recent zombie flick 28 Years Later and its sequel The Bone Temple, helmed by Nia DaCosta. Other recent credits include Gladiator II and The Running Man. He is repped by Wintersons and Vault Entertainment.
Agudong stars in and exec produces the hit YA films in Tubi’s Sidelined franchise and will be seen coming up in Amazon’s series adaptation of Stephen King’s Carrie. She is repped by AEFH, Gersh, Trilogy Talent, and Hirsch Wallerstein Hayum.

title: Late-Night Went Really Dark This Summer
full_content:
Jimmy Fallon has spent most of the summer as the sole torchbearer for late-night on broadcast television.
The Tonight Show host has been palling around with Katseye, trying on QVC wigs, starting his own microdrama, interviewing almost everyone involved in The Odyssey and making fun of the President.
He has, essentially, held down the fort of late-night all by himself. Jimmy Kimmel has been on his annual summer holiday and Seth Meyers has been largely off since the middle of June and will return at the end of September. Stephen Colbert, of course, is off writing a Lord of the Rings movie after being unceremoniously axed by CBS.
Meyers was off between June 18 and July 13, returning for two weeks before departing on July 30 and will eventually be back on September 21. This is much longer than recent breaks; last year he was off between July 18 and August 12 as well as the last week of August and in 2024 he was off the last two weeks of August (although admittedly it was an election year, which may have played into things).
Watch on Deadline
“We got a break coming up. I wish we didn’t. We like being here with you guys, but we’ll be back, we’ll be refreshed,” he said on an episode of his YouTube series Corrections.
“We’re about to take a very long hiatus and when we take very long hiatuses, one of the things that people say is that we’re going to miss so much. Because of that, we, through back channels, reached out to the White House and he agreed he’s not going to be weird. Until we get back,” he joked.
Kimmel has been taking the summers off since 2020, having baked in the idea to his contract with ABC. His show has been guest hosted by the likes of Anthony Anderson, Colman Domingo, Ike Barinholtz and Tiffany Haddish with Rosie O’Donnell filling his seat this week.
This long summer break is also interesting given that it coincides with Emmy voting season. Only John Oliver is on air this week as voting starts tomorrow so voters won’t be swayed by the latest monologue from Kimmel or Stewart as they choose who will win Outstanding Variety Series (although given the current rules, all five nominees – The Daily Show, Jimmy Kimmel Live!, Last Week Tonight, The Late Show and Saturday Night Live – could win an award in September).
Late-night hosts taking time off during the doldrums of summer is not a concern, in itself, but this year’s broadcast line-up feels like a harbinger. Many believe that the storied Tonight Show will be the last late-night franchise on air – Fallon is currently signed up to host through 2028, much like Meyers – but the cancelation of The Late Show, CBS deciding to move away from late-night altogether and the likelihood of Kimmel leaving sooner rather than later makes it feel like a sign of things to come.
The fact that Last Week Tonight’s John Oliver only signed up for a one-year deal, rather than his traditional three years, is also a worry, although that says more about the state of his employer, Warner Bros. Discovery, which is in a complicated corporate takeover situation, than the state of late-night comedy.
Yes, there’s still The Daily Show but the Comedy Central show is itself is on a longer hiatus than last year, essentially taking all of August off, returning on September 8, and Andy Cohen’s Bravo talker Watch What Happens Live is still a thriving spot for reality gossip.
Ad spending on linear late-night shows is clearly continuing to fall; ad intelligence agency Guideline noted that spend went from $439M in 2018 to $221M in 2024.
The narrative is that late-night is being replaced by YouTube shows.
Trevor Noah and Conan O’Brien are prospering with the former Daily Show host having nearly 5M subscribers on the Google-owned platform and the former Tonight Show has nearly 10M subs for his Team Coco channel.
But the new breed of “late-night” shows on YouTube such as Julian Shapiro Barnum’s Outside Tonight and Ben Gleib’s Good Night are struggling to break through. Some of Barnum’s Outside Tonight episodes are receiving hundreds thousand viewers, but the channel has fewer than 8,000 subscribers, while many clips of Good Night get only a few hundred views.
Fallon hasn’t addressed the fact that he’s largely alone on late-night island this summer, but he did recently tell USA Today that he feels some responsibility to carry the genre into the next generation
“The idea of it is that it’s just someone that you can talk to that’s there for you, that you can laugh, and you can know what’s going on in pop culture in the world,” he said. “I think that’s just needed.”

title: ‘Your Friends And Neighbors’ Creator On Making Emmy History And How Jon Hamm Turned The Tables On Don Draper – Contenders TV Nominees Studio
full_content:
Apple TV’s Your Friends and Neighbors has been nominated this year in the marquee Emmy category of Outstanding Drama Series. It marks the first-ever Emmy nomination for the series, and it has been achieved in just its second season. It also made a kind of Emmy history as becoming only the second series to score the prestigious nomination without being nommed in any other category in the same season (the first was Big Love in 2009). That indicates the series, which will be heading into its third season in 2027, is becoming a word-of-mouth hit, not just with audiences but also with Television Academy voters.
It is well deserved, and creator/showrunner/writer/executive producer Jonathan Tropper joined Deadline’s Contenders Television: The Nominees Studio to talk about how it got to this point and how much might have had to do with the wild second season. Joining him was co-star Hoon Lee, who plays series star Jon Hamm’s cohort Barney Choi.
Watch the conversation below and scroll down for photos from the event.
The series sees Hamm, back in a suit a la Mad Men’s Don Draper, being fired as a hedge fund manager, dealing with a recent divorce, and trying to pick up the pieces in wealthy Westchester’s Westmont Village, where he turns to stealing from his neighbors’ homes only to discover a host of secrets and affairs hidden within those compounds. In the second season he continues the practice only to be confronted by a new neighbor (James Marsden) who threatens to expose him, an act that once again could put his whole family at risk.
“I’m not sure what it is about the second season specifically that made it catch on. I think in some cases, it’s just the fact that we came after the first season. You know, if I sat down and thought about it, second seasons are generally a little denser,” Tropper mused. “There’s more character complexity because we’ve already built the world. And so I think in the binge culture, the fact that people can sit down and watch 19 episodes as opposed to just the first nine episodes probably gave us a little more staying power. And I think it’s one of those shows that just had a wonderful word-of-mouth spread.”
RELATED: Contenders Television: The Nominees Studio – Deadline’s Complete Coverage
Indeed. And was he surprised by that single Emmy nomination? It WAS surprising and surreal. “We were in Europe, so it was the end of the day for us. We had no idea they were being announced that day and my phone just started to blow up. And, you know, I couldn’t really wrap my brain around it until I really started hearing from a lot of friends in L.A. who in real time were learning with the nomination. And then I began to realize that we were in that conversation [which] was really exciting. It’s really great,” he said.
As for his initial desire to tackle this particular world, it was something that had been on his wish list. “This is a show I really wanted to do for a long time. I just had to get to a point where people would let me make this show. Due to a handful of circumstances. I came up more on the side of television action shows, but I had been writing novels that were more set in worlds like this, and that dealt with these types of situations and journeys,” he said. “And I think I was just biding my time till somebody trusted me enough to do a show like this. I lived in Westchester for 15 years. I knew this world really well, and I know it’s really right to me for exploration, and I think it was just a combination of my own maturation and the ideas coinciding to to bring this show forward.”
As for the casting, and notably getting Hamm, as Andrew Cooper, to return to world later than but still in the universe of a Don Draper? “I mean having Jon Hamm in that role is interesting because you really can’t shake the specter of Don Draper. I think that follows him the minute you put him in a suit, you see. And the way I viewed it is kind of a deconstruction of that character. Or, you know, as John likes to say, you know, ‘Don Draper sold the American Dream and Andrew Cooper bought it.’ And I think we started from there,” Tropper said.
Lee is just one of a sterling cast of supporting players getting rich roles, Barney Choi being one of the buzziest. What did Lee think of the opportunity?
“I think the great appeal of it is being able to give voice to sort of all of your inner turmoil and your inner chaos,” he said. “A lot of the times I’ve been asked to play characters for Jonathan that are sort of organizers of the world or as fixers or operators, and that necessitates a kind of level-headed approach, so to be able to let fly with neuroses after neuroses and sort of allow the character to really spin out was incredibly fun for me to start to, to dabble in, And now that’s just building as the stakes go up for the entire situation, as it becomes more invested in Coop’s world, he starts to really unfurl. And that’s proven both fun but also challenging. And that challenge is always interesting. Like the general feel of the show, it’s incredibly fun to do.”
