title: Standing With Afghan Women
full_content:
In the five years since the Taliban seized power in Kabul on August 15, 2021, Afghan women have become the most persistent source of resistance to the group’s efforts to transform Afghanistan. The exclusion of women and girls from public space is at the center of the Taliban’s extremist state-building project—a project that has also included dismantling institutions, subordinating the judiciary to religious authority, eliminating political opposition and civic activity, silencing independent media, and diverting male and young female students from schools with broad-based formal curricula to madrasahs that instill the Taliban’s ideology.
Many Afghan women are refusing to accept this radical transformation of Afghanistan’s social and political order. Some are protesting in the streets despite the extraordinary threats they face. Others are organizing underground schools to fill gaps in education and collaborating closely with Afghans in exile to prepare legal action against the Taliban’s abuses. Against the odds, Afghan women have built a tenacious resistance movement, inside and outside the country, that is working to alleviate conditions and provide opportunities, however limited, for women and girls.
Yet most foreign governments, including those who have publicly condemned the Taliban’s swift and sweeping repression of women since 2021, have done little to support Afghan women’s efforts. Indeed, many are expanding their diplomatic engagement with the Taliban, which may further embolden the group to tighten its repression and advance its extreme policies. The Taliban’s odious treatment of women should in itself be sufficient to compel foreign countries to reconsider their approach. But the strides the Afghan women’s movement has made offers them another reason to resist normalization and instead to invest directly in Afghan people. Afghan women are the most organized constituency resisting the Taliban’s hardline agenda—and they are preserving the human capital, institutions, and political networks with which a stable and pluralistic Afghanistan could one day be rebuilt.
STILL IN THE FIGHT
Afghan women had received education and participated in professional life—if unevenly—for decades before the Taliban first seized power in 1996 and imposed oppressive policies that dismantled women’s rights and opportunities. After the Taliban regime fell in 2001, Afghanistan, with the support of the United States and other international partners, made remarkable strides in restoring and advancing the rights of the country’s women and girls. By 2021, an entire generation of women had grown up with some access to education. Women, especially in urban centers, worked as doctors, lawyers, judges, journalists, and public servants. They became a significant presence in political life, filling more than a quarter of the seats in Afghanistan’s parliament and serving as ministers and diplomats.
After the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the group swiftly imposed policies that reversed decades of progress for women and girls. In addition to barring women’s access to education, employment, and public services, it dismantled key institutions such as the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the Afghan Independent Human Rights Commission, and the High Commission to Eliminate Violence Against Women. The regime also closed women’s shelters, imposed a strict dress code, and restricted women’s access to public spaces. Every year, these measures have become more expansive and entrenched, reinforced by the 2024 Law on the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice and the promulgation of more than a hundred decrees that touch on nearly every aspect of women’s lives. More than 3,000 morality inspectors have been deployed across the country to enforce the Taliban’s decrees in public spaces and to pressure male family members to ensure women’s compliance within the home. One former civil society worker described the suffocating effect of these laws in testimony related to the UN Security Council, commenting, “I am afraid that they will ban women from breathing without a man’s permission.” Another Afghan woman compared living under the Taliban to “being buried alive.”
Yet even in these draconian conditions, Afghan women have continued to fight for their rights, meeting the Taliban’s repression with extraordinary acts of courage. Within weeks of the group’s return to power, scores of women marched through the streets of Kabul, Herat, Mazar-i-Sharif, and other cities to demand that the Taliban reverse their newly introduced restrictions. The UN has documented the Taliban’s brutal response to these demonstrations, which has included arbitrary arrests of protesters and their families, enforced disappearances, rape, torture, and other forms of intimidation and violence. Yet women activists have remained defiant, and at times they have drawn support from men. In June of this year, women and men in Herat took to the streets to protest the detention of at least 30 women for allegedly violating the Taliban-imposed dress code. According to Human Rights Watch, Taliban security forces responded with beatings, shots into the crowd, detentions of protesters, and the killing of at least one boy.
As the Taliban have intensified their repression, women have found new ways to continue nonviolent resistance. Women’s groups have become more decentralized and clandestine. As during the first Taliban regime in the 1990s, women activists have organized underground schools to educate girls denied access to formal classrooms. Women who have been shut out of the professional careers they enjoyed before 2021 have mobilized to offer services that the Taliban eliminated. They have opened their own small business and informal enterprises, and they are negotiating with local Taliban officials and community leaders to allow them to keep those businesses operating, to run educational programs, and to provide access to health care and other basic services. Afghan women are also working closely with UN offices, international human rights organizations, and legal experts to document human rights abuses and preserve evidence of arbitrary detentions and gender-based violence.
 Afghan women have continued to fight for their rights.
Women inside Afghanistan and those who were forced into exile have developed increasingly sophisticated and far-reaching networks that not only put a spotlight on the Taliban’s abuses but also call on foreign governments, the UN, and other international institutions and donors to limit their engagement with the Taliban, sustain humanitarian assistance, and protect refugees. Their speaking engagements and social media campaigns have sustained public attention even as international media coverage has faded. And online organizing has helped them navigate constraints such as the Taliban’s restriction of women’s movement inside Afghanistan and visa rules preventing those in exile from traveling internationally.
Afghan women in the diaspora and their allies have also been working to hold the Taliban accountable for their repression. Together, they have pushed governments participating in UN negotiations over a new treaty on crimes against humanity to include recognition of gender apartheid—a system designed to permanently subordinate and exclude women from public life—as a distinct crime under international law. Although the process for incorporating this concept into legal frameworks is long and uncertain, the idea has gained traction among policy leaders; the UN High Commissioner of Human Rights, for example, has described the Taliban’s policies as “gender apartheid” and “gender persecution.” Calling out the Taliban’s system for what it is can be valuable in itself, as it raises the political costs for those moving toward normalization.
Afghan activists are also finding new ways to pursue accountability for the Taliban’s abuses. Last year in Madrid, four Afghan civil society organizations established the People’s Tribunal for the Women of Afghanistan under the auspices of the Permanent Peoples’ Tribunal, an international civil society organization that investigates serious human rights violations. Although the tribunal does not hold binding legal authority, it provides an opportunity to establish evidence and develop legal arguments that could inform future prosecutions and advance international law on gender persecution and gender apartheid. In a series of public hearings, Afghan lawyers, researchers, and survivors of Taliban abuses laid out a case that the Taliban’s systematic repression and exclusion of women and girls since 2021 amounts to gender persecution, which is recognized as a crime against humanity by the International Criminal Court. In December, the tribunal issued its final judgment in The Hague—a symbolic choice given the city’s role as a center of international justice—upholding the charge of gender persecution. The judges also concluded that Afghanistan today qualifies as an “apartheid-like system” and recommended that gender apartheid be codified in international law.
The work that Afghan women are doing today is essential to preserving the possibility of a peaceful and economically viable Afghanistan. The Taliban’s exclusion of women is not just a violation of human rights; it is also eroding the country’s human and economic capital. UNICEF has estimated that restrictions on girls’ education and women’s employment are already costing Afghanistan at least $84 million in annual economic output—a significant sum in an impoverished country where nearly three-quarters of the population is struggling to meet basic needs. The Taliban’s madrasahs, meanwhile, are teaching the next generation to adhere to the group’s hardline ideology. It is the underground schools that are preserving access to the kind of education that will support a pluralistic society and prepare young Afghans for a post-Taliban future. And independent civic organizations are the bodies sustaining the professional expertise and institutional knowledge that will be needed to one day rebuild the country.
SMART INVESTMENT
Despite the extraordinary work of Afghan women to resist the Taliban, foreign engagement with Kabul has done very little to recognize or support their efforts. Instead, several foreign governments have concluded that some form of transactional relationship with the Taliban is the safest route to containing extremism, managing migration, and stabilizing the country. Although Russia is the only country that has formally recognized the Taliban government, China has accepted the credentials of a Taliban-appointed ambassador, and several countries in the region are expanding their diplomatic and economic ties with Kabul. Even the European Commission recently invited Taliban officials to Brussels to discuss migration issues in talks attended by 15 EU member states. Foreign officials raise and condemn the repression of women and girls in such engagements, but it is often clear to the Taliban that these concerns are not their interlocutors’ top priorities. Thus, as the Taliban increases their repression, the diplomatic costs they face are diminishing rather than increasing.
The last five years should serve as sufficient proof that further cooperation with the Taliban will not moderate the group’s behavior. Despite U.S., EU, and UN Security Council demands that the Taliban prevent terrorist groups from using Afghanistan as a safe haven, for example, the UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team has found that the Taliban maintain a “close and symbiotic” relationship with al-Qaeda and that several other extremist organizations continue to operate in the country.
Some interaction with the Taliban may be unavoidable, but foreign governments should not take steps that confer legitimacy on the regime, which would only embolden the group to deepen its repression at home. Instead, they should restrict their contact with the Taliban to existing diplomatic channels and craft policies that prioritize Afghanistan’s long-term stability.
Part of that effort must include the meaningful inclusion of Afghan women in international diplomacy. The Taliban regime systematically excludes half the population from any kind of political representation; the rest of the world should not follow suit. Diplomatic efforts today too often grant the Taliban a formal place at the table while limiting contact with Afghan women to informal consultations. At other times when a government has systematically denied political participation to a substantial part of its population, most notably in the case of apartheid South Africa, international institutions have devised innovative ways to include those denied political representation. The same can be done with Afghanistan. The UN should establish a formal mechanism that integrates Afghan women into formal, substantive deliberations related to Afghanistan’s future. Such meaningful participation would send a clear message that the UN and its members reject the Taliban’s claim to be the sole political voice of Afghanistan as long as the group excludes half the population from public life. It would also ensure that decisions about Afghanistan are informed and shaped by actors representing constituencies beyond the Taliban.
Governments and donors should also provide humanitarian assistance and sustained institutional support to Afghan women–led organizations inside and outside Afghanistan. I have heard from Afghan women that cuts to international humanitarian and development assistance, including the loss of funding for education, health clinics, and women-led organizations, have harmed them as much as the Taliban’s policies have. Indeed, more than 100 UN-supported community health facilities closed last year; 50 percent of women working for civil society organizations inside Afghanistan surveyed by UN Women in 2025 had lost their jobs because of funding cuts. If a women’s movement is to confront an authoritarian order, it needs resources. Even modest funding can help if it arrives without restrictions and is guaranteed for several years, enabling staff to focus on building relationships, conducting research, and engaging in sustained political advocacy rather than constantly pursuing short-term grants.
One cause in particular need of investment is the education and professional development of Afghan women and girls. Foreign governments and donors should consult with Afghan women to determine how their money will best be spent. But as a starting point, they should support accredited online and in-person education programs, scholarships for educational opportunities inside and outside the country, professional fellowships in neighboring countries, visa facilitation for opportunities abroad, and the distribution of computers, software, and satellite technologies to Afghan students and professionals.
 A durable political order can come only from the Afghan people themselves.
Foreign governments must also protect Afghans who have fled Taliban rule. Iran and Pakistan together have forced out millions of Afghans who sought refuge in those countries, effectively condemning the women and girls among them to suffer the Taliban’s persecution. Governments with negotiating leverage over Tehran or Islamabad, including Western governments, should press them to halt these forced returns. Countries such as Germany that have signed deals with the Taliban to allow them to deport Afghan migrants to Afghanistan should reconsider such arrangements. Wealthier countries should also provide greater assistance to those hosting refugees. These protections are an investment in Afghanistan’s future. The diaspora networks that Afghan women and men are building today hold the expertise, relationships, and institutional capacity that could prove critical to reconstructing the Afghan state when a political opening emerges—the same way Afghan refugee communities played a vital role in rebuilding the country after the Taliban’s fall in 2001.
The United States has a particular responsibility to protect the Afghan women who worked with American institutions, in civil society organizations, or as human rights defenders before the Taliban takeover and have since left Afghanistan. Some have been stranded in third countries since Washington suspended its refugee admissions program in January 2025 and subsequently imposed sweeping restrictions on the entry of Afghan nationals. The U.S. government must resume processing and admitting Afghans referred for U.S. refugee resettlement and restore viable pathways for vulnerable Afghans, particularly women and girls, to apply for refugee resettlement. It should also restore the Temporary Protected Status that applied to Afghans already in the United States until the Trump administration terminated it in July 2025.
Finally, foreign governments must support efforts to hold the Taliban accountable for its abuses. The United Nations’ Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan, its Office of the Special Rapporteur for Afghanistan, and Afghan women–led initiatives to gather evidence for legal proceedings all require funding to support their work and pay their staff. Afghan women campaigning for the codification of international laws on gender persecution and gender apartheid also need sustained diplomatic backing from foreign governments if they are to advance their agenda.
BREAKING THE CYCLE
For too long, Afghan women have been placed at the center of others’ political projects but excluded from actual policy decisions. After the U.S.-led 2001 military intervention, Western governments pointed to women’s hard-won rights as symbols of success but then denied women seats at the table in negotiations with the Taliban that culminated in the group’s return. Now, the Taliban have built their radical vision for Afghan society on a policy of gender apartheid. Although there is no moral equivalence between the two, both are manifestations of the same problem. The Western countries that spent 20 years helping a generation of Afghan women gain the education and training necessary to advance their positions in society, only to largely abandon them after 2021, should recognize the moral and strategic imperative of helping those who today are continuing that fight in the harshest of conditions. It is not up to Western countries to “save” Afghan women. But these governments do need to reckon with the sins of the past and break a destructive cycle by meaningfully aiding these women’s efforts to shape their country’s direction in every way they can.
A durable political order can come only from the Afghan people themselves—it can be neither imposed by external actors nor negotiated with those who suppress the majority of the population. Afghan women are essential to this project. They had proved their resilience, creativity, and strategic thinking long ago, but their resistance to Taliban rule over the past five years has served as further confirmation. A pluralistic and peaceful Afghanistan is in the world’s interest. To support the struggle of Afghan women is to support those who are keeping the hope for that future alive.

title: The Cost of Keeping China Out
full_content:
Travelers returning from China often report having seen the future. The country’s advances in frontier commercial technologies are visible in the robots that make and serve food in restaurants; the drones that deliver food and medicine; and the deployment of industrial and humanoid robots on factory floors. Even outside China, most of the world is now familiar with Chinese electric vehicles that are as affordable as they are sleek, with massage chairs and swappable batteries winning over passengers from London to Santiago.
Most Americans, however, are unaware of this future. Chinese EVs are effectively absent from the U.S. market, blocked by 250 percent tariffs and broad national security restrictions. And a bipartisan fear has prevented many frontier Chinese technologies, including drones and robots, from reaching U.S. shores. Apart from a handful of products, mostly consumer electronics, the U.S. market is largely oblivious to the fruits of China’s advanced manufacturing ecosystem.
The United States has its reasons for this blind spot. As early as the second Obama administration, if not before, it became clear that China was not playing fairly in business. Successive administrations have used a slew of trade remedies and official complaints to the World Trade Organization to fight back against unfair subsidies, and rulings by the federal Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) have tried to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies from falling into the hands of Chinese actors. Since 2017, Chinese firms have also found themselves the targets of heightened security reviews.
Today, many actors in Washington think the United States should do even more to disengage from Chinese business. Members of Congress are pressuring American pharmaceutical companies to discontinue clinical trials in China, for instance, citing concerns that China’s research and development ecosystem has ties to the People’s Liberation Army. Others are proposing legislation to ban Chinese ownership of U.S. farmland, ostensibly to protect the U.S. food supply and critical infrastructure.
Calling out China’s gains as ill gotten is frequently justified. Defensive responses also feel satisfying—as if the United States could level the playing field and instantly create effective American competitors by locking out Chinese firms that have scaled up and advanced unfairly. Unfortunately, this approach does little to advance American economic and security interests. Chinese firms are no longer merely efficient producers or copycats; in terms of knowledge and production capability, they are increasingly global leaders in many industries. Denying them access to the American market harms U.S. competitiveness, hinders U.S. efforts to build industrial capacity at home, and ensures that U.S. industry and consumers remain far from the frontier of technological advancement.
Instead, Americans must reckon honestly with the scale of China’s industrial and technological progress. The United States need not embrace Chinese imports and investment unconditionally, but it must recognize that its own long-term competitiveness depends on its companies and consumers being exposed to the cutting edge. U.S. President Donald Trump’s vague proposal for a joint “Board of Investment” with China, announced after his May summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, seemed to suggest Washington was moving in this direction. But nothing concrete has come from the board, and managing investment flows at the leader-to-leader level is certainly not efficient.
A more mature strategy of selective openness is possible. The United States should permit carefully structured Chinese investment in areas in which the economic and technological benefits are substantial while imposing stringent safeguards to mitigate security risks. Building the political confidence to sustain a selectively open market for Chinese direct investments requires skilled, transparent, and thorough regulatory oversight. With such an approach, Washington can penalize some imports but still permit access to the U.S. market through investments in American production facilities. There is a clear precedent for this strategy. It is, in fact, exactly what China did to Western companies for decades.
TROJAN HORSES?
Since the 1990s, China has required global investors to operate under conditions that are designed to advance its national development goals. When foreign automakers or cellphone manufacturers wanted to take advantage of China’s cheap labor force, Beijing required that the firms use local supply chains, transfer technology, share management with Chinese firms, provide workforce training, and offer security protections (for example, localizing data and submitting to government oversight). The goal was always to ensure that foreign companies invested in ways that fostered a Chinese ecosystem. As Jeffrey Immelt, then chief executive of GE, said of China in 2010, “I am not sure that, in the end, they want any of us to win, or any of us to be successful.”
Indeed, GE spent decades accessing the Chinese market through joint ventures that eventually seeded Chinese competitors. China is now home to both private and state-owned companies such as Midea, Haier, and State Grid that rose up to compete with GE in everything from home appliances to power generation and transmission. Many are even taking their strategies global—including to the United States.
Chinese firms in frontier sectors like EVs, robotics, and life sciences especially want access to the vast U.S. consumer market. These firms face narrow profit margins at best at home—a result of the overcapacity and “involution” that came from excessive state investment and hypercompetition in specific sectors. If companies want to survive, they need foreign markets to prosper, and the United States remains the largest consumer market in the world. Companies such as the electronics and EV conglomerate Xiaomi and the battery maker CATL have publicly pined for U.S. market access, signaling that they would make significant investments in the United States in exchange for access. So far, however, the U.S. government has blocked such investments because of security concerns. An array of technologies are imagined to be modern Trojan horses. EVs, for instance, are not simply cars; they are traveling networks of sensors, software, computers, batteries, and communications systems capable of collecting data, mapping cities and infrastructure, and integrating with national grids. The fears range from reasonable (Chinese-connected vehicles mapping U.S. critical infrastructure) to far-fetched (remote control and even weaponization of vehicles on the road).
These realities require vigilance. But the answer is not to reject all Chinese investment unless it poses zero security concerns. Such an approach risks isolating the United States economically. If American firms don’t have to compete against the global leaders, they will increasingly sell things only to Americans. The United States will end up an island of legacy firms and practices, and the isolation will weaken American dynamism, reduce competitiveness, and erode broader economic security.
A SMARTER GATEKEEPING
Instead, the United States can adopt strategic terms for investment, as China did. Trump’s Board of Investment remains something of a mystery—a talking point only, so far—but it is not difficult to imagine it drawing from the many regulatory tools in Washington to create and sustain an overall investment structure for Chinese companies. In fact, imposing such a regime should be fairly simple for Washington because it already has much of the institutional sophistication to implement such terms. In addition to CFIUS, the United States has a substantial arsenal of tools to monitor, selectively ban, and condition Chinese investments. A host of regulatory agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and the Federal Communications Commission, can make targeted rules for firms in specific sectors, like life sciences, networked EVs, and robotics. Rules about data localization, required local partnerships, and supply chain diversification can help ensure that Chinese supply chains are not just imported into U.S. production.
Washington can and should upgrade these tools to shape Chinese investment on its terms. CFIUS, for example, imagines the most far-fetched risk scenarios and judges whether they can be mitigated. The interagency committee’s approvals for sensitive investments and acquisitions frequently involve “national security agreements”—special corporate governance arrangements devised collaboratively between firms and CFIUS personnel with provisions for cybersecurity protection, data management, and continuous monitoring of firm decisions by national security specialists appointed to boards.
This is a good beginning for a robust investment control system, but these agreements focus only on protecting national security—not enhancing economic benefits. To be more aggressive, they could also mandate that companies with Chinese investment have special corporate governance boards that monitor and execute economic requirements, including workforce training, diversification of suppliers, technology transfers, and more.
While the specific administrative solution may evolve with experimentation, the central task is clear: Washington needs more systematic assessment and coordination. It needs a structure that is both more open and more targeted in mitigation and governance. This requires greater coordination among industry-specific regulators. Indeed, given that multinationals have complex corporate supply chains and ownership patterns, even deciding the national identity of firms requires coordination across the U.S. government. CFIUS may not think a company is controlled by Chinese interests, for instance, but Commerce may deem it sufficiently connected to a “foreign adversary.” The ability to resolve these regulatory complexities is important, since it is only through good bureaucratic coordination that Washington can both recognize the risks of technologies and also harness their benefits.
THE TESLA MODEL
China’s playbook for EVs is especially instructive. Beijing began encouraging domestic EV and large battery production in the early 2000s, largely through subsidies and industrial policy. Private companies like CATL and BYD made progress with batteries, but the industry, especially large state-owned producers, needed competitive pressure to upgrade the cars they made to meet consumer tastes. In 2019, Beijing decided to balance the risks and rewards of inviting Tesla, then the global leader in EV manufacturing, into the Chinese market at scale. They lifted the joint-venture requirement, and Tesla became the first global automaker to operate a production facility in China with no local partner.
The Shanghai government offered impressive incentives for Tesla’s Gigafactory 3 in Shanghai, including land and subsidized loans. But the Chinese government, which was wary of having an American company mapping roads and collecting data on Chinese nationals in cars, insisted that Tesla store all the personal data of Chinese drivers in China. In 2024, it also required that Tesla use a Chinese company—the Internet giant Baidu—for navigation services inside China and that it localize all mapping data in the country.
Tesla’s production in China soared; even during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Shanghai factory was producing 140,000 cars a year, and localization of supply chains (85 percent by 2020) brought costs down. Tesla became profitable in 2020 for the first time on the strength of the Chinese market, and Shanghai had become an export hub for the rest of Asia and Europe by 2022.
Baidu, meanwhile, used its time working with Tesla to develop frontier autonomous driving technologies and has now deployed “robotaxis” in Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates, and beyond. Perhaps most important, the success of Tesla in the Chinese market helped propel the EV industry there and served as inspiration for homegrown challengers such as BYD, pushing them to focus especially on design and consumer experience. BYD now sells more EVs globally than Tesla does, and Tesla is pushing a cheaper version of the Model Y to compete with companies like BYD and Xiaomi.
For the United States, this is the great irony: the investment and manufacturing expertise it needs to compete with China can increasingly come only from China. For years, analysts have instead proposed working with allies and third countries to construct a scaled market outside China—one with common rules that can serve as a counterweight to China’s sheer size and operate parallel to it. This idea is at least a decade old and has taken many forms, from the Obama-era Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement, to the first Trump administration’s campaign to rally allies to exclude Chinese telecom companies, to the Biden era’s Indo-Pacific Economic Framework and Transatlantic Trade and Technology Council. All three administrations sought to build coalitions of countries with common rules or standards to collectively rival China’s scale.
Despite their theoretical merits, however, all these efforts have either failed or scored only narrow gains. And now it is too late for such a vision: Chinese technologies have reached a tipping point of sorts, becoming ubiquitous in too many countries. The moment for massive, allied coordination to decouple drastically from China has passed. Selective collaboration on particular technology safeguards or supply chain diversification may be feasible, but most of the world has accepted a future with substantial Chinese economic presence in their countries.
Even the United States’ closest traditional allies, Canada and the United Kingdom, seem to recognize this new reality and are approaching China with pragmatism. They are wary of China but consider enduring interdependence a fact of life, especially when the United States keeps changing its own approaches trade. Ottawa and London are embracing Chinese investment and exports, but with creative rules to better balance the costs and benefits.
Canada, for example, has now abandoned huge tariffs on Chinese EVs in favor of import quotas with an eye to localizing production through carefully structured joint ventures with Canadian companies. Chinese firms are already localizing production in the EU, and a recent EU proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, would require limits on foreign ownership alongside supply chain localization and technology transfer requirements. These rules allow Chinese companies access to Canadian and EU markets but ensure that local production systems benefit. A similar strategy is possible in the United States.
TIKTOK SUCCESS
The United States does not need to choose between naive openness and blanket exclusion. Indeed, the Trump administration has on at least one occasion chosen a smarter path. ByteDance’s TikTok operation in the United States, which collects vast amounts of data on American users and uses an algorithm to push content, raised some legitimate national security concerns. Although the Trump administration’s process for handling these concerns was tumultuous, in the end, ByteDance agreed to sell its U.S. business to an American-controlled joint venture in which the Chinese company retained a minority share. Control over the TikTok software and its upgrades went to a U.S. team. All personal data must now be stored in the United States. These arrangements are subject to monitoring and reporting and prove that selective openness for Chinese direct investments is possible.
Arrangements for securing robotic automation or safeguarding biomedical data would, of course, be more complex. And some Chinese investments should be refused. But the United States possesses the institutional capacity to craft serious protections. It can welcome investment in areas in which it strengthens American industry, while also imposing enforceable safeguards. The best outcome would be selective openness alongside a sustainable industrial policy strategy and, eventually, coordination with other large markets on governing risks transparently. The harder task is political: acknowledging that the United States is already behind in several vital industries and that the barriers Washington has built are costing the United States more than they are protecting it.

title: Africa Can’t Afford to Squander Its Demographic Opportunity
full_content:
For decades, observers have chalked up Africa’s slow economic growth to corruption, weak institutions, and poor leadership. But these explanations miss a deeper force at work. The single most powerful variable shaping the speed of economic growth, stability, and the chance of democracy taking root across African countries is the age structure of their populations.
A country tends to be most productive when its fertility rate declines enough that working-age adults outnumber children and elderly people in need of care. When young adults make up a large share of the population—and they are educated, in good health, and able to find work—an economy can really take off. Societies whose populations are older also tend to be more democratic and less violent than those with younger ones.
Africa’s fertility rate is still roughly double that of Latin America and South Asia, and the median age in sub-Saharan Africa today is 19.5 years, compared with 29.0 in South Asia, 34.0 in South America, and 43.0 in Europe. But in a few decades, the prime demographic window is expected to open in many African countries: as millions of African citizens mature into working age, the continent’s economic growth could accelerate sharply. Yet the same conditions that can unlock prosperity and democracy can also cause a country to combust if it is governed poorly. If there are not enough jobs to go around, young adults may rise up or be seduced by the promises of strongmen rulers. African countries must thus start preparing today for their moment of opportunity.
ACT YOUR AGE
In Africa, prospects for prosperity are still largely determined by demography. Currently, the continent is home to 22 low-income and 23 lower-middle-income countries. Because poor countries have limited domestic capital and attract little foreign investment, labor is the primary engine of economic growth. According to analysis using the Pardee Center’s International Futures forecasting platform, growth tends to accelerate when there are at least 1.7 working-age people for each child or elderly person. But today, the continental average is just 1.4 working-age people per dependent.
As countries move into middle-income status, the availability of capital becomes more important than labor for driving manufacturing- and services-led growth. And as countries become even richer, technology and higher-value services, such as finance, steadily become the dominant factor driving economic expansion, overtaking both labor and capital. China, and what are known as the Asian “tiger economies”—Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan—all followed a similar pattern: a large working-age population first drove rapid growth, then capital accumulation and technology transfers added fuel to the fire.
Most African countries have not yet benefited from the demographic structure that launched these Asian countries. Africa’s transition was delayed by a uniquely heavy historical burden. The continent’s transition was first slowed relative to other regions because of the removal of working-age people through the slave trade; then, colonial rule left populations poorly educated and disconnected from the infrastructure and institutions needed to participate in the post–World War II surge in trade, industrialization, and technology diffusion. For centuries, Africa’s exceptionally high prevalence of deadly diseases, including malaria and sleeping sickness, also kept mortality higher and population growth slower than in temperate climates, even when women bore seven or more children over a lifetime.
From the 1950s to around 1981, the ratio of working-age people to dependents in Africa was either stuck at low levels or declining, even as these ratios were already trending upward across much of Asia and Latin America. Over the past 45 years, the ratio has slowly started to increase, but it remains below 1.4 across much of the continent. The economic growth Africa achieved from the first years of the 2000s through the mid-2010s was driven to an unusual degree by the high price of oil, copper, and iron ore, itself stemming from China’s industrial expansion and rapid urbanization, not from a favorable age structure.
But Africa’s young population is maturing. The number of African states with a median age above 30 is projected to roughly triple between 2025 and 2050. Fertility has been declining across most of the continent, while improvements in child survival and women’s education reinforce that trend. Forecasts using the International Futures platform indicate that Africa as a whole will reach the 1.7-to-one working-age threshold around 2053, with northern and southern Africa and several island states arriving much earlier. Our modeling also suggests that, with the right policies, governments could speed up the opening of the prime demographic window by a decade. The uneven transition means that opportunity will arise country by country, not all at once. If leaders prepare for it, even more African countries will count themselves among the fastest-growing economies in the world.
THE YOUNG AND THE RESTLESS
The same demographic structure that can unleash economic growth, however, can also be a source of political instability if mismanaged. Youthful societies place immense strain on schools, health clinics, and labor markets, which in turn erodes public trust in governments that cannot keep pace with demand for services. And when young adults—who are generally better educated, more willing to take risks, and more likely to mobilize politically than their older counterparts—make up a large share of the population, and when the economy offers them few ways to advance, the risk of unrest rises sharply. Such a dynamic was at play during the Arab Spring uprisings that began in 2010, and it recurs across today’s most volatile African states: the Central African Republic, Chad, Mali, Niger, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Uganda.
According to research by scholars such as Jack Goldstone and Richard Cincotta, the predictive power of median age is remarkably consistent. The risk of internal conflict and revolutionary upheaval remains elevated for as long as a country’s median age stays below roughly 25.5 years. Crossing that threshold is one of the best predictors of declining conflict risk. Political turbulence falls further, and substantially, once median age passes 30.0—even before a society reaches full demographic maturity at 35.5. As of 2025, only a handful of African states had a median age above 30.0.
To be sure, whether youthful grievances escalate into turmoil also depends on the government’s capacity to contain dissent. States with abundant resources and weak institutions, such as Algeria, can pour money into policing and surveillance to suppress unrest in the short term. But without accountable institutions, investments in security lead to corruption and elite capture rather than long-term stability. Consider, for example, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, South Sudan, and Sudan, where wealth from natural resources temporarily shores up regimes without political legitimacy. The risks from resource dependence and a young population compound each other: both independently raise the likelihood of civil conflict, and where they coincide, the risk is greater still.
Recent African history bears this out. Data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, a political violence research nonprofit headquartered in Wisconsin, show a marked rise in riots and nonviolent protests alike across the continent since the 2010 Arab Spring. These incidents generally take place in urban areas and are driven by a combustible mix of rising education levels, limited job opportunities, rapid urbanization, and the spread of social media. Kenya’s tax-related protests since 2023, Mozambique’s post-election unrest in 2024–25, and youth-led demonstrations over public services and spending priorities in Moroccan cities in 2025 all fit this template: better-educated, connected young populations mobilizing against elites who control resources and offices they cannot access through ordinary political channels.
AN OLD MAN’S GAME
Societies whose populations are young are not just more prone to unrest but are also poor candidates for stable democracy. Research by Goldstone, Cincotta, and other scholars such as Jennifer Sciubba has shown that societies with very low median ages and high fertility, such as Egypt, are generally governed by authoritarian regimes. That is in part because rapid population growth typically outpaces the maturation of the civic institutions that democracies depend on to function, including independent media, legal advocacy organizations, and labor unions. In young societies, these bodies rarely have time to develop the depth and independence needed to check executive power. In the absence of inclusive growth and widespread civic engagement, frustrated young people will sometimes support strongman rulers who promise order and jobs, as they have in Ethiopia and Rwanda.
Societies whose populations are older tend toward stable democracy. Mauritius, with a median age of 35.5, is the only African country whose demographics are auspicious in this regard. Research has shown that liberal democracies throughout the twentieth century have tended to consolidate once median age rises into the mid-30s, typically alongside the emergence of a larger middle class and a more diversified economy. (There are, of course, exceptions. Belarus, China, Cuba, Russia, and several Gulf states remain politically stable and autocratic, despite having older populations.) Intermediate societies, with median ages around 30, often produce mixed regimes—neither fully autocratic nor fully democratic—in which elections coexist with executive dominance, weak checks and balances, or contested rules of political competition. Algeria and Morocco fit this profile.
This is not to say that ordinary people in societies whose populations are young should accept the rule of despots or that autocracy is likely to give rise to an effective development strategy. For every example of economic progress under an autocracy, there is one of decline. But once a baseline of order and development is achieved from the working-age population expanding faster than the number of dependents, incremental democratic reform becomes far more sustainable. In other words, Africa’s demographic transition could also come with stability and a democratic transition.
A TALE OF TWO COUNTRIES
A comparison between Ghana and South Korea illustrates how a government can both influence and take advantage of age structure. In the late 1950s, both countries were newly independent, had a similar median age—about 18 years—and similar levels of income. South Korea moved earlier on agricultural reform, mass basic education, family planning, and public health, driving fertility below the replacement level by 1984. By 1999, there were 2.6 working-age people for each dependent—among the highest such ratios ever recorded, matched only by China and the Asian tiger economies. Crucially, South Korea also quickly urbanized. By 1982, 60 percent of South Koreans lived in cities, so that people and firms were concentrated in ways that raised productivity and deepened labor markets.
Ghana’s demographic transition unfolded on a different timeline. Fertility remained near seven births per woman through the 1960s and has fallen to about 3.4 today. Ghana is not expected to enter its own prime demographic window of opportunity until around 2033—half a century behind South Korea, although still earlier than most of its West African neighbors. Urbanization, too, arrived later: Ghana only recently became 60 percent urban. Ghana’s high proportion of dependents kept household savings low, limited the tax base, and prevented the labor market from expanding in ways that would otherwise have supported faster industrial growth.
South Korea was well placed to influence its age structure because it received large amounts of foreign aid and was governed by an elite focused on industrialization and rapid growth. Between 1960 and 1980, the United States and other countries, such as Japan, sent South Korea $39 billion in aid (in constant 2021 values). Ghana, over the same period, received $6 billion. Both countries were ruled by corrupt militaries for a time, but South Korean leaders tended to invest their ill-gotten gains domestically while Ghanaians invested theirs in London and Paris. (Today, much of that money is parked in Abu Dhabi.)
South Korea embarked on a vital agricultural transformation that increased productivity. Today, 94 percent of land in South Korea is privately owned and is therefore governed by secure, enforceable rights that incentivize investment and allow for land reallocation. Meanwhile, 80 percent of land in Ghana is held communally, and many farmers work merely to subsist.
 Societies whose populations are older tend toward stable democracy.
But soon, the same forces that lifted South Korea into the ranks of advanced economies will be felt across much of Africa, albeit unevenly. It is up to African governments to make sure the prime demographic window of opportunity opens and to make the most of it when it does. Their starting point should be reducing infant and maternal mortality by expanding access to health care for children and pregnant women. When more children survive to adulthood, families do not feel the need to have many children as insurance against loss, and fertility begins to fall. In addition, voluntary access to modern contraception and sex education gives women and their families the option to have fewer children.
Educating girls is the single most powerful way to reduce fertility rates, but the effects of doing so take more time to realize. The longer girls remain in school, the later they tend to marry and begin childbearing, which both lowers fertility directly and raises women’s future productivity and earning potential—reinforcing the link between demographic change and economic growth. Investments in water, sanitation, and basic health infrastructure are also helpful because they help prevent diseases that drive high mortality and, in turn, high fertility. Influencing fertility rates is not just a matter of service delivery; shifts in gender norms, attitudes toward child marriage, and reproductive autonomy also matter. Although these shifts tend to unfold gradually, politicians, media campaigns, and civil society engagement can nudge people toward wanting smaller families.
Ultimately, a demographic dividend translates into growth only if the resulting cohort of working-age adults can find productive work. African governments must prepare by linking vocational and technical training to actual labor demand—for example, by offering employer-designed apprenticeships in construction, agricultural processing, logistics, renewable energy, and digital services. Governments can also widen opportunity by making it easier to start small businesses, expanding credit guarantees and digital finance, and improving transportation links and energy provision. Removing legal barriers and collateral requirements that disproportionately prevent women from obtaining credit and holding assets, while enforcing equal access to jobs and promotion, would also help.
Civic institutions need time to mature alongside the population. Governments can improve the odds of a democratic transition by protecting independent media and courts, strengthening election management and legislative oversight, enforcing term limits, and creating opportunities for young people to participate in political parties and local government. Involving the youth in civil society can also improve intergenerational understanding between aging elites and the people they govern.
THE AGE OF AGE
Africa’s demographic profile is set to look markedly different by midcentury. Its labor force will continue to expand as those in China, Europe, and other aging economies contract. If African countries can make even modest productivity gains, their growth rates should outpace the economies of the now graying societies that drove global growth for the past half century.
Yet Africa can’t become the world’s bright spot unless the region’s governments take action today. The stakes are considerable. Modeling from the African Futures program suggests that if African countries add roughly two percentage points to average annual economic growth—through faster fertility decline, better-managed urbanization, stronger ability to generate jobs for a growing workforce, more integrated trade, and higher agricultural productivity—the continent’s economy in 2050 would be 50 percent larger than under a business-as-usual scenario. Its population would be about 166 million smaller as prosperity further reduces fertility, and income per capita would rise from roughly 28 percent of the global average to 36 percent.
If governments squander the opportunity through weak governance, underinvestment in health and education, or the inability to absorb a growing workforce, the same demographic momentum that could deliver growth will instead become a source of instability—just as the rest of the world ages and shrinks.

title: Google Pixel 12: Everything we know so far
full_content:
Google Pixel 12: Everything we know so far
The Pixel 11 is pretty vanilla. Will we see some more flavor with 2027's Pixel? Find out here.
The Google Pixel 11 marks another year in which Google is reusing the design started with the Pixel 9 series, but if history is any indication, we could see a big shake-up with the Pixel 12.
Google's Pixel phones have been gaining traction in the market over the past few years, owing to Google's "iPhone-like" approach to the series hardware design and software leanings. Even Google's marketing looks a lot more like Apple's these days, but we're hoping Google continues to maintain its historic spirit of innovation in the next round of devices.
And that's where Pixel 12 comes in. Pixel phones have looked the same for the past three years, but they've always packed an experimental surprise that keeps everyone guessing. From squeezable sides to radar-powered gesture sensors, and even the new HiLight LED on the back of the Pixel 11, it's a wonder what Google will think up next. Let's explore all the leaks and rumors for Google's next device and see what they have cooking, shall we?
Price and availability
We fully expect the Google Pixel 12 family to debut next August, following a similar release cadence to the past few Pixels. Per one leak, Google will likely continue releasing four models for the Pixel 12 family: the base Pixel 12, the Pixel 12 Pro, the larger Pixel 12 Pro XL, and the foldable Pixel 12 Pro Fold.
Unless something drastically changes over the course of the next year, there's also a high likelihood that each model will see another price increase. RAM and storage are at a premium right now, and prices are expected to continue to rise throughout 2027 (and maybe beyond) as AI data centers hog the world's supply of RAM and storage modules. The trickle-down effect is more expensive consumer electronics, which everyone is familiar with at this point.
Spec bumps galore
Every year, people expect the usual spec bumps to occur. A faster processor, better battery life, faster charging speed, etc. So far, Google has always met that expectation, albeit Tensor processors have always been slower than competing chips from Qualcomm, MediaTek, and Samsung Exynos.
While we don't know too much about the Tensor G7 processor that will likely power the Google Pixel 12 series, a few leaks give us some clues as to what's possible on the next chip. First up is a potential RAM upgrade (via Reptalica), with Google reportedly testing out LPDDR5x and LPDDR6 versions of Tensor G7. Looking at the numbers over the years offers a sneak peek at what this could bring:
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
- Pixel 1 (LPDDR4): ~4.2Gbps
- Pixel 2-5 (LPDDR4X): ~4.2Gbps (same speed, lower power requirements)
- Pixel 6-7 (LPDDR5): ~6.4Gbps
- Pixel 8-11 (LPDDR5x): ~10.6Gbps
- Pixel 12 (LPDDR6 rumored): estimated ~14.4Gbps
Given the state of RAMageddon and the chipset crisis right now, it's entirely plausible that Google will remain with LPDDR5x for one more year just to save on costs. Still, we can hope for a sizable Tensor speed boost in 2027 if the cards line up right.
Next, we're looking at a potential battery capacity upgrade for the Pixel 12, if one comment from a Google rep holds any water. When asked about silicon-carbon batteries during the Pixel 11 event, a Google representative said the Pixel team was looking into implementing them.
Now, that comment doesn't say the company will definitely implement silicon-carbon into future Pixel batteries, and it doesn't specifically say Pixel 12, either. However, given that Samsung just began using 5% silicon-carbon content in the batteries on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, the likelihood that Google follows suit next year is pretty darn high.
What I'd like to see
Google once again is using an outdated PowerVR GPU in the Pixel 11, a mistake the company made with the Pixel 10 and appears not to have learned from. On the Pixel 12, we're hoping Google uses a modern GPU that supports the latest Vulkan standards and delivers the gaming performance people expect from $1,200+ phones.
I'd also like to see Google switch up the design to make it more ergonomic. For years and years, Pixel phones were known for their comfortable, rounded edges and contoured lines that fit nicely in a human hand. With the Pixel 9, Google went a very flat route all around, once again going with a very iPhone-like look.
Google has historically stuck with a specific design language for 2-3 years at a time, so if history repeats itself again, we should be in for a big redesign with the Pixel 12.
Additionally, I'd like to see Google take flicker accessibility more seriously. Pixel phones have had the worst PWM dimming rate for years, and while the Pixel 11 sports the same "sensitive eyes" feature that launched on some Pixel 10 models, that setting still doesn't go far enough in solving the problem for flicker-sensitive people like myself.
Google generally does a great job with bespoke accessibility features, like the amazing sign-language-to-text tool that launched with the Pixel 11, and I know they can get this one right if they want to.
Lastly, I'd love to see HiLight be a little more...interesting. I got super excited about the Pixel Glow leaks and what we thought was a tease at Google I/O in May, and it turned out to be a tiny LED on the camera island instead of a glowing statement. HiLight is also very basic so far, at least as of the Pixel 11's launch, so any improvement here is sorely needed to make this a useful (or even just interesting) feature.
It'll be some time before we see an official Pixel 12 announcement, but I'm fully expecting plenty of leaks to happen over the next several months. That's always been the case with Pixels, and there's no reason to think that'll dry up this time.
Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Whether it's VR, smart home gadgets, or something else that beeps and boops, he's been writing about it since 2011. Reach him on X/Bluesky/Threads or Instagram @Gwanatu

title: Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Which Android smartwatch should you buy?
full_content:
Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Which Android smartwatch should you buy?
Two new smartwatches with enticing features and designs.
A pretty Pixel
With new finishes, customizable face designs you can generate yourself, and solid specs, the Google Pixel Watch 5 may just become the best new Android smartwatch of 2026.
Pros
- Custom generated watch faces add a unique spin
- Ultra bright screen
- Google Health Premium offers advanced AI insights and coaching
Cons
- Sort of a bland upgrade in look from the Pixel Watch 4
- Same processor as Pixel Watch 4, only boosted
- You need Google Health Premium for advanced insights
An iterative update
The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is not a huge step up from the Galaxy Watch 8, though it offers a more powerful processor, bigger battery, and advanced AI metrics that make it worth considering.
Pros
- More powerful processor
- Advanced AI health insights not locked behind a paywall
- Ultra bright screen
Cons
- Battery life isn't great
- Not a huge upgrade from the Galaxy Watch 8
- Designed isn't as sleek and refined
The Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 debate is an interesting one. While you might think the Pixel Watch makes the most sense for a Pixel phone owner and the Galaxy Watch for a Galaxy phone owner, this isn't always the case. Some people prefer one phone brand and another watch brand. With that said, it's not such a cut-and-dried decision. Let's dive deeper to help you decide.
Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Design and battery life
Why you can trust Android Central
The Google Pixel Watch 5 has the usual domed display, giving it a sleeker, more elegant look. But it's still the same usual look, and Shruti Shekar opines that her early hands-on is getting sort of bland. That said, she admits that Pixel Watch is still "one of the more gorgeous smartwatches on the market."
The Galaxy Watch 9, meanwhile, is still a pretty sexy device. It has two side buttons, while the Pixel Watch 5 has a side button and haptic crown. Aside from being more comfortable than the Galaxy Watch 8, the Watch 9's design is largely unchanged.
Both always-on screens are equally bright, and both smartwatches are durable and water-resistant. The Galaxy Watch 9 also meets MIL-STD-810H standards, giving it a slight leg up in durability.
The Google Pixel Watch 5 is rated to last up to 40 hours with the always-on display, up to 72 hours with Battery Saver mode for the larger size, and up to 30 and 48 hours for the smaller size, respectively. By comparison, the Galaxy Watch 9 is rated for up to 30 hours with the always-on display. In my tests, having worn one for the last several weeks, it never lasts a full day. The good news is that it charges quickly.
Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Power and performance
The Pixel Watch 5's Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor is largely the same as the one in the Pixel Watch 4, but with increased processing power. It goes up against the Snapdragon Wear Elite processor in the Galaxy Watch 9, which should offer snappier performance.
Since both run Wear OS, you get a similar experience, though each adds its own flavor. Samsung's One UI Watch 9 brings more customization, while Google includes features that leverage Gemini. For example, in addition to the standard themes and complication styles, you can use Nano Banana to generate a custom theme. It's easily one of the most fun new features of the watch.
When it comes to health tracking, Google has a leg up. The Galaxy Watch 9 works with Samsung Health, but Google Health Premium has enticing features for Pixel Watch wearers. The caveat is that you need a subscription for the AI features.
You can unlock the helpful Google Health Coach, which walks you through training plans, nutrition, and more in a conversational manner. You get virtual coaching and guidance. Even if you don't sign up for Google Health Premium, fitness buffs will love the new weight- and rep-logging, rest timers, and a workout builder.
Also coming to Pixel Watch 5 is Health Guardian, which can analyze and provide data about breathing trends and irregular heart rhythms, and even alert you of breathing emergencies. It can also measure blood pressure trends and assess insulin resistance.
Samsung is no slouch in this department, though. Samsung Health adds new features to this watch, including a new Vitals dashboard, Trail Run mode, improved hydration management, and an energy score.
Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Specs
| Category | Google Pixel Watch 5 | Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 | 
|---|---|---|
| Compatibility | Android 12.0 or higher | Android 13.0 or higher | 
| OS | Wear OS 7 | Wear OS 7 (One UI 9) | 
| Colors | Matte Black, Polished Silver, Satin Pyrite(41mm, 45mm), Champagne Gold (41mm only) | Graphite, Cream (40mm), Graphite, Silver (44mm) | 
| Swappable Band | Yes | Yes | 
| Battery | 332mAh (41mm), 465mAh (45mm) | 390mAh (40mm), 445mAh (44mm) | 
| Battery Life | 41mm: Up to 30 hours, 48 hours (Battery Saver) 45mm: Up to 40 hours, 72 hours (Battery Saver) | Up to 30 hours | 
| App | Google Health | Samsung Health | 
| Heart Rate Tracking | Yes | Yes | 
| Stress Tracking | Yes | Yes | 
| Blood Oxygen | Yes | Yes | 
| GPS | Yes (built-in) | Yes (built-in) | 
| Sleep Monitoring | Yes | Yes | 
| Water Resistance | 5ATM, IP68 | 5ATM, IP68 | 
| Mobile Pay | Google Wallet | Samsung Wallet, Google Wallet | 
| Storage | 64GB | 32GB | 
| Screen Size | 1.2 inches (41mm), 1.4 inches (45mm) | 1.34-1.47 inches | 
| Screen Type | Actua 360 | Super AMOLED | 
| Screen Resolution | 456 x 456 | 438 x 438 (40mm), 480 x 480 (44mm) | 
| Peak Brightness | 3,000 nits | 3,000 nits | 
| Dimensions | 41 x 12.3mm (41mm), 45 x 12.3mm (45mm) | 42.7 x 40.4 x 8.6mm (40mm), 46 x 43.7 x 8.6mm (44mm) | 
| Weight | 31 grams (41mm), 36.7 grams (45mm) | 31.5 grams (40mm), 34 grams (44mm) | 
Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: What else you need to know
The Google Pixel Watch 5 supports satellite SOS communications, and it comes with a two-year trial. This is crucial for outdoor adventurers. That said, if you fall into this camp, you might prefer a watch like the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 instead. That brings up a good point: Shekar notes that Google is overdue to launch a Pixel Watch Pro to compete in this space, too.
Both support gestures, a nice-to-have feature for quickly dismissing or picking up a call or performing another desired action if your other hand is otherwise occupied. In terms of sensors, both come with the usuals, including advanced sensors such as temperature, SpO2, and ECG.
Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Which should you choose?
Choosing between the Google Pixel Watch 5 and the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is not as simple as choosing the model that matches your phone. Both work well with either brand's device, though you do get some benefits by matching. This includes advanced health metrics in the Samsung Health app on Galaxy phones and features like camera controls on Pixel.
The Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better health companion if you plan to sign up for Google Health Premium. If not, it's a wash between the two, as they both do an equally good job. That said, the Pixel Watch 5's battery life is reportedly much longer, which might be a dealbreaker for some. It's also a sleeker design. But it's not a massive upgrade from the Pixel Watch 4.
Overall, both smartwatches offer distinct but equally good experiences. I'd go with the Pixel Watch 5 because if it lives up to the Pixel Watch 4's reputation as one of the best Android smartwatches, it will easily be the best new Android smartwatch this year. Its style, functionality, and features are best suited to everyday users. And you can unlock plenty of familiar Google experiences right from your wrist.

title: One UI 9.5 leaks continue: Samsung eyes a glass UI with shiny edges and 'depth'
full_content:
One UI 9.5 leaks continue: Samsung eyes a glass UI with shiny edges and 'depth'
Think Liquid Glass.
What you need to know
- Additional One UI 9.5 rumors surface online, as a tipster claims Samsung is chasing a glass aesthetic that delivers "visual depth" for its elements.
- It seems Samsung would apply this to its home screen widgets, such as Now Brief, as well as in its Phone app and more.
- One UI 9.5 rumors got underway as One UI 9 Beta 5 rolled out, claiming development had begun on the Galaxy S26.
Another round of One UI 9.5 rumors concerns its UI, but in reality, it feels like we're caught in a time loop.
Early this morning (Aug 14), SamMobile highlighted a set of leaked screenshots that tipster Fahad Ali posted on X about One UI 9.5's UI. The tipster calls out the software's UI "polish," and it seems Samsung is approaching its 9.5 update with a glass design in mind. Many elements, such as Now Brief and floating UI elements in Samsung-made apps, resemble shinier glass along the edges.
Certain elements reportedly offer a blur when over objects, which is something we've become accustomed to over the years of phones and software design. Another aspect Ali points out is the "subtle backdrop shading." It looks like Samsung is trying to facilitate more separation, detail, and "visual depth" between its UI and the background (or app).
The Phone app looks the same (so far); however, Ali states Samsung has moved the search icon to the floating navigation bar at the bottom. This icon is currently placed at the top of the app, between the new contact button and the three-dot menu. Another post on X claims Samsung could add App Lock in One UI 9.5 to secure certain apps with a password, biometric, or other verification method.
Clear as glass
This is the new thing for phones, isn't it? The glass UI style. Apple already has Liquid Glass so, in a way, it's not completely new. I don't know how to feel about it. These are early snapshots, and they're focusing on these elements, not everything as a whole. Maybe my sentiments will change if Samsung feels this is right.
Rumors about One UI 9.5 started earlier this week, which is funny since Galaxy S26 users don't have One UI 9 yet. Samsung rolled out One UI 9 Beta 5 for S26 users, leaving testers with a 1.1GB download. A handful of fixes were detailed in its patch notes, alongside the August 2026 security patch. What we were most curious about was the 9.5 update rumors by a tipster on X. The tipster suggests Samsung has started developing One UI 9.5 for the Galaxy S26 far earlier than previously.
You shouldn't expect this update anytime soon, as rumors claim it might not debut until April or May 2027. What has us concerned is Samsung's history of software updates. One UI 8.5 was met with heavy delays throughout its development. There's also a chance that the 9.5 update Beta Program won't begin until late this year.

title: US Judge says Google Play Store isn't doing enough to help users find rival app stores
full_content:
US Judge says Google Play Store isn't doing enough to help users find rival app stores
This has to change.
What you need to know
- A report from inside a recent court visit between Epic Games and Google highlights the lackluster state of its rival app store search process.
- Judge Donato states Google must do better to let users find what they're looking for and to remove the third-party app store-specific page via the "Are you looking?" banner.
- Recently, Aptoide returned to the Play Store through Google's Play Catalogue Access Program.
If you thought Google's battle with Epic and rival app stores was over, think again. New reports claim that a U.S. judge is not happy with how things have progressed.
A report by The Verge walks us through a recent court visit between Epic Games and Google. The reason for the recent court visit is that the former claims the Play Store (Google) is "still making it too difficult to install rival app stores." Details from inside the courtroom state an Epic lawyer walked U.S. Judge Donato through a brief demo of how difficult the process is.
In the demo, the lawyer showed that typing "store for apps" in the Play Store's search box provides no such results. Instead, Judge Donato was confused when Walmart appeared. "Wait, why did Walmart come up?" he asked, before stating, "That's not good." Judge Donato ordered Google to fix this, stating the Play Store should understand what the user intends to find, no matter how they phrase it.
Another jarring issue is the Play Store's "are you looking for?" banner that appears frequently when searching for rival app storefronts. As an example, Judge Donato, after viewing a demo, asked, "Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?" Epic states that if users search for a rival store, the banner forces them to tap on it before sending them to a third-party page for other options.
The Verge highlights Epic's argument, which says this may deter new stores from placing their store on the Play Store, as well as "big, established" companies like Amazon. Judge Donato also wants this problem corrected. He told Google, "Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever."
Judge Donato expects these changes to arrive on the Play Store within one week.
Do better
Interestingly enough, Aptoide was mentioned in this report. Earlier this week, Aptoide returned to the Google Play Store. This app store was previously removed from Google's store under its old ruleset that prevented such competition. Aptoide was allowed to return to the Play Store through Google's new Play Catalogue Access Program. Qualifying third-party stores are allowed to publish their stores on the Play Store through this program.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
This program was the result of Epic and Google's long-standing anti-competitive battle over how the Play Store operated. We'd been down this road for years. In 2025, the Epic Games Store was allowed on the Play Store, in what CEO Tim Sweeney called a "total victory." Epic had accused Google of having anti-competitive practices against third-party developers. This kickstarted a long battle between the two companies, and Samsung even got roped into the fray.
Android Central's Take
This is all about choice. It's all about not scaring users into thinking they're doing something wrong when they're not. Epic argued that Google deployed "disadvantages" and scare tactics when users attempted to sideload its apps. Users were given pop-ups that made it seem like a security risk. It didn't leave Google in a positive light. Now, third-party app stores can display their content. Display their alternative path for users looking for something different.
