title: Trump’s dumb border wall
full_content:
About 22 miles south of the former mining town of Patagonia, Arizona, down a winding, unpaved mountain road that passes cows grazing on open range, stands a cottonwood tree believed to be at least 200 years old. The “grandmother” tree, as some locals call it, is imperiled and already showing signs of stress, almost as if it knows its fate. The leaves are yellowing prematurely, falling to the ground at the height of summer. On July 27th, a construction crew felled three neighboring trees to build an extension of President Donald Trump’s wall along the US-Mexico border.
Trump’s dumb border wall
The US has the one of the most advanced “smart” surveillance apparatuses in the world. So why does this administration insist on building environmentally destructive, physical walls?
Trump’s dumb border wall
The US has the one of the most advanced “smart” surveillance apparatuses in the world. So why does this administration insist on building environmentally destructive, physical walls?
An activist climbed up the last tree standing two days later and ever since, someone has sat on a platform hoisted onto the tree’s branches. They say they’ll sit there as long as it takes, because as long as someone is in the tree, it can’t be cut down.
The protest is about more than one cottonwood. “This tree represents a literal line in the sand against border militarization in general,” said Russ McSpadden, the Southwest conservation advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity.
In recent weeks, the Department of Homeland Security has revived its effort to wall off the border, dispatching construction crews to remote parts of Texas, Arizona, and the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation lands to finish Trump’s wall — and has waived environmental laws to get it built, causing backlash from the tiny desert town of Ajo to the even tinier ghost town of Terlingua.
This latest construction push is happening despite record-low encounters along the southwestern border. In fact, encounters at the southwest border dropped almost immediately after Trump took office — not because of any new infrastructure, but because he effectively shut down asylum. Despite the steep decline in migrant crossings, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed along party lines in 2025, gave Trump an additional $46.5 billion to finish building the wall.
The border wall is more than just a wall; it’s a vast surveillance network of interconnected drones, towers, and cameras. Even in areas where there’s no visible barrier separating the United States and Mexico, CBP relies on this “virtual wall” to track migrants. This vast surveillance apparatus is far more effective than a wall, and it’s already largely in place.
In the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, activists from surrounding communities have set up an encampment on private property near the cottonwood tree to support the protest. They take turns cooking meals and use a pulley system to transport food and water to the person sitting in the tree. They know they’re being watched. Trucks from Vision Quest Solutions, a private security firm that advertises itself as veteran- and Native American-owned, roll up and down the fresh dirt road just south of the tree. The activists track the various contractors that are building the road: Fisher Sand & Gravel, BJ Drilling, Stinger Bridge & Iron, and others.
Henry, a community organizer from Tucson who is participating in the encampment, said that a DHS helicopter flew “dangerously close” to the tree on August 10th.
“This movement was started and held down for a long time by local environmentalists who care really deeply about these ancient cottonwood trees,” said Henry, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym. He is among a newer group of activists “who see it as an opportunity to physically stop border wall construction.”
The planned construction projects differ by region. In Arizona’s San Rafael Valley, where an older fence already divides Mexico and the United States, DHS is building a wall featuring 30-foot-tall steel bollards. The plan is to have a “double wall” throughout the Arizona-Mexico border — one that runs through the Tohono O’odham reservation, Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, and the San Rafael Valley. To achieve this, DHS contractors are tearing down the old fence, replacing it with the new bollards, and building an entirely new wall a few dozen feet away. The cottonwood tree sits directly in the path of the second wall.
“They’re approaching the tree from both sides with their work crews,” Henry said. “I don’t really know what their plan is once they don’t have anything else to do.”
In Big Bend National Park, Customs and Border Protection is building what it calls a “Technology & Patrol Road,” or a “smart wall” system of sensors, cameras, and surveillance towers accessible via a new road — even though there’s an existing road that cuts through the park.
Responding to mass outcry about recent construction in Big Bend, CBP chief Rodney Scott said that DHS isn’t building a wall. “CBP is building one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations,” Scott said in an emailed statement. “What people are seeing right now is survey and design work—NOT construction of a wall through the park.” (The statement was also posted near-verbatim on DHS’s X account. )
Unlike in other areas along the border, Scott said, CBP isn’t building a 30-foot wall or installing stadium lighting in Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.
But outraged locals, joined by environmentalists from across the country, charge that CBP doesn’t need to build a 30-foot wall to destroy local ecosystems. Over the weekend, contractors started digging into Mariscal Mountain, a massive limestone ridge, ostensibly as part of the survey and design work needed to build its patrol road.
You can call it what you want. You’re destroying what we’re trying to protect.
— Billy Miller, a river guide and landowner in Terlingua, Texas.
CBP maintains that its goal is to ensure Big Bend remains open to the public. According to agency spokesperson John Mennell, the “smart wall” CBP plans on installing in the area is proactive, not reactive. Though the national park and Border Patrol’s greater Big Bend sector — which encompasses 165,154 square miles — has historically seen fewer crossings than other parts of the border, Mennell said that the buildup of security elsewhere could push migrants into Big Bend.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued the Trump administration last year, arguing that waiving environmental laws to build Trump’s wall “violates the foundational principle of the separation of powers rooted in the US Constitution.” But a federal judge effectively closed the case in March, citing two laws that let DHS disregard nearly three dozen federal laws — including the Endangered Species Act, the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, and the Clean Air Act — to “ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and roads” along the border. A separate lawsuit, filed by the Center for Biological Diversity, a local church, and Billy Miller, a river guide and landowner in Terlingua, Texas, is ongoing.
“Their lawyers — the contractor’s lawyers, the federal government’s lawyers — told us they would give us 30 days’ advance notice before any ground disturbance,” Miller, who has been a river guide in the area for 22 years, told The Verge. “But they just started destroying the river corridor this past week without telling us anything.”
The government’s attorneys, he said, countered that there hasn’t been any ground disturbance, since what they’re doing is “grubbing and pioneering to create access roads to the river.”
“You can call it what you want,” Miller said. “You’re destroying what we’re trying to protect. Y’all were supposed to tell us about it.”
Miller said that he and other locals have been told that the new CBP roads won’t be open to the public; only Border Patrol will be able to use them. “That’s heartbreaking. You’re going to destroy our national park, or take away private landowners’ property, and create roads nobody can use?” he said. According to Mennell, the CBP spokesperson, the National Park Service will decide whether the roads will be open to the public.
“You’re taking a wilderness area that’s really hard to get through, really hard to walk through on foot, and now you’re creating a brand-new road? They’re creating roads that smugglers could use, if there were smugglers out here in the first place.”
CBP also plans on installing vehicle barriers that locals say will block their access to the Rio Grande, which would threaten Miller and other river guides’ livelihood. In addition to destroying landscapes, jeopardizing livelihoods, and endangering migrants, the border wall threatens migratory species across the Southwest, including Sonoran pronghorns and Mexican gray wolves.
Over the last two weeks, the small, tight-knit community has been invaded by hundreds of construction workers. “Some businesses, like the Starlight Theatre, which is the most popular restaurant in town, have put up a sign that says they refuse to serve border wall workers or border barrier construction workers,” said Miller.
Though Trump received 55.6 percent of the vote in Texas’ Brewster County, the community is almost universally opposed to the wall. Miller has friends and relatives who “voted for Trump without really thinking that he would ever try to build a wall out here,” he said. “And now they are kicking themselves in the ass for voting for him.”
Locals share the opinion that the wall isn’t about border security or immigration. It’s about money. Some of the contractors, they point out, are run by major Trump donors. Fisher Sand & Gravel, one of the contractors working on the wall in Arizona, reportedly lobbied Trump directly, and was awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract during his first term.
On Wednesday, over 100 people attended a protest in Big Bend National Park’s Santa Elena Canyon. Their chants of “no road, no wall, no wire, no way” echoed off the surrounding cliffs.
Michael Ryan, a retired National Park Service river ranger who attended the rally, said some people he talked to drove more than 100 miles to be there. “We never thought we would see anything like this,” said Ryan, who has lived in the Big Bend region for 35 years. “We used to think more Airbnbs in the area was about the worst thing that could ever happen to us, and now the scope and scale of this construction is mind-boggling.”
In Arizona and Texas alike, locals see the wall as not only wasteful but destructive.
“They could spend this money on more agents if they wanted to, more infrared cameras, more motion sensors, more drones,” said Miller, the Big Bend river guide. “Even though that’s, to everybody out here, a complete waste of money, that would be more effective than what they’re planning.”

title: Sonos finally added Live Activities controls for your iPhone lockscreen
full_content:
Sonos released an update to its mobile app that finally introduces support for iOS’ Live Activities, giving iPhone users quick access to playback controls on their lockscreen. The added functionality is a “much requested, anticipated, and needed feature,” according to a post Sonos shared to Reddit today that was spotted by 9to5Mac.
Sonos finally added Live Activities controls for your iPhone lockscreen
The frequently requested feature is now available with the latest update to the Sonos iOS app.
While some features like displaying album art are not available, the Sonos Live Activity provides basic details and controls when listening to music or podcasts through a Sonos system without having to fully unlock your iPhone and open the app.
Support for Live Activities and lockscreen controls similar to what’s already available in the Android version of the Sonos app was teased by the company’s CEO Tom Conrad during an interview with Bloomberg last February. And following backlash to a major Sonos app update in 2024, support for Live Activities is off by default but can be enabled by navigating to both the Sonos app’s preferences as well as the Sonos app section of iOS’ settings.
Once it’s turned on, the Live Activity will appear “after you initiate playback and then close the app” and displays the name of the group or room where audio was last playing from and the title of what you’re listening to. After playback stops, the Live Activity will automatically disappear from your lockscreen after 15 minutes.
Support for the Apple Watch and CarPlay is included, but while the Live Activity will be displayed on your wrist or in your car, the controls aren’t supported there. It’s not known if or when those controls will ever work, but Sonos says its team is still working to improve the new feature, and when it comes to album art, the company is exploring “alternative ways to enhance the lock screen experience.”

title: The Analogue Pocket gets a Supreme makeover in red or gold
full_content:
Analogue and Supreme are teaming up to release metallic versions of the Analogue Pocket handheld in red and gold as part of Supreme’s fall / winter 2026 collection.
The Analogue Pocket gets a Supreme makeover in red or gold
Supreme is launching a few gadgets with its next collection, including metallic Analogue Pocket handhelds.

title: YouTube is changing how it counts views to give the numbers a boost
full_content:
YouTube will soon count a view as soon as a video starts to play, lining up with the system used by Instagram, TikTok, and its Shorts videos. The update will go into effect on August 24th, “which means creators will likely see their total view counts increase faster moving forward,” the platform says.
YouTube is changing how it counts views to give the numbers a boost
By tracking views from the instant a video starts to play, YouTube’s new counter works more like TikTok, X, and Instagram.
Instagram and TikTok similarly add a view to a video when it starts to play or replay, while X counts a view when a user watches a video for at least two seconds. YouTube applied Instagram and TikTok’s view-counting method to Shorts last year.
YouTube says it’s going to keep its original view-counting method under an “engaged views” metric in its Analytics dashboard. As my colleague David Pierce notes, it’s not entirely clear how YouTube counted views before this, but “it’s generally accepted wisdom that you have to watch 30 seconds of a standard YouTube video for it to count.”
The change won’t impact creators’ earnings or their eligibility for the YouTube Partner Program (YPP), according to the blog post. This isn’t the only creator-related update YouTube has made lately, as the platform is also upping the requirements needed to join the YPP next year.
“Historically, we’ve used multiple view counting systems across different formats,” YouTube says in its update. “However, we’ve heard that creators want to eliminate this metric confusion and accurately understand their true exposure… We hope that having metric parity across all formats gives creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure.”

title: ChatGPT's new Computer History tracks your Mac activity to create a timeline -  but should you let it?
full_content:
ChatGPT's new Computer History tracks your Mac activity to create a timeline - but should you let it?
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- ChatGPT's Computer History creates a timeline from your app and website activities.
- From the timeline, you can incorporate your work into your conversations.
- The option is only in the Mac app and only for certain types of accounts.
ChatGPT now has a new feature that sounds like a productivity boost but may trigger concerns among privacy-minded users.
On Thursday, OpenAI introduced its new Computer History feature. Now hitting the ChatGPT Mac app, but only for Pro, Business, and Enterprise accounts, Computer History is an opt-in skill that can capture your activities across the apps and websites you use on your Mac. Those activities are then turned into memories and a timeline where you can incorporate them into your conversations and research with ChatGPT and the Codex coding tool.
Also: How to use ChatGPT: A beginner's guide to mastering OpenAI's chatbot
The feature is rolling out globally in most regions, but with access in the UK, Switzerland, and the European Economic Area to follow in the next few weeks.
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET's parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
Replaces Chronicle, no screenshots required
Computer History builds on and replaces the ChatGPT Chronicle feature, which can monitor your screen activity to understand what you're doing while you work. As described by OpenAI, Computer History uses fewer tokens and offers more privacy controls than does Chronicle. Plus, Chronicle takes screenshots to capture your activities, while Computer History records your interactions with apps and websites but doesn't capture your screen, microphone input, or system audio.
By drawing from the generated timeline, you can ask questions about recent work, pick up where you left off with certain activities, understand how you work based on the apps and websites you use, and turn your workflows into new skills. That can be helpful whether you use ChatGPT for requests and research or you use Codex to build and refine code for your projects.
Also: How to keep your conversations with ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot or Claude as private as possible
"Computer History creates an interaction-event stream from allowed apps and websites," OpenAI said on its page describing the new option. "Events can include clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, app switches, and context that MacOS exposes through its accessibility system. Computer History periodically turns these events into text summaries and local memory files."
The timeline organizes your activities by day and time. Each captured item displays a title and summary of the activity, the apps or websites you used, a suggested skill for repeatable work, and options to see the memory file in Finder or delete the item entirely.
Ways to use the Computer History feature
OpenAI offers a few examples of what you could ask ChatGPT based on Computer History.
- "What was I working on before my last break?"
- "Where can I find the proposal document I was looking for earlier today?"
- "Give me a list of tasks I've worked on today and their status."
- "Prepare a summary of what I did yesterday."
Also: How to create flyers with AI that people won't hate: 8 tips (and prompts) that really work
Curious so far? To enable Computer History in the ChatGPT Mac app, go to Settings, select Integrations, and then click Computer History. Turn on the feature and then review the privacy and permission details. If prompted, turn on the Memories option. (Computer History requires Memories so it can use activities across your chats and tasks.) Choose which apps and websites to add to your history and then follow the prompts to set up the necessary MacOS permissions.
Computer History seems like a useful way not only to incorporate your activities into your ChatGPT conversations but also to use the AI to help you organize and manage your work. But this also sounds like a potential privacy risk.
Is Computer History safe and secure?
With ChatGPT capturing what you do, where you go, and which tasks you handle, the AI is collecting a lot of information about you -- both professionally and personally. Is Computer History safe and secure?
To address privacy concerns, OpenAI has set up a few conditions and requirements.
Also: How OpenAI's agent escaped: Sprung by humans in a series of preventable events
First, Computer History is an opt-in feature. You need to actively enable it to use it. With a Pro account, you can do that yourself. With a Business or Enterprise account managed by your company, the designated administrator has to grant access to employees.
Second, you choose which apps and websites Computer History should record. The permissions let you include only the ones you want and exclude any you don't. That means you're able to block ones that display more sensitive content.
Third, you can pause the collection at any time and resume it later. You can also turn off the feature completely.
Fourth, you can clear the history of any recorded activities so that ChatGPT won't remember or store them any further.
Despite these precautions, there is still one potential headache. As OpenAI states: "Computer History files can contain sensitive information. They are not encrypted by Computer History, and other programs running as your MacOS user may be able to access them. Protect your Mac account and exclude sources you do not want included."
Also: I tried the new ChatGPT Desktop App for Linux - but I'll stick to my browser for now
That lack of encryption concerns me. Though OpenAI may not be spying on your activities, savvy hackers who know how to snag this information could learn about your work. For that reason, you do want to exclude any unwanted sources and secure your Mac. Further, you'll probably want to use Computer History selectively, at least at first, until you see how it works and whether it truly is a productivity boost.

title: Apple is warning users of new spyware attacks - what to do if you're a target
full_content:
Apple is warning users of new spyware attacks - what to do if you're a target
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Apple is warning certain users about targeted spyware attacks.
- These attacks are aimed at journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats.
- Anyone notified should enable Lockdown Mode on their iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
Apple is warning certain users about a new round of targeted attacks designed to infect their iPhones, iPads, and Macs with what it calls mercenary spyware. If successful, the spyware is able to bypass any built-in encryption to access your private files, snoop on your conversations, capture your audio and video, track your locations, and control your device.
Also: Older iPhones have an unfixable security flaw - why it can't be patched and the models affected
Sharing the latest details with TechCrunch, Apple said that it sent the notifications to select customers on Thursday across 110 countries. The spyware is dubbed mercenary because it's typically carried out by, or deployed on behalf of, nation states. Further, the attacks aren't aimed at the average person but rather at people with prominent roles in society, including journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats. Still, if you're a victim, the damage can prove devastating.
"Such attacks are vastly more sophisticated than regular cybercriminal activity, as mercenary spyware attackers apply exceptional resources to target a very small number of specific individuals and their devices," Apple said in an updated support page about its notifications. "Mercenary spyware attacks cost millions of dollars and often have a short shelf life, making them much harder to detect and prevent."
As described and displayed by John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at security research center Citizen Lab, the notice appears on your device as an Apple Threat Notification. The actual text reads: "Apple detected a mercenary spyware attack targeted at your iPhone. There are actions you can take now to help protect your data and device."
These attacks often come in waves. Apple sent out such notifications twice during 2024, warning users about mercenary spyware attacks directed against them. On its notifications page, the company said that it has sent users these warnings multiple times a year and to date has alerted people across more than 150 countries.
Also: You're charging your phone all wrong: 6 common myths, debunked
One company in particular that has often been accused of fomenting such attacks is NSO Group. The maker of the infamous Pegasus spyware typically denies any culpability, claiming that it sells the product only to intelligence and law enforcement agencies in their fight against terrorists and criminals. However, Apple and other firms have sued NSO Group, while vendors have been forced to patch software vulnerabilities exploited by Pegasus.
If you do receive a warning, what should you do?
First and foremost, enable Lockdown Mode on your device. This security feature blocks most message attachments and link previews, restricts advanced web technologies, limits incoming FaceTime calls, disables features like SharePlay and Game Center, and stops certain Apple service invitations.
Lockdown Mode also removes shared photo albums, excludes location data from shared images, requires devices to be unlocked before they connect to accessories or computers, blocks unsecure Wi-Fi networks, and prevents device management profiles from being installed.
To enable Lockdown Mode on an iPhone or iPad, head to Settings and select Privacy & Security. Swipe down to the bottom of the screen and tap Lockdown Mode. Then just tap the link for Turn On Lockdown Mode. On a Mac, go to System Settings, select Privacy & Security, choose Lockdown Mode, and then click the button to turn it on.
Also: Why Apple's iOS 26.6 is worth installing (it's not just for the 91 security fixes)
Otherwise, there are other actions all Apple users should take whether or not they're targeted by these spyware attacks.
- Always update your device to the latest software version with the latest security fixes.
- Make sure you protect your device with a passcode, Touch ID, or Face ID.
- Turn on Stolen Device Protection.
- Use a strong password and two-factor authentication for your Apple Account.
- Install apps from the App Store.
- Use strong and unique passwords online and passkeys where supported.
- Don't open links or attachments in emails or text messages from unknown senders.

title: I tested an Android app that lets anyone fight censorship - and shows your impact in real time
full_content:
I tested an Android app that lets anyone fight censorship - and shows your impact in real time
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Snowflake Volunteer is a new Android app that lets you help fight global censorship
- The standalone app allows more people to connect to Tor, even under oppressive regimes.
- The app turns your phone into a proxy and requires no technical knowledge.
Snowflake Volunteer, a new Android app recently revealed by the minds behind the Tor Project, has now landed on the Google Play Store as a way for the general public to help fight global censorship.
Not everyone can lend high bandwidth, set up Tor volunteer nodes, or campaign politically in what has become aprox worldwide fight for our right to privacy, amid tightening controls by states and governments that restrict our access to the internet and online services.
But this doesn't mean we can't all contribute in a small way. Snowflake Volunteer developers argue that a convenient way to help is already in our pockets -- our smartphone can be used to provide others with access to the privacy-protecting Tor Network. Snowflake Volunteer is described as a "single-purpose app that gives volunteers control over when and how they contribute."
Also: The best secure browsers for privacy: Expert tested
So, what is Snowflake Volunteer, how does it work, and how did the new Android app perform during hands-on testing? ZDNET decided to find out.
What is Snowflake Volunteer?
Developed in partnership among Android app studio Bloco, the Tor Network, and Guardian Project, Snowflake Volunteer is a standalone Android app that allows users to lend their internet connections to others to create Snowflake proxies for accessing the Tor Network.
Snowflake Volunteer is based on the Tor Project's Snowflake, which debuted in 2019. Neither Snowflake nor Snowflake Volunteer is designed for anyone living in an oppressed country; instead, they are projects for individuals living in countries that do allow access to the Tor Network -- and are happy to lend this freedom to others.
What is the Tor network?
The Tor Network, accessible via the Tor Browser, is a free way to access the web and .onion addresses while reducing the risk of being tracked. Connections are anonymized through volunteer-run nodes that bounce traffic among themselves, creating high levels of obfuscation and making it extremely difficult for third parties to monitor.
Also: 5 ways to scour the dark web for your data after Google kills its free report
It also allows users to access online websites and services typically blocked at the ISP level by states and oppressive governments. It's private enough to be a favorite of activists, journalists, and whistleblowers.
How does Snowflake Volunteer work?
Once installed and enabled, Snowflake Volunteer connects with people who need a proxy to access the Tor Network. While Snowflake simulates a user's traffic as a video call via WebRTC, it actually routes requests through proxies and maintains "short-lived" connections that are constantly moving, making them difficult to block, unlike static server addresses or IPs.
However, if a Snowflake proxy is blocked, the connection can simply jump to another one.
Your mobile device becomes one of these proxies, effectively serving as a gateway for people in countries with high levels of censorship to access Tor -- and the online freedoms they can't access through standard internet browsers.
Also: This privacy-first chatbot is taking off - here's why and how to try it
The more individuals who install and run either the traditional Snowflake package or lightweight Snowflake Volunteer, the more robust and ever-changing the network becomes -- which means it will be far more difficult for oppressive regimes to block.
By May, after launching in April, Tor recorded roughly 1,300 unique proxy IP addresses actively working in the pool each day. A month later, this had risen to approximately 1,700 Snowflake proxies, a month-by-month increase of 29%. At its height, there were over 2,100 active daily proxies -- and so while the numbers are rising, there's still work to do.
Hands-on with Snowflake Volunteer
I went hands-on with the new Snowflake Volunteer app, putting it through its paces to see if it delivers all it promises to would-be volunteers.
Installation
You can download Snowflake Volunteer on Google Play and F-Droid. The app's code is open source, and developers can also explore the app on GitHub or create their own forks.
Also: You're being tracked online - 9 easy ways to stop the surveillance
For most of us, Google Play is the easiest route. Visit Google's app repository, select the app to install -- that's all. You don't need to sign up for an account or give out advanced smartphone permissions to run the software.
Snowflake Volunteer is currently available in eight languages.
Settings and options
You can decide how the app works and when by changing the following settings, most of which can be accessed in the top-right corner of the app's dashboard:
- Enable/disable: Found on the central screen, you can enable or disable the app, and the process couldn't be simpler. Toggle the button on or off.
- Charging: Since the app does require some juice, you can choose to lend your connection only when the phone is charging. Enable "Charging only" if you don't want the app to use battery life while you're on the move.
- Wi-Fi: You can choose to have the app run only when you are connected to Wi-Fi, rather than a cellular connection, so you don't incur unexpected cellular data usage or bills. Enable this setting under "Unmetered network only."
- Background use: You can allow the app to ask Android to run in the background, which is useful if you want to help whenever your other conditions -- such as Wi-Fi connectivity only -- are met.
- Limits: You can also decide on how many people you are happy to help simultaneously. You can allow up to five connections at the same time -- but keep in mind the more simultaneous connections, the more bandwidth you may end up using.
Also: Privacy in the AI era is possible, says Proton's CEO, but one thing keeps him up at night
Performance
What immediately stands out about this app is the sense of community it's trying to foster: When you enable Snowflake, it says "finding someone to help" while scanning, rather than the more direct language we're accustomed to in apps, such as "establishing a connection."
The app's central dashboard also displays in real time how many people you're helping, how many connections you've allowed over the course of a day, and how many bytes have been sent and received. There's also a "statistics" panel in the top-right menu that documents connections by date.
Do you need to worry about which websites people are accessing through your Snowflake app? For example, what if someone is using your device as a proxy to visit illegal websites or engage in criminal activity? According to the developers, there's no risk to volunteers when someone connects to your proxy, as "their visible browsing IP address will match their Tor exit node, not yours (since you're an entry point)."
There are a couple of points to keep in mind, however, if you plan to download and run this app.
Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you're giving up
First, it won't run if you use battery optimization -- this setting has to be turned off, and so if you are using an older Android handset with an aging battery, you might have to avoid it for now.
Second, if you are connected to home Wi-Fi and on limited bandwidth, this could affect how much bandwidth you'll have left at the end of the month. Active Wi-Fi or cellular is necessary, and you need to be happy for connections to link up to your proxy device.
Battery life
To see whether running this app daily would be a problem for the average user, I ran a series of tests. I allowed up to five simultaneous connections and waited until at least one connection was using my smartphone, a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold6, as a proxy before starting a three-hour run, with 88% battery life. I also did not use any other apps during this time.
(Note: This test was performed during a heatwave in the UK, so the phone's average daytime temperature may have contributed to the gradual loss of battery. My phone is several years old, too, so its battery doesn't hold or manage charge as well as it used to.)
- Starting power: 88%
- After one hour: 84%
- After two hours: 81%
- After three hours: 79%
This test isn't indicative of what you may experience, but it's useful for determining whether turning your phone into a proxy quickly depletes your battery. Based on these results, not by much.
Snowflake Volunteer: The verdict
Snowflake Volunteer, currently available over at Google Play and F-Droid, is an impressive app that can quietly assist others living in oppressive countries.
Most apps serve a purpose, and we generally download them for our personal convenience, such as a banking app to manage our finances, a social media app to stay in touch with friends and family, or weather and map apps to make our daily lives easier.
Also: This blazing-fast, super-private browser delivers a brand new beta - try it for free
But considering how powerful our pocket computers have become over the past decade or so, it seems like a missed opportunity not to use them for others' benefit. I think this is what makes Snowflake Volunteer appealing: it is a quiet, unobtrusive app that lets you contribute to something important without any inconvenience.
The community of users is small, but I can see it growing steadily over time, especially as volunteers realize there's no technical expertise required to help out. Considering how well the app is designed and the minimal power it requires, this is an app I intend to keep on my smartphone for the foreseeable future.

- The feature works on both the app and desktop versions.
- It's only open to Google AI Pro or Ultra subscribers for now.
Several years ago, Google Meet introduced a feature that takes notes during your virtual meetings. As of this week, Google's meeting software can now sit in and take notes on your in-person offline meetings, too.
Designed to let you focus on the meeting instead of taking down what was said, Meet's new feature is rolling out this week to both the app and desktop versions. The app version started rolling out on Aug. 11, while the desktop version started on Aug. 14. If you try your desktop version and don't see it, try the app.

There's no shortage of apps, software, and even devices designed to transcribe meetings, but this feature goes beyond simply recording and transcribing. Just like Meet's virtual version, the feature uses Gemini to build a structured summary and a complete transcript into a Google Doc, automatically saves the file to Google Drive, and emails you a link. Best of all, it does it without requiring you to purchase or install anything extra.
Google does explain that you'll need to let everyone present know Gemini will be taking notes. The feature supports eight languages -- English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish -- but only one at a time. The feature works best, Google added, for meetings lasting between 15 minutes and 8 hours.
How to use Google Meet to take in-person notes
To use Meet's new note-taking feature, look for the "Take notes" button beside the "New" button. When you tap the button, Gemini will automatically start taking notes on what it hears. When the meeting is over, press the button to stop recording.

The feature is available to the standard and plus tiers if your account is on a business plan, but if you're an individual, you'll need a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription.

Building a vinyl system can be a major task: you'll need a turntable and bookshelf speakers, and if they're analog, you'll also need a preamp, maybe an amp, too. Then, you'll need records and a place to store them. Vinyl can be a demanding and space-consuming hobby.
Also: This Bluetooth-only Marshall home speaker sounds so good, I can forgive the missing Wi-Fi
Many people are low on space for several reasons, but an all-in-one suitcase turntable isn't an option for someone with a sophisticated ear. A soundbase like the Victrola Soundstage can help you build your vinyl system up rather than out, without compromising sound quality.

It's quite impressive
The Victrola Soundstage sits underneath your turntable. The Soundstage was made with Victrola's Wave and Automatic turntables in mind, but as long as your turntable has a preamp or you have an external one, it'll work with the Soundstage.
The Soundstage's sound profile leans warm, with a greater emphasis on low and lower-mid frequencies. You end up with a very punchy, deep bass response with minimal distortion, making hip-hop and pop tracks highly enjoyable, whether you're listening passively at low levels or having a maxed-out volume jam session.
Also: I swapped my Bose and JBL speakers for this floating Turtlebox - and it's seriously tough
I spun BTS's "Arirang" album and enjoyed the high-energy A-sides, while the slower, more relaxed B-sides offered just as much bass with a little recession in the upper range. Upper-mids get a little lost, but vocals aren't drowned out by bass.
This emphasis on low frequencies, with slight damping at higher frequencies, is a combination of the analog medium and the Soundstage's tuning. You'll get more of the smaller details in a higher-resolution digital format, but the Soundstage's texture and bass reproduction make for an enjoyable listen.
However, the grainy, textured vinyl sound comes through well in BTS's "no. 29" and "Swim," which have much quieter moments. In short, I'd describe the Soundstage's sound as similar to that of a warm, bass-forward smart speaker that can replicate vinyl's texture. So, if you like the auditory feel of vinyl, the Soundstage still preserves it, despite its digital prowess.
I also spun Michael Jackson's "Thriller," and the Soundstage shone so much more. I'd like to attribute it to the analog recording methods of the 1980s, compared with the highly digitized methods used on albums in the late 2020s. Even with "Thriller," the Soundstage's upper-mids were still recessed, but it had much more color and a more present midrange.
Also: I brought a Bose, Sony, and JBL speaker to the beach - this one's my new outdoor essential
The Soundstage's bass response is a lesson in physics. It uses force-opposing diaphragms to reduce vibrations, thereby avoiding record scratching or cabin shaking. You can feel most of the Soundstage's vibrations underneath it, where the subwoofer resides. The Soundstage's feet keep it from making direct contact with your table or stand, giving the air room to disperse.
As a result, the Soundstage makes the age-old rule of not placing your speakers on the same surface as your turntable null and void.
So many ways to connect
There are RCA, optical, Sub-out, and USB-C inputs on deck for connecting external devices, and Bluetooth and Auracast are available for digital connections. Victrola's Auracast is open, meaning you can connect the Soundstage to non-Victrola devices that are Auracast-compatible.
The Soundstage serves as an Auracast transmitter and receiver, enhancing its digital versatility. However, receiver mode only works when connected with other Victrola speakers. So, you can spin a record and put the Soundstage in broadcast mode with the included remote or by double-pressing its knob, and connect to compatible headphones or speakers. Or, you can start a broadcast from your compatible phone, and Victrola speakers can easily join.
Also: I tested Sonos' new beta features on iOS and Android - how to opt in and what to expect
Though the Soundstage's Auracast role might sound like a bummer, it does make sense. If you're streaming music on your phone, you can create a whole-home speaker setup via Auracast, and the Soundstage can join the broadcast.
You can also take a trip to the pre-soundbar era, and use the Soundstage as a soundbase for your TV via an optical connection. The Soundstage's USB-C ports can connect to a PC to act as speakers, or you can plug in a USB-C drive with audio files.
Don't forget the objective
You'll find that powered bookshelf speakers can deliver more separation and imaging, but they likely won't deliver the punchy bass you can feel in your chest that makes you want to get up and dance. The Soundstage does.
If you don't have the space for the several components that can make up a vinyl setup, the Soundstage solves your problem without the tinny, hollow, and downright unfun sound of a suitcase record player.
ZDNET's buying advice
If versatility is what you're after, you'll find that the Victrola Soundstage excels at it. For beginners with minimal space looking to upgrade their setup, the Soundstage is certainly an improvement over low-quality speakers or an all-in-one suitcase record player. With so many analog and digital connection methods, you can squeeze a lot of use out of the Soundstage.
Also: 48 hours later with the Google Home Speaker, I can't stop talking to Gemini (even if it's imperfect)
If you're a more seasoned vinyl enthusiast, you'll enjoy the Soundstage's compact frame, especially if you're looking to build a second (or third) vinyl setup away from your main one. It will be bassier than your balanced, audiophile-grade speakers, but it is very fun, and sometimes that's what matters more.

Google Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 9: Why I'm considering the upgrade this year
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
Google's latest smartphone, the Pixel 11, isn't an earth-shattering upgrade from the Pixel 10 -- or even the 9. The 6.3-inch physical form factor, 12GB of RAM, and overall build is the same. However, the Pixel 11 has double the base storage and two generations of processor improvements under its belt. With the addition of the Google Tensor G6, the Pixel 11 represents a considerable upgrade in processing efficiency and CPU performance.
Also: Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: I'm a fan of both foldables, but this one wins
If you're a Pixel 9 user who held off on the Pixel 10 last year, the new Google Pixel 11 may just be enough to convince you to upgrade, especially when you consider how the phones' specifications translate into real-world applications.
Specifications
| Category | Google Pixel 11 | Google Pixel 9 | 
| Starting price | $899 | $799 | 
| Display | 6.3-in Actua \| OLED \| 422ppi \| 120Hz \| 3,000 nits peak | 6.3-in Actua \| OLED \| 422ppi \| 120Hz \| 2,700 nits peak | 
| Processor | Google Tensor G6 | Google Tensor G4 | 
| RAM | 12GB | 12GB | 
| Storage | 256GB \| 512GB | 128GB \| 256GB | 
| Main Camera | 48MP Wide \| 13MP UW \| 10.8MP Tele | 50MP Wide \| 48MP UW | 
| Selfie Camera | 10.5MP | 10.5MP | 
| Battery | 4,985mAh \| Pixelsnap \| Qi2 | 4,700mAh \| Qi | 
| Finish | Frost, Pistachio, Hibiscus, Obsidian | Peony, Wintergreen, Porcelain, Obsidian | 
The biggest camera changes
Let's address the elephant in the room: The Pixel 11 features a camera system redesign over a simple upgrade. Instead of the incremental camera upgrades we tend to see in phone launches, the Pixel 11 features a substantial resolution reduction: from 48MP in the Pixel 9 to 13MP on its ultrawide camera.
Also: Google Pixel 11 Pro vs. Samsung Galaxy S26: I compared the two Android flagships, here's my pick
However, the new Pixel 11 also features a telephoto camera, moving from a dual-camera system to a triple-camera array. The telephoto lens is a dedicated zoom lens for capturing clear images of distant objects. This is the second time we've seen a telephoto camera on a base-model Pixel, the first being on the Pixel 10.
Looking into how Google made the upgrades to the new Pixel 11, it appears the company used lower-resolution wide and ultrawide sensors to make room for a telephoto option, potentially to avoid pushing the Pixel 11 into Pro territory and increasing its price.
The main camera went from 50MP to 48MP, which isn't necessarily a substantial enough change to meaningfully affect image quality, especially when you consider that aperture, pixel size, and image processing are much more important than a 2-megapixel difference.
The new Pixel 11 also features upgraded computational video features, including major improvements in ultra-low-light video and 4K cinematic blur.
Is the price increase worth it?
Like many other consumer tech companies, Google is raising the price of its smartphones. The 2026 Google Pixel base model will sell for $100 more than the previous generation, now starting at $899 instead of $799.
You'll pay more, but you'll also get twice the base storage with the new Google Pixel 11. It starts at 256GB of storage and 12 GB of RAM, compared to the Pixel 9's 128GB of storage for $799.
Also: Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: I'm a fan of both foldables, but this one wins
Writer's choice
All in all, we're not seeing a big redesign with the Pixel 11. The similarities may outweigh the differences between the two base model Google phones.
However, the biggest and most noticeable difference will probably be the Tensor G6 performance, which could make the phone substantially faster while running cooler and potentially lasting longer. Also, the addition of a telephoto camera could offer a different photo experience. Taken together, these could offer a compelling reason to upgrade if your phone feels sluggish, or has taken a beating over the last two years.

Google Pixel 11 Pro vs. Apple iPhone 17 Pro: How the new Pixel competes with its biggest rival
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
The Google Pixel 11 Pro and the Apple iPhone 17 Pro are two very different smartphones, but they're each positioned at the top of their respective lineups. They each target power users who want the best on offer but don't need a big 6.9-inch display, and both phones have flagship chipsets, 6.3-inch AMOLED screens, versatile cameras, and multiple AI-powered features. But should you go for iOS or Android?
Also: Google Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 9: Why I'm considering the upgrade this year
I haven't had a chance to compare their camera performance yet, but here's how Google's new Pixel 11 stacks up against its Apple rival.
Specifications
|  | Google Pixel 11 Pro | Apple iPhone 17 Pro | 
| Display | 6.3-inch AMOLED; 3,600 peak nits | 6.3-inch AMOLED; 3,000 peak nits | 
| Battery | 4,850 mAh; 30W charging; 25W wireless | 4,252mAH; 40W charging; 30W wireless | 
| Camera system | 50MP Main, 48MP Ultrawide, 48MP/5x Telephoto, 42MP Selfie | 48MP Main; 48MP Ultrawide; 48MP/8x Telephoto; 18MP Center Stage Selfie | 
| Processor | Tensor G6 | A19 Pro | 
| Connectivity | 5G | 5G | 
| RAM/Storage | 12GB/16GB, 256GB/512GB/1TB | 12GB/256GB; 512GB; 1TB | 
| Price | Starting at $1,099 | Starting at $1,099 | 
You should buy the Google Pixel 11 Pro if…
1. You want Gemini over Siri
The Pixel 11 Pro naturally offers a better Gemini experience than the iPhone. Google says it has co-designed the Tensor G6 chip's silicon architecture alongside the latest AI models from Google DeepMind to deliver better quality and lower latency. While the company is again aiming to "offload everyday, routine tasks" by letting you order groceries or book rides through Gemini, it has also introduced a way for the smart assistant to dial businesses to "complete tasks for you." While Gemini communicates, you'll get a live transcript view and the ability to take over the conversation at any point.
Also: This Google Play Store trick saved me over $100 on the Pixel 11 Pro XL - here's how
A smarter AI addition to the Pixel 11 Pro is contextual AI, which can pull relevant information from across your favorite apps more efficiently. Then there's Rambler, a new voice-to-text feature that lets your phone automatically remove filler words like "um" and format your thoughts with greater clarity before you hit send.
The iPhone will have similar Siri capabilities with iOS 27, but we'll have to wait until September to see them. If you buy a Pixel 11 Pro (or Fold), you can also get 6 months of the Google AI Pro plan with expanded usage limits in Gemini, 5 TB of cloud storage, and Google Health Premium at no cost (a $119 value).
2. You want a notification light on your phone
Google is bringing back my favorite long-forgotten, useful feature, the notification light, in a new form. The new Pixel 11 Pro series has HiLight, an array of ambient LED lights built around the camera's flash to "give you light-based communications on the back of the phone." So, when you keep your phone face down and receive a notification, you can know what it's about without turning the phone over.
Also: Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: How the big Android foldables compare
At launch, Google is offering two HiLight functionalities: one for contacts and one for Gemini. You can assign a color to your favorite contacts so you don't miss an incoming call from them. The other use case is to receive a soft visual cue indicating when Gemini is listening, thinking, and responding.
Google said it is looking for ways to expand HiLight in the near future, including expanding its Favorite Contact notification feature to messages. But as of now, it had no comment on when this would become available.
3. You want an Android phone
For those of us who find home in Android's ecosystem, the Pixel 11 Pro is undoubtedly a better buy than the iPhone 17 Pro. It brings all-new Android 17 features, a bigger main camera sensor for better photography and videography chops, a decent battery boost, a brighter screen, and more capabilities with the Tensor G6 chip. Google is also adding Camera Looks, a new feature that lets you create your own set of distinct film styles like iPhone's Photographic Styles. All of this is paired with the much-loved smooth Pixel UI experience.
You should buy the Apple iPhone 17 Pro if…
1. You record yourself often
If you are a vlogger or want to start recording yourself more often using your phone's selfie camera, the Apple iPhone 17 Pro is the better choice. Apple equipped the iPhone 17 series with a new 18MP Center Stage camera housed in a square sensor. The square sensor lets you shoot landscape selfies and videos without needing to turn your phone.
Also: How to download iOS 27 right now (and which iPhone models support it)
Apple's software in the viewfinder automatically repositions its framing based on the number of people in the photo, and it works surprisingly well. It makes the process of shooting oneself a lot easier than its rivals from Google and Samsung. In comparison, the Google Pixel 11 Pro has a decent selfie camera, but it won't be enough if you need a reliable, flexible front-camera experience.
2. You live in Apple's ecosystem
Google has made it easier for iPhone users to switch to Android on both the software and hardware fronts with products like PixelSnap for MagSafe accessory compatibility and software like Android Switch for device migration. However, if you already own a MacBook, iPad, or Apple Watch, the iPhone 17 Pro is the better phone to purchase. It will seamlessly integrate into your workflow and pair with all other Apple devices.
Also: 5 underrated iOS 27 features that make my iPhone way better - and none are Siri AI
Going for a Pixel 11 Pro in this regard will cost you more than just replacing your phone; you'll need to replace an entire hardware ecosystem. If you're planning to purchase a Pro-level iPhone for under $1,000, I'd suggest buying the iPhone 17 Pro right now, since the iPhone 18 Pro series is likely to see a price hike when it launches in September.

The Pixel's new 'HiLight' reminds me of the golden days of Android phones
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Pixel 11 Pro models have a pulsing light indicator on the camera bump.
- HiLight pulses in response to incoming calls and Gemini interactions.
- Expanded functionality may be coming, but don't expect it at launch.
I remember when life was much simpler, when I could just plop my phone down and know exactly when and how to respond to it depending on the color of its teensy-weensy LED indicator.
Back in college, flashes of green meant someone on Facebook -- likely my studymates -- had sent a message to grab lunch or meet in the library. Blue meant that I had missed calls. And yellow meant that those same study mates were sending me Snapchats instead of studying.
Also: Google Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 9: Why I'm considering the upgrade this year
Then, the power efficiency of OLED panels paved the way for always-on displays, and the need for more context on our screens meant that the LED indicators of the 2010s became insufficient -- and eventually extinct. (It didn't help that every phone manufacturer wanted to design their devices like supermodels: thin and stylish, leaving no room in the chassis for extra parts.)
For a moment, I thought that I'd never feel the nostalgic minimalism of yesteryear, but the Google Pixel 11 Pro series has changed my mind. With the newest models, Google is introducing HiLight, a pulsing indicator that replaces the temperature sensor in the camera bump -- and it's very promising.
How it works
Like the notification LEDs on older Android phones, HiLight signals to the user when an alert is incoming. For now, the feature is limited to phone calls and Gemini interactions, meaning it'll display an aura of color when someone is calling you, or when Gemini is listening, thinking, and responding. That's it.
From our early observations, the LED indicator isn't particularly bright or easy to spot across the Pixel 11 Pro phones (the base Pixel 11 does not feature HiLight). Instead, it's more of a subtle beacon that you'll have to train (or retrain) yourself to peek at and understand.
Also: Google Pixel 11 Pro vs. Apple iPhone 17 Pro: How the new Pixel competes with its biggest rival
The feature also works hand in hand with the Pixel's "Flip-to-shhh" gesture, as they're both intended to promote digital well-being. Google told ZDNET that the wave of colors in HiLight was designed with accessibility in mind, so that even users with color blindness can discern it.
The elephant in the room
The big question mark with a feature like HiLight is what more it will be able to do. Google hasn't had the best track record of maintaining products over the past decades; in this case, it replaced the temperature sensor that some users dearly loved, so I'm not holding my breath for HiLight to become anything significantly greater.
However, some more surface-level integrations, such as messages, general notifications, and even calendar events, make so much sense. And it would truly mark the return of the old-school notification LED.
Also: The new Pixel 11 isn't enough to make me give up my Pixel 9 Pro - here's why
Google says it's working on integrations with the Messages app -- which I'm guessing will be centered on favorited group chats and contacts -- but the company hasn't confirmed any other future plans, such as opening up to third-party apps and services.
That's something we've seen before with Nothing's Glyph interface, but the design of the UK brand is much more polarizing. Given the Pixel's popularity, Google should have a greater chance of developer adoption. Hopefully, it doesn't keep those interested waiting too long.

title: Google Workspace lets Gemini access your company data by default - how to shut it down
full_content:
Google Workspace lets Gemini access your company data by default - how to shut it down
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Internal AI access can create compliance and privacy risks.
- Workspace admins can turn off intelligence sources.
- Google gives Gemini access to Workspace data by default.
I have long accepted one fundamental truth: Google knows everything that I do. I've been using Gmail as my primary life dashboard for over a decade now. Apart from the occasional ad in my Gmail interface, Google really hasn't abused my trust. But still, Gmail sees all. Gmail knows all.
Every email message I have sent or received since before Hamilton opened on Broadway has been processed through Google's voracious data maw.
So, when it comes to the Gemini chatbot, I haven't been too upset that Google's AI seems to know what's in my email or my Google Docs. In fact, that capability helped me out at one point. I actually want Google's AI to do more, but the tech has a limited number of messages it can process. The AI crashed and burned on a more complex research task.
Also: Google is training AI on even more of your data now, unless you opt out - here's how
But not everyone wants Google to access everything in Gmail, Docs, Calendar, and Chat, particularly professionals who use the commercial Google Workspace service.
And yet, did you know that Google defaults to allowing Gemini access to all Workspace services? In this article, I'll show you how that process works. Then, I'll show you how to turn it off for your company.
What is this dark magic?
The good news is that while Google does automatically expose your company's Workspace data to Gemini, the tech giant doesn't use it for training or even use it outside your company's domain. Nor does Google share prompts or generated responses with other users or other organizations. It also doesn't create an AI-specific database from your documents and email messages.
Also: I tried Claude Cowork on my Gmail inbox after Gemini choked - and it saved me hours of work
This fact converts concerns around Workspace AI use from a potential five-alarm fire with deep regulatory and privacy implications to more of a corporate policy issue.
Gemini is available in Chat, Drive, Docs, Calendar, Meet, and Gmail. This capability means you can interact with the AI from whatever work surface you are currently using. To increase the relevance of AI responses while in those workspaces, Gemini accesses Workspace data as part of its response analysis.
Workspace considers each of these sources to be a Workspace Intelligence Source. On the surface, there's an interesting question you might raise. If Google considers each of these buckets a Workspace Intelligence Source but doesn't use them for training, how can it use them in AI queries?
Also: How to keep your conversations with ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, or Claude as private as possible
The answer is as old as Google itself: search. Google indexes all your Workspace sources (as it has since the beginning). When Gemini receives a prompt, the AI uses real-time Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Basically, Google searches the Workspace data as it would during search, retrieves relevant information it has permission to touch, and then formulates a query answer.
Internal data governance
However, just because your corporate data isn't shared with Gemini or used in its training, that doesn't mean you want it all available for AI use, even internally.
The most obvious reason you might want to restrict this capability is for compliance and regulatory reasons. You might have client contracts or regulatory restrictions that explicitly prohibit AI scanning and data retrieval from company information. You might also be subject to regulations that prevent data sharing, even internally.
Another reason is to enforce necessary departmental isolation. It's always possible that an AI could produce an answer that accidentally includes confidential records (think HR complaints, private deals, and more) and provide those answers to employees working in other departments.
Also: Why enterprise AI agents could become the ultimate insider threat
The same principle applies to the rising level of insider threats, both perpetrated by humans and by AI. The last thing you want is curious (or malicious) employees querying an AI to circumvent departmental safeguards to access information they shouldn't be privy to.
Even if you don't have curious employees, if Workspace data is automatically surfaced to the AI, innocent queries could give employees access to sensitive company info that happens to be living in a Google Doc or a Chat log.
How to shut it down
Log in to an account that has admin access to your Google Workspace. Then point your browser to admin.google.com. You'll see your main dashboard.
Click Generative AI (at 1) and then Gemini in Workspace (at 2). You'll see the Gemini in Workspace page. Now, click the Workspace Intelligence Sources block.
You'll get the individual settings page for the entire organization. Here, you can click an option to disable the source for the whole business.
I ran into an issue when I tried to turn off a feature for an individual user. You can enter a user into the users block (shown at 1). But when I tried turning off one of the sources, like Drive and Docs (at 2), there was no interface to disable the feature.
When I asked Gemini why I couldn't take that step, I was told it's because that selector is marked as view-only. To turn off features for individuals, those users would need to be moved to their own organizational units or added to a new group.
So now you know.
Will you let Gemini access your Workspace Intelligence Sources or shut it down immediately? Let us know in the comments below.

I turned an old Android phone into a server for my LAN - here's how and why
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Termux makes it easy to get a Linux terminal emulator on Android.
- With Termux, you can turn your phone into a server.
- Termux is free to install from F-Droid.
I often adapt old phones and tablets for uses other than their intended purpose. Usually, it's just for fun; sometimes there's a method to my madness. Over the weekend, I decided to try turning a phone that had been resting silently in a drawer into a server…specifically, a Linux server.
That's right. I wanted to see what I could do with Apache and a few other bits and pieces. In the end, I wound up with a fun little website as a test, and now I'm going to show you how I did it.
Also: I found a free Android app that makes deleting photos as easy as swiping left
It starts with Termux.
What is Termux?
Termux is a free, open-source Linux terminal emulator that lets you run a Linux environment on Android. It's not exactly a 1:1, perfectly binary-compatible match (there are some permissions issues and a few other quirks that prevent it from behaving exactly like a true Linux distribution), but it's close enough.
You can install Termux from the Google Play Store, but don't. The version available on the Play Store is out of date. Instead, you need to install F-Droid (download the APK from the F-Droid site and then sideload it), and then install Termux from within that app.
Also: How I converted my Android phone into the perfect bedside clock - and why it makes sense
Once it's installed, you'll find yourself at a Linux terminal, where you can begin setting up your server.
Installing the necessary packages
What you install will depend on what you want to serve up. Let me walk you through the process of getting an Apache server up and running along with a basic PHP-based website.
1. Update the packages
The first thing you need to do is update the software within the emulator. To do that, issue the command:
pkg update
2. Install SSH
pkg install openssh
3. Locate your IP address
To find the IP address of your Termux environment, issue the command:
ifconfig
4. Find your username and set a password
Next, you need to find your username with the command whoami. You can then set a password (that you'll use for SSH) with the command:
passwd
5. Start the SSH server
Start the SSH server with the command:
sshd
6. Log in with SSH
Open a terminal window on a Linux or MacOS machine (or a Windows machine with SSH installed) and connect with the command:
ssh USER@IP:8022
Where USER is your username, and IP is the Termux IP address.
7. Install the LAMP server
Install the necessary components for the LAMP server (as well as git and wget) with the command:
pkg install apache2 php php-fpm mariadb git wget
8. Start the Apache server
You can now start the Apache server with the command:
apachectl start
9. Test the server
Open a web browser on your network and point it to http://IP:8080 (where IP is the IP address of your Termux environment). You should see "It works!" printed on the page.
Create a site
At this point, you can either start building a website from scratch or download a sample site, such as one of the ones I found from this collection of PHP sample sites. If you're going the PHP route, you'll need to start the PHP server with the command:
php-fpm
Also: My favorite SSH clients for Android - and why you need them
You can download one of the sample sites into the Apache document root and test it out. To do that, change into the Apache document root with the command:
cd /$PREFIX/share/apache2/default-site/htdocs
You can use git to clone one of the sample sites with:
git clone https://github.com/amoldalwai/E-learning-Website.git
If you're demoing the E-Learning site, rename it with the command:
mv E-learning-Website learning
Point your web browser to http://IP:8080/learning/home.php (again, where IP is the IP address of your Termux server), and the site will appear.
Also: How to run Android apps on Linux
You now have a working website running on a spare Android phone. Get creative with it: There are all kinds of experiments you can do, such as installing a Nextcloud server, a database development server, a CMS, or even (if you want to get really complicated) a home automation server.

Google wants you to use its phones less and its AI more - but who's buying it?
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Google claims to want to change your relationship to technology.
- A dominant theme at its Made by Google event was how to use its phones less to "be more present".
- It's using this idea to sell agentic AI, I argue.
Google wants you to use your phone less. Yes, that new Pixel 11 Pro that Trevor Noah, Peggy Gou, Stephen Gerrard, and Pinkpantheress promoted at its Made by Google event -- it wants you to put down to be more present.
Google's VP Rick Osterloh got on stage to talk to Trevor Noah about how his phone is just too dang distracting, and how he'd love to put it away. Hmm, I wonder if there are a few companies we can blame for that. Are they in the room with us?
Also: Every Pixel device announced at Made by Google 2026: 11 Pro Fold, Pixel Watch 5, and more
"Your phones can do so much, but getting all that done today requires you to do all the work, all the tapping, and scrolling," Osterloh said to Noah to kick off the show.
It's a fair point. Everything we do starts with our phones, and sometimes responding to one message feels like cutting off one of the Hydra's heads: several more distractions just pop up in its place. Osterloh complained that after checking a notification, he often falls down a rabbit hole of dog videos.
Google has a proposed solution for us: it's combatting these distractions with HiLight, a new feature on the camera bar of its Pixel 11 Pro models that glows when an important contact is calling. Google says it's one way users can stay informed about who is reaching them without having to constantly check the home screen.
Right now, it's limited to calls only, but Google says HiLight will support text message notifications soon. The feature is "one of the many ways our latest hardware will help you be more present," Google says in its press release.
Also: The Pixel's new 'HiLight' reminds me of the golden days of Android phones
But does anyone really believe that Google wants us to have a healthy relationship with technology? It isn't selling tech minimalism; it's selling agentic AI posing as minimalism. Instead of having you respond to a text that asks about restaurant reservation details, Google wants Gemini to find those details in your inbox and send them for you. Instead of coordinating an event yourself, it wants Gemini to create the invite and handle the details.
You might be doing less, but Google, through the integration of apps and AI, knows a whole lot more about you in the process.
Don't get me wrong -- these updates sound helpful if they work as promised. But those three minutes I spend organizing a GCal event, ordering an Uber, or responding to an important text aren't the reason my screen time is so high. Rather, it's the social media platforms like Instagram and Google's own YouTube that suck the most time from my day.
It's not the time spent on "menial tasks" that occupies all my time, but they are the most appropriate for agentic AI to handle, hence Google's emphasis on them. And at Made by Google, the company leveraged our poor relationship to technology to sell us more of it.
Also: I bricked my iPhone to prevent doomscrolling - how life has been after six months of use
Google's future is built on agentic AI, and its next generation of its smart wearables, like the intelligent eyewear it launches later this year, will be driven primarily by voice commands. To get users comfortable with speaking to their devices instead of a touch interface, Google wants to prime users for this change by bringing it to smartphones and watches first.
"Real leaps forward -- like what we're seeing right now -- doesn't happen that often," Osterloh said at the event. But it is happening now. Agentic updates like the ones Google unveiled last week give users a new command over their technology.
Also: Google's new AI Search box is here - along with agents and 5 more upgrades
Will these agentic updates actually reduce our screen time? I'm skeptical. Will they prime us for an era of technology where smart wearables are at the center of our device ecosystem, taking photos and sending them through smart glasses or ordering Uber Eats through miced smart rings? That future makes a little more sense to me.
I'll continue to use these devices at the same rate that I already am, but instead of endlessly staring at them, Google is prepping us for a future that replaces visual screens with talking -- and more information about you in the process.

You can turn an old Android into a Raspberry Pi alternative - but know this first
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
ZDNET's key takeaways
- Raspberry Pi boards have skyrocketed in price this year.
- There are pros and cons to using an old phone as a Raspberry Pi replacement.
- Here's a way to unlock your handset's power without risking bricking it.
With demand from AI data centers sending RAM and storage prices through the roof, Raspberry Pi buyers have been among the many victims of this trend. We've seen the prices of single-board computers skyrocket to the point where two 16GB Pi 5 boards cost the same as a MacBook Neo.
No wonder there's been a huge spike in interest in turning an old Android handset into a portable project computer.
Also: You're charging your phone all wrong: 6 common myths, debunked
After all, it looks like the perfect portable computer because it is a highly optimized portable computer, and most of us have a few old handsets sitting in a drawer or on a shelf somewhere, doing nothing.
But… there is a but. Several, actually. Before I tell you what you need to do to turn that old phone into a portable powerhouse for your projects, I'm going to list both the pros and the potential pitfalls of using that old handset.
The pros
It's a smartphone -- a portable, self-powered computer you can slip into your pocket. At first blush, it looks like the perfect system. And that initial infatuation might make you think that it's the superior option.
Also: How I survive summer without AC: My top hot weather coping tips, tricks, and gadgets
Not only is it free (or cheap, since the secondhand market is flooded with old Android handsets), but it also has a built-in battery, a display, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and even cellular connectivity. On top of that, it should be loaded with RAM and storage -- and if you're lucky, it might have a microSD card slot -- a camera, a CPU that usually has better single-core performance than a Pi, and a USB-C port for expansion.
Perfect.
As for software, one way to make use of your hardware is to use Termux -- an app that's both an Android terminal emulator and a Linux environment -- on Android without the hassle of rooting the handset. (Never rooted an Android smartphone? You have no idea about the horrors of bricking a handset.)
Throw proot-distro on top of Termux, and you have the power to run Linux distributions, again, without rooting.
So far, so good, right?
The cons
A smartphone is a very different animal from a Raspberry Pi. There are no GPIO pins, so anything and everything that you'd plug into the Pi this way is a no-go without a lot of futzing about with FT232R boards (and even with a lot of futzing, it can be unpredictable).
You also lose out on Ethernet and a bunch of USB ports, so you'll have to rely on docks, dongles, and such for any expansion.
Also: This Mac dock gives me lag-free dual displays with no sketchy drivers - for $150
Termux also puts obstacles and limitations in your way, stuff relating to power management and storage access, and you'll have to become familiar with things like wake lock and bypassing storage limitations.
Termux can also be buggy, and you'll no doubt be spending a lot of time in the wiki.
On top of all this, I can't even guarantee you'll be able to do what you want. Hopefully, someone's gone ahead of you, and you can walk in their footprints.
One really big limitation of using an Android handset for this type of endeavor is that some ports (ports 1024 and below, which are considered privileged network ports) are off-limits to apps that aren't rooted. Doesn't sound like a big hurdle -- and for the most part, it isn't -- but if you try to build something around certain apps, they can fail. One such app is the ad-blocker Pi-hole, which you'll only get to run on rooted hardware. I know this because I encountered this limitation earlier this year, which is why I used an ESP32-S3 board instead.
This is going to be one of many hurdles, speed bumps, and dead ends that you encounter.
If this is your first time trying something like this, you'll quickly learn why the Raspberry Pi is as popular as it is.
A way around Termux limitations is to install something like postmarketOS, but this involves rooting, and you need a compatible handset.
OK, here's how to get started
Because I have no idea what you want to do with your Franken-Android handset, I'll show you how to install Termux and make a few tweaks to it. After that, you're on your own.
The quickest, easiest, safest way to get Termux is via F-Droid. Either download the APK file directly, or download and install the F-Droid app, and download it through that. Either way, you're going to have to navigate a few security permissions screens (allow everything or things will break).
Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and an Apple Watch helped track my progress
Got it installed and open? Good! Next, update everything by typing the following:
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y
Hit ENTER, sit back, and wait for everything to refresh. Keep an eye on the screen because there you might be prompted for some inputs (say yes to everything).
Next, you need to set up the storage. For this, type the following, then press ENTER, and when prompted for permissions, be sure to allow them.
termux-setup-storage
Next, install the tools you'll need. For this, use:
pkg install proot-distro git openssh
Next, we need to give Termux access to the phone's hardware:
pkg install termux-api
Now you need to flip over to the F-Droid app and search for and install the Termux:API app.
Back to Termux, and now it's time to get Linux installed:
proot-distro install debian
Finally, you're ready to get into Linux… all it takes is one command:
proot-distro login debian
We're in!
From here, you have all sorts of projects to choose from, from a self-hosted password server, media server, file syncing, to web server.
Good luck!
