- Join the free Side Hustle Nation Community. The free Facebook group is the best place to connect with other side hustlers and get your questions answered.
- Download The Side Hustle Show. My free podcast shares how to make extra money with actionable weekly episodes.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is there such thing as an online focus group?
Yes! Several companies facilitate online consumer research focus groups, which is great because that means you can earn money from the comfort of your home or office. Check out our full list to learn more.
How much do focus groups pay?
The pay for focus groups depends on how long the session lasts. Most commonly, you’ll find rates average around $100 an hour.
Where can I find legit paid focus groups?
Companies like Respondent, Fieldwork, and FocusGroup.com are all legit facilitators of paid focus groups. Or, for the best results, you might try an aggregator service like FindFocusGroups.com, which pools together focus group opportunities from several sources. Be sure to check the list of providers on Side Hustle Nation as well.
How do online focus groups work?
Online focus groups work either via conference call or more commonly, through a group video chat to more closely mimic the in-person experience. A moderator will lead the group discussion and participants can chime in through their webcam and computer microphone or phone line.

title: Upskill and Earn: The Proven Path to $150/hr From Home
full_content:
Here’s a proven path to $150 an hour, right from home. Maybe you’ve got a good job you like. But when you look ahead, the salary ceiling feels capped, the red tape runs deep, and the chances to move up are slim.
At some point it hits you: this path won’t get me where I want to go, and nothing changes unless I change it.
For Hermela Felten, she carved out a new path with better pay and far more time freedom, and she’s here to walk you through it.
Hermela runs easeintoearnings.com and Feltech Digital Solutions. A few years ago, she was a college advisor in the DC metro area, spending 2.5 to 3 hours a day just commuting.
When COVID sent her remote, she suddenly had about 2.5 hours of her day back, and that small taste of freedom set everything in motion.
Tune into Episode 749 of the Side Hustle Show to learn:
- how to upskill into a high-paying, in-demand skill for free
- how networking can help you skip the job-application line
- how to turn that new skill into your own part-time freelance business
(Curious if a Salesforce pivot could work for you? Here’s a free 5-day challenge: sidehustlenation.com/salesforce)
Sponsors
- Quo (formerly OpenPhone) — Try it for free!
- Shopify — Sign up for a $1 per month trial!
- Gusto — Get 3 months free of the leading payroll, benefits, and HR provider for modern small businesses!
- Wealthfront — Start earning up to 4.30% variable APY today! Terms and conditions apply.
- Monarch — Get an extended 30-day free trial!
Why She Made the Pivot
Hermela loved her job, but her college salary was capped at about $53,000. Raises followed the department budget, and moving up often meant waiting for someone to retire.
She’d been listening to financial independence shows like ChooseFI, which preach a simple idea: mind the gap between what you earn and what you spend, then invest the difference.
Hermela was already great at keeping her expenses low. The problem was the income side.
Then she heard Bradley Rice’s story. He had pivoted into a Salesforce career and reached financial freedom much faster. She realized she could make the same move and stop letting an income ceiling hold her back.
How She Got Her Initial Traction
Hermela’s move into Salesforce wasn’t a huge leap. She was already Salesforce-adjacent at the university, and being an academic advisor turned out to be a lot like being a consultant.
Upskilling for Free
Salesforce offers two paths:
- work inside one organization
- consult for many
Consulting fit her skills best. She learned the technical side for free on Trailhead, Salesforce’s training platform, and did a 12-week boot camp to prep for the administrator certification.
Her guiding rule throughout: “focus on what you have.” Nearly every skill you already own is transferable.
Networking Past the Line
The bigger unlock was networking. Instead of applying blindly, Hermela got loud about her pivot on LinkedIn.
She’d message people at organizations she admired with a genuine note, mention something specific about them, and end with an ask for a short chat.
She focused on hiring managers, directors, and a few peer-level connections, the people who could actually open doors.
Three Offers Before She Was Even Certified
That outreach worked. Hermela landed three job offers before she finished her certification, each one contingent on getting it, and all through networking rather than blind applications.
She turned down a project manager role at a consulting firm, holding out for something more technical, and accepted a Salesforce admin job serving nonprofits.
It paid $73,000 fully remote, up from her $53,000 college salary. Staying in-demand mattered too, so she kept sharpening skills like pairing Salesforce with AI.
The Six-Figure Offer, and a Bold Ask
About six months in, a past networking contact came back with a new offer: $105,000, nearly double her old salary.
But Hermela cared about time as much as money, so she asked a bold question: would they be open to 24 hours a week instead of 40?
They said yes and prorated her pay to around $63,000.
With low costs and no commute, that was still a win, and it handed her back two full working days to build something of her own.
Building Her Own Freelance Business
Those two extra days became a freelance consulting business.
Her first client only needed 5 to 10 hours of Salesforce help, more than enough to start.
To learn the business side, contracts, invoicing, and finding clients, she took Bradley Rice’s freelance training through Talent Stacker.
More clients came the same way her jobs had: through networking with other independent consultants.
She positions herself as a Salesforce consultant for mission-driven organizations, piggybacking on the popularity of the software itself.
And she’s clear about her limit: she wants to work just 20 to 24 hours a week, so she built the business to fit her life, not the other way around.
How She Prices Her Work
Hermela’s work comes in two flavors.
- Project-based, like helping a client adopt a new marketing tool, where consultants bid on a defined scope.
- Managed services (which she leans toward): ongoing, recurring support billed as a monthly retainer, which smooths out the feast-or-famine of one-off projects.
She thinks of each client as a “bucket of hours,” anywhere from 5 to 40-plus hours a month, scoped so they only pay for work they actually have.
She keeps it to about four clients at a time.
Rates range widely, from $50 to $75 an hour on the low end up to $250 for specialists, with a sweet spot around $125 to $150. Her own retainers land closer to $150 to $200 an hour.
Designing Life Around Coast FI
None of this is about maxing out her income right now. Hermela’s goal is to cover her living expenses, keep investing toward her targets, and protect her time while her daughter is young.
Because she kept her lifestyle lean through every raise, she’s already reached Coast FI, meaning her nest egg can keep growing on its own without new contributions.
She sees it as a short-term sacrifice for a long-term payoff: front-load the work now, enjoy the freedom later.
It’s an idea I have explored on the show with Andy Hill of Marriage, Kids and Money.
A Day in the Life
On a typical day, Hermela makes client calls and keeps an eye on project and maintenance requests, all within her part-time hours.
She notes that the work has grown more complex over the years, with companies expecting more, so staying sharp matters.
There’s also room to grow without chasing clients directly. She can subcontract with other agencies that need extra help, taking a lower rate in exchange for them handling the client-finding.
As she stresses, this isn’t overnight money, but zoom out and stay patient, and the payoff compounds.
Mistakes or Surprises?
Hermela’s biggest surprise was how much genuine relationships shaped her whole journey. Almost every opportunity, from her first job offers to her freelance clients, traced back to a real connection she’d made.
Her takeaway is one Side Hustle Nation hears often: “your network is your net worth.” Being willing to reach out, stay genuine, and keep in touch turned out to be the most valuable skill of all.
What’s Next for Hermela?
Now Hermela is chasing more time-leveraged income, the kind that doesn’t trade every dollar for an hour.
She recently launched Ease into Earnings, a YouTube channel and Etsy shop where she’s exploring digital products like budget templates and money-management tools.
Hermela’s #1 Tip for Side Hustle Nation
“Think of a side hustle as a way to buy back your time.”

- Join the free Side Hustle Nation Community. The free Facebook group is the best place to connect with other side hustlers and get your questions answered.

title: 27 Best Ways to Get Free Money: Legit $500+ Inside!
full_content:
Is there really such thing as free money? Well, it depends on what you consider “free.”
Over the past few years, I’ve discovered a bunch of ways to make extra money with very little effort.
We’ll call it “almost free” money.
Now I want to be upfront. Individually, these ideas won’t make you a ton of extra cash, but when you combine several of them, the results can start to add up.
Here are a few ways to get some free money for yourself today.
Too Many Choices?
Start here instead. Punch in your name and email below I'll show you step-by-step how to add $500 to your bottom line.
Join the Free 5-Day $500 Challenge
You'll also receive my best side hustle tips and weekly-ish newsletter. Opt-out anytime.
1. Survey Websites and Apps: Up to $140/Hour
Don’t expect to earn an amazing hourly rate with most survey sites, but you can earn gift cards, cash, and other rewards by answering surveys, watching videos, playing games, and shopping online with several reputable apps and services.
I hesitated to include them on this list because you do have to do a little work to earn the money, but the work isn’t usually very hard.
Earn $50-150/hr, with thousands of new studies added each month.
Earn an average of $95 per project, and get notified of upcoming studies you may qualify for.
Patients and caregivers can earn $120/hour while helping advance medical research.
User Interviews
User Interviews is a great resource for connecting with online consumer research studies. So far, I’ve made $212 in about 2.5 hours, and typical rates range from $50-200 an hour.
For more, here’s my full User Interviews review.
Respondent
Respondent facilitates high-paying consumer and professional interviews and remote focus groups. According to the site, the average payout is $140 an hour.
Other Online Survey Options
- Swagbucks – Earn up to $35 a survey with this mega-popular app, and get a $10 bonus just for signing up!
- KashKick – Get paid to answer surveys, test games, and try new products.
- Survey Junkie – Take 3 surveys a day and earn up to $40 a month.
- Product Report Card – Get notified about higher-paying product tests, clinical trials, and online focus groups.
- InboxDollars – Get a $5 bonus just for signing up!
- American Consumer Opinion – Join millions of free members and earn up to $50 per survey.
Related: Paid Research Companies that Pay Up to $100 an Hour for Your Opinion
2. Max Out Your Company’s 401(k) Match: $1,000+ Per Year
Your employer’s 401(k) matching program is probably the single best source of free money in existence.
How this works is your company adds money to your retirement account when you contribute. Most companies offer some sort of retirement plan matching, with the most common structure being 50% of every dollar, up to 6% of your salary.
That means if you make $50,000 a year, and contribute 6% of your salary to your 401(k) — $3,000 a year — your employer would add an extra $1,500 on top of that for free!
It’s a deal that’s tough to beat … but doesn’t really help you if you need money quickly. For faster options, read on.
3. Get Free Money From the Government
Is it really free money if they’re just giving you some of your own tax dollars back? Jokes aside, check out what programs might be available at Benefits.gov.
Even if there isn’t another stimulus check coming, I found over 100 other federal, state, and local financial assistance programs.
And if you run a business or organization of any kind, you owe it to yourself to become familiar with Grants.gov. This is the official database of government grants (free money!) you can apply for.
Down Payment Assistance
Several state and federal programs offer down payment loans — and sometimes even grants — to prospective homebuyers.
If you’re in the market, it definitely makes sense to see what programs might be available in your state.
Childcare Assistance
As someone who’s paid over $2,000 a month for childcare, I know firsthand kids are expensive!
Thankfully, the government has a number of income-based assistance programs to help offset the cost of childcare. Drill down to your city and state to see what may be available.
4. Switch Banks: Up to $500
According to Bankrate, switching banks could pad your account with an extra $50-500!
Why do they give you free money just to move your money around?
Because they know switching banks is a pain! And once you do, you’re likely to be a customer for a while.
Just make sure to check the fine print to make sure you can meet the minimum deposit and monthly balance requirements.
5. Find Missing Money
Did you know there is over $42 billion in unclaimed funds in the United States? This is according to the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators (NAUPA).
Search databases at sites like Unclaimed.org to see if you’re owed any unclaimed money.
Totally random, but I found $35 in Nevada from an older company of mine!
Related: “Secret” Websites to Make Money
6. Check Gift Card Balances
If you have unused gift cards lying around, those could be another source of free “found money.” It’s always nice to score a free meal from a gift card you forgot you had.
And if you don’t want to redeem it, you can try and sell it on eBay or through a gift card marketplace like Raise.
7. Check Your Current Rewards Balances
Many programs, including Capital One and Chase, let you redeem your points for gift cards or cash. For me, this is the virtual equivalent of finding money in the couch.
For example, Chase Ultimate Rewards now ties directly in to your Amazon account, where you can use them to pay for new purchases.
The redemption values often aren’t as strong as they would be when exchanged for travel, but can be a great way to offset more pressing expenses.
8. Get Paid to Save: $50 Per Month
Debbie is a unique app that pays you to pay off your debt and build savings.
After you create your new account, link your existing checking, credit card, or savings accounts so Debbie can track your spending and payments.
Debbie has already paid over $2.3M in cash rewards to consumers, and most users can expect to earn over $50 per month in cash rewards.
As a bonus, they’ll even give you a $5 reward to get started.
How does Debbie make money? Debbie‘s partner banks and credit unions pay them for referring new users, and they pass a portion of that revenue on to you.
9. Refinance Your Debt: $200+ Per Month
Even though interest rates have risen, you may be able to consolidate or refinance your existing debt.
Credible is a great resource to shop for student loan refinancing options, while LendingTree may be worth a look for your mortgage rate options.
If you can score a lower interest rate and reduce your payments, that adds cash to your bottom line every month.
10. Get Free Stock: Up to $200
Robinhood is an online brokerage that gives new customers a free stock when you sign up.
You get $5-200 worth of a fractional share. (Limitations apply.)
I got Groupon (worth about $11), but apparently Microsoft, VISA, and Johnson & Johnson are options.
11. Credit Card Rewards: $200 in 3 Months
This is by far my favorite way of earning free money. By taking advantage of the various sign-up bonuses doled out by banks, my wife and I have earned thousands of dollars in free money and travel over the last few years.
(Please just promise to do this responsibly and don’t spend money you don’t have on crap you don’t need.)
What’s the easiest way to get started? Try a new cash back card on for size.
Credit cards like the Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards Credit Card offer a $200 sign-up bonus after you spend $500 in your first 3 months — with no annual fee. That's up to 40% cash back!
If you know you’re gonna spend $500 in the next 3 months, that’s #freemoney. This card also gives you one of the highest cash back rates, with unlimited 1.5% back on every dollar you spend.
Non-Affiliate Disclosure: All information about Capital One cards has been collected independently by Side Hustle Nation and was accurate at the time of publication.
(If you’re worried about your credit score, don’t be. I’ve opened probably a dozen credit card accounts in the last few years and still have a 750+ credit score.)
The Next Step: Check out my free course, Credit Card Rewards 101: How to Earn Free Cash and Travel by Spending Smarter
12. Get Free Money for Using the Internet: Up to $350/Year
Surprisingly, there are a few companies that will pay you to just to install their apps and run in the background on your devices. These are low-maintenance, low-overhead options to earn from what you’re already doing.
Nielsen Computer & Mobile Panel
Nielsen — the company that’s been reporting TV viewership data for decades — will reward you for sharing your Internet usage behaviors.
All you have to do is download the app to your devices.
As they track your usage you’ll earn up to $50 per year.
The app runs in the background and doesn’t slow down your phone or computer.
MobileXpression
MobileXpression is a market research panel that pays you in exchange for data from your mobile phone.
Download their app and allow it to work in the background recording your browsing habits while on your phone. You’ll earn weekly credits redeemable for gift cards to popular retailers.
Get a free $5 Amazon gift card after your first week (if you’re in the US).
Pogo
The free Pogo app is one of my latest finds.
You’ll earn points by linking your bank and credit card details and sharing your location data.
Based on my results so far, I expect Pogo to be worth around $5-20 a year. You can cash out to PayPal or Venmo.
See my full Pogo app review for more.
SavvyConnect
The SavvyConnect VIP program “uses safe, cutting-edge technology to collect data as you surf the web.”
In exchange, they’ll pay you for your data — up to $5 a month per device.
That means when you connect your smartphone, tablet, and desktop/laptop, you can earn $15 a month or $180 a year.
Permission Research (Desktop)
Permission Research will send you a $10 Visa gift card after you install their software and keep it on your Windows computer for a week.
Safety in numbers: More than 2 million users share their computer usage and browsing habits through this service.
13. Sell Your Excess Bandwidth: Up to $30 a Month
I’ve seen a lot of buzz lately around a new app called Honeygain. According to the site, you can earn up to $30 a month when you share 10 GB a day of “your unused net traffic with data scientists.”
Just install the app (available on Windows, MacOS, and Android), connect it to the Internet, and earn rewards passively. On average, it takes users 48 days to reach $20.
Before you get started though, make sure you’re truly on an unlimited plan as it sounds like this could chew through a lot of bandwidth in hurry!
14. Get Paid to Store Other People’s Stuff: Up to $10,000 a Year
The Neighbor self-storage platform connects people with storage needs with those who have extra space. If you’ve got some excess storage capacity in your garage or elsewhere, list your space here to fill it and get paid.
According to the site, hosts are earning up to $10,000 a year running their own mini self-storage operations.
15. Tap Into Your Home Equity
Since refinancing isn’t for everyone, there’s another way to turn your home equity into cash quickly. If you’re comfortable assigning a portion of your ownership stake over to Hometap*, you can get cash upfront without any new loans.
*Currently available to homeowners in Arizona, California, Florida, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Virginia, and Washington.
How it works is Hometap becomes an “investor” in your property, buying a stake today in exchange for the future value. You have 10 years to buy back their share, either with cash savings, proceeds when you sell the property, or through another bank loan.
Too Many Choices?
Start here instead. Punch in your name and email below I'll show you step-by-step how to add $500 to your bottom line.
Join the Free 5-Day $500 Challenge
You'll also receive my best side hustle tips and weekly-ish newsletter. Opt-out anytime.
16. Get Free Cash Back: $150+ Per Year
Fetch
Get cash back for every receipt, plus bonus payouts for buying specific products and brands. Use referral code BG5MP to get 2,000 free bonus points added to your account.
- Super easy to use
- Tons of cash out options
- Earn more from popular brands
- $0.02 minimum receipt value is on the lower end
- Some rewards have high minimums
Just snap a photo of your grocery receipt with the Fetch app and earn points for every item you purchase from the 250+ popular brands in the app.
I’ve been cashing in my points for free Amazon gift cards, but lots of other options are available as well.
Ibotta
Download the free Ibotta grocery savings app and start earning cash back on the shopping you’re already doing. Use the app to find offers and claim them by snapping a picture of your receipt.
Inside my actual account:
You can cash out your savings to PayPal, your bank account, or a gift card once you hit the $20 minimum.
Ibotta Savers who use the app every month earn over $130 a year! I’ll take it.
Rakuten (formerly Ebates)
If you shop online, consider doing it through Rakuten. The long-running site offers cash back at thousands of stores, including:
- Target
- eBay
- Walmart
- Nike
- Kohl’s
- and more
The average cashback offer is roughly 5%—not necessarily a huge saving, but it adds up, especially if you’re shopping online anyway.
I used the site to get over $200 back on my new laptop from Dell, and love getting my “Big Fat Checks” every few months.
Sign up through my referral link for a $30 bonus, or check out our full Rakuten review to learn more.
Upside
Use the free Upside app to get up to 25¢/gallon cash back on gas at thousands of locations all around the country.
Plus, get a $5 bonus on your first $10 purchase with promo code “sidehustle”.
Upside is a popular cash back app for gas, groceries, and dining. Consistent users earn an average of $290 per year in free money. Use promo code sidehustle to get a $5 bonus on your first $10 purchase.
- Easy to use
- Strong cash back offers
- Variety of payout options
- You have to remember to "activate" your offers
- Participating locations may be limited
- Tight time limits to claim (usually 4 hours)
Many major brands like Shell, BP, Exxon, Marathon, 76, Valero, and Sunoco are available, and you just have to tell the app where you’re filling up and what credit card you’re using.
Upside also gives you cash back at participating restaurants and grocery stores, too!
CoinOut
CoinOut won’t replace your day job, but could pay you up to $36 a year for uploading your shopping receipts.
It’s easy to use and you can cash out for an Amazon gift card as soon as you earn your first $3 worth of coins.
Check out our full CoinOut review to learn more.
Receipt Hog
Receipt Hog is a similar receipt-scanning app, where our independent app tester reported earning $25 a year.
Here’s our full Receipt Hog review for more.
ShopBack
ShopBack is a cool new cashback app that gives you $1 back on every Amazon order.
Not sure if I should admit this, but I placed 95 Amazon orders last year … it adds up!
Quick and easy cashback app with compelling features and strong rates, especially during bonus promotions.
- Free and easy to use.
- 1.5% back on Amazon orders (up to $5 per order)
- Low $5 minimum to cash out.
- PayPal is the only cashout option.
- Have to remember to activate session.
It’s free to sign up and at press time they were even offering new users a $15 sign-up bonus.
Check out our full ShopBack review to learn more.
17. Cut Your Insurance Cost: $489+ Per Year
Want to know the dirty secret of the car insurance industry?
Here it is: your cars are worth less every year due to depreciation, but you keep paying the same amount!
Check out Insurify for a quick and painless quote process to find the best rates on car and home insurance. It’ll take just a few minutes (you can even do it on your phone) and users save an average of $489 per year!
18. Negotiate Your Bills: Up to $300 a Year
Call up your TV, Internet, or mobile service provider and see if they have a better rate plan for you. I find doing this with Comcast every couple years nets quite a bit of cash back to our bottom line.
If the prospect of negotiating is intimidating, services like Rocket Money will do it on your behalf. You only have to pay them a portion of your savings if they’re successful.
Rocket Money also analyzes your spending history and can help you cancel forgotten subscriptions and recurring charges.
It’s an easy way to start spending less.
19. Get Paid to Get in Shape: Up to $10,000
Interestingly enough, there are companies that will pay you to lose weight and get in shape. If this is a goal of yours anyway, these options might make sense!
HealthyWage
HealthyWage is an interesting concept that allows you to win money (up to $10,000!) by betting on your own weight loss goals.
Check out their little betting tool to see how much you could win, and read our full HealthyWage review to learn more.
The downside is you have to put up the money first, and then win it back plus your prize when you reach your goal weight.
CashWalk
CashWalk is an app that pays you to walk, up to $5 every 6-8 weeks.
You earn money by tracking your steps and claiming them each day.
Check out our full CashWalk review to learn more.
20. Put Ads on Your Phone: Up to $36/Year
Download the S’more app (Android only) to get paid to watch ads. You can essentially “rent out” your cell phone lock screen to advertisers.
That sounds obnoxious to me, but the app pays $0.10 per day for every day you unlock your phone at least once. You can swipe to unlock your phone normally and ignore the offer.
That adds up to around $3 a month for not a lot of effort. Just make sure to cash out your points before they expire.
21. Clinical Trials
Also not exactly free money, but you can use websites like CenterWatch.com and ClinicalTrials.gov to find paid clinical trials in your area.
Be sure to check the requirements before applying. The money you can earn depends on the type of trials available.
22. Donate Plasma: Up to $300 a Month
A friend of mine reported earning up to $300 a month donating plasma when she was in college. This can be a time-consuming process, but can help save lives.
23. Get Free Stuff: $20+
Free stuff isn’t quite as good as free money, but if you were gonna have to buy it anyway, it’s pretty close!
When I first heard about RebateKey from a Side Hustle Show guest, I was pretty skeptical.
How it works is companies offer to refund a portion of your purchase on certain products — up to 100% — when you buy through RebateKey.
What’s in it for them, I wondered?
Well, they’re building sales proof, gathering user feedback, and collecting emails. I tested it out and sure enough, a month later, I had a check for the full amount of my $21.95 purchase.
Pretty crazy, but definitely worth checking out to see if they have any products you’re in the market for.
24. Get Money for Your Junk Mail? $50+ Per Year
The Small Business Knowledge Center pays people to send them their junk mail. What they do with it, I’m not entirely sure, but participants earn as much as $20 (in a gift card) every couple months.
The company provides postage-paid envelopes and it sounds like an interesting way to get rid of your junk mail instead of just recycling it!
25. Declutter Your House: $500 or More
Again, these aren’t really “free” since you’re getting rid of some items around the house. But if the stuff is just sitting around collecting dust, it can be an easy win.
Suggested Playlist: Flipping Profits
Buying low and selling high is the fastest way to multiply money. Here's how to get it done.
Bookscouter
Do you have books lying around your house gathering dust? If so, you can sell them using Bookscouter.
Find out how much your old books are worth and use the free app to search buyback vendors to get the best deal. The best part is that you can ship your books for free!
One Side Hustle Show guest took this to the next level, and reported earning up to $4,000 a month flipping books.
Other Resale Sites
Here are some other options to help you declutter:
- Gazelle – Get an instant offer for your used cell phones.
- Amazon Trade-In – Turn your used electronics into Amazon credit.
- Chairish – Online consignment store for furniture, art, lighting, and more.
26. Get Free Money with Your Car: $100+ Per Week
Your car is probably a giant depreciating purchase. Between car notes, insurance, and gas, vehicles are expensive.
Here are a couple innovative ways to offset those costs.
Wrapify: Turn your ride into a mobile billboard
If you don’t care what your car looks like, sign up to have your car covered with a wrapped advertisement with Wrapify.
The money you earn with Wrapify is based on how far you drive so commuters in popular areas can earn $100 a week.
Download the app and as you drive, Wrapify tracks your mileage.
Lyft’s Destination Mode
Now shuttling your neighbors around as a Lyft driver is anything but free money, but one cool “hack” is a feature called “Destination Mode.” A Side Hustle Nation community member pointed this out to me at a meetup, saying it basically makes his regular commute free.
Destination mode lets you specify where you’re headed and Lyft will only match you with ride requests along your route.
27. Review Products and Websites: $5-60 Per Test
UserTesting
If you spend a lot of time online or on your phone, UserTesting gives you an opportunity to get paid for doing just that. UserTesting pays people to test websites and apps.
You can make as much as $60 per test if you qualify, though the standard payout is $10 via PayPal for every 20-minute video you complete.
Make Money Today
With all of the ways to make some “free” or “almost free” money listed above, I’m positive there are a few ways that stuck out as possibilities for you.
Check them out and see if they work for you! Some of them are more labor intensive than others, but for the most part, you won’t have to do too much to start earning money today!
Too Many Choices?

Is there such a thing as free money?
It depends on what you consider “free.” Money is almost always an exchange for value. But over the past few years, I’ve discovered a bunch of ways to make extra money with very little effort.

title: We Bought a “Boring” Business. Running it Was Another Story.
full_content:
Buy a boring business, they said. It’ll be easy. It’ll be fun.
That’s the dream Andrea Palacio and her husband chased when they bought a landscaping company.
The road got bumpy fast, but they still added around $300,000 in equity value in just a couple of years.
Andrea Palacio runs AndreaPalacio.ai, where she helps other business owners put AI to work.
But before that, she and her husband lived on a sailboat for 4 years while running an e-commerce business selling pet supplies on Amazon and Shopify.
When that business stalled, they sold it and went looking for something new. They landed on a South Florida landscaping company, thinking it would be steady and mostly hands-off. Instead, almost everything went wrong at once.
Tune in to Episode 750 of the Side Hustle Show to learn:
- how Andrea rebuilt after losing most of her team and clients
- how simple AI tools gave her back 20+ hours a month
- what buying a business taught her about leadership
Sponsors
- Quo (formerly OpenPhone) — Try it for free!
- Shopify — Sign up for a $1 per month trial!
- Gusto — Get 3 months free of the leading payroll, benefits, and HR provider for modern small businesses!
- Wealthfront — Start earning up to 4.30% variable APY today! Terms and conditions apply.
- Monarch — Get an extended 30-day free trial!
Why a Landscaping Business?
After 4 years on a sailboat, Andrea and her husband felt their e-commerce growth stall.
To keep competing with big pet-supply sellers, they would have needed to invest hundreds of thousands of dollars. They didn’t want that risk, so they sold and looked for a new path.
Andrea watched a lot of YouTube videos about buying businesses. The pitch was simple: buy a company that already works, put a manager in place, and step back.
They wanted something that fit both of them. Andrea is strong online with marketing and customers. Her husband is very hands-on.
Landscaping felt recession-proof, since in Florida everyone has to keep their lawn cut, so they went for it.
The Deal That Fell Apart
They bought the company for $470,000, paying about a 2.3x multiple on net income.
To fund it, they used an SBA loan and put their personal assets, including their home, up as collateral. Quitting was never an option.
Then things unraveled. The seller was supposed to train them, but he disappeared just 5 days after the sale.
Soon after, the manager quit and told the crew they were better off finding other jobs. The team dropped from 12 employees down to about 2.
A Brutal First Month
At the time, Andrea had a 7-month-old and was pregnant with her second son.
She was fielding 50 calls a day while handling marketing, admin, and customer service.
Revenue fell from $70,000 a month to $40,000 a month, and her husband had to do the labor himself.
Digging Out of the Hole
The first move was running Google Ads to win back clients. It was expensive to learn, and they wasted money before getting it right.
Finding workers was even harder. Andrea says she might interview 100 people, have 5 show up, and find just 1 who was decent.
Taking over an existing business and then improving it is its own skill.
Jono Santamaria took the same approach with a laundromat, making a series of changes to grow revenue once he owned it.
Learning to Sell
About half their revenue was recurring lawn care.
The other half came from bigger custom and enhancement jobs, which they didn’t know how to sell. They lost their large commercial clients, like shopping plazas paying $2,000 to $3,000 a month.
Andrea’s husband learned sales the “fake it till you make it” way.
Over about a year, they rebuilt revenue to $60,000 to $65,000 a month, sometimes hitting $70,000, while working 80-hour weeks.
Using AI to Get Time Back
The 80-hour weeks left Andrea feeling like she couldn’t be present for her kids. Something had to change.
Her sister mentioned that ChatGPT had just come out.
Andrea, who calls herself tech-curious, started playing with it and imagined AI handling her phone calls and chasing late payments.
Trial and Error
She first hired an Upwork freelancer to build her idea. Five months later, she had nothing.
A second freelancer built an automation on Make that sent clients a photo, pulled from their CRM, after every service, plus a follow-up text.
Happy clients were sent to a Google review; unhappy ones went to a complaint form.
They also switched from paper scheduling to a CRM called Jobber.
Then Andrea taught herself Make on YouTube and built the AI receptionist she first imagined, which booked appointments right inside Jobber.
She notes tools like Claude Code make this even easier today.
How She Trained the AI
Andrea says the setup is the easy part. Tools like VAPI or Retell AI can spin up an AI receptionist quickly. The real work is training it to say the right thing every time.
So she listened to every call, found the problem spots, and updated the prompt to fix them.
Her big mindset shift was to think in steps and systems, and to train the AI like a junior employee.
If a client calls upset, the AI transfers the call to her. If a client wants an estimate, it books the visit on the calendar. Just two automations gave her back at least 20 hours a month.
Listed for Sale — and a $750,000 Offer
With calls handled and time back, they listed the company for sale. They also hired a friend Andrea had known for 20 years as operations manager in December 2024.
Around the same time, they got an offer of $750,000, well above their $470,000 purchase price.
They also bought a small fertilization and pest control company for $170,000, with the seller financing half.
In the end, they decided not to sell, since selling would leave them without an income source. The business was finally stable and running without them handling calls.
When It Fell Apart… Again
In January 2025, the family moved abroad for six months and left the manager in charge. But the business started sliding. Andrea had also stepped away in September 2025 to focus on her own AI company.
When they returned near New Year, their bank account had $2.50 in it. They discovered the manager, a friend of 20 years, had been stealing.
Five days later, a full truck of equipment worth $10,000 to $15,000 was stolen. The lesson Andrea took away was painful but clear: they had not learned how to lead a company.
Rebuilding Leaner with AI
They let the manager go. Good replacement managers wanted $100,000 or more a year, which the company couldn’t afford. So instead of hiring, they automated more.
Now Andrea’s husband goes to the office just one day a week for sales. AI handles the marketing, which brought in so many leads that May was their biggest month ever.
They also built a dashboard to track their real numbers:
- which crews are efficient
- how long jobs take
- and pay versus what each client is charged
For people, they simply promoted their longest-tenured worker to organize the crews each morning. Andrea says missing those key numbers is exactly why they got robbed without noticing.
What Andrea Learned About Buying Businesses
Andrea’s top warning is to never buy a company unless the seller finances at least part of it, so they keep some skin in the game.
If the idea of owner financing appeals to you, Hannah Ingram did exactly that in Episode 571, buying an entire self-service car wash with the seller footing part of the bill.
Andrea also passed on another deal where clients paid three months late and visits were priced at $25, far below their $60 minimum.
In her own company, clients are billed on the first of the month, before any work is done. She warns that raising prices and changing terms after an acquisition will usually cost you those customers.
Tech/Tools
Here are the main tools Andrea mentioned:
- Make – automation platform for connecting apps and building workflows
- Jobber – CRM built for landscaping and cleaning services
- Claude Code – tool she uses daily to build automations
- VAPI and Retell AI – platforms for building AI phone receptionists
- Upwork – where she hired freelancers to help build automations
Where the Business Is Now
Today the company is leaner and steadier. Andrea’s husband goes into the office about one day a week for sales, and they promoted their longest-tenured worker to organize the crews each morning. Last month the business did $75,000 with 7 employees.
What’s Next for Andrea?
These wins freed Andrea to build her own venture at AndreaPalacio.ai, where she helps other owners run an “AI-first company.”
She launched a program, Crewless, for business owners making that shift — mainly local services plus coaching and consulting.
You can find her on Instagram and YouTube. DM her the word “sidehustle” on Instagram for a personalized plan.
Andrea’s #1 Tip for Side Hustle Nation
“Don’t quit on your goals and dreams.”

title: I Asked Listeners for the Most Random Ways They’ve Made Extra Money
full_content:
Last month, I put out a call for listeners to share the most random ways they’ve made extra money, and the responses did not disappoint!
Some side hustles start with a business plan. Others start with a stranger in a parking garage asking if you want to get paid to drink beer.
That one actually happened to me in Atlanta. The woman worked for a market research company, and they needed taste-testers for a product that hadn’t launched yet.
I invited a couple of friends along, and we each made about $75 sampling what turned out to be Miller Chill.
Later we lived near a place called the National Food Lab, so I went over and did a few more paid taste-testings.
Tune into Episode 751 of the Side Hustle Show to learn:
- the strangest things listeners have been paid to do
- how a few of those random gigs turned into real businesses
- where to find unusual rental and marketplace opportunities
Sponsors
- Quo (formerly OpenPhone) — Try it for free!
- Shopify — Sign up for a $1 per month trial!
- Gusto — Get 3 months free of the leading payroll, benefits, and HR provider for modern small businesses!
- Wealthfront — Start earning up to 4.30% variable APY today! Terms and conditions apply.
- Monarch — Get an extended 30-day free trial!
1. Loading Chicken Trucks
Joe Saul-Sehy from Stacking Benjamins kicked things off with a story from his teenage years. He got hired to go out to a farm and help load chickens onto a truck.
The job sounded simple. Reach into the coop, grab a chicken, put it in the travel coop, but real life was different.
The birds panic and escape, and you chase them around a farm apologizing.
The “right” technique (grab both legs, pull hard, wing damage optional) was enough for Joe and his brother to quit at the first break.
As Joe put it, “that is the weirdest and the worst side hustle I ever had.”
My own one-day teenage gig was cutting out organic dog biscuits in a commercial kitchen for about $10 an hour. Tedious, and it didn’t smell great. But no chickens were involved, so I’ll take it.
2. Uber Eats Delivery, But on a Bike
Cody Berman, author of Retire by 30 and host of The Financial Independence Show, moved to Australia for six months while his wife studied abroad.
Rejected from 15+ jobs in Australia, Cody signed up for Uber Eats — but with no license, he switched to bike delivery, and with no bike, he bought a too-small, single-gear pink bike for $25 on Gumtree, in a hilly suburb.
He earned a few one-star reviews for sweating on people’s food.
His tips:
- Get a bike that actually works
- Go electric if you’re somewhere hilly
- Or just pick a different hustle
3. Selling Snacks at School Lunch
Chandler Bolt from Self-Publishing.com got his start at Scout Camp. His mom sent him with a bunch of snacks, and he came home with a wad of cash and a switchblade knife.
In high school, he turned that into a business for his entrepreneurship class. Every two weeks, he and a friend loaded up a Prius at Sam’s Club until the wheels almost scrubbed, then worked the lunches selling drinks and snacks.
They made $8,000 in profit in about two and a half months. Chandler kept $2,000. As he said, he got paid to go to school. It worked so well that the school shut it down the next year.
I did the same thing at Scout camp, loading up at Costco and undercutting the camp trading post. And our youngest just sold $3 shave ice with a friend on a hot day — about $25 each for an hour’s work.
4. Selling Empty Smartphone Boxes
Jason Butler runs My Money Chronicles, a site about personal finance and side hustles. He’s flipped plenty of normal things: clothes, toys, board games.
The surprise was empty phone boxes. He’d read that someone online was selling them, so he listed a couple of Samsung boxes. They sold within a week.
There’s a whole economy in “worthless” items apparently. An original box can double or triple a resale price (used iPhones, Jordans, LEGO sets), so resellers pay $20-$25 for an empty one.
Same with vintage manuals. (A Charizard-shaped Cheeto once sold for $350, then resold for $87,000 — so check the snack drawer.)
Related: The Best Items to Flip for a Profit.
5. Buying Out a Yarn Shop
Donna Westerkamp walked into a yarn shop that was going out of business.
She asked what they’d do with leftover inventory, got a call from the owner, lowballed a price — and suddenly owned the whole stock.
She resold it on eBay and Craigslist, roughly recouping her cost. “The inventory was atrocious… but I made a ton of money,” she said.
Donna was already in the crafting niche, which matters.
That’s what Shannon Jean recommended in Episode 731: start with what you know.
6. A $5,000 Yard Sale (and a Free Facebook Strategy)
Bill Fortenberry built his company around a strategy he created for his dad’s business, which had a Facebook page and no marketing budget.
He calls it the 1-10-10 strategy:
- 1 post a week
- 10+ photos per post
- shared in 10+ local Facebook groups
Bill needed test cases. Around the same time, he and his wife were downsizing and raising money for a missions trip to Ukraine to help at a youth camp for kids affected by the war. So they held a yard sale.
He took 30 or 40 pictures, put them in a single Facebook post, explained what the money was for, and shared it in local community groups. That one post brought in more than $5,000.
Jeff Rose covered another angle in Episode 706 — the Facebook content monetization program, earning $1,000 a day.
7. E-Bike Rentals
Wanting something to run around a full-time job, Brian Sadler from Wisconsin delivers e-bike rentals to nearby trails, campgrounds, and resort areas.
He did it the smart way:
- built the website first
- borrowed a neighbor’s bike to test the concept
- and befriended campground owners who loved having a new guest amenity (some via paid partnerships).
The lesson: go where your customers already are. We have a scooter episode with Lenny Tim, who spent a couple of years on local SEO before buying a single scooter.
8. Renting Out Your Backyard to Dogs
Marie Frey from Nova Scotia has three kids four and under, including twins, so passive income was the goal.
She’s also a real estate investor, and author of The First 3 Doors: Lessons From Our Rookie Years in Real Estate Investing.
She found Sniffspot, which works like Airbnb for dogs. Dog owners book her backyard by the hour. Setup took a couple of pictures and a price. Bookings are accepted automatically, so there’s no management, and she can block off times when the family wants the yard.
They made about $500 the first year and a little less the second. For something this passive, Marie says any extra money is a win. There’s no labor either — no dog walking, no boarding.
Similar marketplaces worth a look:
- Swimply — rent your pool (hosts earn $5k+/yr; insurance included)
- Neighbor — rent storage space (garage, shed, side yard, attic). Our Neighbor review.
9. Board Game Rentals
Trish is in Kitsap County, Washington, near Seattle. She rents out board games, in her words, “like they’re DVDs from 2004.”
She runs it through her local Board Game Geek guild and rents through the Libib app. She’s building a subscription where people pay $20 a month to borrow four games.
She’s up to over 300 games, all labeled, scanned, and organized like a tiny Blockbuster.
It started because she loves board games as a hobby but can’t read rule books at night, so she’s building a business around daylight gaming.
I like the subscription model better than per-rental. There are challenges to solve — shipping, missing pieces — but it’s a great niche.
10. Renting Out Baby Gear
Ariana Johnson became El Salvador’s first BabyQuip provider — renting car seats, cribs, and strollers to visiting families.
Chatting with them during deliveries, she spotted a gap and launched the blog El Salvador Kids Guide, which now brings sponsored reels and paid trip-planning consultations.
The two hustles feed each other. Some families find the guide and then rent gear; others rent first and come back for advice.
If you’re already the go-to travel planner in your circle, that’s a skill you can monetize — see Episode 670 with Bailey Richert.
11. Digital Nomad Co-Living and Retreats
Danny Flood had been traveling for years as a digital nomad, selling courses online through a partnership with AppSumo.
A friend in Greece invited him to a villa in the countryside, and Danny started organizing co-living retreats there.
The first one had three people, four including him. The next year he expanded to Nepal. Two years later, roughly 35 or 36 people came to the co-living in Pokhara.
Then people suggested a summit. He hosted one with more than 120 participants, with the Nepali government and tourism board attending. He’s back in September for the co-living and a second summit at digitalnomadsnepal.com, with about 40 speakers.
His advice: find a location that isn’t saturated, run it in shoulder season, pick a clear niche, and use good photos. Some of his first posts were just on Reddit.
If events appeal to you, try Episode 634 with Chloe Winstanley, or Episode 297 with Hung Pham on The Culture Summit.
12. Online English Lessons
Monica is the founder of English with Monica. She went from 524 TikTok followers to 70,000 in a year by going live four times a week and actually engaging.
That audience unlocked bootcamps, digital products, and memberships.
There are dozens of sites where you can teach English online, but it’s usually one-on-one, and typical rates might be $10-25 an hour.
If you build your own audience like Monica did, you become a market of one — and that changes what you can earn from the same skill.
13. Turning “Can You Help With My Resumé?” Into a Business
Two callers, nearly the same story — both started by request, not marketing:
Cyril (DareToCloud.com)
Cyril, a guitar teacher, was asked by a student’s mom to help with her CV.
He was great at it, got her up to speed on a required CRM, and she landed her dream job.
His realization: the real skill was communicating clearly to a specific person — “a CV is basically a landing page for a human.”
That’s now what he does for a living (website maintenance and SEO for B2B companies).
Balkisu Fidelis (Kisu’s CVs Collection)
Balkisu started by helping a friend apply for a job. Later that month, the friend referred someone else. Before long, people were paying her to write and improve CVs and cover letters.
Both started by request, not from marketing. That’s a great sign — if people ask for your help without you even trying, that’s real perceived expertise.
Years ago, Austin Church from Episode 417 told us to pay attention to what wants to happen. There’s also the Tim Ferriss line: what would this look like if it were easy?
If a project has sat on the back burner for years, maybe it doesn’t want to happen. And that’s okay.
14. Affiliate Marketing Without an Audience
Anthony Smith makes money recommending digital marketing products — no big audience, funnels, or paid ads. Here’s an example of his Stan Store.
His first sales came from simply sharing useful info with people already looking to grow their businesses.
His takeaways:
- People respond to authenticity — you don’t have to be an expert
- Consistency beats perfection
That’s sales 101 — be a listener first and a problem solver second.
Your Turn

If you have a fun, random, or creative side hustle to share, I’d love to hear it and possibly feature you in an upcoming episode.

title: $500/Week as a Mystery Shopper: Getting Paid to Shop, Eat, and Snoop
full_content:
Getting paid to eat at restaurants, tour apartments, and run your car through the wash 20 times in an afternoon? That’s mystery shopping — a $2 billion industry most people have never heard of.
Mercedes Eckert has been doing it for 13 years and has helped over 25,000 shoppers get started through her company, iShopAGP.com.
Her personal best: $600 in a single day without getting out of the car.
She also runs ShopQuest, a free site where you can browse mystery shopper jobs in your city.
Tune into Episode 752 of the Side Hustle Show to learn:
- how mystery shoppers actually get paid
- how to stack jobs together into a $600 day
- the common scams to watch out for
Sponsors
- Quo (formerly OpenPhone) — Try it for free!
- Shopify — Sign up for a $1 per month trial!
- Gusto — Get 3 months free of the leading payroll, benefits, and HR provider for modern small businesses!
- Wealthfront — Start earning up to 4.30% variable APY today! Terms and conditions apply.
- Monarch — Get an extended 30-day free trial!
How Much Money Can You Make Mystery Shopping?
One of Mercedes’s shoppers recently did a few apartment mystery shops and made $850 in less than two days. She toured units as a fake renter and rated the leasing agent.
Based on iShop’s data, side hustlers average $200 to $500 a week. You’re paid by the job, not the hour. Mercedes’s best day was $600. Her easiest shop paid $300 for 30 minutes of taking screenshots on her couch.
If you want an hourly number, the low end is around $25 to $40.
Can You Do It Full Time?
Yes. Mercedes knows one shopper who makes over six figures a year doing this full time. Another shopper made $65,000 and change in 2025.
Most people fit it around a job, though. They shop after work or on their days off.
Who Hires Mystery Shoppers and Why
Big companies want to know what is happening in their stores from a real customer’s point of view. They cannot be everywhere at once, so they hire it out.
That feedback gets used in a lot of ways:
- Updating the training manual
- Hiring more staff
- Sometimes letting staff go
Mercedes says the goal is usually coaching, not firing.
One thing to know: the brand does not hire you directly.
Companies outsource their mystery shopping programs to separate companies called providers. You contract with the provider.
That means you are not going to roll up to Target and hand the manager a business card.
How to Find Legit Mystery Shopping Jobs
There are somewhere between 100 and 150 provider companies out there. You can research them yourself, or you can go through a mystery shopping organization that trains you and connects you with partners they have already vetted.
Once you are contracted with a provider, you can start picking up shops the same day.
Mercedes named Reality Based Group as a good one to look at. But she says the “best” provider changes depending on what you want to do.
Every provider has its own set of clients. One might specialize in the auto industry, with car dealerships and mechanic shops.
Another might be loaded with food shops — fast food, casual dining, fine dining. After a few shops, you will figure out what you like and which companies have it.
iShop, MSPA, and What an Organization Actually Does
I had signed up with MSPA (Mystery Shopping Providers Association) years ago and assumed it was some kind of industry certification.
Mercedes explained that iShop does essentially the same thing MSPA does. They are just newer.
Neither one is a provider. They are recruiters and trainers.
They give you a home base, train you, and connect you with legitimate companies. Most mystery shoppers are with one or the other.
Do Not Sign Up With 100 Companies at Once
New shoppers often want to see every single shop available. Mercedes says slow down.
Start with a handful, learn the ropes, then expand.
Signing up with 150 providers at once is like signing up for DoorDash 150 times. You will just get overwhelmed.
Skip the Apps, Go to the Websites
Mercedes does not send new shoppers to apps. There are a few mystery shopping apps, but they are third parties, not the actual providers.
Go to each provider’s website instead.
On an app, you will not see everything that is available, and what you do see tends to be the lower paying shops.
What Is Route Shopping?
Route shopping is how shoppers make the big money. You pick a day, string together several shops, and knock them out in one trip.
You can do the same type of shop at 5 different locations. Or you can mix it up, which is what Mercedes likes to do.
She would line up a few apartment shops, then drop a breakfast shop and a lunch shop in between so her meals were covered. Then she would add a gas station shop so her gas was covered too.
The important part: you build the route yourself. It does not come as a package. You can pull shops from several different companies into one day.
What the Work Actually Looks Like
One of Mercedes’s favorite routes was car washes. One day a month, she would go out and get her car washed about 20 times. She never even got out of the car. She made $600 and was home in time for dinner with her kids.
Each shop meant:
- getting the wash
- noting the name of the employee who greeted her
- snapping a few photos inside the car wash
- and filling out the report
The report usually took her under 15 minutes.
You can do reports from your phone, but Mercedes prefers a laptop. It is cleaner, there is more room on the screen, and she is not getting notifications while she types.
Most reports are questionnaires. Some ask for a written narrative in complete sentences, which trips up more people than you’d think.
Also, you almost never need a disguise. Providers use rotation instead, meaning a shop you do this month may be locked to you for 30 days.
Do You Have to Pay Out of Pocket?
Mercedes says sometimes. A car wash, restaurant, or movie theater can’t be judged unless you’re a paying customer. You pay up front and get reimbursed on payday.
Plenty of shops require nothing, while apartment shops are the best example — you tour, evaluate, and spend nothing.
Pay schedules vary by provider, and PayPal is the most common method.
Mystery Shopping vs. Merchandising
I tested an app called Hetal, where the job was to go to Target and scan the aisles.
One assignment covered about 65 aisles and took roughly an hour and 45 minutes. It worked out to about $20 an hour.
Mercedes pointed out that this is technically merchandising, not mystery shopping. A lot of mystery shopping companies offer both, so you will run into it.
The difference is simple. Mystery shopping is about evaluating customer service. Merchandising is about the merchandise — taking pictures, putting stickers on products, that kind of thing.
Merchandising usually pays less, and it is more likely to be paid by the hour. Some shoppers love it and some hate it. Given the choice, most would rather do a true mystery shop where they are getting paid to do something they were already going to do.
How to Build a Good Reputation as a Mystery Shopper
Mystery shopping is a $2 billion industry, but Mercedes says it is also very small. The key players all know each other, and word of mouth spreads fast.
There are really only two things you need to do.
- Do good work. Do not flake on shops you agreed to take. Turn in your reports on time and follow the instructions.
- Get in front of the company reps in person. That mostly means conferences. There are only two mystery shopping conferences, and Mercedes runs one of them.
When a shopper does good work, providers tell each other. It is not a competition between them. They will pass your name around for you.
iShop’s conference is in Vegas this year. The first was in 2022, last year drew over 100 people, and they’re hoping for 200.
Worried about saturation? A VP at one provider told Mercedes they release 35,000 to 40,000 shops a month and still need fresh faces.
Mystery Shopping Scams to Avoid
Two show up constantly:
- The check in the mail. Someone sends a check, maybe $2,000, and asks you to cash it. One of Mercedes’s shoppers did and had her bank account compromised.
- The gift card ask. Buy 10 gift cards, scratch off the codes, send them over. You’ll never see that money again.
The rule: if anyone promises you money before you work, it’s a scam.
One more check — look at the email domain after the @ symbol. If it’s Gmail instead of the company’s real site, walk away.
Tools/Tech
- MileIQ — mileage tracking. You’re an independent contractor, so miles are a write-off.
- ShopQuest — free directory of shops in your area. Launched 3 months ago with thousands of listings.
A single sign-up system across all providers is what her team is working toward. Shoppers used to mail in paper reports, so the tech is moving fast.
Can You Get Paid to Travel as a Mystery Shopper?
Yes, and Mercedes has done it. She has been paid to fly to other states and to stay at out-of-state resorts.
She has a friend who mystery shops all over the world — Dubai, China, the UK, and Hawaii. Mercedes brings her to the conferences to talk to shoppers about traveling for work.
About three weeks before this interview, one of her partner companies called to say they needed people for resort mystery shops in Cabo San Lucas.
The trick is finding the providers that specialize in travel, since not every company has those clients.
Is Paid Mystery Shopping Training Worth It?
Why pay for training when you can sign up with providers for free?
Mercedes’s answer comes down to three things.
- Charging for training is industry standard – every mystery shopping organization charges for training.
- Providers don’t train you – they’re there to get a job done and are slow to answer emails.
- People who complain about the money – when someone complains that shops only pay $6 or $7, she asks if they started through an organization. The answer is always no.
iShop offers free training, paid training, and ongoing support. If you complete a shop incorrectly, you don’t get paid — so the details matter.
Mistakes to Avoid
The biggest is trying to figure it out alone. That’s how people end up with $6 shops and quit.
The second is sloppy work. Flaking, late reports, or a narrative that gets kicked back will hurt you fast in an industry where everyone talks.
What’s Next for Mercedes?
The conference and the new platform are the two big things right now.
But what she says she loves most is the testimonials. Shoppers who paid off debt, paid for a wedding, or got paid to test drive a luxury car.
One used her mystery shopping money for IVF treatments, got pregnant, and is now expecting her second.
On the business side, working directly with the provider companies has become a two-way street. The providers do not get paid if the shops do not get done, so they need shoppers who will actually show up.
One company rep told Mercedes they filled four hard-to-reach areas with her shoppers.
For finding new shoppers, iShop leans on word of mouth, social media, and ads. Her take is that you should never stop trying new marketing.
Mercedes’s #1 Tip for Side Hustle Nation
“Just show up.”

title: The $2k/Month Mushroom Side Hustle That Bought a 70-Acre Farm
full_content:
What if a spare closet could turn into a farm, a warehouse, and 70 acres of land?
That’s roughly the path Kyle Beaver took. Kyle runs Ten Mile Mushrooms in rural Pennsylvania, along with Pro Grow Club, and he grows gourmet and medicinal mushrooms like oyster, lion’s mane, and reishi.
Before mushrooms, Kyle spent two years working state fairs in Pennsylvania, selling stuffed pretzels out of a food truck.
Watching people drive 3 hours for a pretzel taught him what he wanted in his own business: something niche, something nobody nearby was doing, and something he could run in a very small space.
A Google search for businesses you can run in a small space led him to a mushroom growing page from the UK. Almost 10 years later, that search has turned into a multi-six-figure operation.
Tune in to Episode 753 of the Side Hustle Show to learn:
- how to start growing gourmet mushrooms for $300
- where to sell mushrooms and what they’re worth per pound
- how a $1,000/year farm can unlock a $600,000 land loan
Get Personalized Side Hustle Ideas

How Kyle Found the Mushroom Business Idea
Kyle wasn’t searching for mushrooms. He was searching for businesses he could run in a small amount of space.
The UK page he found broke down how much money you could earn per square meter each year. That got his attention. So did the fact that nobody in his area was growing these mushrooms.
He checked local farmers markets and found no competitors. Even the large supermarkets near him still don’t carry gourmet mushrooms today.
Kyle grows wood-loving species, the kind you’d find in the wild. That includes:
- oyster
- lion’s mane
- reishi
- other medicinal types showing up in mushroom coffee
“Nobody’s doing this in the area. I haven’t even heard of these mushrooms,” he said.
What It Costs to Start a Mushroom Growing Side Hustle
Less than almost any other agricultural business.
- Kyle’s actual startup cost: $300 – straw and poly tubing, oyster mushrooms grown in a spare room with no fans or coolers
- Farmers market setup: $200-300 – a tent, table, cash box, and a small business insurance policy (typically $1M, and cheap)
- A full grow-and-sell setup: a couple thousand dollars
He had no money and no credit when he started.
His advice is to get a few grows under your belt before building out a real grow room — a closet, spare room, or front porch is genuinely enough to begin.
How Much Money Can You Make Growing Mushrooms?
The grow tent behind Kyle on our call is 4 square feet. It produces 16 pounds of mushrooms every two weeks — and it doesn’t have a shelf in it yet.
- Farmers market retail: $24–$30 per pound fresh, sold in half- and quarter-pound packs
- Wholesale to restaurants: $10–$12 per pound, roughly half the margin
- Per grow block: a $10 block yields 2–4 pounds, producing $60–$80 of retail revenue
That’s north of 75% gross margin on cost of goods.
For comparison, Kyle cites industry figures showing an acre of corn nets negative $150.
Specialty mushrooms are one of the few crops where a genuinely small farm still clears a living.
Understanding Flushes and Yields
Grow blocks usually give 2 to 3 good flushes, or rounds of growth. The first flush is always the biggest.
Most commercial growers only take that first flush. After harvesting, you’d wait another two weeks before seeing any new growth, which creates a traffic jam in a small grow room.
If space is tight, there’s still a use for spent blocks. Bury them in the garden and you can get another pound or two.
Kyle also warned about the “infinite mushroom hack” you’ll see online, where you regrow mushrooms from scraps over and over.
Mushrooms get genetically weaker each time you do this. Commercial growers start fresh every week instead, which is how Kyle can count on 50 pounds a week.
Where to Sell Mushrooms: 4 Sales Channels
For a small mushroom farm, there are four main outlets:
- Farmers markets – the highest price per pound
- CSAs – subscription boxes for local produce
- Direct to customer – online sales of kits, dried mushrooms, and tinctures
- Wholesale – restaurants and other buyers
Farmers markets are where things took off for Kyle. Shoppers walk past table after table of familiar vegetables, then stop when they see something they’ve never seen before.
Kyle has never run his own CSA, but he’s been part of several. A mushroom-only CSA is tough, so it works better to team up with other farmers and offer a full box.
Why Selling Grow Blocks Beats Selling Mushrooms
Kyle’s revenue didn’t scale from mushrooms. It scaled from what he built around them.
- Tinctures came first – a $45 jar that sells instantly once customers hear it’s made in-house
- Dried mushrooms followed
- Grow blocks turned out to be more profitable than the fresh product
The real inflection point came a couple years into farmers markets, when another farm asked him to supply ready-to-fruit blocks in bulk.
That one request changed the trajectory.
He now ships starter blocks to small farms across the country — filling a supply gap Kyle didn’t know existed until somebody asked him to fill it.
How a Small Farm Can Unlock a USDA Land Loan
To be considered a farm, you need to:
- Sell $1,000 of agricultural products a year
- Register an LLC as a farm and show income
- After 3 years of tax returns, apply for a USDA Beginning Farmer and Rancher loan through the Farm Service Agency
- Up to $600,000, zero down, very low interest
Kyle’s loan financed an 8,000 square foot warehouse and a 70-acre homestead at 3% interest — $1,900 a month. A conventional raw land loan runs 8–12%.
Mushrooms also qualify as urban farming, which sidesteps most state acreage requirements.
Agritourism and Airbnb: Making Farmland Pay for Itself
A handful of bookings a month covers Kyle’s entire $1,900 loan payment.
Current and planned listings:
- An Airstream-style trailer – the first unit
- A small camper out back
- A second-story apartment inside the warehouse itself
- A cabin under construction, bought cheap from a nearby amusement park campground
Location does much of the work. He’s 12 minutes from an amusement park, beside a UTV and four-wheeler riding area, and on the edge of Pennsylvania’s coal region — where land dilapidated by mining now draws quad riders.
The standard rule of thumb for short-term rentals: within an hour of a metro, 30 minutes of a regional destination, close enough to town to hire cleaners.
This connects to Episode 686 with Garrett Brown, the land hacking episode I recommend if this idea appeals to you.
How to Find Grants for a Small Farm
Grants have become a major revenue source. Kyle said they’ve been awarded hundreds of thousands of dollars for the coming year.
One pending research grant could cover his salary and every employee’s salary for a year. He expects grant projects to nearly double revenue in 2027.
One catch: many grants are reimbursement-based. You spend first, submit receipts, and get paid back, so you need some cushion.
Here’s where Kyle looks:
- grants.gov – the biggest source for federal grants, though not the easiest site to use
- SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) – offices in all four corners of the country, with at least four grants a year that apply to most farmers
- Farm Service Agency and your local USDA office – once they know you, they’ll send opportunities directly. Kyle got a $15,000 marketing grant with a one-page application
- sam.gov — the government registration side of the process
- Local business development groups — Kyle’s is called SEDA CoG, and most areas have something similar with state or city grants for small farms
Tools/Tech
- AI tools – Kyle uses AI for grant research and for creating application materials. He says it’s easily doubled how many grants they can apply for
- Content Creator MACHINE – the all-in-one platform Kyle uses to post social media, run email marketing, build funnels, and manage customers as a CRM
- Go High Level and Pablo – similar all-in-one platforms Kyle mentioned
- YouTube – Kyle credits it with teaching him how to build his entire farm and fix nearly everything on it
- Grow fans and growing tech – makes the day-to-day operation of a grow room easier
A Day in the Life
Kyle is in the middle of stepping out of the operator role and into the owner role. They now have a manager and people in set positions.
Much of his day is spent talking with the other small farms his business supplies across the country, troubleshooting and walking growers through problems.
His mornings start at 5 a.m. with the gym, then email and computer work. Around 8 a.m. the crew arrives, and about ten minutes later something breaks.
“So then I’ll become a mechanic or a welder for an hour,” he said. You can also find him at @GrowMushMore on YouTube.
Mistakes or Surprises?
Kyle’s biggest surprise wasn’t about money. He set out to become a business owner and ended up passionate about ecology and small agriculture.
He didn’t expect the community either. Kyle was a lone wolf for years before realizing he needed mentors and people who had walked the path ahead of him.
He also sees where new growers get stuck, and it isn’t the growing. Mushrooms are fairly easy to grow, especially if you buy blocks from a supplier.
“A lot of folks are just getting tripped up at the we need to actually sell these things,” he said.
Sales and marketing is the skill that decides whether a mushroom farm works.
What’s Next for Kyle?
Kyle is focused on Pro Grow Club, the monthly grow kit program at progrowclub.com. Surveys from the past year showed that most of his audience are complete beginners who’ve never heard of these mushrooms.
He also runs a program called Farm Launch, which helps people start a profitable mushroom farm within six weeks.
He expects that within three years there will be success stories of people who started with one or two blocks in a closet and went on to buy their own property.

title: $3k a Month Renting Out Mobility Scooters Part-Time
full_content:
I love a good rental business: buy something once and get paid for it over and over again.
It’s a cool model, and this week’s guest found a creative approach to it in the mobility scooter niche.
Lenny Tim from LAMobilityScooterRentals.com is a serial side hustler and entrepreneur involved in the e-commerce and YouTube space. He built his scooter rental to $3k a month in his spare time.
Tune in to the Side Hustle Show interview to hear how:
- Lenny discovered his niche
- found his first customers
- expanded his fleet and operations
