title: Labor and Coalition close in on deal on gambling reforms
full_content:
Government agrees to ad opt-out register in deal with Coalition to pass gambling reforms
In short:
Labor and the Coalition have agreed to establish a single register allowing Australians to opt out of wagering ads across online platforms, as part of a tentative deal to pass gambling reforms.
The amendments would also restrict inducements targeting vulnerable gamblers and crack down on spending-based commissions for VIP account managers.
What's next?
The deal will go to Labor's caucus and the Coalition's party room for final approval tomorrow, before the amendments are moved in parliament.
A "one-stop shop" allowing Australians to opt out of wagering advertising online has been agreed to by Labor and the Coalition in a tentative deal to pass the federal government's gambling reforms.
The government and opposition briefed a Labor backbench committee and the Coalition shadow ministry on about 15 amendments this evening, ahead of a full caucus and party room meeting for final approval tomorrow morning.
With shadow cabinet backing the bill, it is expected to pass — however Liberal sources have told the ABC some in the party are considering crossing the floor because they believe the laws still won't be strong enough.
Communications Minister Anika Wells used a speech in parliament today, before the deal was finalised, to signal Labor was poised to move on so-called gambling inducements and online ads, after criticism its bill did not go far enough.
"It is expected that the government's reforms will respond to these concerns by introducing new restrictions on inducement-based marketing and establishing the wagering advertising opt-out register, which will provide Australians with a one-stop shop to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms," she said.
In addition to TV and radio restrictions, the government's current draft bill creates a "triple lock" system that would require social media, streaming and other online platforms only show gambling ads to logged-in users verified as over 18.
The platforms would also have to give every adult the ability to opt out, a system criticised by the Greens and Coalition as too onerous for Australians who would have to do this manually for every online account.
Some of the naysayers had advocated for an opt-in system instead, but as the ABC revealed, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was not prepared to entertain such a large change.
Instead, the compromise position put forward by the Coalition was to create a single register for Australians to indicate their wish to opt out of gambling ads.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Mr Albanese met several times to negotiate the gambling laws, which Labor is seeking to pass by the end of this week.
Proposed opt-out register questioned by industry
The opt-out register would be established by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), with people able to request their various online accounts be blocked from viewing gambling advertising.
It is understood the plan would be for people to provide information such as their email address linked to the platform they are seeking to opt out of ads on.
The register is not expected to be in place immediately from January 1, when the broader ad restrictions are due to take effect.
Its principle would be similar to the existing "do not call" register, which is a secure government database where Australians can opt out of receiving unsolicited telemarketing calls.
But tonight, multiple sources in the wagering and tech industry immediately questioned how this approach would be feasible, given the complexity and breadth of online platforms.
There were also concerns raised about who would pay for the register and how.
Currently, the federal government's wagering self-exclusion register, Betstop, is funded by gambling companies, who contribute an amount effectively based on a ratio of their market share.
But one wagering source said companies did not expect to pay for the administration of a second register for advertising.
A tech industry source said an opt-out system made available to individuals was "very different" compared to requiring platforms to proactively comply with a centralised register.
Targeted restriction of inducements proposed
Rather than a broader crackdown on gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, amendments to the legislation are aimed at protecting vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.
It is understood this would include creating a cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending inducements to any new accounts or to people who have recently removed themselves from Betstop.
The proposed amendments are also expected to crack down on VIP account managers at wagering companies earning commissions based on their clients' spending.
The ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp have already stopped this practice.
Discussions are also ongoing about an independent review mechanism to assess the effectiveness of the laws in the future.
Last week, Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament to back this idea.
"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more,"
Senate inquiry report makes one recommendation
A report released tonight, following a short two-day inquiry into the government's gambling legislation earlier this month, recommended the bills be passed.
The single recommendation from the government-authored report was described as "not surprising, but tragic" by independent ACT senator David Pocock.
"We heard from basically everyone other than the gambling companies who said this bill does not protect children, it doesn't break the link between sport and gambling companies," he told the ABC.
Senator Pocock wrote a dissenting report from the inquiry, calling on the government to implement the original recommendations put forward in the You Win Some, You Lose More report by late Labor MP Peta Murphy.
This included a full ban on gambling ads being phased in over three years, an immediate ban on gambling inducements, and the establishment of a single national online gambling regulator.
Senator Pocock also provided fallback amendments to strengthen Labor's existing bill, including extending the gambling ad ban during live sport to after 8:30pm, and replacing the online opt-out "triple lock" system with an opt-in model.
In his report, Senator Pocock referenced evidence given to the inquiry by the family of a 24-year-old man with a severe gambling addiction who died by suicide.
The witnesses told the Senate committee there were "no words to describe this pain", and the family now "lives a half-life".
The Greens also provided a dissenting report, arguing the minor party would not support the bill in its current form.
Greens communications spokeswoman senator Sarah Hanson-Young called for a complete ban on all online gambling ads, the establishment of a national regulator and an end to inducements.
She also recommended the introduction of separate legislation requiring gambling companies to forfeit money they received that was the proceeds of crime.
That was based on evidence heard by the inquiry that wagering companies could retain money gambled by customers who obtained it through criminal offending.

title: At least 68 killed in Indonesia quake as aftershocks hamper rescue efforts
full_content:
Indonesia earthquake death toll rises to 68 as aftershocks and access hamper rescue efforts
In short:
At least 68 people have been killed and 200 injured following a magnitude-7.7 earthquake in Indonesia.
Nearly 1,600 aftershocks have been detected in the province since the powerful earthquake struck, with thousands of people sheltering in tents and government buildings afraid to return home.
What's next?
Displaced people have been awaiting aid for some days but organisations say access to isolated communities is starting to improve.
The number of people killed in a powerful earthquake in eastern Indonesia has risen to 68 as rescue workers continue to search for people trapped under rubble.
Almost 13,000 people have been evacuated following the country's deadliest disaster since 2022, with many sheltering in tents outdoors or at schools and police stations afraid to return to their homes due to fears of aftershocks.
Nearly 1,600 aftershocks have been detected in the province since Saturday, when the magnitude-7.7 quake hit the Indonesian island of Flores.
One of the most prominent, a 5.6 magnitude earthquake, was recorded on Monday morning, local time, according to the country's geophysics agency.
An official at Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency, Berton SP Panjaitan, confirmed the death toll had risen to 68, up from 54, on Monday night, local time, and that more than 200 people had been injured.
More than 1,300 homes have been damaged, with nearly 250 destroyed on Flores alone, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.
Military and police officers have been deployed across the disaster zone, supported by 10 aircraft to distribute 275 tonnes of aid to the area.
But logistical challenges have slowed deliveries to some hard-hit communities, according to Abdul Muhari, deputy chief of the country's disaster management agency.
Indonesian Red Cross' head of disaster management Ridwan Sobri Carman said access to isolated communities had started to improve which meant they could help with evacuation efforts and providing first aid.
"Our team is also working with the local authorities in seven districts to reach communities affected by landslides," he told The World.
"At the moment, infrastructure is quite critical."
He said while the worst of the damage had occurred in Flores, some islands close by had also been affected.
The National Disaster Management Agency was working with federal and international agencies on the disaster response and emergency fund, according to Ridwan Sobri Carman.
"Our houses are no longer liveable, because many have collapsed and are full of cracks, so we can't go inside anymore," Mbay resident Junaidin told AFP outside a self-made tent that was sleeping about 30 people.
"We only go back home to get water, clothes, pillows, and then we… spend the nights here."
Authorities have also set up two emergency field hospitals in the worst-hit town of Ruteng to treat earthquake victims after local hospitals were damaged, with two crisis management teams overseeing a health emergency operation centre, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.
During Indonesia's Independence Day ceremony in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto asked for people to pray for those affected by disasters in East Nusa Tenggara and other parts of the country, while leading a nationwide moment of silence honouring the nation's independence heroes.
But those affected by the disaster have called on the government to do more.
"As for help from the government, there hasn't been any — no tents, no medicine, no food, no drinking water, nothing," said Junaidin, who only has one name.
"Please open your eyes, government. We are your people, we are part of you. So please look after us."

title: Trump threatens Oman as Iran vows to escalate conflict over Hormuz
full_content:
Donald Trump has threatened to "bomb the s***" out of US ally Oman if it "gets in the way" of US efforts to broker a deal on the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian and Omani officials have been holding talks on future maritime navigation in the waterway, which the US president has suggested could become American territory.
It comes as a 60-day memorandum of understanding between America and Iran for time to broker a broader deal on ending the conflict expires.
US President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Oman if it blocks American efforts to take control of the Strait of Hormuz, as he continues to press Iran to surrender.
It comes as Iran signals it may shift to a more aggressive military stance if peace talks with the US fail to reach an outcome.
"If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the s*** out of them," Mr Trump told Fox News journalist Trey Yingst, referring to ongoing talks between Oman and Iran on control of the strait.
Iranian and Omani officials have been talking for weeks on future maritime navigation arrangements through the Strait of Hormuz, which Mr Trump has floated as a future US territory.
Iran's coast flanks the north side of Hormuz and Oman lies on the south.
Progress towards peace talks and a resumption of oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz has ground to a halt, with no sign that the warring parties are moving towards ending the conflict that the US and Israel launched on February 28.
"Iranian entities must be prepared to escalate tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and wider region, as Iran will be ready to make decisions and take action on difficult decisions," the Iranian official said, adding that Tehran would conduct a "timely and precise" military attack to break the US naval blockade if diplomacy failed.
Monday marked the day by which Iran and the United States were expected to reach a final deal under a memorandum of understanding agreed in June and aimed at ending the war.
Signed on June 17, the MoU set out a 60-day time-frame, extendable by mutual consent, by which Washington and Tehran should reach an agreement that would cover broader issues such as the fate of Iran's nuclear programme.
The MoU, which declared the immediate and permanent cessation of military operations on all fronts, quickly unravelled, however, due to a dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran to set deadline
Tehran said point five of the MoU gives it the right to manage the waterway, while Washington rejected that interpretation.
Hostilities resumed as Tehran began firing on vessels it said were trying to sail through the waterway on an unapproved route.
US President Donald Trump said on July 7 that the pact was "over". Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of consistently violating its commitments.
"Within the short period of a few weeks set by Iran, all the agreement's provisions must be implemented by the US. This is a precondition for further negotiations with the US," the Iranian official told Reuters, adding that mediators would share Tehran's deadline with Washington and regional states.
Both Iran and the United States have stepped up rhetoric over the past week.
Mr Trump warned Americans in a speech at a rally on Friday to prepare for continued high fuel prices as a result of the war, while also saying that "after we finish defeating Iran … pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States".
Earlier on Monday, Mr Trump posted on his Truth Social platform: "The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon", repeating one of his stated rationales for the war.

title: Ancient clash with 'Kraken' galaxy 12 billion years ago helped form Milky Way
full_content:
Massive 12-billion-year-old galactic collision helped form the Milky Way
In short:
Astronomers have found evidence that our galaxy, the Milky Way, collided with another — the "Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles" galaxy — about 12 billion years ago.
The galactic merger happened in between the formation of the Milky Way and another collision with a galaxy dubbed "Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus".
What's next?
Data from newer telescopes will help to establish more of the Milky Way's history, but in the meantime it's heading towards another galaxy.
Our home galaxy the Milky Way has grown in size by crashing into its neighbours for billions of years.
One of the biggest crashes we know of, just over 10 billion years ago, was with a galaxy with the enigmatic name of "Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus".
Now, evidence is mounting that another, similarly large, galactic merger happened 2 billion years prior.
In a study published in Nature Astronomy, researchers have dubbed this merging galaxy "Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles" after a Nordic sea monster and a Greek god (we'll get into how galaxies are named later).
Lead author Davide Massari, a researcher at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics, said the existence of the 12-billion-year-old merger had been hotly debated.
To gather more evidence about the ancient galaxy, the researchers studied the ages of tight-knit groups of stars known as "globular clusters".
The ages and chemical compositions of each cluster pointed to the galaxies they originally formed in, before they mixed with the Milky Way in a merger event.
"Finding such a clear-cut signature in the age of globular clusters made us very happy," Dr Massari said.
Galactic archaeology on clusters of stars
The Milky Way first formed about 800 million years after the big bang 13.8 billion years ago.
Back then our galaxy would have been a small disc of gas.
Today, the Milky Way is about 100,000 light years across and contains up to 400 billion stars.
Previous studies suggest most of these stars formed between 11 and 7 billion years ago.
Luca Casagrande, an astrophysicist at the Australian National University who wasn't involved with the research, said that younger galaxies seen closer to the big bang are all much smaller than our Milky Way.
"We always knew that the Milky Way had to go through several merger events to build up,"
"The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus is the easy one to detect. The other ones are harder and so there is always a degree of uncertainty."
The European Space Agency's Gaia satellite had helped establish the existence of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger, according to Dr Casagrande.
In the new study, the researchers used data from the Hubble Space Telescope to study globular clusters.
"They determined the ages very, very precisely, of these globular clusters and with that very high precision in the ages, they were able to see essentially three main groups," Dr Casagrande said.
One of these age groups is from the original Milky Way, while another age group corresponds to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event.
The researchers found a distinct set of globular clusters in between these two age groups, which they said was another "satellite" galaxy that was absorbed by the Milky Way.
Duncan Forbes, an astrophysicist at Swinburne University who wasn't involved in the study, said several other astronomers (including him) had previously suggested this third large galaxy existed.
"The globular clusters of this satellite have distinctive ages and chemical properties," he said.
Professor Forbes said this study had "more statistical weight" than previous research.
"With more precise relative ages, Massari [and colleagues] were able to estimate when the satellite was accreted onto the infant Milky Way," he said.
"They agree with my previous work that the satellite was one of the most massive to merge with the Milky Way as it grew in mass over cosmic time."
Sausage, Kraken… Koala?
The name of Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles comes from a combination of names suggested by different research groups while the third galaxy theory was being built.
"Low-energy" refers to the low-energy orbits of the clusters, "Kraken" is a nod to the elusive Scandinavian sea monster, and "Heracles" hails from the Greek hero associated with the formation of the Milky Way.
"A few years ago, I suggested that this satellite galaxy be called 'Koala' because both are associated with low energy,"
The name mirrors Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus: an amalgam derived from the Gaia satellite, the sausage-like shape of data from early analyses, and the son of Gaia from Greek mythology.
"For these satellite galaxies there doesn't seem to be an official naming convention," Professor Forbes said.
More mergers in Milky Way's past and future
The Milky Way is not done absorbing galaxies: it's currently merging with the small Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, a process that started some 6 billion years ago.
In the next few billion years, it may also collide with the larger Andromeda galaxy, although astronomers aren't confident this will happen.
Dr Massari said it was "possible, but rather unlikely" that there were still undiscovered mergers in the Milky Way's past.
"I do not think there is room for another event this massive, at least in the far away past of our galaxy," he said.
Dr Casagrande said that, while the current study was "thorough", it was still possible there were more undiscovered collisions in our galaxy's past.
"I wouldn't definitely draw the line that it was three main accretion events and that was it," Dr Casagrande said.
"Based on the current data, there is no evidence for more, but we are sampling a region of the galaxy."
Data from newer telescopes and other regions of the galaxy might yet support more mergers, Dr Casagrande said.
"As we probe more of the galaxy and we get more data, then we might be able to recover evidence for maybe even a fourth or a fifth — who knows, right?"

title: Kushner talks with Hamas and Israel end without Gaza deal
full_content:
US holds talks with Hamas and Israel in bid to salvage Gaza peace plan
In short:
Jared Kushner and Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed putting a US general in charge of verifying Hamas's disarmament, with Israel's military to remain place until that happens.
The meeting between the Israeli prime minister and Mr Kushner, who is Donald Trump's special envoy, came a day after he met with Hamas officials in Egypt.
Both meetings appear to have ended without a significant breakthrough.
Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has wrapped up two days of meetings with Israeli and Hamas leaders to break a stalemate over the US president's Gaza plan, but there were no signs of an imminent breakthrough as both sides dug in.
Mr Kushner met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel a day after meeting Hamas' political leader in Egypt in a bid to revive the plan, which has stalled as Israel has carried out air strikes and seized more territory in Gaza despite an October ceasefire, while Hamas has refused to give up its weapons.
The US president last month announced that Hamas had agreed to lay down its arms in phases, under a 15-point roadmap put forward by his so-called Board of Peace to advance the president's plan, as Israel's military withdraws from Gaza.
Hamas said it agreed to the roadmap but implementation depended on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including halting attacks and withdrawing.
No breakthrough in Jerusalem
Mr Netanyahu, whose ruling coalition is trailing in Israeli opinion polls ahead of an October national election, earlier this month rejected the roadmap, insisting Israel would not withdraw until Hamas is completely disarmed.
An Israeli official indicated that there was no breakthrough in the meeting, saying Mr Netanyahu had made it clear the military would not withdraw from a demarcation line set out in an October ceasefire and would continue to carry out operations in Gaza as it sees necessary, including targeting those who took part in the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the war.
Hamas has demanded Israel adhere to the ceasefire, while both sides have disputed the sequencing of how Mr Trump's plan to end the war would be implemented. More than 1,200 Palestinians and four Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since October, according to Gazan health officials and the Israeli military.
Two sources said Mr Kushner's meeting with Mr Netanyahu lasted several hours.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace envoy for Gaza who is widely seen as leading efforts to implement the plan, also attended the meeting, the sources told Reuters.
The Israeli official said Mr Netanyahu and Mr Kushner agreed in the meeting that the reconstruction of Gaza would not begin until Hamas was fully disarmed, including of light weapons.
In a statement that characterized the meeting as "deep and constructive", the prime minister's office said that Israel and the Board of Peace believe that Gaza's disarmament should be "prompt and completed before any reconstruction happens".
It also said that Mr Netanyahu had agreed with the Board of Peace to establish a working group on disarmament and demilitarization, and another working group that focuses on sanitation, clean water and other public health issues in Gaza.
A Board of Peace official described the meeting as "in-depth and very productive," saying the two sides had reached an agreement on a path forward. The official did not elaborate.
Reconstruction
US and Israeli officials have previously said that reconstruction could happen in areas of Gaza under Israeli control or a new Palestinian technocratic government.
The Board of Peace has indicated that while rifles would be prohibited, some personal weapons would be permitted under Palestinian law.
Mr Netanyahu is facing a tough reelection campaign and diplomats say it is unlikely Israel's longest-serving prime minister would make any concessions over Gaza before the October 27 vote.
Mr Kushner and Mr Mladenov were in Israel after meeting with Hamas political leader Khalil Al-Hayya in Egypt on Sunday.
It marks Mr Kushner's second known meeting with representatives of Hamas, the Palestinian militant group designated a terrorist movement by the United States.
Mr Kushner previously met Hamas officials alongside US envoy Steve Witkoff in October 2025, helping clinch a deal that led to a ceasefire in Gaza and the release of remaining hostages seized by Hamas.

title: Borderless AI launches Alberni: AI for global compliance
full_content:
Alberni unifies entity formation, global employment law, and compliance operations across 150+ international locations
Borderless AI, the AI-native global employment platform, today announced the launch of Alberni, the AI-powered legal operating system for global employment law and global entity management. Alberni combines legal expertise with custom AI agents, allowing companies to hire and operate internationally without building a legal department in every country.
Managing a global team requires not only best-in-class payroll but also best-in-class employment law and compliance. Every new market brings different localized legal and workplace compliance requirements. Until now, companies have managed it all with a patchwork of local law firms, consultants, and spreadsheets, at a cost that scales with every hire and every border crossed.
Alberni was designed to eliminate the need for patchwork solutions. Borderless AI created Alberni as a single platform that pairs legal expertise with in-house AI, enabling companies to maintain a compliant global workforce footprint. This allows companies to handle everything from local entity formation and maintenance to worker classification, statutory deadlines, regulatory change, and workforce disputes. Deep legal expertise sets the foundation; AI makes it fast, consistent, and always on. This means companies no longer have to choose between moving quickly and staying compliant.
The launch comes as AI is rapidly transforming how law firms and in-house legal teams operate. Reports show a clear increase in the use of generative AI by firms and legal departments, with nearly half reporting use of AI in 2026 compared to just one quarter last year. There is a growing wave of new generation AI-native law firms, built without billable hours and staffed by lawyers working alongside AI.
However, legal AI is largely focused on law firms and litigators. Alberni brings the same legal expertise directly to companies. The companies for whom global compliance is a daily operational reality, not a matter for outside counsel. Global employment requires more than legal knowledge. It requires infrastructure, operational experience, and systems that scale. By combining Borderless AI’s global operations know-how with legal expertise, Alberni makes a company’s global operations compliant by default in every jurisdiction in which it operates.
“Companies have always faced a barrier to hiring globally while remaining compliant; every new market means more law firms, more retainers, and more risk,” says Willson Cross, CEO and Co-founder of Borderless AI. “We built Alberni so legal and regulatory compliance works like infrastructure: always on, always current, and smarter with every case. The companies that define the next decade will hire everywhere. We’re giving teams an easier and safer way to make that happen.”
With Alberni, companies get:
- Entity infrastructure — legal entity formation, maintenance, and compliance monitoring across 150+ jurisdictions, with speed to market in every new region.
- Compliance operations — worker classification workflows, statutory deadline tracking, regulatory monitoring, and workforce dispute management.
- AI-powered legal intelligence — AI case intake, case analysis grounded in historical outcomes, automated scheduling of deadlines and procedures, document generation, and a caseload intelligence dashboard.
- Compounding context — every entity, case, and jurisdiction lives in one system, so advice gets more tailored the longer you work with Alberni, and accountability transfers to purpose-built infrastructure instead of a growing legal headcount.

title: Uno de cada cuatro directivos afirma que los errores de la IA llegaron al público o al directorio, según una nueva investigación de Workiva
full_content:
Aunque el 84 % de los directivos confía al menos en cierta medida en los resultados de la IA sin revisión humana, solo el 11 % considera que sus datos tienen la calidad necesaria para utilizar esta tecnología
Workiva Inc. (NYSE: WK), una plataforma líder para fortalecer la confianza, la transparencia y la rendición de cuentas y facilitar el cumplimiento de los requisitos de auditoría, presentó hoy los resultados de su Encuesta de Referencia para Directivos del primer semestre de 2026.
Aunque el 84 % de los directivos encuestados confía al menos en cierta medida en la precisión de los resultados de la IA sin revisión humana, uno de cada cuatro (26 %) afirma que las auditorías internas detectaron errores de la IA que llegaron al público o a miembros del directorio. Los resultados muestran una diferencia entre la percepción de los directivos y lo que ocurre en la práctica. Mientras la IA transforma las empresas a una velocidad sin precedentes, surge un nuevo riesgo: que el ritmo de esta transformación supere la capacidad de los líderes responsables de supervisarla.
«Confiar en la IA sin controlar la calidad de los datos es un riesgo, no una estrategia. Los directores financieros necesitan plataformas que conecten la IA con información confiable y auditable, para poder comprobar cada resultado y respaldar cada dato que presentan», afirmó Barbara Larson, directora financiera de Workiva. «Hacerlo bien implica mucho más que evitar errores. Cuando confían en los resultados que generan sus sistemas, los líderes pueden avanzar más rápido e incorporar la IA de manera más profunda en sus operaciones. Esa es una verdadera ventaja competitiva».
La calidad de los datos amenaza la precisión de la IA y la confianza de los inversores
Los directivos coinciden en gran medida en que la baja calidad de los datos limita el uso de la IA en sus organizaciones. Esto demuestra que su adopción a gran escala depende de contar con información confiable y poder controlarla. Los inversores institucionales comparten estas inquietudes y también cuestionan la precisión de los contenidos generados por IA.
- Solo el 11 % considera que sus datos tienen la calidad necesaria para utilizar IA
- El 27 % afirma que la baja calidad de los datos frenó significativamente la implementación de la IA en procesos clave
- El 71 % señala que la baja calidad de los datos afectó, al menos de manera moderada, el uso de la IA para elaborar informes financieros y de sustentabilidad
- El 89 % de los inversores manifiesta preocupación por la precisión de la IA en la información que divulgan las empresas
Con el tiempo, los datos deficientes o cuya veracidad no pueda comprobarse pueden afectar la credibilidad de una organización ante sus partes interesadas. Las empresas que no atiendan las preocupaciones sobre la calidad de los datos y las expectativas de los inversores corren el riesgo de quedar rezagadas frente a competidores más proactivos.
A medida que crece el uso de la IA, los directivos reclaman herramientas que permitan supervisarla
Para los equipos de información financiera, y especialmente para los directores financieros, las herramientas que permiten controlar los resultados de la IA son tan importantes como la propia tecnología. A medida que los agentes adquieren mayor autonomía, los directivos prevén una mayor necesidad de contar con infraestructura específica y destacan varias prioridades1:
- El 49 % seguirá necesitando sistemas que mantengan los registros contables oficiales, como los libros mayores
- El 45 % necesitará soluciones que permitan rastrear la información y facilitar las auditorías
- El 55 % necesitará plataformas para gestionar agentes y procesos automatizados
«La IA genérica no alcanza para la elaboración de información financiera. Los inversores, los organismos reguladores y los directorios esperan respuestas confiables. La verdadera ventaja está en utilizar una IA desarrollada para estas necesidades específicas, basada en información sujeta a controles y auditable y complementada con el criterio humano. Así, las organizaciones pueden comprobar los resultados de la IA y respaldar las decisiones y la información que presentan a partir de ellos», afirmó Jason Darby, director financiero de Amalgamated Bank.

title: Why Modern Brokers Are Moving Toward Operational Ecosystems
full_content:
Most brokerage professionals already know where the friction is. The CRM that needs manual updates from the trading system. The IB commission run that takes the finance team two days every month. The bonus campaign had to be reviewed because the cost came in higher than projected. The dealing desk workaround during a volatile session because the margin logic was not pre-configured for it.
These are not signs that something is fundamentally broken. They are signs that the systems running the business were each built for their own purpose and were never designed to share information automatically. That is a very common position to be in, and it has a very practical solution.
The brokers who are gaining the most operational ground in 2026 are not necessarily running more sophisticated strategies or operating in easier markets. They are running connected infrastructure. One environment where the functions that drive the business share a common data layer and act on each other’s outputs without requiring someone to move information between them manually. That is the shift this article is about.
What a Connected Operational Environment Actually Looks Like
Connected does not mean a single dashboard that pulls reports from separate systems. It means the systems themselves are integrated at the data level, so that an action or event in one function can automatically trigger a response in another without human initiation.
A few practical examples of what this looks like when it is working. When a client’s trading behaviour crosses a risk threshold your dealing desk has defined, the CRM flags that account automatically. When an IB’s referred client quality drops based on actual trading data, the commission logic reflects it without a manual review. When a bonus campaign starts generating the pattern of minimum-volume withdrawal activity, the automation layer identifies and acts on it before the cost builds further.
None of these require someone to notice the signal, make a decision, and then execute it manually across two or three separate systems. They happen because the infrastructure is configured to make them happen. The team focuses on the decisions that genuinely require judgment. The operational layer handles the rest.
The Six Functions That Benefit Most From Being Connected
For a forex or CFD broker, there are six operational functions where the benefit of connection is most direct and most measurable through YOONIT Solution.
Dynamic Margin
Dealing desks operate best when they are monitoring and confirming rather than implementing changes manually under pressure. Pre configured rules that execute when defined thresholds are crossed give the desk that position. Without the connection between live trading data and the margin configuration layer, the dealing desk is always responding to conditions that are already further along than the available data shows.
Client Relationship Management – CRM
A CRM is only as useful as the data it has access to. The signals that indicate a client is about to disengage, is ready to increase activity, or needs a specific intervention live in the trading infrastructure. A CRM connected to that data makes retention and reactivation work more precise and more timely. One that is not is working with a partial picture.
Copy Trading
Copy trading environments generate risk in ways that are not always visible in the individual account view. Follower concentration across a single strategy, execution quality under heavy simultaneous order flow, cross-server replication consistency. These are operational considerations that require visibility at the ecosystem level, not just the account level. Real time monitoring at that level is what allows proactive management.
IB and Affiliate Management
Partner networks scale cleanly when commission logic is automated and performance data is connected to actual client trading behaviour. Without that connection, the administrative overhead of managing the network grows with it. With it, the network can grow without the back office growing proportionally.
Bonus and Campaign Management
Campaign performance is visible in real time or it is visible after the fact. When the campaign management layer is connected to live trading data, eligibility rules and abuse detection run continuously. When it is not, the review happens after the campaign has run and the cost has been incurred. The difference in commercial outcome between those two positions is significant across a full year of campaign activity.
MAM and PAMM
Managed account structures require automated allocation, transparent fee calculation, and a complete audit trail to operate professionally at scale. These are not optional features for a serious managed account offering. They are the operational foundation that makes the product credible to investors and manageable for the ops team.
The YOONIT Trading Solution
YOONIT is the connected operational ecosystem PLUGIT has built for forex and CFD brokers on MT4 and MT5. Six integrated modules covering each of the functions above: Dynamic Margin, CRM, Copy Trade, IB and Affiliate Management, Bonus Automation, and MAM/PAMM.
Each module works independently for brokers who want to address one specific function. Together they form a unified operational layer where data moves automatically between functions and configured rules execute without manual initiation. YOONIT does not replace existing trading infrastructure. It connects to it, running natively on the platforms already in use.
What Brokers Are Seeing When the Infrastructure Is Connected
The practical improvements that follow from moving to a connected operational environment are consistent across brokers of different sizes and different product focuses. The dealing desk operates against pre configured rules rather than implementing changes manually under pressure. Operations teams spend less time on reconciliation and more time on decisions that require judgment. Partner commissions are accurate and paid on schedule without a monthly manual process. Estos premios distinguen a las empresas que están impulsando la evolución de los servicios financieros en distintos mercados mediante soluciones innovadoras y de vanguardia.

La solución está integrada directamente en la plataforma unificada de banca y pagos de i2c y evalúa el riesgo en tiempo real en el momento de autorizar cada transacción. Así, las entidades emisoras pueden detectar operaciones fraudulentas con mayor anticipación, simplificar sus procesos y mejorar la experiencia de sus clientes sin afectar las tasas de aprobación.
“Nos enorgullece que Global Finance Magazine haya reconocido a i2c como la empresa de tecnología financiera más innovadora de América Latina”, afirmó Matt Pearce, vicepresidente de gestión del riesgo de fraude y operaciones de disputas de i2c. “A medida que los pagos digitales se expanden en la región, las instituciones necesitan formas más ágiles e inteligentes de gestionar el riesgo sin sumar complejidad. title: Demand for AI-native security chiefs jumps 256%, Christian & Timbers research finds
full_content:
Every company that moved to replace a CISO in the first seven months of 2026 named agentic AI expertise as the top requirement, up from fewer than half a year earlier
Demand for AI-native chief information security officers and chief security officers rose 256% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to research from executive search firm Christian & Timbers.
We already saw demand surge before the Hugging Face incident became public, with CEOs, CIOs, and boards asking us to find CISOs who’d actually secured agentic systems.Share
Overall CISO and CSO replacement activity rose 45%, from 22 companies in January through July 2025 to 32 in the same span of 2026, out of roughly 100 companies Christian & Timbers advised on security leadership this year. The more significant shift was in what those companies asked for. In 2025, nine of the 22 named deep agentic AI expertise as the most critical qualification for the new hire. In 2026, all 32 did, representing a 256% increase and, for the first time, a universal requirement.
“A candidate could walk into a final round twelve months ago with a strong traditional security record and some AI exposure on their résumé, and today that same background gets filtered out before the first conversation,” said Jeff Christian, founder of Christian & Timbers. “The role moved so fast that most sitting CISOs are still building the case they were hired to build two years ago, while the board in the room with them is already asking about agent identity and machine-speed incident response.”
The findings draw on Christian & Timbers’ inbound search activity and approximately 100 conversations between firm partners and CEOs, presidents, division presidents, COOs, CHROs, VPs of talent, CIOs and CTOs, conducted between January and July 2026.
Two requirements come up in nearly every search, Christian & Timbers says: hands-on experience securing autonomous AI agents, and the ability to translate that risk into terms a board can act on. Candidates with a strong traditional record but no agentic AI depth are no longer reaching final rounds.
The shift lands days after the industry’s first confirmed autonomous AI cyberattack. An OpenAI model running a cyber-capability benchmark escaped its sandbox, reached the open internet and compromised Hugging Face’s production systems without human direction, according to the Cloud Security Alliance’s July 28 post-mortem.
“We already saw demand surge before the Hugging Face incident became public, with CEOs, CIOs, and boards asking us to find CISOs who’d actually secured agentic systems,” said JC Christian, President of Christian & Timbers. “Hugging Face gave every CEO who was still weighing the decision a very concrete reason to move this quarter instead.”
Christian & Timbers reports that the CISO is second only to the CIO in current replacement activity, and that the most AI-advanced companies have begun requiring every role to be AI-native, with demonstrated experience deploying large language models or agents for productivity, revenue acceleration or, in security’s case, risk reduction.

title: Researchers find the first significant link between AI adoption and revenue growth
full_content:
New study of 500 enterprises conducted by Larridin and Carnegie Mellon University reveals organizations with concrete evidence of AI deployments and results grew revenue faster than those with weaker signals
Larridin, Inc.®, the platform measuring AI-powered work across the enterprise, today announced findings from a new study, Do AI Adoption Signals Predict Company Performance?,conductedin collaboration with researchers at Carnegie Mellon University.
For the first time, researchers have identified measurable connections between companies’ visible AI adoption signals and subsequent revenue growth. Examining more than 500 publicly traded U.S. companies (excluding the five largest AI chipmakers), the study found that companies providing the most specific AI disclosures in public 10-K filings achieved an 8% advantage in revenue growth compared with those that provided the least detail.
The strongest finding centers around “narrative concreteness,” or how clearly a company describes deployed AI systems and quantifiable results in its regulatory filings. The results suggest that companies documenting named AI deployments and measurable outcomes tend to grow faster than organizations relying primarily on aspirational or generalized AI language.
“Generalized AI investment alone tells us little about a company’s ability to create value,” said Ameya Kanitkar, co-founder and CTO of Larridin. “What matters is identifying where AI is being deployed, measuring adoption and workforce proficiency, understanding how customers and employees are benefiting, and connecting those efforts to quantifiable business results.”
AI Evaluation Signals Predict Growth
The study, Do AI Adoption Signals Predict Company Performance?, evaluated companies using seven AI-related signals, including Larridin’s scores on adoption, proficiency, impact, and maturity index, as well as three measures derived from SEC filings and hiring data: narrative concreteness, investment intensity, and AI-hiring builder rate. Researchers compared those signals with revenue growth, operating margins, and stock returns while controlling for industry sector, company size, and prior growth momentum. All seven AI signals show a relationship to revenue growth.
However, most of the broader adoption and composite scores became less predictive after accounting for the company’s industry sector, company size, and existing momentum. Narrative concreteness, the extent and depth of information about AI deployments in the 10-K filing, carries information not explained by those factors.
The study is the first to show that a signal of AI adoption correlates significantly with faster revenue growth, though not with better operating margins or future stock performance. This means that companies demonstrating the clearest understanding of how they are investing in and deploying AI technology appeared better positioned to grow the top line, but those investments had not yet translated into measurable cost efficiencies or investor returns.
The findings also do not support the speculative narrative that companies are adopting AI primarily to reduce headcount. While the study did not directly measure layoffs, the absence of a relationship between AI adoption and margin expansion suggests that AI is not yet functioning as a broad-based labor-cost reduction strategy. At this stage, companies appear to be using AI more to expand capabilities than to reduce costs. As the paper concludes, “in this sample, AI adoption is a top-line story, not yet a cost story.”
“The study suggests companies are using AI primarily to expand capabilities, improve customer experiences, and create new growth opportunities,” said Shixiang (Woody) Zhu, Assistant Professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, who led the research team. “At this stage, AI’s measurable impact is appearing more clearly in revenue growth than in operating margins or stock performance, indicating that its value goes beyond cost reduction.”

title: Cash, Trust and Resilience in an Increasingly Digital Payment Landscape
full_content:
For more than a decade, payment innovation has been framed as a transition from physical to digital money. Yet the latest findings from the Federal Reserve reveal a different reality: consumers are not choosing between cash and digital payments. They are choosing both.
According to the 2026 Diary of Consumer Payment Choice, cash remains an integral part of Americans’ financial lives. Four out of five consumers continue to use cash, 90% report having no plans to stop using it, and nearly half now keep cash on hand for savings or emergency preparedness. The study also found that Americans made an average of 47 payments per month in 2025, with cash accounting for 14% of all payments, making it the nation’s third most frequently used payment method. These findings demonstrate that while payment technologies continue to evolve, consumers continue to value flexibility and maintain a mix of payment options rather than relying on a single method.
Consumer behavior tells a different story than technology headlines
Innovation in payments has been extraordinary. Digital wallets have become mainstream, peer-to-peer transfers are nearly instantaneous, and consumers can complete purchases with a tap of a phone or smartwatch.
The Federal Reserve’s decade of consumer payment research suggests payment habits evolve gradually rather than abruptly. New technologies expand the range of payment choices available to consumers, but they do not necessarily replace existing methods that continue to serve distinct purposes. Consumers continue to use cash because it offers characteristics that digital payments cannot fully replicate. It is universally accepted, immediately accessible, requires no technology or internet connection, and functions independently of third-party networks or electrical infrastructure.
Cash remains a trusted foundation for payment resilience
Perhaps the most significant finding from the Federal Reserve’s latest research is not simply that Americans continue to use cash, but why they keep it. The growing number of consumers holding cash for emergencies reflects a broader recognition that digital systems, while highly reliable, are not immune to disruption.
The research found that 76% of consumers carried cash during 2025, while 45% stored cash separately for savings or emergencies. Average emergency cash holdings increased from $306 in 2024 to $364 in 2025, suggesting that more consumers view physical currency as an important component of financial preparedness.
This behavior highlights an important aspect of payment choice: consumers value not only convenience, but also reliability and control. Power outages, severe weather events, cyber incidents, telecommunications failures, and network disruptions can temporarily limit access to electronic payment systems. During these moments, cash provides immediate continuity because it functions independently of electricity, internet connectivity, and third-party networks.
For many consumers, that resilience creates trust. Cash settles instantly, remains directly accessible, and works regardless of technology availability. Interestingly, while only 16% of consumers identified cash as their preferred in-person payment method, many more continue to use it regularly. This suggests that cash increasingly serves as a trusted and dependable fallback option, even for consumers who primarily rely on cards or digital payments.
Rather than indicating resistance to innovation, these findings demonstrate that consumers value having multiple reliable ways to pay. As payment systems become increasingly digital and interconnected, maintaining access to cash remains an important component of resilience, helping ensure continuity, confidence, and choice across a wide range of circumstances.
The future is coexistence, not competition
Too often, discussions about payment innovation are framed as a competition between physical and digital money. In reality, successful payment ecosystems are built on coexistence.
Central banks, financial institutions, retailers and payment providers all share an interest in ensuring that consumers can access reliable payment options across a wide range of circumstances. This means supporting innovation while maintaining the resilience of existing infrastructure.
Demographic trends provide additional insight. The Federal Reserve’s research also highlights that cash use remains higher among older adults, lower-income households, and rural communities. These findings underscore that maintaining access to cash continues to support accessibility and payment choice across diverse segments of the population.
Planning for resilience requires preserving payment choice
The lesson from the Federal Reserve’s latest research is clear. Building the future of payments is not about choosing between physical and digital forms of money. It is about creating a resilient ecosystem in which consumers can rely on both. As payment systems continue to evolve, preserving access to cash remains an essential part of ensuring trust, continuity, and choice for all Americans.
About the Author: Jim Petit leads the Currency Management Solutions division for Giesecke+Devrient (G+D) in the United States. With decades of experience across payments and financial services, he brings a perspective shaped by G+D’s work with central banks and financial institutions in over 100 countries. For more information, please visit www.gi-de.com.

title: AIG expands cyber insurance offering to help businesses manage cloud outage risks
full_content:
New Parametric Cloud Outage Solution Helps Businesses Protect Against Cloud Disruptions and Receive Faster Claims Payments
American International Group, Inc. (NYSE: AIG) today announced a new Parametric Cloud Outage Solution, providing clients an additional layer of cyber insurance protection to help them recover faster from business interruption losses resulting from cloud service outages and cloud provider downtime. These events can disrupt operations, customer transactions, and access to critical business applications.
Parametric insurance provides a predetermined payment when a specific event or policy trigger occurs. AIG’s new Parametric Cloud Outage Solution triggers are based on a predefined formula that considers cloud service downtime and the associated potential financial impact. Covered events may include outages affecting cloud infrastructure, software-as-a-service platforms, or other cloud-based technology services, subject to policy terms and conditions.
Enterprise spending on cloud infrastructure services has increased steadily among businesses of all sizes. According to Synergy Research Group, global enterprise spending on cloud infrastructure services reached $129 billion in the first quarter of 2026, an increase of 35% from the prior year, the highest growth rate since 2021.
“As businesses increasingly invest and rely on cloud-based solutions to better serve customers and run critical operations, even a short outage can have significant operational and financial impacts,” said Tracie Grella, Global Chief Underwriting Officer of Cyber Risk Insurance at AIG. “AIG’s Parametric Cloud Outage Solution is designed to give organizations faster access to funds when disruptions occur, helping them respond with greater confidence and certainty while complementing their broader risk management and insurance programs.”
AIG’s Parametric Cloud Outage Solution’s key features include:
- A shorter waiting period of two hours
- No monetary retention following the waiting period
- Transparent, predefined policy triggers
- Rapid claims assessment and payout process
- Ability to manage cyber and cloud outage coverage through a single insurance policy
Developed in partnership with Parametrix, a leading provider of digital infrastructure insurance solutions, the parametric formula is backed by Parametrix’s proprietary monitoring of more than 750 data centers globally and tracking over 9,000 software and other technology providers (e.g. SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS).
“In today’s environment, carriers and brokers are increasingly looking for ways to bring additional value and innovation to insureds,” said Sharon Haran, Chief Commercial Officer at Parametrix. “Our Cloud Outage Solution creates an opportunity to do exactly that, and we are delighted to work with AIG to bring this solution to their insureds. Leveraging technology and parametric structures, this solution delivers relevant protection for a growing operational risk in a simple, scalable, and economically viable way.”

title: Z-Library Official Domain and the Challenge of Retaining Paying Customers
full_content:
A public library once stood at the center of every town. People walked through heavy doors and searched dusty shelves with quiet focus. Modern reading habits moved that same feeling onto screens. The smell of paper faded yet the wish for knowledge stayed alive. E-libraries now carry the torch in a faster world where time slips through human hands like sand through an hourglass.
Why Readers Stay Loyal to Digital Libraries
People return to familiar places for simple reasons. Comfort matters. Ease matters. Trust matters. An e-library that feels smooth and reliable becomes part of daily life. Reading turns into a rhythm much like morning tea or late night radio. In this space Z library remains a leading option for readers across the globe because it offers broad access and a calm reading experience that fits modern routines.
Paying customers often expect more than files on a screen. They want stable service clear search tools and a sense of order. Many readers feel buried under endless subscriptions across music film and news platforms. A reading service must avoid becoming another noisy market stall. It needs the quiet mood of an old bookshop hidden on a rainy street where every shelf feels carefully placed.
The Balance Between Access and Value
Readers today move fast from one service to another. Loyalty can vanish overnight. One weak experience may send people elsewhere. That challenge pushes e-libraries to think beyond price alone. Good structure matters more than loud promises. Clear categories smooth navigation and reliable access build habits over time.
Strong reading habits grow through small details that often go unnoticed:
- A Simple Reading Flow
When readers search for material they prefer a path without friction. Slow pages broken links and clutter drain patience fast. A smooth reading flow keeps attention on ideas rather than technical problems. This quiet efficiency works like a good stage crew in a theater. Nobody notices the workers behind the curtain yet the show cannot survive without them. Paying users often remain loyal when every visit feels calm and predictable rather than stressful or confusing.
- A Sense of Discovery
People enjoy finding new material in the same way music fans enjoy hearing an old favorite song on the radio. Discovery creates emotional connection. A strong e-library keeps readers curious without overwhelming them. Smart organization and thoughtful recommendations guide readers toward fresh interests. This feeling of exploration gives value beyond simple access. It turns reading into a living habit instead of a task completed and forgotten after one session.
- Consistency Builds Trust
Trust grows slowly like a tree beside a country road. Readers notice stable service even if they rarely speak about it. Clear design dependable access and familiar structure create confidence over time. Paying customers often stay where they feel comfortable. Sudden changes or confusing systems weaken that connection. Stability matters because people already face enough noise during daily life. Many seek reading spaces that feel steady and calm rather than chaotic.
That steady feeling often becomes the hidden thread connecting readers to one platform for years rather than months.
What Keeps Readers Coming Back
Human habits rarely depend on logic alone. Emotion plays a quiet role behind every choice. Readers often return to spaces that feel welcoming and familiar. A dependable e-library becomes part of ordinary life much like a favorite café or an old park bench beneath autumn trees.
Retaining paying customers means understanding those emotions without turning reading into a sales pitch. Readers want freedom simplicity and comfort. They want a place where knowledge feels open rather than locked behind endless barriers. When an e-library protects that feeling it keeps its place in the modern reading world with quiet strength and steady purpose.

title: Greenpeace Pictures of the Week
full_content:
From calls for climate action in the Philippines and Switzerland, to protests demanding permanent protection of Raja Ampat. Here are a few of our favourite images from Greenpeace work around the world this week.
🇵🇭 Philippines – Greenpeace Philippines and frontline communities challenge Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to ensure that his administration’s vision of development will protect people–not polluters–as he delivers his fourth State of the Nation Address (SONA), warning that the country cannot claim genuine progress while millions of Filipinos continue to bear the growing costs of extreme heat and the climate crisis.
🇨🇭Switzerland – The drought in Switzerland is continuing and is casting a shadow over the National Day with bans on open fires and fireworks. This summer shows what lies ahead for us. Due to global warming, summer droughts and the risk of weather-related forest fires will continue to increase.
Greenpeace activists are therefore in no mood to celebrate. On Thursday 30 July 2026, they unfurled a banner on the shores of Lake Constance at Mannenbach-Salenstein harbour bearing the slogan ‘No reason to celebrate. Climate action now!’. They are calling on Switzerland to finally acknowledge the climate crisis and take appropriate action: 100 million Swiss francs are needed for immediate measures to tackle heatwaves and protect the climate.
🇮🇩Indonesia – Greenpeace activists staged a peaceful, non-violent protest to reiterate their call for the full and permanent protection of the Raja Ampat ecosystem. This action involved unfurling banners reading “Protect Raja Ampat, Stop Dirty Energy” and “Is Your Car Powered by Forest Destruction?” just as Industry Minister Agus Gumiwang Kartasasmita pressed the button to open the Gaikindo Indonesia International Auto Show (GIIAS) 2026, the largest annual automotive exhibition in Indonesia.
🇪🇸Spain – Artificial smoke, ashes, burnt logs and a black banner outside the Congress of Deputies reading “Spain is burning. Your inaction is killing us”. This is how Greenpeace Spain activists peacefully protested this morning in Madrid to show their solidarity with the thousands of people affected by the fires, as well as demanding that political groups and administrations act and engage in real politics to address the climate emergency. All this at the start of a fourth heatwave and with much of the country affected by historic fires that have already claimed 15 direct fatalities and displaced more than 100,000 people.
🇳🇿New Zealand/Aotearoa – Greenpeace New Zealand activists dropped an 18-square-metre banner from a giant rimu tree to call for conservation land protections on New Zealand’s West Coast. They are protesting government reforms to conservation laws that would make it easier to commercially exploit and sell off public conservation land. The activists are recreating an iconic image from one of New Zealand’s most famous conservation campaigns, which successfully stopped native forest logging on public land across the country.
🇩🇪Germany – Greenpeace documents dead zones through research carried out on Boris Herrmann’s research yacht, the Malizia Explorer along the German Baltic Sea coast. Greenpeace scientists test the water with a CTD-Probe among other methods, for nitrate and phosphorous levels, temperature, oxygen and salt levels and for PFAS.
High numbers of factory farms lead to an increased production of liquid manure, which is later spread onto the fields, with traces eventually landing in the open seas after rainfall. These substances lead to detrimental conditions in the water and the sea bed, including so-called dead zones. Drone images of the Malizia Explorer just off the Schleswig-Holstein coast.
🇬🇧UK – As Shell announces record profits an electric advan outside Big Ben at Westminster is showing images of the damage caused by wildfires across Europe. The images raise awareness that the biggest polluters continue to profit while ordinary people bear the brunt of the costs of these climate disasters. It’s time to hold Shell accountable and demand they pay for the damage they’ve caused.
Greenpeace has been a pioneer of photo activism for more than 50 years, and remains committed to bearing witness and exposing environmental injustice through the images we capture.
To see more Greenpeace photos and videos, please visit our Media Library.

title: Trillions within reach, yet governments’ Global Tax Treaty draft lets the richest climate polluters off the hook
full_content:
New York – As the fifth round of negotiations on the Global Tax Treaty – also known as the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation – opens today in New York, Greenpeace International is calling on governments to raise their ambition. Gaps in the draft text, published in full for the first time, must be addressed so that global tax rules can help solve the connected climate, nature, and inequality crises, rather than letting corporate polluters and the super-rich profit while everyone else pays the price.
Nina Stros, Global Senior Policy Expert, Greenpeace International said: “Governments and delegates still have not grasped what is at stake but they face a simple choice. Create global tax rules to speed the transition to a fairer, more resilient future by disincentivising investment in environmentally destructive industries, ending tax-dodging, and holding wealthy polluters to account. Or keep shielding polluting corporations and the super-rich while communities pay the price through higher bills and climate devastation. The money is right there. It is about time governments recognised this once in a generation opportunity to make those most responsible for the climate, nature and inequality crises we are facing pay their share, and reclaim trillions of dollars to invest in our shared future.”
While the world recently saw its first-ever trillionaire, the largest oil and gas corporations are reporting another bonanza in second-quarter profits. Meanwhile, record-breaking heatwaves, rising ocean temperatures and the cost-of-living crisis continue to put communities under pressure worldwide.[1]
The newly published ‘zero draft’ of the Global Tax Treaty falls far short of the ambition needed to hold the wealthiest polluters to account. Negotiators must push back against the disconnect between this draft and the realities of the climate and inequality crises communities face.[2][3][4]
Despite 24 countries making submissions aligned with strengthening the Treaty’s Sustainable Development article, the text does not go beyond the high-level clause already in the terms of reference.[5][6] Governments are left with far too much room to continue with business as usual, rather than creating a clear new legal obligation to hold wealthy polluters to account through national and global tax mechanisms. Similarly, the polluter pays principle appears nowhere in the current draft. The article on taxing high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) has been weakened since the last round of negotiations in January 2026, reducing obligations on countries to act. The draft also fails to include any provisions on minimum profit taxation of multinational companies, or on the taxation of extractive industries and natural resources.
Ucizi Ngulube, Tax Justice Campaigner, Greenpeace Africa, said: “The global majority championed this United Nations process because the current global tax system is fundamentally unfair, serving a handful of wealthy nations and billionaires at the expense of everyone else. As we head into INC-5, countries must remain ambitious. We don’t need vague promises, we need bold proposals that stop the exploitation and inequality, and hold the ultra-rich polluters accountable for the climate damage they leave behind.”
By closing loopholes on profit-shifting and tax havens, and setting new taxes, nationally and globally, on the profits of the biggest polluters and on extreme wealth, countries could unlock public funds urgently needed for climate action, nature protection and essential public services.[7]
Mayor Melchor Mergal, Municipal Mayor of Salcedo, Eastern Samar, Philippines, survivor of super-typhoon Haiyan and member of Greenpeace delegation in New York said: “I have seen what the increasingly frequent and devastating storms can do to a community, and I know what it takes to rebuild. The money is needed for stronger homes, schools and health centres that can safeguard our communities against the next storm. The funds exist. What we are missing is the political will to make those most responsible pay for the damage. A strong treaty would give communities like mine the means to recover and to build real resilience through making polluters pay.”
Greenpeace International is calling on negotiators in New York to strengthen the sustainable development and HNWI articles in line with the proposals countries, experts and civil society groups have put forward, to include the polluter pays principle into the text, and ensure the treaty can reclaim at least one trillion US dollars per year in public finance for climate action, public services and a fair transition.
ENDS
A Greenpeace delegation, including Mayor Melchor Mergal, will be at INC-5 in New York. The delegation is available for comments or interviews before, during and after the talks.

[3] In April, 57 countries met in Santa Marta, Colombia, to advance action on ending coal, oil and gas dependence. The final synthesis report highlights under-taxation of fossil profits as a barrier to a just transition, concluding that progressive tax reforms are necessary. 141 countries also voted for a just transition away from fossil fuels under a UN General Assembly resolution endorsing the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion on climate change in May.

title: Wildfires and climate change: Why the smell of smoke is a global health warning
full_content:
Last week I woke up to a hazy, orange sky, a red sun, and the smell of burning wood drifting through the Montreal city air.
Smell is one of our strongest ties to memory.1 As someone who has spent years camping with friends, I have always associated the scent of burning wood with warmth, laughter by the fire, and a deep connection to nature.
This time, the smell made my stomach sink.
That scent did not come from a nearby campfire. It was millions of hectares of boreal forest burning across the continent. My throat tightened as I thought of the thousands of people, especially Indigenous communities, forced to evacuate while their homes burned to the ground.
Smoke knows no borders
We are actually witnessing a global ecological shift. Canada’s devastating 2023–24 wildfire seasons saw 20.4 million hectares burn down. These were not isolated events. We’re seeing forests burn around the world, from Australia’s bushfires and Mediterranean blazes to the burning Amazon; climate-driven fire seasons are increasingly common occurrences.
Climate change and wildfire smoke do not respect geopolitical borders. In 2023, haze from Canadian fires crossed the Atlantic and caused air quality alerts in western Europe. Pollution anywhere speeds up climate disruption everywhere. If we treat ecological collapse as just a local problem, we miss how interconnected the climate crisis really is.
And right about now, the images of wildfires surging from across the world create a real sense of global emergency. Do you feel this, too?
Health risks of wildfire smoke exposure
We can’t keep seeing wildfire smoke as just a seasonal problem. The fine particles found in wildfire haze carry toxic chemicals, heavy metals, and black carbon that go deep into our bloodstream.
Recent research confirms that breathing in wildfire smoke raises the risk of heart disease, stroke, and lung problems for months after the smoke is gone. The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) also warns that extreme fires could increase by up to 50% worldwide by the end of the century if emissions are not reduced.
We must urge our leaders to consider this: What is the point of short-term economic growth or rising stock markets if the simple act of breathing outside becomes dangerous for our health?
Need for political courage and systemic change
One of the most frustrating aspects of this dire situation is the gap between what politicians say and what they actually do.
Governments may issue air quality warnings and talk about climate targets, but many still use public money to support fossil fuel projects and support industrial practices that worsen global warming. For example, in Canada, billions of tax dollars are set to fund fossil fuel projects, even as the country falls behind on its emissions targets.
Calling fossil fuel expansion short-sighted during a climate crisis is an understatement. While oil company CEOs rake in excess profits, frontline communities and families pay the real price through health problems, food insecurity and higher living costs.
Forest management and Indigenous fire stewardship
For over a century, industry-led forest management has focused on putting out all fires, clear-cut logging and planting monoculture tree plantations. Unfortunately, this has led to dense, uniform forests, turning them into giant tinderboxes during climate-exacerbated heatwaves.
To change this, we need to move from just fighting fires to caring for forests in a holistic way that respects nature and Indigenous knowledge:
- Restoring Indigenous fire stewardship: For thousands of years, Indigenous Peoples in North America, Australia, and South America have practiced cultural burning, which means controlled, low-intensity fires during cooler seasons. Recent research shows that returning land and fire management to Indigenous communities helps clear dangerous undergrowth, restore biodiversity, and prevent major wildfires.
- Resilience from diversity: Instead of managing forests by planting fast-growing trees that benefit the timber industry, experts recommend focussing on ecological diversity. A mix of tree species, ages, other vegetation and structures in the forest makes ecosystems stronger in the long run.
- Protecting primary and old-growth forests: Ancient forests store huge amounts of carbon and keep soil moist much better than young tree plantations. Protecting these old-growth forests is one of the most affordable and effective ways to fight climate change.
Reason for hope: Global climate solutions for wildfire prevention
The solutions we need already exist. If we recognize how serious this crisis is, we can move forward together and achieve real change by:
- Respecting and supporting Indigenous-led solutions → For millennia, Indigenous Peoples and local communities have respected and defended nature. Their experience shows that the resiliency of forests is strongest when the local people who rely on them have the power to care for and manage their territories.
- Stopping the flow of government subsidies to fossil fuels and Making Polluters Pay → Moving government support from fossil fuels to green energy, forest restoration, and community resilience can address the real causes of climate change. And instead of making wealthy polluters wealthier, we should make them pay for the harm they cause.
- Global Climate Accountability → We need to treat the climate emergency as a real international health and security crisis. Countries must keep their promises under the Paris Agreement and work quickly to cut methane and carbon emissions. If we lower global temperatures, forests will be less likely to burn to the ground.
Taking back our future
The smell of firewood should continue to remind us of nights under the stars with friends, not the loss of our homes or our future. We already have the knowledge, tools, and solutions to protect and restore forests. Now is the time to ask our leaders for a long-term vision, while we can still safely breathe the air around us.
Julie Amira Byrnes is Engagement Manager at Greenpeace International
