title: Oil disaster unfolds in protected marine area as Russian shadow fleet tanker leak accelerates off Oman
full_content:
Oman – New satellite imagery analysis by Greenpeace Germany indicates that oil leakage from the Russian shadow fleet tanker Caroline Bezengi, grounded in Oman’s Al Hallaniyat archipelago, has accelerated and is now estimated to have spread across roughly 600 square kilometres – a fourfold increase over just the last two days.
Nina Noelle, international environmental disaster expert at Greenpeace Germany, said: “This is a drastic increase, indicating a deterioration of the vessel’s condition. Satellite imagery analysis suggests that the oil spill covered 45 square kilometres up until 26 July. By 2 August it had expanded to around 150 square kilometres, and imagery from 4 August indicates that it now extends across roughly 600 square kilometres .
Hanen Keskes, campaigner at Greenpeace MENA said: “Even relatively small oil spills can have long-lasting consequences for marine ecosystems with chemical residues that persist in marine sediments for years, compromising their ecological resilience. With the oil leak from the stranded Caroline Bezengi now accelerating, the environmental consequences will be severe, threatening coral reefs, seagrass meadows and coastal habitats that support endangered sea turtles, migratory seabirds and marine mammals in the Hallaniyat Islands. Sea turtles rely on the islands’ beaches for nesting and egg-laying, while many seabird species depend on the islands as critical breeding sites. The surrounding waters are also home to the rare Arabian Sea humpback whale.”
Large stretches of Al Qibliyah Island’s shoreline appear to have been affected, while additional oil slicks extend far out to sea, further polluting and damaging this protected marine ecosystem. The tanker has reportedly been leaking oil since it ran aground in June, following a suspected limpet mine attack that resulted in the flooding of the engine room, and urgent action is needed to contain the spill and prevent further harm to marine life and local livelihoods.
The situation surrounding the tanker Caroline Bezengi is yet another alarming example of the serious environmental risks posed by Russia’s so-called shadow fleet. Sanctions are being circumvented using ageing and poorly maintained tankers, putting coastlines and marine ecosystems at risk in order to maintain revenues that help finance Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
With oil apparently leaking at an accelerating pace and the tanker stranded in a difficult location, there is an imminent risk of an unprecedented oil disaster from a broken tanker, with devastating consequences for the region’s coastlines and marine ecosystems.
Greenpeace urges the Omani authorities and all relevant regional bodies to act immediately to assess all remaining options to contain the spill, secure the tanker’s cargo and conduct a comprehensive, independent assessment of the ecological damage. Where additional capacity is needed, Oman should urgently request international assistance for expertise, equipment and resources as required.
The Caroline Bezengi is stranded close to Al Qibliyah, an uninhabited island in the Al Hallaniyat archipelago, within a marine protected area. According to reports, the tanker was nearly fully loaded when it ran aground and estimated to be carrying around 800,000 barrels of oil.
The difficulties surrounding the Caroline Bezengi reflect wider concerns raised by previous Greenpeace investigations into Russia’s shadow fleet.[1] The vessel lost its flag registration in Cameroon on May 29, and is since listed as ‘flag unknown’ by the International Maritime Organisation. Omani authorities reportedly ordered the Shanghai-based owner to act, but received no response. The tanker is not insured by any recognised Protection and Indemnity (P&I) club, but an opaque insurer called Arsenal Kyrgystan, apparently based in the Kyrgyz Republic, according to information for October 2025 obtained by Greenpeace Nordic from Danish authorities.[2] It is unclear whether that cover remains valid and will make sufficient funds available for emergency measures, clean-up, ecological restoration and compensation.
Without an accountable owner and clear, adequate insurance or even a responsible flag state, Oman and affected communities risk being left to fully bear the environmental and financial consequences of this unfolding disaster.
ENDS
Satellite images from the Greenpeace Global Mapping Hub available in the Greenpeace Media Library
Notes:
[1] Previous Greenpeace investigations into Russia’s shadow fleet: Greenpeace has actively targeted Russia’s “shadow fleet”, a network of aging, underinsured oil tankers used to evade sanctions, through a combination of direct ocean protests, investigative research, and environmental modeling. Activists from Greenpeace Germany, Greenpeace Nordic, and Greenpeace CEE/Ukraine have staged direct peaceful actions, such as painting messages on offshore bunker refuelers and protesting in European waters to highlight the double threat of war funding and catastrophic oil spills. To hold governments accountable, Greenpeace Germany published a comprehensive report cataloging 192 high-risk shadow fleet tankers, which helped inform subsequent EU sanctions, and developed interactive oil spill simulations to visually demonstrate how potential leaks from these decaying vessels would devastate coastal ecosystems.
[2] Information obtained via an FOI request to the Danish Marine Authority (DMA) by Greenpeace Nordic in 2026. The web-site for a company under this name, claiming to provide marine insurance services can be found here: https://arsins.kg/en/about. The DMA obtained this information from the captain of the Caroline Bezengi, when it moved in and out of the Baltic in 2025 and 2024.

title: Greenpeace International’s anti-SLAPP lawsuit continues after North Dakota courts largely reject Energy Transfer’s attempt to avoid accountability
full_content:
Amsterdam – In regards to the North Dakota District Court issuing a “narrowly tailored” anti-suit injunction, Greenpeace International Senior Legal Counsel Strategic Defence Daniel Simons said:
“Greenpeace International’s anti-SLAPP case against Energy Transfer in the Netherlands will continue and the central arguments are not impacted by the anti-suit injunction issued by the North Dakota District Court. As directed by the North Dakota Supreme Court, the anti-suit injunction is ‘narrowly tailored’ so as not to interfere with key claims in Greenpeace International’s anti-SLAPP case.
“The North Dakota courts have cleared the way for Greenpeace International to continue pursuing justice under Dutch law. The only limitation imposed pertains to Greenpeace International asking for a finding that the North Dakota District Court case ‘lacked legal foundation.’ However, these are not central claims for the anti-SLAPP case.”

title: Saving the ‘Amazon of Europe’ from Big Ag’s next megafarm
full_content:
Just weeks after witnessing thousands of people in Croatia protesting against an invasion of giant chicken farms in their towns, I found myself packing my bags again. The Big Ag corporate interests planning to quadruple Croatia’s poultry production haven’t given up, and now have their eyes on another pristine corner of Croatia.
This time, I traveled to Croatia’s northeast, right on the border with Hungary, where a fiercely dedicated community is fighting to keep a megafarm from destroying an area widely known as the ‘Amazon of Europe’.
Grassroots resistance against the Chicken King
My journey started with a bus drive down from Budapest to the border, where the Drava River divides Hungary and Croatia. This region, right where the rivers Drava and Mura meet, is the stunning Mura-Drava-Danube UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.
Covering 930,000 hectares along 700 kilometres of rivers, this is a biodiversity hotspot with rare habitats such as floodplain forests, gravel and sand banks, river islands and oxbow lakes. It’s an ornithological haven packed with rare bird species including black storks, marsh harriers and the highest density of breeding pairs of white-tailed eagles in continental Europe.
But Big Ag MHP Group, Europe’s biggest poultry player, led by the infamous billionaire ‘Chicken King’ Yuriy Kosiuk wants to turn this paradise into an industrial zone.
The Legrad-Donja Dubrava Citizens’ Initiative, a grassroots group leading the opposition to the farm, warns that this facility will house a staggering 1.8 million chickens annually. The 50,000m2 facility will pump 30 million liters of groundwater annually from its own wells for technology and cooling, while producing 1 million litres of wastewater per year.
I was invited here by Korina and Emil, a local couple who are spearheading the grassroots resistance. They are not your typical activists; rather they are ordinary people who are taking action to defend the place they live. Emil took me on a tour to see exactly what we are up against. First, he showed me an existing megafarm linked to Perutnina Ptuj–Pipo, the same company behind the new project, which is already operating nearby. We then visited the site of the proposed expansion.
Locals told me the company is rushing to open its doors as early as next month. The threat is immediate, but this community isn’t backing down.
The protestival on the riverbank against corporate greed
The community is incredibly creative with their protest tactics. A few weeks before I arrived, they had already made waves with “kayaktivism,” with around 60 activists launching onto the river to take striking photos that exposed how dangerously close the facility is to the water. They traded paddles for microphones and organised a “Protestival” right on the riverbank, attended by hundreds of people and representatives from various organisations, musicians and local grassroots groups.
The energy was electric. Traditional Croatian folk musicians shared the stage with rock legend Darko Rundek, all standing united against corporate greed.
All waters are connected, different communities threatened by the same Big Ag playbook
Back in my hometown of Budapest, the Danube river is my favorite part of the city. And water doesn’t care about borders. The Danube River, which flows through Hungary and forms part of the border between Croatia and Serbia, joins the Drava, flowing into the sea and the global oceans. So what happens here matters.
The people of northern Croatia’s struggle against the Veliki Pažut industrial poultry farm is a real David and Goliath fight – a small community standing up to international corporations to defend an area they love. But sadly, it is the experience of many communities world over.
- In Spain, communities are organising against the construction of a new factory farm cramming one million hens and producing over 235 million eggs a year.
- In Mexico, the iconic cenotes of the Maya rainforest are being polluted by illegal pig farms, threatening the water supply for indigenous communities across the region.
- In Nigeria, the world’s largest meat company, JBS, is planning a US$ 2.5 billion expansion that locals fear will threaten livelihoods and undermine food security.
All over the world local communities are threatened by the same Big Ag playbook: bulldozing lands, extracting profit and leaving behind pollution and contamination. So this isn’t just a local dispute over a construction permit. It’s a battle between community and corporate extraction.
We can’t let Big Ag use our rivers as a sewer for their industrial waste.
Locals showed me the way. I proudly took a stand to protect their land, and the beautiful Drava river against corporations like MHP, that only serve billionaires and their shareholders.
Just like in Sisak, Croatia, where local people drew a line and the Chicken King backed down, today, on the banks of the Amazon of Europe, the message to Big Ag remains exactly the same.
Not here, not anywhere.
It’s time to cut through corporate lies, cut agriculture emissions and shift towards sustainable agroecology.
Sign now!
Dániel Nyitray is Global Campaign Lead for Big Ag at Greenpeace International based in Hungary.

title: Indigenous resistance is key to building a post-extractive future
full_content:
True allyship can only take hold when we recognise that Indigenous peoples’ struggles are intricately bound up with our collective fate. Our greatest hope against ecological breakdown is to support Indigenous sovereignty and actively join the global resistance against extractive industries. This is a matter of our mutual survival and liberation.
“If you have come here to help me you are wasting your time, but if you have come because your liberation is bound up with mine, then let us work together.”
— Lilla Watson, Gangulu woman, ‘Aboriginal Activists’ Group
What is extractivism?
Differing from the simple act of harvesting a resource (such as cutting down a single tree), extractivism is an economic model that treats the Earth as an endless storehouse of raw materials. Nature is commodified and extracted at an industrial scale and exported to enrich distant interests, while local communities (often Indigenous) bear the devastating ecological and social costs.
It’s no coincidence that the concept of extractivismo (extractivism) originated in Latin America – a region that has served as ground zero for over 500 years of imperial plunder, while simultaneously remaining the global heartland of Indigenous frontline resistance.
The battle over recognition and sovereignty
For many Indigenous communities, resisting extractivism looks like a fundamental struggle to exist in the eyes of the law. States have long used the denial of Indigenous identity as a tactical weapon to erase land claims, clear territories for corporate concessions and evade legal accountability under international law.
Nevertheless, Indigenous movements have generated some of the most vibrant, historic and effective mobilisations in recent memory. An Indigenous Environmental Network (IEN) report found that Indigenous-led resistance in North America has successfully delayed or stopped greenhouse gas pollution equivalent to at least 25% of annual US and Canadian emissions.
Through decades of tireless organizing, Indigenous leaders secured foundational frameworks like ILO Convention 169 and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). These instruments serve to enshrine the principle of self-determination, establishing that Indigenous peoples alone have the right to define their own identities, institutions and relationships to their territories.
The high cost of defense
Frontline Indigenous defenders routinely face systemic intimidation, land theft, state criminalization and lethal violence. According to data from Global Witness, while Indigenous peoples represent roughly 6% of the global population, they consistently account for more than one-third of all land and environmental defenders murdered worldwide each year.
Colonial states also spread racist and prejudiced narratives about supposed Indigenous inferiority. These myths have permeated many levels of society and led to a profound disconnection not only from Indigenous peoples but also ancient traditions, their wisdom, knowledge systems and ways of relating with the Earth and other living beings that we sorely need to revive.
Confronting ‘green extractivism’
Today, Indigenous movements are also challenging accelerating demand for so-called ‘critical minerals’. Brought about by the energy transition, AI and Big Tech, and the defense sector, this speculative rush for minerals is giving rise to new sacrifice zones.
In her book Extraction, political scientist Thea Riofrancos spotlights frontline Indigenous communities fighting back against ‘green extractivism,’ exposing how the rush for clean energy minerals risks repeating historic colonial harms. To break this cycle, Riofrancos advocates for solutions that move beyond simply swapping gas-powered vehicles for electric ones, calling instead for public transit investments, circular material recycling and a deliberate reduction in overall resource consumption.
In response to today’s intensifying extractive rush, Greenpeace has partnered with other NGOs and experts to launch the Restricted Areas Map, indicating places where mining poses unacceptable environmental, social, cultural or rights-related risks.
Demands of Indigenous environmental movements
Across courtroom battles, frontline blockade and international climate summits, Indigenous activists share a repeating set of demands.
In 2025, Indigenous youth representatives from the world’s primary tropical forest basins, the Amazon, the Congo Basin, Borneo and West Papua, penned their version with the Sira Declaration. Drafted in West Papua, the declaration lays out a call to action for governments, corporations and international bodies to:
- Recognize and Secure Land Sovereignty: Legal recognition and enforcement of customary land titles, enforcing full self-determination and the right to Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC).
- End Militarization, Violence and Criminalization: An immediate end to state-sponsored military operations, arbitrary arrests and violence targeted at Indigenous environmental defenders.
- Halt ‘Green Colonialism’ and Extractive Projects: Resist industrial mining, logging, fossil fuels and speculative critical-mineral exploitation, rejecting any climate ‘solutions’ that turn Indigenous territories into sacrifice zones.
- Direct Climate Financing to Indigenous Communities: Routing global climate, conservation and loss-and-damage funds directly to Indigenous nations and youth-led groups on the frontlines, bypassing intermediaries.
- Center Traditional Knowledge and Youth/Women Governance: Guaranteeing leadership seats for Indigenous youth and women in international climate policy.
Public support for Indigenous leadership
Global public opinion strongly supports these demands. A Greenpeace poll spanning 17 countries across five continents* revealed that 78% of respondents trust Indigenous Peoples and local communities most to protect forests (compared to 49% for governments and 42% for corporations). Additionally, 75% of respondents agree that Indigenous peoples should receive direct climate funding to safeguard their ancestral territories.
Building a just, post-extractivist future
Stopping destructive corporate projects is only the first step. A post-extractive future requires a post-colonial future. In a time as critical as this, non-Indigenous allies cannot remain passive observers. Decolonisation requires that settler populations actively reject the ideology of extractivism by rejecting the commodification, domination and exploitation of Nature.
Indigenous leadership provides practical blueprints for post-extractive societies founded on care, ecological balance and generational/collective well-being. A Greenpeace report highlights inspiring case studies of community-led forest solutions.
*Polling Methodology Note: Countries surveyed include Kenya, South Africa, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Canada, USA, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea, Australia, Denmark, France, Germany, Netherlands, Spain, and the UK.
Tsering Lama is a storytelling manager with Greenpeace International.

title: We are still standing: from Lokolama, our forest continues to speak
full_content:
This story was originally posted by Greenpeace Africa
As the sun rises over Lokolama, the forest awakens long before we do.
Birdsong echoes through the canopy. Our elders are already walking the familiar forest paths they have known all their lives. Barefoot children run freely among the trees, unaware that during August the world is celebrating the Indigenous Peoples Month.
For them, this month is no different from any other.
It is simply another month spent with the forest that feeds them, protects them, heals them and teaches them how to live.
For me, however, this month is a reminder. A reminder that our story deserves to be told differently.
For far too long, Indigenous Peoples have been portrayed as vulnerable communities in need of protection. Yet long before the world began talking about climate change, biodiversity or nature-based solutions, our ancestors from Africa and other parts of the planet were already protecting these forests. They understood something fundamental: you do not own the forest, you belong to it.
I was born in Lokolama, Équateur Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Here, I learned to recognise the trees, to listen to the silence of the forest, and to understand that every river, every peatland and every living species forms part of a fragile balance that we have a responsibility to pass on to future generations.
Our ancestral knowledge is far more than a cultural heritage
Last year, Greenpeace Africa came to our village.
For several days, we walked together beneath the towering trees. We shared our stories, listened to our elders, met with young people, learned from the women of our community and discovered together that our ancestral knowledge is far more than a cultural heritage. It is a practical response to many of the challenges our planet faces today. The expedition to Lokolama and Penzélé showed that Indigenous communities are not merely beneficiaries of conservation; we are its first architects.
The forest is our past, our present and our future
One memory remains especially vivid.
I remember watching the children as they drew their vision of the perfect forest.
Not one of them drew an empty forest.
They drew towering trees, rivers filled with fish, bonobos, birds, butterflies and families living together in harmony with nature.
Their drawings were simple.
Yet they carried a profound truth:
Our forest is our home, our identity and our future
I also remember our conversations with the communities of Penzélé.
We spoke about past challenges and misunderstandings, but above all, about our shared determination to build a future where forests are no longer a source of conflict but a place of cooperation and peace. Because protecting the forest also means protecting the bonds that unite the people who call it home.
Today, as world leaders discuss climate finance, carbon markets, biodiversity and sustainable development, I would like to remind them of one essential truth.
The forests of the Congo Basin did not wait for international conferences to be protected
These forests have been safeguarded for generations by the women, men and young people who live within them.
Our knowledge does not come from books.
It comes from the seasons.
From the rivers.
From the trees.
From the forest paths our grandparents taught us to walk with humility and respect.
This does not mean that we reject development.
On the contrary.
We aspire to quality schools, accessible healthcare, better roads that connect our villages and opportunities for our young people.
But we believe that genuine development can never come at the expense of our identity, our ancestral lands or our rights.
We want to be part of decision making processes
We want to be partners.
Not merely observers.
We want to participate in the decisions that affect our territories because no one knows this forest better than the people who have lived with it for generations.
I am not asking the world to celebrate us.
I am asking the world to listen to us.
To listen to the voices rising from Lokolama, from Penzélé and from countless other villages across the Congo Basin and across the Earth.
Because behind every one of those voices lies knowledge, solutions and a vision of the future that our planet needs now more than ever.
Our shared future depends on our ability to protect the world’s forests.
And protecting forests begins with respecting those who have always been their first guardians.
We are Indigenous Peoples.
We are not the past.
We are an essential part of the future of the Congo Basin.
And as long as the forest continues to breathe,
We will continue walking beside it.
Valentin Engobo Mufia is a Representative of the Tshwa Indigenous People of Lokolama from The Democratic Republic of the Congo.

title: UN tax talks: Global South push for fairer rules as rich nations drag their feet on properly taxing wealthiest polluters
full_content:
New York – As the fifth round of negotiations concludes at the United Nations in New York, an ambitious Global Tax Treaty – also known as the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation – remains within reach. Major improvements to the zero draft text are still needed, however, to deliver global tax rules that will help solve the connected climate, nature, and inequality crises, rather than letting corporate polluters and the super-rich off the hook.
Nina Stros, Global Senior Policy Expert, Greenpeace International Political Unit said: “Global South demands for fair and inclusive international tax rules are starting to shape the text of the Framework Convention, and that is real progress. But without trust and a commitment from all parties to negotiate in good faith, we risk an empty treaty that fails to address problems everyone acknowledges exist. The most ambitious version of the Global Tax Treaty can only be built on truly international tax cooperation, where every voice counts, including those of the communities hit hardest by the climate crisis, not just predominantly those of the wealthiest polluters and their patrons.
“Outside these negotiating rooms, people are living through extreme weather and rising bills, paying for a crisis they did little to cause, while the wealthiest polluters keep profiting. Too many countries are losing revenues to tax havens. The Global Tax Treaty is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to correct the unfairness and the dysfunctions of existing tax agreements and the broken corporate tax system. It’s time for every country to step up and bring concrete solutions that work for people and the planet.”
Key takeaways from INC-5 include:
- A strong Global Tax Treaty is still a long way off, but the developments from this session were encouraging. Negotiations moved from the abstract to the concrete. The draft text is moving towards a fairer allocation of taxing rights over multinational profits, which could overhaul the unfair and undemocratic system currently shaped by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
- Global South countries showed strength and unity, many coming together to defend strong language on fairer allocation of taxing rights and to push for more robust articles, including on taxing high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) and on harmful tax practices. Some emerging and middle-income economies played a bridge-building role, including regarding the article on sustainable development; arguably a sign of wider shifts in global power and of a growing understanding that this treaty is instrumental in delivering other UN agreements, like those under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
- Wealthy nations, particularly in Europe, favoured complaining over proposing solutions. Despite countries championing climate action in other global forums, European countries mostly stayed silent on sustainable development here, and many called for changes that would defend the status-quo of corporate and super-rich tax-dodging. They must move from complainer to solution-seeker, not only to rebuild trust with the Global South and unlock ambition, but so that their own people benefit from the hundreds of billions of dollars a year that could be reclaimed by holding the wealthiest polluters to account.
- Momentum is building towards environment-aligned tax and spending. Several Global South countries signalled they would bring forward new proposals to strengthen the treaty’s environmental tax and sustainable development provisions in Article 4, which some Global North countries have expressed interest to explore. With more ambition, this could lay the legal foundations for global and national progressive polluter taxes, while ensuring that governments’ tax and spending policies support global climate and environmental agreements.
- Heightened discussions on Article 6, concerning the taxation of high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), particularly across G77 countries, showed that cross-regional cooperation and alliances hold a significant potential for a bolder outcome.
There was also broad support among countries for bringing civil society and other stakeholders into future Conference of Parties (COP) meetings, which will be vital to raise ambition and hold countries to account through this process as it moves towards delivering the treaty.
Negotiations for the Global Tax Treaty will continue until mid-2027. The sixth round of negotiations will be held in Nairobi from 30 November to 11 December 2026, followed by three further rounds of negotiations next year. Greenpeace will continue to attend, urging every country to be guided by the realities their people face outside the negotiating room, and to hold negotiators to the promise this treaty represents.

title: Greenpeace Pictures of the Week
full_content:
From protests against oil and gas in the Black Sea, to documenting drought impacts in Germany. Here are a few of our favourite images from Greenpeace work around the world this week.
🇧🇬Bulgaria – Greenpeace activists from five countries painted “NO GAS + OIL” on the side of the abandoned tanker “Kairos”, part of Russia’s shadow fleet, anchored off the coast of Burgas, Bulgaria. The activity protested against the toxic dependence on oil and gas, which funds wars, fuels corruption, and endangers marine ecosystems and local communities.
🇩🇪Germany – During a forest tour in Reiersdorf, Brandenburg, Greenpeace highlights the extreme fire risk posed by pine monocultures, showing how structurally diverse mixed forests with deadwood cool the ground and naturally prevent wildfires.
🇳🇱Netherlands – Activists from Greenpeace Netherlands have modified the names of several train stations following yet another tropical day this summer. Stations were renamed to ‘Hotterdam Centraal’, ‘Amsterwarm Centraal’, ‘Grillversum Media Park’, and ‘Smelthogenbosch’. With temperatures soaring well above 30°C and a record number of tropical days, the campaign highlights the reality of the climate crisis caused by fossil fuels and emphasizes that these extreme weather events are no longer exceptions. The action calls on politicians to take decisive steps toward phasing out fossil energy ahead of the Climate March in Amsterdam on September 12.
🇩🇰Denmark – Danish fjords, lakes and coastal waters are plagued by oxygen depletion due to decades of pollution from industrial pig farming. Greenpeace Nordic is on an expedition to measure and document the extent of the problem, as well as nitrogen pollution, which originates mainly from pig manure spread onto the fields.
🇩🇪Germany – Drought impacts Rhine River’s water level in Germany. The river Rhine shown here with a very low water level in Cologne.
Greenpeace has been a pioneer of photo activism for more than 50 years, and remains committed to bearing witness and exposing environmental injustice through the images we capture.
To see more Greenpeace photos and videos, please visit our Media Library.

title: Danish expression of the day: Lokummet brænder
full_content:
What does lokummet brænder mean?
This is a fantastic, very visual expression used when disaster strikes. Literally translated, it means “the outhouse is burning”, but a more accurate translation would be “we’re in deep trouble” or (to stick with the toilet-theme) “Shit has hit the fan”.
Where did lokummet brænder come from?
While the exact year the idiom was coined isn't recorded in the official dictionaries, it stems from the days before indoor plumbing. Most apartments in Danish cities didn’t come with plumbing, and therefore communal outhouses were used.
Picture one of them catching fire: it wouldn’t just be dangerous, it was a chaotic, foul-smelling, and an incredibly urgent disaster.
The phrase has clearly survived the modernisation of plumbing and remains a staple of informal Danish slang today.
READ ALSO: What’s up with Copenhagen apartments' minuscule bathrooms?
Why is lokummet brænder worth knowing?
This term pretty perfectly encapsulates the Danes’ dry and dark sense of humour.
The expression is incredibly common in conversational Danish and you may even come across it in business settings, though most likely in more modern, laid-back offices, when describing a stressful deadline or a failing project.
Examples
Vi er bagud med projektet, og kunden ankommer om fem minutter. Lokummet brænder!
“We are behind on the project, and the client is arriving in five minutes. We're in deep trouble!”
De er bagud 3-0, og der er kun ti minutter tilbage af kampen. Nu brænder lokummet for alvor for landsholdet.
“They are down 3-0 with only ten minutes left in the game. Shit’s really hitting the fan for the national team.”
Jeg glemte min kones fødselsdag i morges... lokummet brænder.
“I forgot my wife's birthday this morning... I'm in massive trouble.”

title: The most common Danish e-mail sign-offs and what they really mean
full_content:
Med venlig hilsen/Venlig hilsen
This is the most standard, go-to sign-off. It’s neutral, inoffensive, but kind. Literally, it translates to “with friendly greetings” or “friendly greetings”, however, a more accurate translation would be “Kind regards”.
Mvh/Vh
Mvh or Vh are abbreviations of the above. Although almost just as common, these might come across as slightly colder in tone.
Venlige hilsner
Venlige hilsner is the plural of Venlig hilsen, and interestingly, in making it plural, it seems to increase the friendliness of the sign-off. While you might use the singular Venlig hilsen in neutral contexts, such as communication with your electricity provider or landlord, Venlige hilsner might be considered when writing to someone who you have or will have physical contact with.
Kærlig hilsen
Kærlig hilsen translates literally to “loving greetings”, but more accurately to “Lots of love”. This is how you might sign off an email to a close friend, or a birthday card to your grandparents. It would be unusual to use this in business contexts and might lead to some raised eyebrows.
Kh
Kh is the abbreviation of kærlig hilsen. This one may be marginally more common in business emails, but is still unusual. We recommend steering clear of using Kh and Kærlig hilsen in business or formal contexts, if you’re not fully comfortable with the term.
Hilsen
Hilsen translates literally to “Greetings”, but more accurately to “Regards”. It’s neutral and standard, but perhaps lacks personality and may even be how you sign off an email if you’re slightly ticked off with someone.
De bedste hilsner/Dbh.
De bedste hilsner translated to “best regards”. Although perfectly acceptable and appropriate to use, de bedste hilsner, or dbh for short, can be viewed as being slightly more old-fashioned and formal, with some feeling that it is outdated or “un-Danish”. If this is your preferred sign-off, go for it! But just be aware that de bedste hilsner isn’t quite as common as the English “best regards”.
Mange hilsner
Mange hilsner translates to “Many regards” and falls into a similar category to “Med Venlig Hilsen”. However, this one is far less common and is possibly seen as being slightly less formal. Mange hilsner is a perfectly appropriate sign-off to use with colleagues, but Med venlig hilsen might be a better option if you’re writing to clients and customers.
Knus/kram/kys
These sign-offs translate as “hugs” (knus/kram) and “kisses” (kys). It goes without saying that these should only be used with close friends and family. It would in most circumstances be viewed as inappropriate to include these in a work email.
På forhånd tak
På forhånd tak translates to “Thanks in advance”. You can use this simply as a sign-off, or add it as the final line before an additional sign-off, such as Med venlig hilsen. It’s a good one to include when communicating with customer service, or after having asked a for a favour or for a task to be completed.
Keeping it short: /
Some people like to keep it really short, and simply use a forward-slash followed by their name: “/John”. It’s to the point, works in all languages, and is a bit difficult to read any further meaning into.

title: More than 150 million in Europe face temperatures over 35C on Friday
full_content:
Temperatures are set to surpass 30C for around three out of five European residents (excluding Turkey) -- amounting to around 350 million people, according to an analysis based on German weather service forecasts and 2025 population projections from the Joint Research Centre, with results consistent with the Austrian NGO Klimadashboard.
Europe is the fastest-warming continent and in some places is ill-equipped to deal with hot weather.
Scientists have shown that recurring heatwaves are a clear marker of global warming, primarily caused by burning coal, oil and gas -- and warn they are set to become more frequent, longer and more intense.
Repeat heatwaves and drought have fuelled a historically hot summer of wildfires, and contributed to the deaths of thousands of people.
READ ALSO: Western Europe experienced hottest June-July on record
In France, temperatures climbed even higher, with weather service Meteo-France recording 42.5C in Chateaumeillant in central France, the country's highest reading on Thursday.
Paris hit 38C and much of the country was under a heatwave alert.
In Italy, similar temperatures were forecast to affect 29 million people, particularly along the west coast, in the Po Valley, the south and on Italy's islands.
Large parts of the Iberian Peninsula also sweltered, with around 25 million people affected in Spain. The country's Aemet weather agency recorded temperatures of 37C in central regions on Thursday.
In the UK, temperatures also reached 36C or higher in 40 locations across central and southern England. The country is on track to record its hottest ever summer, the Met Office said this week.
The heatwave has fanned wildfires across Europe. In northern Greece, hundreds of tourists were evacuated by boat as a forest fire bore down on two popular resorts, while crews in central England's West Midlands region battled blazes damaging homes amid drought conditions.
AFP calculates the figures using a method similar to that of Klimadashboard, cross-referencing population density with the weather forecast model from the Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD) -- Germany's national meteorological service -- published at 0300 GMT.
Residents are counted if the model forecasts temperatures above 30C or 35C at their location at any point during the day.
As the model has a resolution of approximately 6.5 km it does not fully capture urban heat-island effects, when cities are significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas, David Jablonski of NGO Klimadashboard told AFP.
Consequently, the analysis "likely underestimates the number of people affected in densely populated urban areas", the organisation notes on its "European Heat Tracker" website.
In London, temperatures hit 38.1C at Kew Gardens, making it the fifth-hottest day on record for Britain, according to official weather agency the Met Office.

title: Danish word of the day: fræk
full_content:
What does fræk mean?
Fræk is a commonly used word in the Danish language and has three main meanings.
- Cheeky, naughty or rude: when used to describe behaviour - especially children’s behaviour - it means misbehaving, talking back, or just generally doing something they know they’re not supposed to.
- Sexy or risqué: In an adult context, fræk means physically attractive in a provocative way, or something which is sexually suggestive.
- Cool, Edgy, or Audacious: When describing inanimate objects (like a car, a dress, or a piece of design), it means something is visually striking, bold, or cool.
Where does fræk come from?
Fræk comes from the Middle Low German word frech. In early Danish history, it was actually a compliment used to describe a brave or fearless warrior. Over centuries, "bold" morphed into "brazen" and "shameless," eventually softening into "naughty" or "rude".
Fræk with the “sexy” or “risqué” meaning, is a more modern twist on the word, and according to the Danish dictionary (Den Danske Ordbog), only officially took hold in the Danish language around 1966, mirroring the cultural shifts of the 1960s.
Why is it worth knowing?
This word is incredibly common in Denmark. You’ll very commonly hear parents calling their kids fræk (or en frækkert, the Danish equivalent of “a cheeky monkey”).
However you might also come across fræk on dating apps or when out enjoying Danish nightlife.
Understanding the difference between fræk used for children and adults shows a mastery of the Danish language.
Examples
Nu skal du ikke være fræk!
"Don't be cheeky!"
Hun havde en ret fræk kjole på.
"She was wearing a pretty sexy dress.”
Han har købt en lille fræk sportsbåd.
“He’s bought a little cool sports boat.”

title: The best places to buy English books in Copenhagen
full_content:
The independent shops:
Tranquebar is great independent bookshop in the heart of Copenhagen. They offer a wide selection of books, both in Danish and in English, from romance, philosophy and poetry to children’s books, cook books and more.
Books & Company can be found outside of the hustle and bustle of Copenhagen City. Hop on the train (or take a bike-ride up north) to Hellerup, where you’ll find this lovely independent bookshop opened in 2009 by an American woman.
Another independent shop to consider is Ark books, an international non-profit, volunteer-run bookshop which has been a part of Nørrebro since 2014. This bookshop is unlikely to have top-selling books on their shelves, but rather a curated selection of interesting and quirky books. Visit this shop if you’re looking for a new book to read and are open to suggestions.
Although New Mags might not be the place to go if you already have your heart set on a book, this beautiful shop is worth a visit if you’re in the mood for perusing beautiful coffee table books, cook books, magazines, children’s books and more.
The Pond is a cute little book shop and cafe in the Nørrebro neighbourhood of Copenhagen. They pride themselves in being an LGBTQIA+ book shop, run by nonbinary staff, selling queer books, and offering a safe, inclusive space for all.
The chains:
This one is at the top of the list for a reason. Although Politiken’s Boghal isn’t exactly a chain, it also doesn’t seem fair to put it with the “independent” shops, as it’s owned by the major Danish newspaper, Politiken.
Politikens Boghal is a big and fantastic bookshop, just off the main town square, Rådhuspladsen. Although their main selection of books is in Danish, they also have a big section of English books. If you happen to have a membership with Politiken, this will give you a 10 percent discount in the shop.
Although the, at the time, 123-year-old company behind Arnold Busck went bankrupt in 2020, many of the iconic shops were purchased and rescued by other companies. JP/Politikens Hus bought the famous, multi-story flagship store on Købmagergade in the heart of Copenhagen. Although the shop predominantly sells Danish books, you will also find a good selection of English ones.
Bog og Ide is another chain which you’ll find scattered across most of the country. Their online store has a great selection of English books, and most of their Copenhagen shops will also have a dedicated English-language section.
Although Saxo isn’t a physical shop, this is the Danish webshop where you’ll find the absolute best selection of English books. If you’re an avid reader, consider getting a Saxo membership. From 79 kroner a month (59 kroner if you're under 28), you get free shipping and a member's discount (usually around 10 percent, but this varies) on all orders.
Other
Vangsgaards Antikvariat claims to be the Nordic region’s biggest antique bookshop, and is known in Copenhagen for its impressive selection of books. While you’re most likely to find Danish books, you will also find books in other languages. They even have a search function, allowing you to look up the book you’re trying to find.
If you’re the type of person who takes pride in owning books, and you get a kick out of admiring them all lined up on your book shelf, this option probably won’t be one for you. However many expats don’t realise that Danish libraries have a massive selection of English books. You can look them up on their website or app Biblioteket (a handy one to install as it will update you on approaching hand-in deadlines, as well as keep you informed on local events) and either reserve them, or add yourself to the wait list for them.
You’d be surprised by how many English books pop up on secondhand platforms like Vinted and Reshopper, and often for exceptionally good prices. If you’re wondering what second hand platforms are best to use in Denmark, take a look at the list we compiled.

title: What to do if you encounter a wolf in Denmark
full_content:
The pamphlets, developed by The Ministry of Green Transition, include useful information for everyone, so we’ve decided to highlight some key points.
READ ALSO: Wolves approaching humans in Jutland may have been 'actively fed'
- Stay still and keep calm. It’s very rare that wolves approach people, but if you do come across a wolf who isn’t shy towards humans, and who comes closer than 30 metres, keep very still, stay calm, keep an eye on the animal, and if possible, take a photo or video as documentation.
- Don’t follow the wolf, as this might stress or anger it. Give it time and peace to distance itself from you.
- If you feel uneasy, make some noise. If the wolf doesn’t leave by itself, shout, clap your hands or wave your arms around. This signals that you’re a human, which in itself is usually enough to scare off a wolf.
- Keep eye contact. Never turn your back on an approaching wolf, but continue looking directly at it. Show dominance in the same way as you might over an aggressive dog.
- Stay seated, if you see a wolf from your car. A wolf doesn’t associate vehicles with humans and is therefore unlikely to interact with cars. Stay in your car until the wolf is gone.
- Back away slowly if you and the wolf notice each other when you’re very close to each other. If the wolf feels threatened, it may growl and show its teeth. This isn’t necessarily a sign that it’s going to attack you, but rather that it’s afraid. Give it some space, and it will naturally flee.
- If the wolf attacks, kick and hit it. We have yet to experience any human being attacked by a wolf in Denmark, but if it does, you need to use physical strength to ward off the wolf. Use this tactic too, if the wolf attacks your dog.
The Ministry of Green Transition has also published recommendations on how to avoid attracting wolves to your garden or home if you live in an affected area.
- Stop feeding wild animals such as deer, hedgehogs and more.
- Don’t leave out food waste. Meat attracts wolves especially much, and wolf pups are naturally curious and will learn to associate humans with food if they repeatedly find food in the same place.
- Protect your pets. Bring your pets in at night, and don’t let your dog roam too far, as wolves can take interest in them, as they see them as equals.
And lastly the Ministry of Green Transition has made a list of recommendations for how you can protect your dog against wolves.
- Keep your dog on a lead, as these are less likely to be viewed as a threat to wolves.
- Keep your dog close if you meet a wolf.
- If you’re out hunting, keep your hunting dogs close, and as a minimum where you can see and hear them.
Wolves are a protected species in Denmark, but they can be shot if they are deemed to be a “problem wolf”, a term used for wolves that are not shy around people, roam urban areas, have attacked livestock behind wolf-proof fences, or are a danger to human safety.
If you do spot a wolf, make sure to report your sighting on ulveatlas.dk, to help the Danish Nature Agency keep track of Denmark’s wolves.

title: Europe battles new wave of wildfires
full_content:
Friday was expected to see some 150 million Europeans -- particularly in France, Germany, Spain and Italy -- experience temperatures over 35C, according to AFP calculations.
And temperatures of over 30C were set to affect some 350 million residents, accounting for three in five people in Europe (excluding Turkey), an AFP analysis of German weather service and Joint Research Centre population data found.
The historically hot summer has contributed to the deaths of thousands of people -- and increased the risk of forest fires.
Here are the latest developments:
READ ALSO: More than 150 million in Europe face temperatures over 35C on Friday
France
A forest fire in the Landes region of southwest France reignited early Saturday forcing the evacuation of another 100 residents and holidaymakers around the town of Luglon, authorities said.
The fire, which has been burning since Thursday, has now devastated 15.8 square kilometers (six square miles) of forest with some 650 people forced out of their homes, said regional government prefect Gilles Clavreul. Some 550 firefighters are in the battle against the flames near the eruption of another fire in July that covered 37 square km of land. Clavreul said he had asked the government to send a Chinook water-bombing helicopter that has been sent by Australia to help with France's wildfire crisis.
READ ALSO: 500 evacuated as new wildfire breaks out in south-west France
Germany
In Germany's Eifel region, just across the border from Belgium, some 1,400 firefighters on Saturday battled to contain a major fire that has forced the evacuation of some 1,800 people from Hurtgenwald – a town of 9,000.
READ ALSO: Wildfire forces evacuation of 1,800 people in North Rhine-Westphalia
Spain
A fire in the northeastern region of Aragon is raging for a sixth day and has affected more than 15,000 hectares, but firemen say they have halted its spread towards population centres and two monasteries, one of which has roots in the 10th century.
Some 1,000 people from 18 different villages and settlements remain evacuated, though weather forecasts call for some welcome light rain and lower temperature.
Belgium
A wildfire at the Fagnes natural park in eastern Belgium, near the border with Germany, has ravaged almost 8.5 square kilometers of forest, authorities said. The fire started Friday and spread rapidly through the night.
Firefighter reinforcements from all of Belgium and from Germany have been called in.
Croatia
More than 100 firefighters and two water bombing planes battled through the night to contain a major forest fire that broke out on Friday on the Croatian island of Dugi otok, threatening a large number of homes.
Another major fire, which engulfed vineyards and olive groves on the Peljesac peninsula further south, was also brought under control on Friday evening, following a fierce battle involving 240 firefighters and three planes.
Serbia
Serbian authorities said late Friday they were battling 25 serious forest fires, including one which has devastated 25 sq km of land at the Deliblatska national park near Belgrade.
Greece
Firefighters remain on high alert in Greece, where the risk of fire remains very high in several parts of the country due to strong winds.
More than fifty agricultural and forest fires have broken out in the last 24 hours, most of which were brought under control quickly, according to the fire service.

title: EU pushes back as US revives trade pressure on bloc
full_content:
Washington's ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, called on the bloc Friday to "align" the provisions of two landmark new laws on environmental and human rights supply chain standards with the EU-US trade deal struck last year.
"Now it's time for the EU to deliver," Puzder posted on X, along with a US government document detailing a long list of "concerns" with the rules.
"The United States will take any actions necessary to address unreasonable burdens on US commerce absent a solution that addresses these concerns," the document warned.
Responding to Puzder's message, European Commission spokesperson Arianna Podesta said the EU continued to "exchange on both tariff and non-tariff issues", with the United States, calling the process "constructive".
But she added: "We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation."
The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) requires large companies to fix the "adverse human rights and environmental impacts" of their supply chains worldwide, while the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requires them to provide information on their climate impact and emissions, and steps to limit them.
"The directives' extraterritorial reach and costly and onerous supply chain due diligence obligations will adversely impact the ability of US businesses to compete on a level playing field in the EU market," read the US document.
The EU has already dialled back the scope of both laws under pressure from businesses both inside and outside the bloc, delaying implementation and sparing smaller firms, but the US document said that did not go far enough.
Puzder's comments came a day after he hit out at the bloc's carbon border tax, CBAM, which he charged was "a tariff in substance, no matter the 'climate policy' label".
Separately, the EU was among dozens of trading partners flagged in a White House report Thursday as risks regarding "illegal transshipment" from China -- where goods are sent through third countries to avoid paying sweeping levies imposed by President Donald Trump.
The report, which also targeted Mexico, Canada and Japan, vowed to tap artificial intelligence to help detect illegal practices in future.
"The EU shares the US objective of tackling customs fraud," the commission spokesperson said in response to the accusations.
Podesta said Brussels was "engaging" with Washington to better understand the report's "potential implications for the EU," while noting that the document found the EU transshipment risk to be "embedded within broad legitimate trade flows."

title: On the Agenda: What's happening in Denmark next week?
full_content:
Monday, August 17th
Black Hole Week, hosted by the Center of Gravity, starts on Monday, August 17th. The event kicks off with a micro-opera: a lyrical performance dedicated to black holes. Black Hole Week includes lots of other great educational events, including Science & Cocktails, where you can learn about black holes while enjoying a cocktail, a talk about where black holes come from at The Round Tower, and more.
Tuesday, August 18th
Court case between Dansk Folkeparti and Radikale Venstre
The chairman of the Danish People's Party (Dansk Folkeaparti), Morten Messerschmidt, and the political leader of the Social Liberal Party (Radical Venstre), Martin Lidegaard, are expected to meet in the Court in Frederiksberg on August 18th. This is a civil lawsuit in which Messerschmidt has sued Lidegaard for defamation, due to his statements that Dansk Folkeparti want to deport citizens based on their skin colour.
Wednesday, August 19th
The Danish Democrats’ Summer Meeting
The political summer meetings are in full swing, and this week the Danish Democrats (Danmarksdemokraterne), Denmark’s right-wing populist party, are hosting their summer meeting on August 19th and 20th in Nyborg on the island of Funen.
Thursday, August 20th
Thursday sees the start of a large variety of cultural events, one of them being Kulturmødet Mors, a cultural event which takes place in Mors in North Jutland. The event celebrates art and culture through debates, performances, workshops, exhibitions and more. More than 32,000 visitors are expected to attend the event which start on August 20th and lasts until August 22nd.
Louisiana, one of Denmark’s most famous modern art museums, kicks off its much anticipated event, Louisiana Literature, which starts on Thursday, August 20th. This annual event celebrates modern literature through interviews, dialogues, readings, performances and musical interpretations. The event takes place all weekend and features many Danish authors, but also international authors such as Douglas Stuart, Katie Kitamura, David Szalay, and more.
One more cultural event takes place, this one nestled between the Black Diamond library and the Danish parliament, Christiansborg, in a secret garden. The event takes place every Thursday evening until mid-September. This week’s event features musical performances, artistic interpretations of poetry and talks on the topic of “trust”.
Liberal Alliance’s Summer Meeting
On Thursday, August 20th, one of Denmark’s centre-right political parties, Liberal Alliance, hosts its annual summer meeting, which this year takes place at Egelund Castle in Fredensborg in North Zealand.
Friday, August 21st
Copenhagen Cooking and Food Festival
Copenhagen Cooking is an annual food festival which takes place in the heart of Copenhagen. Every year at the end of August, the country’s best chefs, restaurants, producers, cultural institutions, and foodies gather for a 10-day celebration of Copenhagen’s diverse food scene. This year’s programme includes everything from outdoor, communal dinners, a day dedicated to the Danish smørrebrød, and an event revolving around Spanish jamón (ham). If you’re a foodie, this is an event you won’t want to miss.
A handful of Fridays throughout the summer, streets across Copenhagen are closed, as roller-skaters zoom through the city. The routes change each time, and are roughly 20km long. Between 500 and 1000 people take part in each event. The trip starts and finishes at Next House, close to Copenhagen’s Central Station, begins at 7.30pm, and takes roughly two hours.
Saturday, August 22nd
On Saturday and Sunday, Esbjerg’s annual music festival takes place in the city’s harbour on the west coast of Denmark. This year’s lineup features big international names such as Pet Shop Boys and Kelis (known for her song Milkshake), and big Danish names such as Rasmus Seebach, Dizzy Mizz Lizzy, Suspekt, and more.
Opening of Hovedstadens Letbane
The Greater Copenhagen light rail (Hovedstadens Letbane) opens the last stretch of its route August 22nd, allowing passengers to travel the entire route from Ishøj to Lundtofte north of Lyngby. The opening will be marked by a public festival at Gladsaxe Town Hall with music and activities. The full opening of the light rail system includes 17 new stations, connecting Rødovre and Lyngby, adding to the existing 12 stations between Ishøj and Rødovre.
With the season for Octoberfest approaching, Reffen are kicking things off with a party dedicated to good beer. The event invites micro-breweries to their pop-up bars, as well as talks, tastings, and beer bingo.
Sunday, August 23rd
On Sunday, August 23rd, you can go for a walk around the stone embankment around Copenhagen's new (and controvertial) peninsula, Lynetteholm and get a full sense of how large the peninsula will be. The full walk is 7.5km long, but a shorter 4km option is also available. The event requires registration, and includes free coffee, snacks, talks and more.
READ ALSO: Party demands new environmental scrutiny of Copenhagen artificial island project
On Sunday August 23rd, DSB (Danish State Railways) invites everyone to what they call Cykelsøndag or “Bike Sunday”. The S-trains, which run from central Copenhagen through Zealand to many of the capital’s suburban towns, will be free, and bike-related events have been planned, such as free bike repairs in Ishøj, bike rides and pancakes in Hareskoven, mountain biking in Rude Skov, and more.

title: LATEST: Europe's battle with wildfires continues
full_content:
A historically hot summer has contributed to the deaths of thousands of people -- and increased the risk of forest fires. Here are the latest developments:
Belgium fire doubles leading to heavy smoke pollution in Germany's Monschau
A wildfire raging in a nature reserve in eastern Belgium, the biggest to hit the country in recent history, has more than doubled in size in 24 hours to affect some 3,000 hectares (7,500 acres), authorities said.
The Wallonia regional government said more than 250 firefighters and other emergency personnel were mobilised through the night, but that "conditions remain challenging" two days after the fire's outbreak in the High Fens park.
On Sunday, the entire area along the German border to Belgium was shrouded in thick, yellowish smoke.
According to German authorities, the flames are now just three kilometres from the German border. Although the fire was not expected to spread into the country, significant smoke pollution was likely, so on Sunday morning, authorities "urgently" advised residents in three districts of border town Monschau in North-Rhine Westphalia to leave their homes by 10am.
The town said on its website that it "cannot be ruled out that there will be increased, significant smoke exposure and smoke fallout starting in the morning."
Four arrested over Croatia fires
Croatian police said they had arrested four people suspected of starting some of the wildfires that have swept parts of the Adriatic coast in recent days.
The four are suspected of setting fires that scorched pine forests and olive groves as Croatia battles a wave of blazes fuelled by drought and heat.
France gets a grip on wildfires
A fire in southwestern France has burnt 1,700 hectares since Thursday, but "the situation is developing more favourably", with no major flare-ups in the night, according to regional prefect Gilles Clavreul, thanks in particular to falling temperatures.
The circumstances of another fire in the northeastern Ardennes had improved, a local official said. Around 100 hectares have been burnt since Saturday, a situation described as "unprecedented in the recent history" of the department, according to the deputy director of the Ardennes fire service, David Gouzou.
READ ALSO: 500 evacuated as new wildfire breaks out in south-west France
Greek island fire
Firefighters were battling for a second day to contain a forest fire on the Greek Aegean island of Skyros, as the local mayor voiced hope it could soon be brought under control.
"Within the day I believe the fire will be fully extinguished," Skyros mayor Kyriakos Antonopoulos told state TV ERT.
Germany
In Germany's Eifel region, just across the border from Belgium, a major fire that forced the evacuation of some 1,800 people from Hürtgenwald – a town of 9,000 – was improving on Sunday although the flames had not yet been completely extinguished.
Residents were able to return to their homes as the situation around the Gey district had "eased sufficiently," the Düren district stated on its website Saturday evening.
The spread had been halted and there was no longer any immediate threat to the district from the forest fire, authorities said.
According to reports, around 1,600 emergency personnel remain on site.
READ ALSO: Wildfire forces evacuation of 1,800 people in North Rhine-Westphalia
Spain
A fire in the northeastern region of Aragon is raging for a seventh day and has affected more than 16,000 hectares, but firemen said on Saturday they had halted its spread towards population centres and two monasteries, one of which has roots in the 10th century.
On Sunday, France is sending 100 firefighters, 16 fire engines and a helicopter to support the operation.
As a precaution, authorities sent an emergency ES text alert on Sunday, asking people hiking or engaging in other activities in forest areas to remain in urban environments and not venture into the mountains due to the proximity of the forest fire to Peña Oroel mountain.
Over 1,000 people from 20 different villages and settlements remain evacuated, though weather forecasts call for some welcome light rain and lower temperatures.

title: Today in Denmark: A roundup of the latest news on Monday
full_content:
Copenhagen celebrates Pride peacefully without arrests
Thousands of people attended the Copenhagen Pride festival on Saturday, including Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, without police having to make any arrests.
"There have been no assaults, and we have had no arrests in connection with Copenhagen Pride, so it's gone well and without any major issues," Mads Østermark from the Copenhagen Police said after the event. "There can always be some minor issues when there are a lot of people on the streets and when people are drinking alcohol."
The parade on Saturday was the culmination of a week of celebrations as Copenhagen Pride marked its 30th anniversary.
"In a world where rights are being rolled back and democracy is under pressure, we must fight for the basic democratic values, and of course that also means that two men can be together and that a rainbow family can have good conditions," Frederiksen told TV2 during the parade.
The Liberal Party was the only party from Denmark's right-wing opposition which took part in this year's event, a decision Jakob Engel-Schmidt, tax minister from the Moderate Party, told TV2 was "a bit sad".
Danish vocabulary: en smule trist – a bit sad
Red-Green Alliance calls for ban on US company Palantir
Denmark's far-Left Red-Green Alliance has called for a ban on the use of software from the controversial US company Palantir by Danish police, intelligence services and other public agencies.
Ahead of the party's group meeting on Monday, the party's leader, Pelle Dragsted, said his party aimed to demand in upcoming budget negotiations that money be put aside for helping these agencies that use Palantir's products replace it with Danish or European software.
"We are concerned about whether Palantir can be used by the United States to gain access to sensitive information about Denmark and Greenland. This is about digital sovereignty and being able to stand on our own two feet," he said.
"We must not be vulnerable in relation to Trump and his government, which, as we know, uses every vulnerability and dependency as a means of pressure."
Dragsted also said that the government must push ahead with its agreement to lower VAT on food, threatening to trigger a government crisis if the agreement is not fulfilled.
"This is not a threat, it is a fact," Dragsted told the Børsen newspaper.
The proposal has been met with harsh criticism from economists, who warn, among other things, that it is an expensive and inefficient way to help citizens.
Danish vocabulary: et forbud – a ban
Man flown for treatment after stabbing in Horsens
A man was flown to hospital for treatment by helicopter on Sunday after he was stabbed in a violent assault in central Horsens. Police cordoned off the area after the attack and blocked the nearby roads. Police officers were out on patrol on Sankt Helene Vej and Sønderbrogade, the two most affected areas.
The cordon was lifted at 1.30am on Monday morning. Police have concluded that the stabbing was an "isolated incident" and have told residents there is no risk that the situation "may develop further".
Danish vocabulary: knivstikkeri – stabbing
Denmark gets unified emergency psychiatric hotline
Denmark is launching a nationwide psychiatric emergency hotline, which anyone in Denmark can access by ringing the 112 emergency number or contacting their local regional emergency doctor, or lægevagten.
The scheme was first announced in 2023 as part of a psychiatric agreement between all the parties in the Danish parliament, but it has taken until now to be rolled out across the country.
If a citizen or their relative calls the emergency medical service with a mental health issue, the service can then trigger a psychiatric referral to a consultant with psychiatric skills.
The new function is staffed by nurses and social and health assistants with psychiatric experience in close collaboration with the regions' psychiatric specialists.
The scheme was developed after three people were killed at the Field's shopping centre in the summer of 2022 by a man who had spent years in and out of psychiatric treatment.
Danish vocabulary: sygeplejersker – nurses

title: Denmark launches unified emergency psychiatric hotline
full_content:
The scheme was first announced in 2023 as part of a psychiatric agreement between all the parties in the Danish parliament, but it has taken until now to be rolled out across the country.
Essentially, the new scheme means that anyone calling 112, whether for a physical or mental health issue, can receive emergency assistance. In the case of an emergency mental health issue, a call will trigger a referral to a consultant with psychiatric skills.
The new function is staffed by nurses and social and health assistants with psychiatric experience in close collaboration with the regions' psychiatric specialists.
Callers who need to go to hospital can still be picked up in an ambulance and treated by paramedics if needed, before being brought to emergency psychiatric evaluation.
One of the aims of the new scheme is to provide help before a situation worsens or develops to the extent that the patient requires inpatient treatment.
The scheme was developed after three people were killed at the Field's shopping centre in the summer of 2022 by a man who had spent years in and out of psychiatric treatment. The incident sparked a debate about psychiatric treatment in Denmark, including a request for a national emergency line for psychiatric issues.
Mia Kristina Hansen, spokesperson for national mental health association Sind, said a year after the attack that she was disappointed that the new emergency line was not yet in place.
"If the perpetrator had called and they had said that someone needed to drive out to him and help him, I think that would have made a huge difference," she said.
Ida Auken, health and church minister, welcomed the new scheme, saying that it is part of a new "historic" improvement in psychiatric treatment in Denmark.
"For a lot of people with mental health issues, the psychiatric emergency line will be a quick and easy way to access treatment," she said in a press statement.
The new scheme will be monitored closely for further evaluation.

title: SAS launches direct route from Denmark to India for first time in 17 years
full_content:
The new route will start from October 1st and will be trafficked by Airbus A330s, meaning that there will be 266 seats available on each flight. Flights will continue at that frequency throughout the year.
In a press release, SAS said that the direct route will strengthen Copenhagen Airport's position as an important transit airport, as it offers routes to other major European destinations and longer routes to cities like New York, Boston and Toronto.
Paul Verhagen, the airline's commercial director, described the new route as "an unusual milestone for SAS", which would "open the doors between Scandinavia and one of the world's most dynamic economic centres".
SAS has not had a direct route between Denmark and India since 2009, according to airline industry site Check-in.dk, when the route between Copenhagen and New Delhi was closed to save costs.
Air India currently flies between Copenhagen and New Delhi in northern India, while Mumbai lies on the west coast.
Copenhagen Airport is not only Denmark's main airport, but also the closest major airport for much of southern Sweden.

title: Excessive kissing and cutting socks: Denmark's weird and wonderful wedding traditions
full_content:
The ceremony
We’ll start off simple: the ceremony. Nothing too shocking happens here. The ceremony either takes place in a church or at a town hall, the latter being the more popular, and faster of the two ceremonies, taking at the very most 15 minutes. A church wedding will include hymns chosen by the couple.
The ceremony includes similar traditions as in other countries: the groom shouldn’t see the bride before she walks down the aisle, typically accompanied by her father; they don’t spend the night before the wedding in the same bedroom; rice is thrown over the newlyweds as they leave the church or town hall.
Dress code
When trying to plan your outfit, there are a few colours which should be avoided at a Danish wedding. White is strictly reserved for the bride. Avoid anything white, cream-coloured, light beige, or even a white dress with flowers on. Black is the colour of mourning and should also be avoided at weddings. Red in old traditions symbolises that you have had a romantic relationship with either the bride or the groom. Red might not necessarily be off-limits, but it may be a good idea to ask the bride or groom for their opinion first. If in doubt, ask!
Kransekage
After the ceremony, a larger group of guests will be invited to have champagne and kransekage, a traditional Scandinavian confection made from marzipan, sugar, and egg whites. It is shaped into stacked, concentric rings to form a tall, cone-shaped tower decorated with white icing.
Dinner
The number of guests usually thins slightly for the dinner, which takes place after the kransekage has been eaten.
Removing your jacket
Guests can’t take their jackets off until the groom does. On a hot summer’s day, you’ll often feel a sigh of relief as guests realise the groom has taken off his jacket, after which they follow suit.
Kissing… lots of it!
If any celebration should contain lots of kissing, surely it’s a wedding? The Danes wholeheartedly agree, and have therefore invented some fun games for the newlyweds to take part in.
Don’t be surprised when the wedding guests start hammering on the tables. This is the ritual performed to get the newlyweds to stand on their chairs and kiss. When guests start stamping their feet, this is the newlywed’s cue to crawl under the table and kiss.
You’ll often find the guests have some fun with this, getting the bride and groom to do one after the other.
When the bride or groom leave the room
Kissing isn’t just reserved for the bride and groom. When either the bride or groom leave the room (as inevitably happens when they need to go to the toilet), the opposite sex line up to kiss the newlywed who was left behind on the cheek.
Songs and speeches
If you’ve been to any big Danish gathering, it won’t surprise you that Danes really like to sing together.
A fun Danish tradition is the custom of taking a well-known song (often from the Danish Højskolesangbog, a book of songs written with the purpose of being sung at folk high schools, but sometimes also popular, international songs), and replacing the lyrics, making them unique to the couple being celebrated. The new lyrics will be printed out and passed around to guests, who will then sing the song to the well-known melody.
READ ALSO: Why do Danes love singing group songs at family gatherings?
Danish weddings also come with an awful lot of speeches, often making the dinner-part of the wedding drag on - especially if you don’t speak any Danish.
Hurra!
The Danish “Hurra!”, similar to the English “Hurray!” is used at most big celebrations. Originally used by soldiers as a battle cry, today it’s used to cheer on a newlywed couple, or a birthday boy or girl. The “hurra” is often used at the end of a speech, where the speech-giver will instruct the rest of the guests on how many “hurra”’s to do. The most common ones are:
- Three short and one long: “Hurra! Hurra! Hurra! Hurraaaaaa!”
- The nine-times hurra!: “Hurra! Hurra! Hurra!” times three.
- The long live “Hurra!”: “[Name] længe leve! Hurra! Hurra! Hurra!” (“Long live [name]!” in English)
The wedding waltz
When the dinner at long last is over, and at the very latest at 23.59, the dance floor is opened by the newlyweds with a traditional wedding waltz (brudevals in Danish). The waltz is to the melody from Danish ballet, Et Folkesagn (“a folktale” in English), composed by Niels W. Gade in 1854. Guests surround the newlyweds, clapping along to the beat of the song. As the song progresses, guests close in on the newlyweds, making them waltz in smaller and smaller circles.
Cutting the sock
As guests have closed in entirely on the newlyweds, making it impossible for them to continue their waltz, the groom is lifted into the air by male guests, his shoe removed, and the tip of his sock cut off (yes you read that right!)
This odd tradition is meant to symbolise that a bride will take care of her new husband, his clothes included. Cutting off the tip of the sock was a way for the new wife to prove her darning skills.
Removing the bride’s garter
The more daring couples sometimes also include the fun and slightly risqué tradition of removing the bride’s garter. Here the groom will crawl under the bride’s dress and remove the garter, either with his hands, but typically with his teeth. The groom will emerge to cheering guests, and then toss the garter to the group of unmarried male wedding guests - making it the male equivalent of the bouquet toss.
Dancing
A Danish wedding is, if anything, a really great party. Expect dancing until the early morning hours, and don’t be too surprised if you wake up with a hangover.
